The Bureau: XCOM Declassified not only fails to grasp its strategy based roots but struggles to smoothly incorporate some of the most basic elements of gameplay.
Set in the 1960′s you take the role of William Carter, a CIA agent with the task of delivering a mysterious object, as things don’t turn out as planned Carter finds himself caught within a global alien invasion. After showing the ability to command, Carter is brought into the XCOM project to combat the new alien threat and keep it hidden from public domain.
While the story has plenty of potential, filled with plot twists and interesting concepts that promised much however the abysmal animation quality and equally poor dialogue stomps on any attempts for the story to blossom. As your character speaks to others, it won’t take long for you to notice the constant repeat of three animations that just feel artificial, along with poor voice acting that simply changes tone every sentence making it impossible to take anything they say with any care. Plot holes run amok with many of the side quests, and dialogue not connected to the main focus of the storyline.
The Bureau tries to blend the turn based strategy of the XCOM series with real time cover based shooting. Promoting teamwork and RPG elements to overcome challenges works well on paper but poor execution through AI simply makes many of the strategy components redundant. Often finding my partners simply refuse to take any useful cover unless directly told to do so, however when they take position the poor AI simply takes over, soon making them move out of cover instantly. The AI will often struggle to perform basic tasks, watching myself go down right next to an ally as they simply stand on my face watching my hp slide down to zero.
While enemies are based on those featured in previous XCOM games, within The Bureau they lack the identity and unique traits that made combat diverse, tense and tactical. As you progress through the game, enemies will remain the same except for an additional armor or shield bar with the word elite lazily thrown after their names.
Character progression within the game is very limited, offering little combat customization. As you and your squad levels up you are given the choice between two new upgrades, often being the choice between duration and damage. This design has been taken from XCOM: Enemy unknown which worked fine within the game design however playing as a single character through the whole story, and only having two teammates with you at all times means characters simply feel too limited, with a maximum of three skills per class, you’ll soon find your preferred attacks and have no reason to add diversity to your tactics throughout the entire game. Skills are activated by bringing up a battle HUD, giving you access to your own and team skills, during this the game will slow down giving you more time to plan and consider your options. Though slowing down the game reduces the pressure, the game continues to play making many tactical attacks an impossibility. Many times I found myself trying to time my snipers critical strike with turrets and protective abilities however the moment a skill is selected it will begin to play out giving you little time to organize the ambush you planned in your mind, often resulting in a messy and inconsistent first attack.
One of the huge holes apparent within the game seems to be a lack of co-op within the game, the structure of combat and the storyline feel setup for two players. Situations where the main character become split up for short periods of time from the team, as well as the dependency on tight coordinated teamwork scream out for two player interaction. Many flaws within the game, specifically the unreliability of the AI would be overcome and none apparent with a second human player. With a second player the game could be incredible enjoyable and the fact developers missed this opportunity is a great disappointment.
The Bureau is definitely not one of the worst games available for sale, but simply tries to do so many things, it does none of them well. Barely meeting the line of mediocre in any aspects of gameplay giving it no identity on the market, and as such simply giving no reason to buy it especially at a full AAA title price.

Video review (including score):
Hello Neighbor has finally arrived, and with it comes the endless hype generated since its reveal. This hype certainly did not help the game, as it was buggy upon release and has since received a lot of negative reviews. I started playing wondering if my own review would join the masses here, but I actually ended up enjoying the game.
The whole gimmick with this game is that each time the player is caught by the Neighbor, the Neighbor gets smarter. For example, the Neighbor got tired of me breaking in through the same window every time, so he eventually placed a bear trap on the other side of the window. When he got tired of me jumping through that window regardless of the bear trap being present, he ended up just boarding up the window entirely, preventing me from going through the window in the first place. It was an interesting mechanic, forcing me to change up the way I played on more than a few occasions. As the game’s defining feature, it is a bit underwhelming, but it is still a nice feature regardless.
Upon starting the game, the player is just popped down right into the game world. There is no tutorial and no main menu. There is little in terms of direction, so it falls to the player to figure out what to do. The objective is to get into the basement and find out what the Neighbor is hiding, no additional help is provided by the game. As such, it can be quite difficult at times, especially later in the game when the puzzles are more intricate. All of this really goes to show just how well designed the puzzles are. Not only are they reasonably difficult, but they are really creative as well. I would be lying if I said that I did not use a walkthrough for a couple of the puzzles in act 3, where this creativity really shines.
The cartoony art style can be good or bad depending on what the player wants from this game. For a horror game, it was probably not the best choice. Those expecting so will be very disappointed. Even so, I thought the style was great for a game like this. Any sort of realism is quickly thrown out the window in act 2, so a style like this is really fitting and perfectly captures the atmosphere of the game. Despite this, the game can still be scary at times, especially when the Neighbor comes out of nowhere.
Even after the patches, Hello Neighbor is still seriously lacking in polish. There are numerous bugs and other issues that I ran into while playing. I had heard of the bugs that the game suffered upon its release, but I at least expected them to be somewhat ironed out by the time I played, several patches later. In fact, my very first experience in the game was me trying to tip over a trash can only for it to somehow launch me into the sky, forcing me to fall to my death. A great first impression of what was to come.
Objects would oftentimes clip into each other, sometimes getting stuck in walls. At one point, I had managed to get the wrench stuck in a wall. The wrench is required to open certain gates, but luckily I had already used it to open these gates before it got stuck. Had I not, a complete level restart would have been necessary. Bigger objects would sometimes get suck in the walls as well, making constant rattling noises while stuck. I had a trash can get stuck in a door at one point and had to suffer the metallic noises it would make for the rest of the level.
It also is not just objects that can get stuck, the player can get stuck too. I had to restart a level at one point because I got stuck in-between several bushes and a door. Luckily, restarting a level from the pause menu only resets the player back to the start, leaving all progress intact, so I did not lose anything by getting stuck. The version I played on was 1.1.3, so hopefully these issues are fixed with future patches. The devs have been releasing patches every few days, so it might not even take that long.
Aside from the bugs, the game can also be easily exploited. I managed to skip the majority of act 2 by building a platform and jumping from it to get to a previously inaccessible door. I do not mind exploits such as this, but it should be mentioned regardless. I imagine that speedrunners would have a blast finding all of the different ways they can glitch themselves through the levels.
The game’s story is purposely left ambiguous, with many fan theories as to what exactly happened throughout the course of the game. I am all for stories that make you think, but it just did not work here. The dream sequences and the whole shadow beast thing just felt so out of place with the rest of the game. The story tried to play heavily on the “horror” aspect of this game, an aspect that was already lost after the end of act 1, just when the story really started to kick in. A lighter, less serious story may have worked a lot better, considering how zany the game becomes after act 1.
Despite its bugs and storyline, Hello Neighbor is still a decent game. The puzzles are creative and a lot of fun to solve, the art style is good, and the Neighbor AI mechanic adds an additional layer to the gameplay. The devs have been constantly putting out new patches, so the bugs I discussed may not be bugs for long.

Games have been using Twitch well to promote themselves before launch, and Forced Showdown did well in tying the launch discount with Twitch minutes watched. But don't let that gimmick make you overlook a game that's solid in the Action RPG genre. It's roguelite elements in the card deck building genre are pretty good: as there's good card variety here and a nice selection of heroes. Combat does strong at first, in particular in the challenge area, and yet the game is still fair. Now over time, the variety does start to get hurt if you don't keep unlocking new content, which can be a challenge with some of the stuff that the game throws at you at times. But that takes a lot longer then other games in this specific combination of genre elements, and I was still having fun at 10+ hours with no problems. The game delivers in a bang from buck perspective, even without the discount. Just be ready to deal with some performance issues (especially on the end of waves), that never hit game breaking, but are very annoying.

FORCED SHOWDOWN is a twin-stick shooter that introduces a unique card system into the traditional formula. Instead of relying on traditional itemization your upgrades are based on the cards that you put in your deck. What this does is allow you to customize how you want to play your champion while still keeping some of the random nature of a rogue-lite style game. While I don’t think the card system is going to be redefining any genres, it works well and the game represents one of the most polished twin stick shooters in recent times. The solid gameplay and well developed aesthetic gives the game a feeling of quality, much more so than the original FORCED. The game is good, very good but it’s also a game that I believe needs additional content in the future to keep players around. So far following this game I’ve come to trust the developers are planning on supporting this game to a great degree, and hopefully more campaigns and characters help flesh out an already great addition to the twin-stick genre.

Very good first person puzzle game similar to Portal.
Offers a decent amount of difficulty while still being rather intuitive, however I did get completely stuck once and had to look for some hints online. There are some really unique mechanics that unfortunately cannot be described without spoiling the story, however I can say that I've never played anything quite like it before.
What really makes this game shine is the music and the voice acting. Unlike Portal, the player character in this game has a voice, which allows the story to unravel throughout the course of the game through banter between the player and the (totally-not-Glados) AI character that's watching you. Unlike most games with mid-gameplay dialogue, I never had any issues where the characters would cut off if I progressed too far--everything was very well paced. The music is haunting, and does a great job of setting the haunting tone and atmosphere of the game, perfectly framing the story as it unfolds.
My only complaint? It's very short. Like, really short. However, despite its length, I really enjoyed it, and would definitely recommend snagging it in a sale.

If you've played The Talos Principle, Portal, or any game of that type, there is no reason to play The Turing Test. If you haven't, you should play them instead of The Turing Test.
Since it is a completely linear puzzle game, there are only really three elements which matter:
- The puzzles
- The story
- The environment/atmosphere
The puzzles are mediocre. There are quite a few mechanics here, many more than you would need for a 4-5 hours game. The problem is that they never amount to a challenge. Passed the first 20 minutes trying to figure the basics, you will never encounter a puzzle that will even pretend to resist you. In fact, quite often, you might even complete puzzles without using all the tools at your disposal, because you do not need them.
The story is ok. You can basically guess where it is going 30 minutes in. There are "shocking revelations" throughout the game, but they don't really impact the story overall, instead acting as little nuggets of life to make the characters feel a bit more relatable. The moral/ethical dillema presented is never really explored. And yes, you get to choose your ending, but it's really just a "press the button or don't" deal.
The atmosphere is ok. Nothing to write home about. Atmospheric music, servicable visuals, just enough lore to not put you to sleep, pretty good voice acting. You'll most likely forget about it and never come back to it.
The Turing Test is not a bad game. It's just your average space meal. If you are starving, you will push it down your gob, and it will keep you satiated for a few hours. But if you're not on the verge of death, you have no reason to want to ingest the tasteless, joyless mixture.

King of Dragon Pass is a great game with an old school interface. It might be rough around the edges to start, but that's to be expected from the era it came out in. Some people in the reviews have mistaken the PC interface to be an inferior port of the mobile version, but it's actually the other way around: the mobile port improved the interface to suit touchscreen devices. I don't think the PC interface is that complicated or difficult, but it is probably the main thing that might not get you into the game.
Once you get past that slight hurdle, there's a super rich CYOA game underneath. King of Dragon Pass is made up of managing your clan and (somewhat random) events. Your job? To be the best descendants that you can be of your tribe, whatever that means. Tradition paves the way.
The random events are numerous. About the only common thing each run will have is bumping into the ducks nearby. Besides that, there's a huge wealth of events, some of which have long running consequences.
Then there are the hero quests, where your tribe reenacts myths of old through hardcore storytelling and cosplay. Recreating it faithfully produces boons for you. Deviating from the myth might bring calamity, or it might be a story told so hard, it REWRITES THE MYTH IN THE PAST. Intense stuff.
Basically, if you like reading, and watching a tribe grow/dwindle, and want to unite everyone under your banner, then King of Dragon Pass is quite possibly the best game for you.

If you never played a Paradox or a Hearts of Iron game, this is a great game to start.
Set in the prelude and during WW2 Hearts of Iron 4 offers a great freedom in terms of tactical and strategical decisions. For example, while playing as Japan you have the option to either go to war with China or make them your puppet. If you do decide to go to war you have multiple ways of going about it. Should you either starve the from supplies by raiding their naval convoys and bombing their factories before taking a land offensive or go balls deep into the enemy frontlines with your divisions full of artilery support combined with air superiority or even multiple naval invasions is your choice. As the game can be started in either early 1936 or mid 1939, there is a lot of potential for replayability escpecially with the fact that you can choose any of the available countries in the world meaning that you can do stuff such as making USA communist, breaking free of British rule as India (if you have the Together for victory DLC) or recreating the Roman empire as Italy. The only real issue with the game I have is the multiplayer which unless played with friends is painfully slow and frustrating as well as the fact that the game slows down a lot in longer games due to the sheer amount of units present in the map world. Even though there are issues in the base game there are an incredible amount of mods in the workshop which either aim to fix those issues (like the AI or end war confences) or completely revamp the game world adding new countries or alternate timelines like the mod Kaiserreich ( which I highly reccomend to try) which takes place in a timeline where Germany won WW1 and the mod is arguably more developed than the base game.
Overall a good game especially for newbie to grand strategy games but might lack longevity for experienced player however it holds great potential in the modding community. Would reccomend to try out and if you're not sure about how to play it check out some YouTube guides and letsplays, for me they got me into the game and other paradox games.

I love 3D puzzlers like Portal 2 and The Talos Principle. Imagine my surprise when there wasn't a surge of puzzlers after Portal's success in 2007.
This game is...well, I'm not sure how to put it. Its graphics are great; the best of all 3D puzzlers. However, the puzzles themselves aren't all that challenging. I'm certain a grade 3 student could do them given enough time. My average time per puzzle is about 3 minutes (they get longer and more challenging in the later levels/optional levels).
The game's story is below average. It also feels like it caters to a grade 3 student. It touches themes that have already been covered years ago and doesn't add anything new to the sci-fi genre. It is probably the most predictable story you can imagine. Right from the get-go, you already know what happens next. If the game's title doesn't spoil it for you, then the semblance of the antagonist in 2001: A Space Odyssey will.
The game does give off a spooky vibe - it feels like it could've been a really effective horror/puzzle game split with combat elements, yet it remains a puzzler and only a puzzler. That's okay.
Story - 5/10 (Average)
Graphics - 8/10 (Awesome)
Puzzles - 5/10 (Average)
Overall the game gets a 7/10. It's a good game. It just does nothing new. It had so much potential but that's alright. Hopefully someone will pick up where they left off and make something really amazing.

For some the visuals and the story may be compelling to stick with it, but I'll find a better use for my gaming time. Only saving grace for me was that I got this through Humble.

There are a few annoying problems beyond that.
1. The game boasts "full controller support" but literally the very first thing you need to do is dig out your mouse and keybaord and click on Accept to install some Unreal Engine 4 stuff. I'm playing this on my couch with a controller, so that was an annoying start.
2. The game has subtitles but they're very tiny and hard to read, and there's no way to adjust the size. Worse, the game has many audiologs, and *none* of those (that I found) have subtitles. That seems like a serious omission.
All told, a somewhat fun game but barely rises above average. I'd give it a weak 3 out of 5.

Complete hunter bias. Supposedly the Elder Kraken and the Wraith are the only exceptions, but even then, 1/2-3/4 of the hunter team has to be full blown ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to lose. After more playtime, I now know that the Wraith and Elder Kraken are no exceptions.
Both sides get spawned in the same exact spot maybe 15-20 seconds apart.
Speed is about the only advantage that the monsters have, but the maps are so small that it takes no effort to cut the monster off. And actually, if the trapper has a pet, most of the time it'll ignore the tracks and lead the hunters to cut off the monster anyway.
All the hunters get the arena/trap, rendering the main point of the trapper class void and further screwing over the monster. The trapper now gets a global tracker ability to replace the trap, which must have a cooldown of a 30 seconds or less because the "Tracked by global tracker" is about all you see when you're trying to sneak around and eat creatures.
The arena lasts forever, which when you're stuck facing level 20+ players with maxed out, OP hunters, renders everything pointless.
Apparently the hunters can instantly respawn, regardless of what the timer says, as long as they go back to dropship when they go down. When they respawn, the dropship puts them on or very near the monster.
There's a match timer of around 5 minutes. In that time the monster is expected to magically kill all the hunters in a lesser/unevolved state or elude the hunters, eat tons of creatures, evolve twice, and destroy the power relay. All the hunters are expected to do is either kill the monster or wait out the timer. Also, the monster can't damage the power relay while there are hunters nearby.
There aren't a lot of obstacles on the maps, but the monster has to avoid alerting "birds" every ten feet, while the hunters have to avoid maybe half a dozen plant traps in the entire map. The birds get alerted even if you're not that close, while you basically have to purposely walk over and step on a very specific spot for the plant to get you. The NPC creatures on the map will attack both sides, but they pose absolutely no real threat.
Either there are a metric ♥♥♥♥ton of hackers or everyone has already figured out all the exploits to this and that to make the hunters literally invincible. Even when you have them separated and their medic isn't healing them, you will pound them for days and barely make any progress, and this is only at the lvl 20 mark.
The hunters get all sorts of useful buffs from special creatures on the map while the monster gets nothing but climb speed and the extraordinarily rare ability to eat faster.
There are multiple OP hunters in each class. One of which is a trapper that can harpoon you from the other side of the map, and with perks, or hacks, the tether is indestructable. Another one has an ability that greatly reduces the respawn timer, as if it wasn't short enough already.
The hunter perks are extremely helpful while the monster perks are mostly useless, especially considering all the other factors.
Basically there's 3 ways each match will go;
1) The hunters will bum rush the monster and kill it at stage 1.
2) The monster will get ungodly lucky and the hunters will clump up so that its attacks harm multiple hunters at once. All while at evolution stage 1 or 2.
3) The hunters will designate a runner who is to run and hide across the map the second they start to lose the fight to the monster. The monster then has to constantly fight off waves of attacks all while still trying to evolve. Eventually, either the hunters spawn too rapidly and the monster can't recouperate in time or the timer runs out and the hunters win. (Technically 4, but who's counting?).
There are a lot of bugs where the game will get stuck during loading and such that requires a relaunch to get away from. Tons of connection problems as well. Eating and climbing with the monsters bug out a lot, making it take a lot longer to do what you're trying to do.
The players, not characters, are by far the worst part of the game, but that's typical nowadays. Toxic as can be, screaming racial slurs, squeakers like no tomorrow, "♥♥♥♥♥ this, ♥♥♥♥♥ that", dumb trolls, mindless people not doing anything, etc.
There also isn't any sort of real singleplayer/PvE mode that allows you to progress. There's a training mode where you face bots, but the bots are really tough, you barely get any credits from it, and it only pays out for ~3 matches and then you get nothing. It also doesn't apply towards daily or periodical challenges. Clarification for you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out there, bots aren't slow, dumb, or make mistakes like people do, and unless you play on easy(I'm not even sure if you can change bot difficulty, and I don't really care), the bots are better than most players that you will encounter. I guess maybe if you select certain characters that the bots just aren't capable of fully utilizing, things might be easy, but I chose not to waste much of my time with training mode.
If you're the type of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ person that loves easy, one-sided games then you'll probably like this, as long as you play hunters.
I personally find it extremely easy and boring to play as the hunters, but it's also pointless and infuriating to play as the monster.

Things you'll do in 'Lili: Child of Geos': Pick flowers, smash pots, torment spirits, drop out of school, overthrow a corrupt and cruel government, free slaves, collect hats, and rescue a guy's pretzels.
Despite the game's simplicity, it manages to be utterly addictive. The world is gorgeous, and the characters that fill it quirky and adorable. The game's humour is also fantastic, and there's a bunch of references to well-known media.
Some advice I have for new players: Don't bother buying keys. Convert your flowers to money and you'll quickly have enough to buy the skeleton key, thus rendering buying small keys a pointless waste. I had enough for the skeleton key before reaching the third zone (there's four in total). Also pick as many flowers, smash as many pots, and rip the flowers off spirits as much as you can. Even if you don't want the achievements for it, it'll still be helpful in getting resources.
All in all, it was a very cute, quirky, and memorable game. Possibly one of the best I've ever played, in fact. There were a couple of minor issues (slightly awkward camera controls, occasionally getting stuck), but nothing game breaking. It's a solid 10/10 for me. And tbh, even if the rest of the game totally sucked, I'd be inclined to at least rate it a 7 for the fact that there's a genderqueer spirit. Nice.

The new expansion, Nightmare Tide, brings new zones and dungeons. I've only played through two of the three, and I have to say Draumheim is very fun.
The gist of the game is that you are a hero, one of the "Ascended," who battles against the forces of the various planes (fire, water, death, wind, etc) which are trying to take over Telara, your homeworld. The current expansion takes place in the Plane of Water, which has some fishy stuff going on.
The mechanics of the game are similar to WoW but improved in several areas. One of these is the talent system, which lets you choose three trees to spend your points in. There are lots of possibilities, and as a result there are only four classes. These essentially act as a base, not an end result. There are also "Instant Adventures" which let you pick up with a group and start questing immediately, which can be a nice change of pace.
One thing I will say WoW does better is the "atmosphere" of the game (food... water... atmosphere!). Rift just doesn't have the fantasy quality through music and art style, and as a result you feel like a lump of pixels running around a parking lot in a dress, rather than a super awesome gnome warlord running around a mountain range in a dress.
People do play this game, though there are fewer servers. Each one feels fairly well populated.
Overall, there is plenty of content, which really is what counts, but the game doesn't have that "feel" like WoW did back in Burning Crusade which, to be honest, is probably not a fair basis for judging MMO's. That was simply a unique time period.
My biased and unsubstantiated rating is 8/10.

King of Dragon Pass is an interesting game. The overall objective is to become King (or Queen) of Dragon Pass. As you rise to the top you have to face trials, challenges, and management in order to ensure your clan comes out on top.
This game has a TON of detail ranging from choices and consquences to how you rule your clan decides how things progress in the game for you and the other clans around you. Really understand this game through and through. From my personal experience if you treat this as a typical sim-management game you will get screwed time and time again. Really think like a ruler whose either a "War leader" a "Balanced leader" or "Peaceful one" don't try to go from one end of the spectrum to another in an extreme fashion. You will lose time and time again. There is no save point only "restore points" and those don't any good. Your choices are literally final.
Your "ring" or "circle of advisors" will help you lead your clan each one has their own viewpoint and "stats" so choose and listen to them very wisely and carefully. Overall though it comes down to YOU making the decision. Don't just click choices left and right. In a strange way. This is like the Witcher games by CD Projekt Red. The choices you make in the "now" will overall affect how things go later on. You can restart over again but know that your "ring" changes each time and events will play out diffently also not to mention how your tribe starts out as well. This game really takes into account for everything. Now of course there might be some issues, and there are. Like for example some choices you make might be straight forward and to your personal opinion it might be the "right choice"  however from time to time the game will go on a tangent and gives you this: "WELL THEN!" response even though techincally it might be the right choice. So choose wisely or you will have chosen poorly.

The Bureau is a TP squad based shooter and is 2K Marins verson for XCOM.  Originally in 2010 being a FPS with really nothing to do with the original games.

The Bureau was a joyless game. The characters were flat and stiff, as was the story. The combat is a watered-down version of Mass Effect, also devoid of any real fun. Easily a third, if not more, of the game play time is spent simply running from room to room in your base; tedious and dull. I never felt really rewarded for any of the missions, it was just and endless progression towards the end. Even when you unlock the UFO, your combat sessions still begin by showing you arrive in the same old copter from the beginning of the game. The game simply refuses to give you any memorable moments, almost spitefully pulling you forward on a short leash.
The combat works, but feels more like an initial draft and not a fully fleshed out system. Since the rest of the game is simply running from room to room on your base endlessly, you'd think they would have crafted a deep, engaging combat system. You would be wrong. It's relatively fast paced, ammo is limited which forces you to scavenge the levels for weapons. I can see how they intended this to keep players from nesting in secure spots for very long. Your party has abilities, several of them directly taken from ME's biotic powers, it's just nowhere near as enjoyable. Even though the maps change throughout the game, the combat itself begins to feel repetitive very early on.
Even at the end, which I won't spoil for those who feel they must play this game, you are asked to make a choice between characters from the story, characters you have no reason to care for one way or the other. It's as if they felt suddenly at the end you must face a terrible decision and arbitrarily shoehorned one in. The ending was terrible and left me very unsatisfied. I did complete it. At 17 hours it's barely a few evenings worth of play, which is a good thing. By that point I was ready to be done.

I couldn't stress you enough: DO NOT buy this scam and buy the original "Painkiller: Black Edition" instead. This is NOT a full remake.
Sure, it has pretty graphics and they added a touch to some levels. They added humor here and there. But that's pretty much the only positives.
You see, they cut a huge portion of the original game. In total, Black Edition (original game + expansion pack) has 32 levels + 3 bonus ones.
"Hell and Damnation" only remade about 15 of them.
On the top of it, the developers dare charge us more money to have some more of the original levels in their DLC.
Please, do NOT buy this even if it is on sale!
I recommend "Black Edition", though. It's a fun fast-paced arena shooter. You have to kill all enemies in an area before the doors open, allowing you to progress. It sounds repetetive, but the various environments make up for it. Also, there are different enemies in most levels, enemies that match the environment. Skeleton knights in the cemetery, evil monks in the monastery, undead military in the military base, ninja... Most of them are melee, but some also have other attacks as well. There are 5 weapons in the game, but we could say there are actually 10, because each of them has a secondary fire mode that is very different and that uses a different type of ammo. The expansion pack adds 2 weapons (or 4).
The level design is mostly linear, but you can also explore a bit and find secret areas.
So if you like this type of shooter in which you don't have to think much and just shoot monsters, then you might enjoy it.
TL;DR DO NOT BUY this scam called "Painkiller: Hell and Damnation". I recommend "Painkiller: Black Edition" instead.

Do you like to read? I love it, whenever whatever I'm reading is well written. Fortunately, that's the case with this piece of literature (not always I have this luck with "visual novels").
Yeah, this is not a game. It's barely audiovisual. There's no voice acting and there's only music if you remember to turn the radio on (I did it only after a while; the other controls are inconsequential). The scenery is monotonous
and you don't need to look at it anyway, because nothing unusual happens and your eyes will be busy reading.
I'm not going to summarize the plot, but it's very well conveyed through dialogue only, without hand holding; even with a few things open for interpretation, there's really no mystery here. Character development is also great. Although there are branches of dialogue, there's no choice and consequence, no multiple endings, no replayability (you'll only need to play the epilogue again if you want the 2 last achievements; it's a very easy one to 100%). It's very short (2 hours tops), but it doesn't feel lacking. The extras are a nice addition: the music is very good, as the short stories.
The only annoying things are the need to keep a button pressed for the main game to go forward (the epilogue corrects that) and the general slowness, including the menus . But they're only a small nuisance, what matters here is the story.
Have a good reading!

OVERALL

This is one of my favorite games. The strategy, management and RPG elements are skillfully combined with a rich narrative set in a fantasy world that manages to avoid being just another Tolkien rehash. The game does not hold your hand (though the tutorial is very useful to get to grips with the basics), and various kinds of information is not overtly shown, leaving it up to the player to seek it out and to pay attention to details revealed in lore, events and the advice of the clan ring members. This makes the whole thing feel less like a system to be gamed, and gives a sense of making decisions that have real weight.
It is also the only game I know of where you can sue a ghost or have a duel with a duck.

The idea behind this game is a good one, it really is. Unfortunately it's poorly executed. It has several bugs that makes the game crash, and depending on how you've set up your clan it can be next to impossible to work around them (good luck winning the game if you can't upgrade one of your key gods temples).
Then there's what's simply poor execution. You get no save slots (thus can't run multiple games at once), you have no vloume control for the background music, no screen resolution or font size settings etc. And for some reason any and all information for the game (and you will need to read it to get through the hero quests) is stored online, not within the game, so any time you click a link in the Lore tab it opens up in the Steam Overlays webbrowser.
Even for something that is essentially a 17 year old game repacked to work on a modern computer it feels rouch and poorly executed. If you want to give it a try pick up one of the other versions instead, but the one you get here on Steam is not worth wasting your money on no matter how good the sale is.

I don't think I've ever felt so burned buying a game day one. Do not let the XCOM name fool you. It has nothing to do with the overall story. If anything this game makes a mess of the overall narrative of XCOM. The story is below average with one little unexpected twist but if anything it's more unexpected because up until that point you don't expect much after hearing all the character's dull droning and uninspired dialog.
The graphics range from sub-par to bland. Strange phenomenons appear all the time, from the shimmering hair of one of your colleagues that change from blond to brunette, all the way to identical twin guards that also bare a striking resemblance to a scientist you just passed down stairs.
The game play is standard cover-based shooting. You move, kill aliens, wave ends, then keep moving; sound like some real white knuckle action? If so, get out more. Sometimes you find an alien weapon and get to use it...that's it. No research, no testing, no means of duplicating the tech. You just have it now and so do your teammates.
Speaking of which, your A.I. partners are dumb as suicidal rocks. You give them orders, to which they either ignore so they can do what they want or they follow orders and keep following them regardless of whether or not they are about to die by continuing to obey. They rarely kill an enemy and are more of a liability than a useful asset. When they take too much damage they fall and you have a short amount of time to get to them before they die for good...not that you'd notice. More than a few times I had a teammate warn me I was standing near an alien-thrown grenade. I would jump out of the way while the A.I. teammate that warned me would sit there and get blown up.
This game was short. I beat it along with all the achievements on the first time around. The DLC mission "Codebreakers" was horrible. Not only is it an obvious mission that was cut out of the original product to make more money and incentivize pre-orders, it is the SHORTEST MISSION IN THE GAME AND ADDS NOTHING TO THE STORY! What do you get to show for it? Another backpack mod thing that you probably won't use.
I've played some bad games in my life but this one hurt. I like the XCOM franchise but this one was nothing but a cheap cash-in that used the XCOM name to boast sales. Do yourself a favor and buy XCOM: Enemy Unknown or continue to play it  if you already own it. This game is only XCOM in name, not in game play nor spirit. Learn from my mistake.

Yeah.... just play a different Xcom, ANY other Xcom. You will be glad you did.

The House of the Dead series has always had a weird history. Mostly known as a cheesy as Hell collection of light gun arcade game with the occasional console port has never had the most positive reputation, but it's remained a staple of the on-rails shooter scene for some time. From it's original line of arcade shooters, to more obscure spin-offs like The Pinball of the Dead, Zombie Revenge, and English of the Dead, none have become more notorious and fondly remembered as The Typing of the Dead. The idea to fuse typing instruction and zombie killing birthed a strange cult phenomena among Sega fans, and it's become a well-remembered example of just how weird things could get on the Sega Dreamcast.
The Typing of the Dead: Overkill is the combination of two HotD games. Not only is it the most recent incarnation of the TotD (there was a sequel to the first game, but it was Japan-only), it's also doubles as a PC port of The House of the Dead: Overkill, the underappreciated most recent installment of the original series. Both versions, both Typing and House, of Overkill are availble in this package, making it a two pronged beast of gore and guttural laughs.
The plot is as simple as it gets: series mainstay Agent G is out on his first case, teaming up with wise-cracking detective Isaac Washington as they investigate the appearance of mutants in the American south and try to stem the ensuing destruction by tracking down one Papa Caesar, crime boss extraordinaire. Throw in vengeful strippers Varla Guns and Candi Stryper, and you've got an♥♥♥♥♥kicking cast of profane mutha♥♥♥♥as who know how to dispose of any undead baddie.
The biggest worry about when I first booted up TTotD:O was how the unusual control scheme would play out. Would I get sick of it? Would I get bored of it? Would it be too difficult to enjoy? Turns out, I was completely wrong about all those, because weirdly enough, this was one of the most satisfying gaming experiences I've had in
. Typing out Polish swears and nonsensical phrases gave the game a level of difficulty that actually had me continously coming back for more and more. How the typing is implemented with the fast-paced on-rails action is so intuitive and logical that it made the game far more white-knuckle and intense than I would've ever expected. Nothing here feels too difficult, and any errors made are purely on you. Instead of getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I found myself laughing and yelling 'NO!' whenever my fingers would foul up and I'd end up dead.
As for the game's campaign, while short, has a heaping ton of replayability with a difficulty scale that'll kill your fingers but still keep you entertained. TTotD:O also has mini games, fantastic (and logical) DLC, a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of fan made dictionaries to download and try, and a spot on port of the original House of the Dead: Overkill. While this port is still fun and is worth playing even if you don't enjoy typing zombies to death, I personally found it lacking that satisfying edge that the main game has.
The game's grindhouse presentation, profane script, and ridiculous set pieces made this the funniest gaming experience I've had in ages. As a hardcore exploitation film fanatic, this game was so far up my alley. The voice-acting is on point, the gratuitous amounts of gore and swearing is enough to make any grindhouse lover at least chuckle out loud, the film grain and groovy 70's music and intermission loading screens give the game a sense of tongue-in-cheek levity that makes it hard not to smile at.
Probably my favourite game of all time. Seriously, this was fantastic, and I know that I'm gonna continue playing it in the future. Check this oddity out for a laugh and/or to have some much need levity in your zombie slaying.
It's hokey, it's fun, and there's enough to sink into it to go back for replays.

OneShot is a story-driven RPG reminiscent of the likes of Undertale. The story follows Niko as he must take 'the sun' and return it to the top of 'the tower' in order to save the world. Along the way, you meet a lovable and memorable cast of side characters and learn things about the world that keep the game mysterious, yet intriguing and always fun. Lastly, as the title suggests,
Oneshot's gameplay revolves around its 'puzzles'. The reason I put puzzles in quotes is because you can hardly call them puzzles... They almost all revolve around finding specific items and combining them in a certain way to help you with whatever objective you are trying to accomplish. While some people may see these as puzzles, the game is pretty linear and practically tells you how to achieve your goal. The reason the gameplay is fun however, is because of the exploration. Contrary to what I mentioned earlier, the game is basically open-world. The maps you are exposed to throughout the game aren't very large, but you can go anywhere at any time, with a few exceptions. Reading bits of lore found on papers and interacting with citizens of this world is very interesting and keeps the player motivated to learn more about the game. Lastly, there are some very cool mechanics that OneShot managed to pull off very successfully. They are unique and tie in with the lore.
Overall: 6/10 - Decent
The driving force of the game, the story, is what keeps OneShot going. The entire cast has lots of personality and are very memorable. The story revolves around the world you are in, which may come across as a downside to some, but the world is so engaging that you seem to forget about this quite frequently. The story is very linear, but there are a few decisions you can make that affect the world similar to the likes of Undertale.
Overall: 9/10 - Amazing
The music is very atmospheric. While not quite as memorable as Undertale, which I keep making comparisons to, it does its job and does it well. There are only a couple songs in the OST that I would listen to outside of the actual game
but that does not stop the entire OST from matching the theme of the game well.
Overall: 7/10 - Good
The game takes about 4-6 hours to complete and coming in at about $11 CAD that is about $2/hr which meets expectations. I highly reccomend picking a day and playing through the entire game in one sitting, it is worth it. In terms of replayability, there isn't much to say here. (Possible spoilers but not really)
Aside from that, I don't see why you would want to replay it, as it is completely story driven, unless you are achievement hunting (which you can go back and do).
Overall: Length - 9/10, Replayability - 5/10
Average: 7/10 - Good
This isn't something people normally include in reviews, but I feel like it is an essential peice of a game. OneShot has a lack of these, but thankfully, it doesn't belittle the gameplay. Here are a few things I disliked about OneShot.
However, these are just a few pet-peeves of mine, and don't belittle the experience to most people.
Overall: 8/10 - Great
Gameplay - 6/10
Story - 9/10
Music - 7/10
L+R - 7/10
QoL - 8/10
Total - 74/100
OneShot is a good quality RPG that is a fine addition to any steam library and I can certainly see why so many people like it. If you enjoy story-based games, I highly encourage you to purchase this game and play it ASAP. If not, I recommend waiting for a sale.

Most important thing: This game is actually F2P. You can quest and explore quite readily without needing an investment beyond time, and even that is fully reasonable. Putting a mere $5 into the game grants access to the Auction House, which is highly intuitive and can generate money very early, if things are moving too slowly for your taste. Beyond that, all investments are entirely optional, depending on how much you enjoy the game and how much more you want to support and explore it.
To briefly address everything else: The combat is your standard MMO stuff, and the quests are the typical uninteresting tedium. However, the lore is surprisingly engaging, and this game's social scene is rather nice. The classes are very fun to build, and builds are quite customizable. The art is nice, though the world can at times be a bit empty. Progressing in power feels very good, and there are many cosmetic/collection options available. The music gets repetitive, but is pleasant enough the first few times. The factions are unfortunately rather binary, with one being the militaristic and unpleasant religious group while the other is a tolerant and progressive misunderstood alliance. Events offer fun cosmetic stuff without needing huge time commitments, and PvP seems fairly well fleshed-out.
Overall, I've had a lot of fun, and intend to keep having fun.

Three Fourths Home is a story based game. It's storming, and you are driving your car through the Nebraska landscape on the way home while having a conversation on the cell phone w/ your parents and brother (conversation in text on the screen). As you drive through the storm you get to know the family's problems and perhaps identify w/ a young adult who's trying to strike out in life for the first time.
The Extended Edition added some new elements to the game, such as the epilogue, an extra scene and the new save system. Overall a good addition to the main game itself, and the epilogue also sheds some light to the main character's past.
Note, this is not a game as much as it is a multimedia presentation w/ a few user interface controls. It has a good story, the art design is nice, and the visuals and sounds create a nice atmosphere, but there's not a lot beyond that. If this story appeals to you go for it, but understand there's not really gameplay as much as reading the story and watching how the visuals interact w/ the story that's happening. It's targeted to a specific audience. For me, it is art, but it lacks some depth either in the gameplay and plot.
The gameplay is fairly simple, all you have to do is simply holding down the Right Trigger button to drive/walk forward (or the right directional key on the keyboard) and then selecting options in order to take part in a telephone conversation. There is not much to do beside that, and I have to wonder why they'd bother adding the button for the wiper, also for the horn. Through the entire time I was driving really slow, afraid I might hit something on the road but nothing really happens.
To sum it up, I was curious about the title, and thought it was well done, but at the same time it won't leave me thinking about it after I've seen it. I'm always happy to try games that do something a bit different, and I appreciate the idea behind the game, but at an hour in length (the rest is used for achievement) and no real resolution to anything my first thought upon seeing the credits role was 'is that it?' Despite the lack of a gameplay, I still recommend this based from my experience with the game, and if you're curious about it, it's a good experience for what it is.

Less a game and more an interesting piece of fiction, Three Fourths Home is definitely not for everyone. Mechanically, it's little more than a conversation tree, a simple keyboard mechanic that (literally) moves the plot along, and some minimalistic graphical effects. If you're looking for much beyond a plot and atmosphere, you're likely to be disappointed.
The heart of Three Fourths Home, then, is the quality of the writing. This is a strong example of the Iceberg Theory (think Hemingway) where the substance is in the subtext. Without giving too much away, this is a story about family and the emotional power of things left unsaid. When you figure out what's going on, it'll either hit you in the feels (I'll admit, it got me a little) or make you say "oh, that's it?" depending.
Before you know it, the story ends. You can replay a few key decision points to change the outcome and stick around for a few achievements, but not much else. Because of this, some might be turned off by the price tag ($4.99 at the time of this review). I received it as part of a Humble Bundle and was not disappointed, though it did leave me wanting more. This, then, is the rationale for my positive review (if Steam had a middle option, I probably would have chosen that): the developers grabbed my interest, and I'd like to see what else they're capable of.

A truly excellent puzzle game, I highly recommend it to anyone who is a fan of first person puzzle games like Portal, or of narrative-heavy games.
I was a tad skeptical when I first started playing. Everything about the game had a very portal-esque feel. I was prepared for a complete rehash. You wake up in a testing facility, receive a gun-like tool to use in solving puzzles, and start moving boxes onto buttons to complete tasks.
However, after the first few puzzles the game rapidly diversified. Showing just how unique and flexible its puzzle system was. The game does an excellent job of introducing a wide variety of mechanics in the puzzles, introducing them one by one in a very natural way such that the player can just keep progressing and progressing without having to stop for tutorials or other interruptions. The story continues to get more and more interesting.
As someone with a deep interest in the philosophy behind the nature of intelligence, and the ramifications of “true” AI, the story began to grip my attention very quickly. The “bonus rooms” start to tell a compelling story-within-the-story that kept me seeking out and solving them. Even without that aspect, the primary story tells an interesting tale of rationality vs emotion, the needs of the few vs the needs of the many, and other such themes. The writers did an excellent job crafting an engaging and unique tale.
The game is short, I managed to 100% it in only two play sessions, but it is definitely a game worth playing.

‘Stuck’ in orbit around Europa / Jupiter you solve 3D Puzzles with mechanics requiring the understanding of order, phase, dimension, human creativity and adaptation. Other reviewers have pointed out that this game is shorter (6 hrs) and easier than Portal or ‘The Talos Principle’; Hooray that is exactly what We need (not to mention that the gaming mechanics are completely different). Enjoy the first playthrough without reading a guide; later achievement of 100% is quick and straightforward and facilitated through good game design.

You control Ava Turing trying to find her colleagues deep in a space colony on Europa. During the journey she has conversations with the colony's AI, T.O.M. about morals, free will, consciousness, and the like. The puzzles never got too hard, which I appreciated since I was very interested in the story and didn't have to admit defeat at any point to see it to its end.

Personally, I fancy PVE more than PVP. There are few PVP games that I enjoy, so far, Evolve being one of them.
I have not purchased or spent money on Evolve previously so my experience is solely that of a F2P player.
The Good:
-Fun gameplay (mixes some PVE elements with PVP)
-Smexy graphics
-Characters and interactions among them are entertaining
-Quick to find a match (on my end at least), some people leave last min whether its a disconnection or whatever reason. They're replaced by bots which is "okay" but I know this bothers some
-Everything is obtainable through in-game currency which you get just by playing
-It's free
The Bad:
-Lack of gamemodes, while different characters keep things varied, I wish there was some alternative modes to play to mix things up even more.
-Chat is blink and you miss the message with no way of going back to see what people wrote
-Lack of skins for some characters, like Jack who I enjoy playing
-The preference system is both good and bad, but I'm putting it in the bad because the issue with it can really ruin the fun. You get to pick which class you want to play on a scale of 1-5, it does its best to give you your number one and if not, your number two and so on and so fourth. Sounds great, right? Well, only when it works. For example, in one match, I had down I wanted to play a Trapper, another person wanted to play as a Medic, We were the only ones in that lobby who wanted to play those two classes. I got Medic and the other person got Support. Why? I don't know. It hasn't happened too much, but it is annoying when you get assigned a role which you shouldn't have been assigned.
Overall, it is a very fun game and I recommend giving it a shot.
Side note: I know some founders have some issues with compensation, however, me not being a founder can't vouch for that. I can only rate it as a F2P player.

Lili: Child of Geos is light-hearted and good for a short casual play. It's a delightful adventure game about a student who needs to collect interesting flowers for her thesis, and she decides to go to the land of Geos to find legendary species. Upon arrival, Lili finds herself thrown into a peculiar society of Constructs and Spirits, where all Constructs are enslaved by the Mayor, a Spirit. Lili decides that saving the Constructs from tyranny is more important than securing her degree, and stays to help defeat the Mayor.
The game revolves around picking flowers; defeating the Spirits require you to jump on their backs and remove their red flower. I was a bit hesitant to buy this game because of the story's premise, but the wonderful graphics and music are evidence of the game's overall great quality. It is definitely worth joining Lili on her adventure.

Fun and free. Red Trigger is a first person game in which you pick up a gun that makes red pillars extent/retract from floors, walls, etc. to help you get yourself from A to B and complete this super short game. The puzzles aren't terribly difficult, but some are pretty cleverly constructed, and the electronic soundtrack was pretty pleasant to listen to during my time with Red Trigger. Player dexterity is about as important here as it is in something like Portal, and my dexterity as a player is pretty terrible, so chances are you'll be able to complete the game as long as you can think your way through the puzzles.
If you like first person puzzle stuff like Portal or The Turing Test, and don't mind a lack of a story or minimalist appearance, Red Trigger is a nice, short fun game that I recommend, because time, money, and frustration my common costs of playing a game, and this game takes less than an hour to finish, costs literally no money at all, and didn't make me angry. This was a win all the way around. Give it a try and if you don't like it, at least your curiosity has been sated. =)

Red Trigger is a minimalistic first person puzzle game that feels a lot like Portal and looks a lot like Superhot. The simple graphics work very well to highlight the puzzle elements and provide a clean futuristic aesthetic to the levels. There are no enemies and only environmental dangers to look out for, which, combined with a relaxing and non-intrusive soundtrack, makes the entire experience quite serene. The only problem that throws a spoon of tar into the proverbial jar of honey is the inconsistent collision detection with the red platforms that could occasionally send players plummeting to their doom after a perfectly executed jump, or at least ruin a good speed run and force a restart.

It's a 'lite' version of the original game and it's expansion. A ton of levels were cut out, repackaged as DLC (and it's still not all of them there). The 'cutscenes' aren't the same as the original, in fact somehow made worse. Samael was changed from his angelic hotness to a generic Grim Reaper image, the English dialogue sounds like an amateur school play, and Eve looks way too mannish.
Functionally, it's a game. The guns work the way they're supposed to, feels good grinding up baddies with the Painkiller staff or pinning them to walls with the Stake Gun. The mob sizes are just as ridiculous, the secrets are as esoteric to get to.
Someone mentioned this feels more like a "fanfic" version of the game, and I agree. Feels like the devs of this version thought they could do it better, and ruined a big chunk of it trying to. Either that or Nordic Games, trying to cash in on all the assets they bought off the corpses of THQ and JoWood, rushed this POS out the door and chopped it up along the way, hoping to milk more money out of the older fans. In either case, this is a bad buy, 'HD' or not.
Save yourself lots of DLC money and go buy Painkiller Black Edition. Get it from GOG, it's a better deal with all the extras.

This game is fan fiction of the original Painkiller.
Everything looks more detailed, but that's about the only upside.
They "re-envisioned" the original campaign, mostly rebuilding the original levels, but still changing lots of things here and there, usually for the negative or for no reason whatsoever. The main change being that the game now throws mainly fast-moving enemies at you, from the very start, and when introducing new enemies, does not allow you to learn about them by introducing them on their own, but adds hordes of other enemies. They also changed the weapons you get, and have you starting out not with the default weapon, the iconic blade fan, but with an endgame weapon.
And in terms of non-gameplay: Over half of the missions from the original campaign, which was designed with a thematic progression, are now DLC.
Get Painkiller Black instead. It doesn't have widescreen mode, the textures are low-res, but at least it was made by people who respect their users.

When I saw all the early previews for what they wanted this game to be I was excited. It was creepy, it was tense, it was dangerous, and it looked fun.
This is not that game.
This is a third person shooter with a stilted plotline, meaningless choices, and hours of walking down a straight path shooting at aliens from behind a chest high wall.
At one point in the game you are told that your forces are doing terribly against the aliens. I was never sure how that could be as I was killing hundreds of them each level.
The problem was that they were trying to build up the tension of putting you in a world where you were outgunned, outmanned, and pretty much screwed. And then put you into a third person shooter which requires you to shoot and defeat enemies left right and center for it to be fun.
The combination doesn't work well.
There's no unlocking weapons, technology, or anything else. You will recieve weapons when you pass levels, and you will gain equipment when your people level up. There's no sense in reall changing loadouts because they'll all feel the same in the end.
Your allies will be remarkably usless at doing anything other than getting themselves killed. I can not remember a single time they pulled me out of a dangerous situation, even when they had the single remaining enemy flanked.
And the choices you can make are rendered moot by the end game. I fought to save one character. Did it make a difference? Maybe, depends on the ME3 "Which button did you choose" ending. Anything before that? Never gets mentioned.
There are better third person shooters, dont' waste your time or money on this one. It just never lived up to it's potential.

This may be a good game for those who drool over the UFO's, conspiracy theories, alternative histories as well as those who love the 50's and the 60s (even though they weren't even born then). This is not such a great game for everyone else.
The game plays like a straight B movie, at best.
It pains me that this game used the Unreal 3 engine instead of Mafia's II Ilusion engine, even though 2K Games owns the former. The differences are apparent and Mafia II came out 3 years ago. The game's facial animations are pretty lifeless, the lip sync is nonexistent, the anti-aliasing is somewhat noticeable, there are some texture pop-ins in the background in open levels, the fire/explosion effects are bad as well. It is ridiculous to still be playing with such graphics in Q3 2013, but at least the game allows you to get a 100 FOV which makes you see a enough of your surroundings,.
The overall visuals resemble some sort of a grainy pallet, as if you are watching the game through the lens of the late 70's camera.
Walking around the Xcom base is one of the best highlights of the game, at least it seems so at first. Once you soak in the fact that most AI models are pretty much lifeless the feeling wears off pretty fast.
Unlike in the Enemy Unknown you will have opportunities to sneak up on enemies and be able to set up mini-ambushes, although your element of surprise won't last longer than 2 seconds, the enemy will always know where you are, and why shouldn't they? There is always only one approach to beating the level. The levels are linear although they do provide for some flexibility with cover. And this is the first game that I have seen (since Splinter Cell Conviction) that allows you to switch cover diagonally.
The game loads the level as you progress - each time you open a door a new portion of the level loads while your character cautiously looks around, it's pretty clever.
The game is moderately easy even on the hardest difficulty wherein your agents DO get permadeath, however you can always reload the checkpoint and start over. That kind of defeats the purpose of the Ironman feature that Enemy Uknown had. But then again, Enemy Uknown did not feature the main protagonist. Or maybe it makes little sense to compare the two games since they have been in a parallel
development for quite some time. If anything, this game's combat is closer to Mass Effect than anything. You can heal your squad in an instant, you can pull enemies out of their cover, zap the enemy's shield, set up turrets, use drones, except somehow you manage to do so in mid-twentieth century America.
The squad AI is so-so. Sometimes they are able to kill the enemy by themselves and sometimes they rush out into the battlefield and get knocked down and later bleed out if you don't rush into the hail of bullets yourself in order to try to save them - which kind of defeats the purpose of a smart squad especially when you are on the defensive - major minus. However, it does feel good when you send an enemy to outflank a turret while you get the turret's attention. Moments like that work in the Bureau's favor.
Your squad mates are sure to run out of cover into the open when they are being flushed out with the grenades. And keeping them in line by rallying them to yourself does not work in the midst of the battle. However, all of this DOES push you forward to be decisive in your actions. Should you take a little too long to outsmart and outgun the enemy you are likely to lose a squad-made.
As for the enemy AI, well, 90% of the time they expose their heads from out of cover - so sniper rifle is essential, even with its 15 bullet ammo capacity. So even on the hardest mode all you need is one head shot to kill a medium strength alien.
There are a few things that bothered me. Some of the human tech you have from the beginning is way too advanced. Stealth? Automatic Squad Heal? Smart turrets? What's cool about the X-Com games is that you always faced overwhelming odds with realistic human tech at first - it's the way of the underdog. It's the challenge that counts. And that's what I expected to get from this game.
The game did not do a good job of building up the tension. The prologue mission has you killing aliens left and right. Your character is a natural right away. Okay, he fought the Japanese and then some Vietnamese, but still...
Sure there is a story: it tries to capture the step by step alien invasion across the US and has you traveling to various hot-spots and points of interest. Recruiting new soldiers doesn't cost a thing. So you may never run out of soldiers. What's nice is the constant dialogue between you and your squadmates - helps with immersion and everything.
The game is, by all means, playable.
B for effort.

Spoilers!
OneShot is a cool little game for it's price. It has these generic little puzzles (combine X + Y to make Z) that oddly, don't seem so droll, and it makes really cool use of the rest of your HD (making you open up images to use as overlays, temporarily changing your wallpaper, etc.), but it is NOT the heartstring-tugger that some of our more normie-detached, fur-aligned, weeb friends would have you believe.
The game's big reveal is the typical "Sophie's Choice", where you're forced into one of two "tough" options:
Save the other world and the hero's stuck there abandoning his family, life and child-like, innocent pleasures.
Send the hero back to his home, so he can eat mommy pancakes while the other world shatters and dies.
Unfortunately, the Maker of the game deflates the potential before it can be realized. NPCs are more excited by who you are rather that what you're there to do, and quite a few even tell you that your "Saving The World" act is really just a delay of the inevitable. So really, why bother?
You'll pick one option, see the ending and then want to try the other ending, not because you were made to realize the gravity of the negative consequences of your decision, but rather, because you hope the other choice feels more weighty, less cliche, equal to how such a difficult decision should make you feel.
Still a good game. Pick it up, especially if it's on sale, even it's just to support the small businessman and his copy of RPG Maker.

I like the idea but I'm not really a fan. Core to the gameplay is the concept of finding objects in the world and using them to interact, but unintuitive level design leads to what is basically trial and error. It's reminiscent of old school adventure games in a bad way -- there's a constant feeling that you've missed something critical to your progress, and so solving puzzles winds up being an exercise in randomly combining everything you can to see what happens each step of the way. It diminishes the feeling of achievement I get when I do achieve progress because it renders it down to a tedious inevitability.
I had to refer to a walkthrough before i left the first room, for example, because the nature of the game's interactions wasn't yet clear to me. After understaning it though, a walkthrough seemed like an appropriate tool if only to streamline the above mentioned inevitability.
It's an interesting experience but not fun to play. That's not to say that fun is the only metric of a game's worth -- if you're looking for something that does things a little differently then consider checking this out. For most, I'd say this one is skippable.

Three Fourths Home is a hard game to review. It's one of those games that make you wish Steam had a middle button between positive and negative. It's a simple story where you play as a girl named Kelly who gets caught up in a storm. While driving home in the storm, she talks to her mother and the rest of her family on the phone.
The gameplay is basically holding down the D button to drive, and clicking on dialogue options. That's really it. The entire game is driving and talking. If that doesn't sound like you're thing then this is definitely not the game for you. Also, each dialogue choice leads to the same result. It's nice to have dialogue options, but don't get this game if you are expecting a real choice game.
All that aside, Three Fourths Home is all about the conversation Kelly has with her family. If you like to play games that are heavy on dialogue, it's worth giving a try. I was personally very emerged in the atmosphere and conversation. I also found the characters to be very relatable. I felt what the game wanted me to feel by the end, and for that I'm giving it a positive review.
Keep in mind that even though this is the "extended edition," it's very very short. I beat the game plus looked at all the bonus material in about an hour and a half. You can always go achievement hunting or go back and pick other dialogue options, but like I said, it leads to the same results and the same ending. I wouldn't suggest paying the full price for this game due to it's length, but I got it in a bundle and it was a good hour spent.
Successfully does what it aims to do; tell a story in style.
I'm lovin' it. Would love to get more games like this to play and review.

I bought this last year when it was on sale but didn't get around to playing it 'til a couple of weeks ago. It is certainly a short game; my playtime as shown here on Steam includes some time after I finished the story and extras where I let the game sit open in order to get the "Listen to the Radio" achievement.
I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed the game - yes, the gameplay is minimal, but the way you get to know the characters through your dialogue choices is well paced and ratchets up the tension as the story builds up to its conclusion.
I haven't done a second playthrough as of yet - I've certainly thought back about whether I'd make some choices differently as the protagonist, and I can see myself doing a couple of playthroughs in order to get some different reactions and bits of information from the other family members. So while the game's features in the store description don't exactly scream "replayability," I think there's some added value if you enjoyed the story the first time around and want to see what more there is to learn. Playing the epilogue and reading Ben's stories definitely added to the experience; it's easy to identify with the protagonist from the get-go but you really get a deeper understanding of her motivations the more you interact with the game.
The base game is currently 66% off as part of the 2016 Summer Sale; if you like story-driven games with very simple dialogue-based gameplay, I'd say it's definitely worth it - I bought it at a smaller discount and feel like I've got my money's worth.

I wish I could give this game neutral feedback, but as a fan of the genre (visual novels/short stories), I feel like I can give it a slightly positive review.  The game is very brief, which is fine, and consists of two telephone conversations (one during the main game, and one during the epilogue) with the protagonist's mother.  The conversation itself feels mostly authentic, but I was slightly distracted by the fact that the mother keeps simulataneously telling your character to be careful driving in the bad weather, but refusing to get off of the phone.  That is a minor complaint, but the bigger problem is that the story doesn't really go anywhere.  The Epilogue is a bit better than the main game, in my opinion, and I do like the very simple art style.  If you enjoy story-based games, and can catch this on sale, I would say it's worth checking out.  It's clear that quite a bit of care went into the crafting of the experience.

"King of Dragon Pass" is one of the most underrated games on Steam, You make text based story choices with some resource management. Because the results are revealed in story, often with hours of play passing, you are not sure what factors accumulated to produce a result. The game displays very little "number crunching" that's available to the player. What the game provides are principals of how your clan should be run. Over time the player comes to understand the logic of how to govern.
The text of the game includes over 600,000 words. Much like reading a very good long novel, the richness of the story is gradually revealed.
I estimate the "long" version of a "normal" difficulty game takes over 20 hours to complete.  I've found the game to have excellent replay value. You can take exactly the same actions in exactly the same situation and produce different results. Even better, taking a different action will often reveal a previously unseen portion of the game.
On the downside, I've found the "hard" version of the game to be tedious. Earlier in 2016 the game was updated with many bugs fixed and new story content added. There are bugs that remain, but they are minor and do not interfere with the game overall.
Unique and very good strategy/rpg game.

Mechanically, it is unlike any other game i have played. Equal parts a tribe management simulator and choose-your-own-adventure game, it is rich in flavor and surprisingly deep, necessitating a fair amount of playthrough to figure out how to do things "right." Not that the game is difficult or unfair in that regard; it is simply complex, with a deep wellspring of intricacies to drink in.
One of its greatest strengths is that - similarly to Alpha Protocol, for an odd but apt correlation - every decision seems to matter. From the seemingly smallest things, such as favors granted or called in on, to every single decision made in the events of the game - of which there are a great deal - choices are called back to and referenced throughout in-game years and even generations. Your tribe's history is shaped not in terms of generic paths, but in a web of events that are intricately linked together. More than anything else, this helps make an ostensibly fantasy game feel "real", or at least tangible.
It's a rare breed of game that manages to take a small budget and do things correctly what many large-budget products fail to do. This game deserves far more recognition than it has, and i can only hope that it is fondly remembered in the future.

Personally, I fancy PVE more than PVP. There are few PVP games that I enjoy, so far, Evolve being one of them.
I have not purchased or spent money on Evolve previously so my experience is solely that of a F2P player.
The Good:
-Fun gameplay (mixes some PVE elements with PVP)
-Smexy graphics
-Characters and interactions among them are entertaining
-Quick to find a match (on my end at least), some people leave last min whether its a disconnection or whatever reason. They're replaced by bots which is "okay" but I know this bothers some
-Everything is obtainable through in-game currency which you get just by playing
-It's free
The Bad:
-Lack of gamemodes, while different characters keep things varied, I wish there was some alternative modes to play to mix things up even more.
-Chat is blink and you miss the message with no way of going back to see what people wrote
-Lack of skins for some characters, like Jack who I enjoy playing
-The preference system is both good and bad, but I'm putting it in the bad because the issue with it can really ruin the fun. You get to pick which class you want to play on a scale of 1-5, it does its best to give you your number one and if not, your number two and so on and so fourth. Sounds great, right? Well, only when it works. For example, in one match, I had down I wanted to play a Trapper, another person wanted to play as a Medic, We were the only ones in that lobby who wanted to play those two classes. I got Medic and the other person got Support. Why? I don't know. It hasn't happened too much, but it is annoying when you get assigned a role which you shouldn't have been assigned.
Overall, it is a very fun game and I recommend giving it a shot.
Side note: I know some founders have some issues with compensation, however, me not being a founder can't vouch for that. I can only rate it as a F2P player.
