I am of extremely conflicted opinions on this game.  TL;DR, this game is unique enough that if you have any interest in its concept at all, you should probably get it at least on sale, in spite of its flaws.
I also will not weigh in on the GOG versus Steam versions debate, as I don't own the GOG version.  The GOG/classic PC version is less expensive, and has your clan tula (lands) improvements shown on a map, while the Steam/iOS version has higher resolution support.
That said, the good:
This is a game of serious choice-and-consequence gameplay that isn't bound up in a single black-and-white morality system.  It can be a serious game of strategic choice and risk-management, as well as role-playing.  The world, in particular, is rather detailed, and while the simulation is rather simple, it does manage to leave a sense of verisimilitude in the world.  Other clans have military and economic strengths where their casualties and losses are recorded, and other clans feud and raid in the background without you.
It also avoids the "snowballing" pitfall of many nation-management games, since there is no real military victory in this game.  You cannot hold territory outside your tula, and only through extreme difficulty can you expand it.  Trying to kill all of a certain species leads to disaster, as you cannot accomplish it alone.  Although the game rarely tells you as much, it's a game of diplomacy, and if you enjoy playing the diplomat route in RPGs, you'll probably enjoy this game.
This is a game that tries the almost unique feat of basically being a visual novel-type choose-your-own adventure game that is also mostly procedural.  It has a complex story made of random events and random characters.  It also has a (non-randomized) worldbuilding lore that has quite a bit of depth and I personally just love mythological stories.
When the game works, it lets you sweat out serious choices of balancing risks like whether to tell your irreplaceable warchief to risk his life to drive off a fierce invading force, or whether to hang back, even if it condemns more of your (relatively more replacable) front-line soldiers to their deaths or even risk losing the battle and seeing your lands raided.
Then, there is the bad:
This is a game that unfortunately suffers quite a bit for simply never telling you the information you need to know to make proper decisions.  At first, it seems like trial-and-error gameplay where you have "hints" provided from your advisors, although you quickly learn they're generally useless as they always give the same advice no matter the actual circumstance.  (The warrior types will advise killing everything or offending anyone who CURRENTLY has a smaller army than you do.  The tricksters will tell you to lie to or cheat everyone you meet.  The diplomatic types base all judgements on who hates you the most at the moment. None of them keep your overarching strategic goal in mind, and they're often wrong, but then again, the results of events are random, anyway, and they always disagree down predictable lines, so that's no real surprise.)  However, when you start to understand some of the mechanics beyond what is just the random events, you start to realize the real fatal flaw in King of Dragon Pass:
In general, I love Crusader Kings 2, but I hate the events in that game because they feel so cheap and two-dimensionally random in a game that is otherwise fleshed-out, simulated, and whose mechanical underpinnings you can not only see and understand, but also manipulate when you understand them.  In this game, it's nearly entirely those random events, and you can't see most of the mechanics, much less understand how to manipulate them properly.
For example, while other clans feud and raid behind your back, you have absolutely no way of knowing this happens.  You will also suddenly find you made an enemy out of a former friend because you made friends with someone they hated, without the game ever giving you ANY hint this would happen.  This is an "invisibility of information" problem that plagues this game to its core: It has a complex set of inter-related parts going on under the surface, but the player is left utterly blind to the workings of these mechanics.
This is worse than mere trial-and-error gameplay.  Trial-and-error gameplay, while frustrating, at least follows a logical cause-and-effect.  You come across three doors, and opening any of the "wrong" doors instantly killing your character at least follows a logical cause-and-effect that you can understand how to avoid the next time you play.  When a friendly clan suddenly declares a feud upon you for slights you don't believe you ever committed, however, there's absolutely no way for the player to understand what caused this effect, or IF it was even any of their choices which caused that effect at all.
It's at times a game that hands you a panel full of buttons, and when you press some, will randomly either pat you on the head or scream at you for what a horrible failure your entire life has been, even when you performed the exact same actions in the exact same sequence, and it leaves the player utterly baffled as to what went wrong.  These are especially bad in the cases of those invisible feuds between other clans - there is never any way for the player to understand that these feuds even exist, so they have no means of understanding when they are treding upon someone else's toes, and therefore, have no reason to expect that event that SAID it resulted in gaining renown will suddenly cause you to instead LOSE renown without there being any warning other than your relations suddenly souring.
It's not that the game doesn't track these things: It absolutely tracks who gets angry for what reason, but it just doesn't
things that should be obvious.  For example, when negotiating within a tribe, it will say "two clans are offended by the concessions you made to other clans," without saying
was offended by
concessions.  There's really no way to find out besides repeated savescumming and trial-and-error sussing out of the key variables. The end result is that you make guesses on too little information, then get told that some of your choices were apparently bad, but not told which ones, with no way of learning from past mistakes.  That really offends some deep-seated gamer part of me: Games should be about learning the mechanics and building up skill to do better the next time, but this game denies that to players.

The Turing Test is a fun little game with a neat story and less than adequate puzzles. The story is an interesting one and brings up a number of topics such as what it means to be a conscious entity, if A.I. can truly be conscious, and what it means to be free. The story is definitely the strongest point of the game and while it's themes are by no means unique or fresh, they are executed well enough.
Where the game falls short is in the puzzles and the gameplay. There are 70 puzzles in the game (77 if you count the bonus puzzles) and in my opinion they are far too easy. Personally, I didn't get hung up on a puzzle until I was in the 40s and even then, once I realized the mechanic that I had to take advantage of I didn't encounter a challenge until at least the last 20 puzzles. The primary reason is that there just aren't enough in-game mechanics when manipulating elements in the puzzles. The difficultly curve is quite flat.
If you've played Talos Principal and enjoyed the story and the puzzles, I do not recommend this game. The story, while good, is not nearly as good and the puzzles are comparitively very easy. I'd give this a 5/10.

A fantastic multiplayer experience with a chunky level of depth, this mod for half life 2 allows users to fight in western conflicts (think The Good, The Bad and The Ugly; For a Few Dollars More) with the title even parodying the movie Fistful of Dollars. Everything from the game environments to the soundtrack pay homage to the film genre that inspired the game and every instance of recollection these details bring forth is satisfying.
The combat within the game is a combination of melee and ranged assaults across several modes of gameplay, with an emphasis on the gunplay using revolvers. An expansive consideration was made to their mechanics including dual wielding to increase ammo and firepower and fanning the hammer for high rate of fire but lower accuracy. These options coincide with a dexterity mechanic where you can decide which hand you prefer using, affecting accuracy across all the revolver mechanics.
Four possible teams exist in the game, each visually distinct with their own sets of voice lines, which in handy when playing the team based modes. But with all this structured combat, how can you persist against the dangers? Whiskey. Lots and lots of whiskey. Found littered throughout each map are bottles of moonshine whiskey that can be picked up to restore health, but cleverly, this comes with it’s own dangers as consuming multiple jugs of the good stuff makes you drunk, lowering accuracy and visually distorting the screen. Alternatively there is a weaponised version of he whiskey that has “infinite ammo”, allowing you to heal other players but not yourself. Most modes of play involve a monetary reward system for killing other players, using buy screens at spawn time and treasure chests hidden throughout the map of three tiers, coinciding with the power of each weapon.
Usually in games this means players that manage to hit top tier weapons are at an extreme advantage, but not so in this game! Battling with these deadly assets has drawbacks such as extremely slow reloads, or low level damage stopping the high damage, ammo count or rate of fire from being too challenging to face. In a lot of ways many of the weapons are a novelty in and of themselves, allowing users to perform all manners of unique tactics, this ranges from a sawn off shotgun used in conjunction with a revolver for short + medium damage dealing, to a bow and arrow that deals damage with silent shots.
My personal favourite aspect of the game is the melee combat, where you can use your fists or three melee weapons to get close and personal. With so much emphasis on gunplay you would think that this side of the conflict was sub par, but several mechanics exist that make it a very exciting way to play. If enemies get too close, a kick mechanic allows you to knock enemies backwards, allowing gun users to fire a shot into their gut, or melee battles to end with one combatant being kicked off a cliff. To even the odds, there is a disarming mechanic that is applied by certain weapons such as the brass knuckles sending your opponent’s weapons cascading off screen while you pummel their face leaving them in a state of panic. It’s quite euphoric.
I’m closing I recommend this game to anyone who plays Team Fortress 2 or Day of Defeat, as the feel of play is a mix of the two. Either way it’s a more satisfying experience than counter strike.

The premise of this game is great, but in my opinion it was executed poorly.
First off the game is not self explanatory in any way, some areas I found to be impossible without looking up a guide. How was I supposed to know in act 3 you need to put the pieces of cake on the plates? How was I supposed to know you had to freeze the globe? If I wasn't asking myself, "how was I supposed to know this?" I was asking myself, "was I intended to do that?" as I would just stack boxes (assuming they wouldn't fall over) to reach areas I wasn't sure I was supposed to go to.
Secondly, as many other reviewers have stated, the physics are floaty. A simple jump can easily be overshot, or if you're walking along a pipe you can fall off easily if you have to step down to a lower one. The game could have benefitted well from tighter controls, as platforming with parachute pants is a little difficult in this setting.

Apparently there are certain doors that the neighbor has to break open for you, but I have no idea if this is random or if there is a set trigger that causes this. I passed this area by following a guide where you open the gate to the trampoline and make a long jump from the roof into the trampoline and escape, but again, I have no idea if I was supposed to make that jump as it was really difficult and took over a dozen tries.
Act 3 is where I gave up. The game just got too cryptic, and without a guide it's basically impossible for a brand new player to find things out. This is a big problem. Maybe the way to fix it would be to have a list of objectives, or maybe a hints menu to help the player out.
All in all, I wouldn't recommend it, not for $30. Maybe $10?

Three Fourths Home isn't a game about coming home and not wanting to be there. Three Fourths Home is a game about holding right.
Three Fourths Home is a tight little (emphasis on the little) visual novel about post-college woman who comes home and doesn't want to be there. As someone who typically loves the not-video game genre with things like Gone Home and the Beginners Guide this is probably the first time I ever questioned where a game like this was worth the purchase.
The visuals are actually interesting even if they are a little static and the sound design is spot-on, placing you in a car ride during a rain storm but it's actually the narrative that was the biggest let down of the game. The subject of having to return from school, back to a small town and back to living with your parents is a story that's becoming more and more real for a lot of people and something video games haven't really tackled. And the portrayal of this feels honest. There's a contrained politeness from the main character when she's talking to her mom and dad but that's where it ends. The story's told through a series of phone calls between the main character and her family but it feels limited and constrained. Characters can only really stress how dangerous a storm is until it gets VERY stale and where we're meant to read into what's not being said and extrapolate and think about the situations, what we find feels shallow and a little predictable.

This game is honestly really, really cute, and quite entertaining at times. The plot is decent, the gameplay is pretty fun, and the world looks absolutely beautiful... but there's one big issue that might be a potential deal-breaker for some people.
I have an Alienware 13 with an Intel i7-5500U processor (2.40GHz), an Nvidia 960M GPU with the latest drivers, and 16GB of RAM. When I'm using the game's "Low" graphics setting, I can get only just above 30fps if I stand still and stare at a wall. If I use the game's "Highest" graphics setting and I'm moving a lot or generally trying to play the game, I can easily end up with less than 10fps. (For comparison, my computer can easily and consistently get anywhere from 120-150fps in Portal 2 without even breaking a sweat.) I have no idea if the problem is with the game or my computer (though I'd be very, very surprised if it was the latter), but this definitely needs to be mentioned, and hopefully fixed.
Other than that, this game is a great experience and a lot of fun, considering that it's a PC port/expansion of a tablet game. Though I was a bit disappointed when I had to play on the "Low" or "Medium" graphics settings to have a framerate better than "slideshow", I didn't really notice it after a while and was simply able to enjoy the game for what it was.
The other thing I'm slightly disappointed by - though in a good way - is that there isn't any way to get the soundtrack! The background music is all really nice and calm for the most part, with simple instrumentation and nice melodies. If there was a $1.99 DLC I'd buy it in a heartbeat.
If the very thought of getting less than 60fps makes you want to throw up and/or throw your computer out a window, I wouldn't recommend this game. For everyone else, though, it's definitely worth at least waiting for a sale - this game is really cute and fun, and it's got a pretty decent price for the five or so hours of playtime.

Remember doing the Town level with only the stakegun? Or the snowy bridge with ninjas? Or the military base with the UFO at the end? Well I hope you do, because this game doesn't have them.
Painkiller Hell & Damnation is basically a prettier but anorexic Painkiller Black Edition. If you've never played Painkiller in your life, start with Painkiller Black Edition, which is avaliable on Steam for only 9,99€ and gives you about 30 levels right off the bat, whereas Painkiller Hell and Damnation, which costs 19,99€ will only give you about 15 of those same levels, some of which are arguably weaker than their original counterparts. That's half the conten for twice the price. And if you want all the singleplayer content for this game you're gonna have to fork over nearly 50€ (assuming you buy the base game + 2 DLC bundles and not all the DLC separately). So Painkiller Black Edition is just a better offer all around.
With that out of the way, what's new in Painkiller Hell and Damnation?
Well, here are my observations from beating the game on Insomnia (Normal difficulty):
-You get a new weapon (The Soulcatcher) which is kind of OP. It shots a saw blade that cuts through several enemies, it's alt-fire acts like a vacuum for souls, which is insanely useful and once you collect enough souls (about 5 or 6) you can use the tertiary fire to convert some of the enemies into your allies for a short period. Overall this new weapon makes the game a bit too easy, but I guess you can just opt out of using it for the most part
-Speaking of weapons, the progression has now been altered, but on the flip side you can use the Battle out of Hell weapons in the vanilla levels. Also some of the weapons have been slightly rebalanced, the most notable exception for me is that the Electrodriver is actually useful now.
-The order of the levels has been redone somewhat. There are now 4 episode instead of the original Painkiller's 5. Train Station is now in episode 2, as opposed to episode 3. You fight the Swamp monster in episode 3 and Alastor in episode 2. In episode 4 you get the Orphanage and Looney Park.  The levels themselves have also been changed to some degree. Like the Colosseum is missing some of it's traps, the Oriental Castle takes place in day instead of night etc.
-The monster placement is different. The only new enemy is a skeleton which appears in most of the levels, but then you have some weird decisions like clowns in the Opera House, bikers in the Train Station, and a complete absence of gladiators in Colosseum. I guess it's good that they wanted to make it a fresh experience but a lot of it feels weird and out of place.
-On that note the conditions for Tarot cards have been improved, in my opinion, with the exception of maybe one or two. You can also unlock two tarot cards per level now AND it tells you if you have fullfiled the requirments, which is a very welcome addition.
-You can the story in co-op although I haven't had a chance to test this feature.
-There's also a story with cutscenes in there but honestly I wouldn't bother, it sucks for the most part except for a few "so bad it's good" moments. Also Daniel is voiced by Duke Nukem, but his performance is kind of boring
-If you buy the "Heaven Above" DLC you can play 5 levels of a top down Painkiller, which can be fun, but the camera is so goddamn bad it made the whole ordeal way more frustrating than it ought to be.
Sadly some problems haven't been fixed from the original - souls still take way too long to appear for no reason, the enemies still get stuck in doorways and a vast majority of the enemies are ♥♥♥♥ing braindead.
So would I recommend Painkiller Hell & Damnation? Well I wouldn't recommend it over Painkiller Black Edition and certainly not with it's current price tag. However if you love the original game and get this one when it's on sale, I think you won't be disappointed. Really the biggest problem with this game is the price tag, because it just doesn't offer enough new content and features to be priced almost the same as a brand new triple A game.

Dogfight 1942 is a good game.
I've already played others titles like this and I appreciate the arcade genre, because also this dogfight is an arcade.
You will have 2 main campaigns in the base game, so I suggest to buy all the bundle in order to play the entire experience.
Missions are fast to be completed, and introductions with teammates speaking and cinematic view of the airplanes are a good part of the game. The game itself is instead a little poor: you fly and shoot using machinegun or missiles or bombs, and sometimes torpedoes, but enemy really fall in a few hit and the dogfights that the title suggests are really fast to be terminated.
Event the ace from enemy troops are easy to take down. Instead I've found better combats in Air Conflicts.
The controls are a bit peculiar: you don't manouver the airplane directly, but the machine gun targeting. So if you follow enemies on screen, your airplane follow the target, rotating and cutting the corners.
Instead I prefer Air Conflict where you move the airplane and if the target is around the enemy automatically it him; this is more challenging than here in dogfight.
The engine is good for a visual impact, if you don't want too much. The only problem is the drop of framerate inside concitated fights... but the scenario is not so complicated, so why this happens?
In any case the game is perfect in bundle with special offers. It grants a good variety of missions and can be terminated in a couple of days. You can always try the random dogfights mode or try with highest difficulty.
In any case not bad.

Mass Effect but with a 60s art style. Teammate AI is a mess with them choosing to take cover in front of enemies or keep running around doing nothing unless you decide to issue commands for them every single second, thankfully this gets slightly better once they level up and can take more damage, and once you level up a few times in which the game becomes a total cakewalk. Other than that the combat is alright and can even become ~~intense~~ sometimes in harder difficulties.
The storyline is a mess; outside the twist near the end it's very disjointed with the game assuming you know things you haven't been told yet (your character acts as if he knows these things too) and some characters vanishing two levels from the end of the game and never being mentioned again.
Like I mentioned before the entire game plays and feels like Mass Effect but set in the 60s (there's even a base you can walk around in and talk to people after missions). I liked the art style a lot and it kept me playing until the end, but the game itself is kind of a mess due to it being stuck in development hell for 5+ years. Even so it's not Aliens Colonial Marines/Duke Forever horrible garbage, just average. If you think the setting looks interesting and want a slightly strategical third person shooter (think Brother in Arms and Mass Effect as previously mentioned) buy it when it's on sale for u$20 and you'll have fun. Hopefully it'll get a sequel in the future that fixes the issues it has (but it bombed so it won't).

For the light gun emulation, V-sync (or maybe even the engine) does not give good mouse control that is needed for a game like this (Mad Bullets seems to have this down).

Winning the Guiness Record for most swearing in a video game, House of the Dead Overkill sure as hell set itself apart from all of the generic party games for the Wii. Then it was made a PS3 game. And now a PC game. There are two games, so I will review both.
Typing of the Dead Overkill is basically HOTD Overkill, but fast typing is needed to kill zombies, rather than a virtual gun. You will be forced to type anything from Grapes to Gilt Edged Chicken F*cker.
HOTD Overkill, which can be selected to play if you would rather use a mouse to shoot rather than a keyboard. This version is a direct port of the PS3 version, which, in turn, was adapted from the original 2009 Wii version. However, like the PS3 version, there are a few extra levels that focus on the shenanigans of hooker Varla Guns and dumb blonde Candi Stryper. Set in 1991 in the deep south of Lousiana, you play as either profane lady's man Isaac Washington or rookie agent "G", killing various zombies (or mutants) to eventually confront sterotypical 1970s B-Movie villian Papa Caesar.
The entire game plays out like a 1970s Grind-house B-Movie. Grainy footage, music from the era and a dramatic narrator. While older HOTD games left a zombie corpse covered in bloody holes when they are dead, this game opts to literally cause the zombie to explode into a pool of blood on the ground. A first for HOTD games is a store that sells guns and perks for in-game cash. This cash is usually received from doing a good job in a level, or just coming across a wad of it in the level itself. Other collectables in levels are paintings, records and statues.
I would narrowly recommend this game. The older HOTD games literally had no replay value, because the levels vary very little. Here, you have more to do after you beat the main game. Upgrading and buying guns, playing minigames and playing a Directors' Cut mode (basically the normal game but each level is extended). If this game is on sale and you are a little bored with your game library, pick this game up, you will have some fun. But, unless you really enjoy the series or you want to learn to type better, don't buy it at full price.
If you want to test a keyboard, this is for you...

I'm a big fan of Paradox games going back to Hearts of Iron 2 but this one just isn't for me.
HOI IV's attempts to simplify HOI3's formula made the game more confusing to me, while also robbing it of depth.
I don't enjoy the convoluted production system.
I don't like the rearrangement of the sea and air campaign manager.
I don't like that armies don't have a proper chain of command anymore (they're just massive collections of divisions with a general at the head).
I do like that the campaign is generally more open-ended, and there is the option to make it more or less scripted to be exactly like WWII. This is huge since, much as I loved the gameplay of 3, it got tiresome playing WWII again and again. This freedom is increased with the excellent addition of the steam workshop and its many wonderful scenarios, some of which are quite well developed.
All that said though, I just can't get into this style of a hearts of Iron game.

The only thing that stops this game from being a masterpiece is the lack of moddability, as an engine I feel it would create virtually limitless possibilities for players to generate their own rich worlds and stories to share around.

To get to the point: only get this on sale. The game isn't bad, but has numerous issues that it is a beta at best.
That out of the way, the biggest issues this game has are AI and paid patches. The AI can be absolutely braindead sometimes (ie. moving units off a war front to begin another push, causing a collapse).
The paid patches is what killed this game for me. Instead of proper Expansions, they add new focus trees (which mods can easily do) and justify the cost with additions that should have been in from the start or patched in for free (like most good devs do when they support their game post-launch). I know they need to make money to push more content out, but making us pay for patches is NOT how you do it.

This is my favourite game on Steam.  It's a low-fantasy village simulator set in Glorantha, the world of RuneQuest, in which you manage a clan.  It has city-builder and RPG elements, but your goal isn't to grow, and you don't roleplay any single character.  Rather, you guide your village nobles into making choices that will increase their reputation among the other inhabitants of Dragon Pass (and we're not just talking people -- we're talking clans, tribes, dragons, gods, spiritual ancestors, beastmen, you name it!) until one of your nobles becomes accepted to lead the region as King or Queen.  There's a ton of depth to the game and the decisions you can make.
There are no animations in this game; it's mostly text.  Hand-painted watercolours depict events as they happen.  It's truly unique.
This version is a bit strange because it clings to some holdovers from the iOS version, which was optimized for touchscreens.  You don't need a touchscreen laptop to play the game, but it makes menu scrolling easier and allows the use of a couple features, such as zooming in and out of the map.

The Turing Test is an enjoyable experience, much like watching “Street Fighter the Movie”. You know it’s not good. The plot makes little sense. Character repeatedly do stupid things that they should know not to do. And many puzzles could easily be solved with the abilities (such as crawling, leaning, and climbing) than anyone over the age of 14 has. But the gameplay is enjoyable enough for a few hours, and doesn’t over stay it’s welcome.
I got this cheap for $10 and think that that was a good price for what I got.
WARNING: This game chugged along for me. After turning off all the useless graphic options (like anti-aliasing ) and lowering the others it could barely do 30fps which is well below my laptops standard output. I don’t know if this will be an issue with everyone else, but it was for me.
Also, this game has intense and constant changes in brightness, with one of the strongest bloom effects I have ever seen in a game. This WILL cause eye strain and I would recommenced playing this only in a well lit area.
Review:
As far as Gameplay goes, it is exactly what you think it would be. A sub par first person puzzler in the vein of Q.U.B.E., Quantum Conundrum, and some obscure Valve I seem to have forgotten the name of… The rooms are nonsense with only a brief line thrown in about why the rooms were built that doesn’t add up even when you don’t think about it; and believe me, you will. The difficulty spikes dramatically. And the mechanics can be… Odd… Let me explain.

This gun you have (that comes out of nowhere and has no purpose other than to solve puzzles) can only hold 3 charges and has no way to swap them out after being collected other than to shoot them into a receptor. Why? Also, you get a gun that you use literally 3 times in the entire game. And only one of those times is to solve a puzzle! And the puzzles. All but two(from what I found) can be solved from any state. And both that require a restart if you mess up come at the end of the game; one of them LITERALLY is the end of the game!

And then there’s the other end of the spectrum. Many puzzles have obstacles like 4 foot platforms you have to lower before you can climb. 6 by 8ft holes in the wall that you have to find a way around instead of crawling through. And energy cores you could easily take with you if she would only stick her hand around a corner to use her gun.

At the same time, many puzzles can have corners you can cut or just be skipped almost entirely by the run function. I can almost guarantee you the ability to run was not in the original game and was added later. It does not mesh well with the puzzles at all! That being said, I quite enjoyed that oversight, and was always looking for cheeky ways to undo the developer’s designs.
This whole things seems unfinished. Just a collage of partial ideas put together to see what works. It’s rushed and semi broken, but that almost gives it a sort of charm… A charm that gets old fast, but luckily the game is quite short. And I will give it credit for being quite good at teaching concepts naturally… Congratulations due where congratulations are due; it’s only fair.

Now the story is something truly interesting. See you play a murderer named Gill T… Wait… No, that was from a story I wrote in Middle School. Ah yes, you play a woman named Ava Turning who works with a robot struggling with being self aware… Yes… Very on the nose that name is.
There’s really not much to say that you can’t already guess. The dialogue is laughably bad, more so when you remember these are supposed to be astronauts. It makes sense coming from the A.I. as he is going through ‘cyber puberty’ and has many a reason to be upset and confused. TOM (The A.I.) is easily the best part of this game and strangely enough, the voice of reason.

All of… ‘that’, culminates to an epilogue that, if you are like me, you will sit through 4 times to see all the slightly different endings (honestly its 2 endings with the ‘bad ending’ having 3 different flavors… two of which are the same flavor inverted… But you don’t know that till you try them out). This segment is an unskipable long 3 minute wall down two corridors, followed by a minute of watching characters move on their own… make that 3 minutes if you get a certain bad ending). It’s a pain, cannot be skipped, and requires a you to be sitting at your computer interacting the entire time.

So what does it all come to? Well avoiding spoilers (
)… Nothing. I understand why its over, but when the only story you have is building up two major problems and then neither is addressed… That leaves you feeling used. And seeing all the different endings? Well, right after your choice, cut to unskipable credits so… Don’t expect a resolution or consequence.

Following in the wake of successful puzzles games like
and
,
might have striking similarities with the former 2 but it still feels more like a tribute rather than a shameless copy.
It feels very natural to compare The Turing Test with the aforementioned games. Even at a glance they have so many things in common it is almost impossible to not draw a comparison between them. Many reviewers have already done this comparison before and they all come to the same conclusion. While the games are incredibly similar, The Turing Test still manages to hold to his own personality (nice unintentional parallel with the game's story perhaps?) and when it shows it's true colors it manages only to succeed.
Puzzle games are a bit intimidating for me. I love their concept but when things get tough I tend to lose focus. I mostly avoid puzzle games unless I know the storyline/graphics/concept is interesting enough for me. However I've come to the conclusion that when it comes to these kind of games, perseverance is sometimes a stronger attribute that problem solving. Not always mind you, but it certainly comes in handy.
The Turing Test has very few simple mechanics which you will learn as you progress through the game. You collect energy beams with your gun which then you can use to power several devices in a stage. There's various colored beams which all have their own uses but the game never gets
complicated. For what is worth I found the Turing Test challenging enough but as I mentioned above puzzle games are not my specialty.
Later in the game, some extra gameplay elements are added with the inclusion of a remotely power robot assistant, but again, it never feels too difficult to handle even for inexperienced puzzle game players.
So how does The Turing Test differentiate itself from the other, dime-a-dozen puzzle games? For me personally, the story and how it's played out was a key aspect of my positive experience with the game.
The premise is this: You play as Ava Turing, aptly named scientist, trapped on Jupiter's moon Europa, on the brink of a world-changing scientific discovery. In the station, the mission's AI T.O.M (Technical Operations Machine), which has the responsibility of monitoring the project, informs you that your fellow crew members have been behaving erratically and it's up to you to find out what's been happening. I won't spoil the story but I will discuss a couple of things about it.
First of all, if you've ever watched
you have pretty good idea about what's happening. The 'AI-gone-haywire' trope has been done before, many a times and it's usually a safe bet when it comes to science fiction. And while Portal had a more humorous approach to this trope, The Turing Test goes a lot more philosophical about it. It's not necessarily preachy and it does raise a few interesting questions regarding what we consider 'intelligence', 'consciousness', 'free will' and many more as you'll hear T.O.M lecture you about robotics, ethics and humanity.
And for what is worth, T.O.M is an exquisite character. The brilliant voice acting of James Faulkner was a core aspect of the game's success believe it or not. The monotone, the robotic color of his voice, you can hear him getting slightly angry, frustrated, even sarcastic at times with just
minor changes in his speech. T.O.M does not have the humor and insanity of GLaDOS. He's much more manipulative, cold and subtle but there are moments where you can see his reasoning. There are times when you get angry with him, understand his reasoning and even sympathize but that's all relevant to your opinion about artificial intelligence. For me it was very interesting to hear what T.O.M had to say to Ava during their albeit short discussions and motivated me to look for the optional areas to delve deeper into the AI's 'psyche' if you will.
There's a weird vibe going on The Turing test. Graphically the game is pretty well done in the amazing Unreal Engine 4 but it is the nature of the game to focus less on graphical detail and more on level design. The simplistic nature of the environment hides a more complicated way of solving puzzles and furthermore I appreciated 'Red herring' moments in which a solution to a puzzle was much more simple than the relative complexion of the devices available to a stage.
The sound and music are excellent and contribute to create an appropriate atmosphere for the game. The music in particular is not constant so when the tracks of the soundtrack begin to play, they set a perfect mood for the game. The ambient sounds are as sci-fi as you can get and they create a good amount of immersion.
The game is relatively short. At your leisure it takes around 4-5 hours to complete and there's a few optional areas which shed light into the lore of the game. There are two possible endings to choose from which I did feel they could have been slightly expanded but I can understand why the developers went with a more abrupt and 'realistic' way of ending things. You don't always need to have long melodramatic cutscenes for the player to make their own interpretations and that's why I can respect both endings.
The Turing Test is pretty well crafted in my book. There's a lot of inspiration drawn from other puzzle games and sci-fi films but it never felt like a ripoff. I thoroughly enjoyed my time and while some of the puzzles felt a bit easy even for me, there were several ones which were challenging enough to give me a nice feeling of satisfaction when I completed them. The game has a near perfect duration, it doesn't drag on and knows when the curtains have to fall. The story raises some fascinating discussions if you're into science fiction stuff and the way it unravels throughout the game feels very natural. All in all, The Turing Test is an excellent recommendation. If you enjoyed Portal and want something a little more serious story wise, then this game is certainly for you.

This is an extramarital offspring of Portal and Talos Principle. The kid cannot match any of his great parents in size, depth or creative ingenuity, but there's no doubt who they are. Seriously though, this is a very solid mix of the aforementioned games and you should like it if you liked them. However, don't expect it to surpass any of them in any way. It's a Portal/Talos Light. Very Light.
P.s.: my actual playing time is higher than what Steam indicates (the counter goes south when one plays offline)

I suppose my opinion isn't a popular one in regards to Three-Fourths Home but I didn't really enjoy the game.
To begin, I loved the art style, sound effects, music and subtly that the game brought when I first booted it up and started playing. I liked the idea of exploring the characters life and background through dialogue and the minimilistic approach the developer took. However, the game felt like reading someones short-story fiction they submitted to a group critique for an undergrad advanced writing course. I'm not much a fan of visual novels, it's not my cup of tea. This one in particular had some beautiful visual elements that matched where you were in reading the dialogue that added to the mood and really played on your emotions. But, after a while the game just really felt like it was dragging on.
If you like visual novels and are drawn in by character studies, this is a great game for you. It really is designed well and the visuals are fantastic. The writing is very well done as well, but it felt like something that kept going for much longer than it should have.
It was an experience more than a game, but I enjoyed it nonetheless. It reminds me of a much simpler version of Kentucky Route Zero

Experimental interactive fiction.
I'm recommending and reviewing this game because it doesn't deserve the "mixed" status it currently has.
Come into this expecting an experience more like "Kentucky Route Zero-lite." If you do, it's worth the entrace fee. We are inventing and defining this medium as we go and I'm enjoying each step along the way. Three Fourths Home being one of them.
This is not a huge powerhouse of narrative exposition, nor is it a "videogame" in the classic sense. Steer clear if those are what you are looking for.
Dialogue does not feel stilted or forced and characters are believable. The premise was sound and made me want to call my mom. It was also just the right length for its content and subject matter. My favorite part of the experience would be Ben's stories. Somebody on this team is a decent fiction writer, which feels odd in this day and age.
My least favorite part would be my fingers getting tired/bored from holding "right" the whole time. That may have actually been intentional though, as driving for a long time can have the same effect.
If you're interested in this type of thing, don't pass it up. Also, play it in one sitting.

Playing this game I fell in love with the characters; the story; the storytelling. Quite simply this is much more about the story than the game. And to me that's not such a bad thing.
The characters are believable, I suppose in part because you get to decide how Kelly should respond and in turn guiding how the other characters repsond. I found myself at times telling her to say what I would say and at other times playing along with the narrative - saying what I think would bring more of the story out for me to hear.
The other part of the believability is how well they're crafted. You don't know their backstory. You get snippets from them. Snippets from other family members. Snippets from Kelly's replies. Enough to make a picture, enough to let your imagination fill in the blanks without thinking the storyteller should have given you more (but wishing they had).
Actually the storytelling is so good I do want more. I want to go back and play it again. Change my answers, try and learn more about everyone. Don't worry, I'm not going to give any spoilers.
So storytelling before gameplay? Yeah that's how this car rolls...through Nebraska...in a storm...but only when holding the buttons down...(play it, you'll see what I mean).
I gotta say, wouldn't you pay such an itty bitty price for an amazingly well crafted and engaging story with believable characters? So why not pay it for a story and game?

A fantastic narrative experience condensed within an hour. The story tackles on themes of parental obligation, disability, and depression and crafts them into a very real, believable experience. The ambiguity of the story overall makes it very relatable.

Even as far as visual novels go, there isn't much to see here. The story is extremely short, though I would say mercifully so. There is an obnoxious "drive" mechanic requiring the player to hold down a button throughout the main story in order to advance the text.
If I were to critique the "gameplay" seriously, I would point out that the dialogue choices are inconsequential, which is corollary to the fact that the player knows nothing of the character whose role they are thrust into. The character does have historical contexts within the narrative but the relevant exposition tends to occur after the fact. For all intents, every dialogue choice you are presented with is a blind and pointless decision.

This is less of a game and more of an interactive story/art project. There is no intense gameplay, there are no intense puzzles, just the story, art, and music. The minimalist visuals and atmospheric soundtrack do well to not only give the narrative proper focus, but also reflect its scale. Three Fourths Home is a peek at the life of a young woman and her family, and it explores family and life issues in a tasteful, realistic manner. Its subtlety fleshes out emotions well in the first part of the game, and while the epilogue felt a bit heavy-handed and harsh at first, it was brought back down to Earth with its climax. Not all the characters are likeable, but that reflects the reality behind the story. The extra content is also a nice touch, fleshing out the world further and giving the feeling that the family's story goes beyond the main narrative. Overall, it is beautiful, subtle, and emotional, and while it's hard to recommend it as a game, it is easy to recommend as an experience.

In this review I'm going to compare Rift to WoW because these are the only fantasy MMORPGs I have played. Rift is a very very pretty game, but at the end of the day It lacks the depth and innovation needed for it to stand out. Beyond the dynamic events which are very fun and provide a vitality and ease to open world raiding that puts WoW to shame I'm just not drawn into the story the way I am with WoW. At the same time I have played WoW so many hours that I know a good deal about the story. In RPGs I find satisfaction when after doing quests for NPC's it changes not only what they say to you but how they interact with you. In Rift, NPC's say the say same thing to you before the quest as they do after the quest, and give you quests to talk to other NPCs when they finish with you, I find it generic. I also found the quest writing boring. I do enjoy the level of customization with regard to the spells and the skill trees, this gives people great flexibility to play classes how they like and to play them all on one character because god forbid someone go level in Rift more than once. Rift is refreshingly low on bugs though which is no small feat in comparison to WoW's buggy instances of long spawn times, bad drop rates etc. After playing Rift I realized I would enjoy WoW a lot more if it had more dynamic events, better graphics, more stylistic realism, and more gameplay customization. Does WoW still even do World bosses? Its important to point out that while Rift is now free to play one can purchase advantages which make it "less time consuming" a bit of a paradox because if you don't want to consume time why are you playing videos games in the first place? Otherwise I don't have a problem with all that, if money isn't a problem for you, you might want to just buy a level 60 character and get right to the latest content in Nightmare Tide. If you are hoping to not spend money then let me tell you up front It starts to feel restrictive when you get to about level 15. You'll only get 3 bag slots, the rest are behind a paywall requiring REX which can be bought ingame at the auction house. Now this is all good but when the price is over 1k platinum its not cheap, a mount costs 2.5 platinum just to provide perspective. Now it might be worth it to shell out $5 for the credits because you also get loyalty points, which lift some restrictions. The idea of starting out with restrictions doesn't appeal and yet in any MMORPG there are restrictions. I wish the bag slots were purchasable with  Planite, thats just me. I like that quests were able to start on their own without an NPC in the Instant fight areas, (again a model for WoW) and that for many quests you could turn them in on the spot without always needing to go back to an NPC. The art of the game itself is top notch and makes the cartoony style of WoW look tired and dated, even though I object to the scantily clad plate wearing female guards, which I just find silly and cliche. These are minor quibbles to the main reasons Rift hasn't met it potential: the lack of a great PVP system. WoW has gone through inumerable PVP overauls over the years but its paid off, the PVP in WoW is really great, for many hardcore PVPers that play WoW, its all they do. Ok so what should you do? If you are still curious play it for the first zone, It won't cost you.  if you plan on playing beyond that be prepared to shell out a little cash, so thats if you want to give it a go beyond approximately level 20. I want to protect whoever may be reading this from the sunk-cost fallacy. Perhaps like myself you want to wait for something fresh like Black Desert or Everquest Next because you don't want to become overly invested in something you know you'll eventually stop playing. As someone who quit their MMORPG It makes more sense to wait for something radically different to replace it.

Red Trigger is a fantastic, first person puzzle game. The gameplay is simple, you have a gun that has 3 "energy beams". You can shoot those energy beams at these red shaped things. When you shoot them, they'll move a certain direction, depending on what way they're facing. After shooting an energy beam at a red thing, you can shoot it again to take back the energy and use it on another red thing. Some red things will even act as switches that will toggle certain things like something rotating or a bridge being activated. Some red things will launch you into the air allowing you to fly around. Hell, sometimes there's red things on red things. The puzzles are great, though I feel they could be a bit more challenging. The art style is very simplistic, but it looks wonderful and the graphics, well, it's an Unreal Engine game. There's only two problems I have. One, the audio is WAY too loud. I have to set my computer's volume to 8 for it to now destroy my ears, and there's no audio slider in the options menu so I can't change it in game. This, of course, can be easily fixed by editing the sounds or adding audio options. Two, there needs to be more levels. Right now, this is a short but very sweet game. There's nothing necessarily wrong with that, but I wan't more. If more levels were to be added in the future, that would be awesome.
To sum it all up: Gameplay is good, puzzles are great and wonderfully designed but could be more challenging, graphics and art style are great, audio is too loud, and more levels would be awesome.
For now, I give it a 9.9/10. Fix the audio then it's a 10/10

This game puts your through linear puzzles featuring the early concept aerial faithplates from Portal, trapdoors, bars that can be used to obstruct hurdles wanting to block your path and basically hard light bridges, all of which you can controll via a lasergun that you point at them from any distance. The aestetics are rather bleak with a tad of eye-cancer and follow the philosophy from Mirrors Edge when it comes to providing the player with hints on the solutions of the puzzles. Though I suppose that's kind of a neccessary evil when the entire map is blank and untextured, which in return begs the question how this game can be as badly optimized as it is. What's neat I guess is that it features some semi-realistic physics, semi-realistic in the sense that it picks wether the laws apply according to the situation. Say you are jumping and activating a faith plate in which case you get teleported to the side of the launch-pad instead of soaring into the sky, timing your jump towards lift-off however can amplify your speed manyfold. Another plus would be good air strafing mechanics although hitboxes can be rather jarring to predict when trying to land a jump or to keep from running into a laser while trying to step on a platform that you can raise from underneath it.
All in all it's a poorly fleshed-out concept that implements some physics-based game mechanics rather well. And seeing how this is a free student project I think it accomplishes what it's trying to do just as well. Just put on sunglasses if you're gonna play the game for over an hour straight trying to get the speedrun achievement that at this point has become an empty trend to pad any game's length. The bane of completionist's existance.
There's also a twisted hallway that rotates gravity as you walk along it just to mess with you.

OneShot is a RPG that has strayed a
off the path of a normal RPG. While it is still very story based, there isn't any loot drops or boss battles in the traditional sense. The characters in the game are very well made, as everyone has a role. In the end I would give this game a perfect score, great job developers.

A lot of people reviewing this game have been under the impression that this is (or is supposed to be) a flight sim game. This is NOT a sim of any kind. This is more of an arcade style dogfighting game. This game is simple, straightforward, and fun if you just want to shoot planes out of the sky. There is no joystick support (in fact the settings and options for this game are very limited) and there is no multiplayer. There is however local co-op. The mission objectives are straightforward and not repetitive. There are some options for customizing your plane (adding numbers on the wings, shark face to the nose of the plane, etc). You do get to fly various planes of the era (American, British, Russian, and German) which is awesome of course. (My personal favorite were the Russian planes in the Russia Under Seige DLC. While slower, they have the most firepower.) I would recommend playing this with the DLC, which should give you about 5-6 hours total of playtime. I don't really understand why this game gets bad reviews, I thought it was a lot of fun. I played it with a Steam controller and that was great. You can't pull through the vertical, for some game physics-related reason but it doesn't detract from the fun. There is great mission variety. It looks and sounds good and it certainly does work in full screen. It is arcade-y yet challenging enough to be fun in Normal mode and very hard in Difficult mode. The aircraft controls are simplified so that you can focus on the flying and shooting. You can change aircraft and other parameters and it offers several game modes. It has good replayabilty. I'll certainly be returning to it to try and pick up some of the awards I missed. It doesn't try to be anything other than what the description and demo video portray it as - a rollicking good time in the cockpit without imposing a huge learning curve on the player and for a few quid with all the DLC, it's a bargain. If that sounds like your thing, buy it, you'll enjoy the ride. 10/10.

I must start off by saying that I didn't test simulator mode or multiplayer, I just wanted to relax and shoot down some planes and this is exactly what I've got. The game has 2 acts(RAF and US) + 2 DLC(Russia, Africa), about 20+ missions and it takes about 5 hours to go through it all without pressuring yourself. I basically started with basic settings and only died once in a battle(and about 10 times trying to land).
All the missions are different and it's a big plus(actually I liked mission diversity a lot, flying inside canyons, battles overseas, bombarding tanks), but I must say that landing didn't feel like the strength of the game. At some point, you'll be asked to land in the field....and you might crash because no one shows you where you can land and where you can't. Apparently, some grass is better than the other same looking grass.
Props for planes, they look great(about 20 different machines), also props for fights, they can be very dynamic and during missions when you are flying into great battles there are planes swarming everywhere shooting from different angles, directions etc. But usually, you have support, your wing with 4 orders that you can give them like protect me or attack my target.
Diversity also shows up in the missions themselves and planes. In one mission you may be asked to bombard tanks, fight with other pilots, again tanks, bunkers, ships. It feels great(and unrealistic, I stopped looking at my stats after I've seen 71 kills after one of the missions in the Act I). As to planes, they have different weaponry, armor, speed, maneuverability, you can also customize how they look.
Honestly, I couldn't take the whole game on one sitting but still, I don't feel like I wasted time. For me 6+.

This game is great, it's fun but, it's obnoxious, very obnoxious.
Let me explain, I'll begin with the weather.
Storms are much too frequent and last way too long, in my last couple of hours, I got stuck with a sand storm that lasted 3 in-game days and it made it very difficult to keep playing, once it stopped, I got 5 minutes of sunny peace then it started raining for the rest of the in-game day and night, once that stopped, I got another 5 minutes of freedom then another sand storm came and ruined it by lasting the rest of the in-game day, it took way too much will power to ignore it.
Now the resources.
This game is very very tedious and painful to play in the beginning, the game has high demand for hard to find resources, take Magnesium for example, it's hard to find, and the giant worm is a prick, but, granted, once you get it, you have alot of it, that's okay, but, the one thing that made me stop playing and take a break is once I got the Habitat and the fabricator up (after wandering for nearly an hour trying to find the needed Gases) I got to the next stage, now, the biggest problem here is, not only do you need to haul around a good handful of Barrels, but the barrels can only hold 100 units of a single gas, but, the Rubber and Plastics require 50 units of said gasses for one peice, and you need alot of rubber and plastics to progress, on the outside that seems okay to someone who hasn't played, but when you're like me and have to travel 1.4km and traverse 2 Giant Worm spawns just for clorine, it really begins to♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, I so badly want to continue but it's extremely tedious and painful I just don't want to dedicate that much time finding the resources to build a dozen barrels, travel upwards of 1.4km for a barrel of gas that's only good for two bits of plastic/rubber, especially when you need alot of plastics and rubber. (another thing to note, is you may end up running out of water and food before you can even get to a point where you can sustain yourself, I only just got a fabricator and I'm on my last canister of water)
Apart from that, the game is fun and you can lose an hour pretty easily on it, the only thing I really want to see changed is the storm frequency and/or length and the consumption of precious rare gases, seriously, 50 units for one bit of rubber is a bit rich if you ask me, especially when you have to dedicate alot of time to go collect said gas, but if you like Subnautica or Ark: Survival Evolved, I recomend this game, it just needs some tweaks (and a bit of optimization)
What you get for the price is pretty good, it's a small game in regards to file size as well which is a plus.
Another thing I want to add is, the game does need some graphical tweaks and more graphics options, one thing that bugs me every now and then is that weird glitch effect, sometimesit freezes the game for a second or two, and the framerate fluxuates constantly.
On the mechanical side, Movement is very slow and painful, stamina recharge is very slow and kind of irritating, but it works, not really an issue, just annoying sometimes, I also tend to find myself getting stuck on the terrain sometimes, which is quite irritating.
and finally, the sound design is very very nice, though the Combat Music tends to play when it doesn't need to and it's quite annoying, I don't know if I'm about to get killed or if it's just the game playing the BGM for no reason.
Anyway, in the games current state, I'd probably rate it a rough 6.5/10, if they just fixed the two main issue I brought up with the resources and the weather, it'll deffinately be a solid 8 or 9/10 in my books.
Quick edit: if they even just change the Gas consumption from 50 to 25, it'll make it much more manageable, so instead of 2 uses, it'll have 4.

I wasn't really into strategy games until I stumbled upon this game. After watching a few YouTubers play this game, I was convinced that it would be a barrel of fun, and I was right.
Now, HOI4 can either be one of two things: a WWII simulation strategy game or a casual strategy game with mods enabled. Mods such as Millenium Dawn: Modern Day Mod add an extra level of replay value, as you're able to play in either 2000 or 2016 as any country you like.
The base game offers a way of learning how to micro-manage, a skill that must be mastered in order to be a real strategic gamer. The detail in HOI4 is fantastic, as you have to take into account different terrains, the types of troops you're deploying and the resources and supplies available to you.
Multiplayer lobbies offer a way to communicate with other players (countries) in order to win the war. This is a wonderful example of where TeamSpeak or Discord comes in handy, as most lobbies ask you to join such sessions in order to communicate via VOIP. This also paves way for serious, hardcore players, who try to either stick to a realistic scenario or go mad for fun.
Hearts of Iron IV rekindled my interest in the Second World War, ranging from the different battles in different environments, to the weaponry and the failures of both the Allies and the Axis. I for one did not know too much about the collapse of the British Empire. Being British, that is a bit silly. I did go on to learn more about the role of the Crown rule of India and how they contributed to the war, reading about various subjects like these during a game's progress.
I think that HOI4 will go down as one of the all-time great strategy games.

Another classic example of Paradox's trying to be fancy and end up with a broken, frustrating experience. And yet, their fanbase will defend them insistently. Apparently, "The player is playing it wrong" is a sufficient excuse for anything that Paradox does wrong.
The peace conference system allows other countries, that are not your allies, to take significant amount of the territory that you conquered, even if that other country was getting crushed the entire time without your involvement. I took over half of Africa and all of Middle east in one war, and Italy magically takes all of Africa and half of Middle east despite virtually zero involvement on the Africa front. It even allows countries that literally did nothing other than suiciding random low-cost ships into the enemy (i.e. zero land unit used) to take lands that you have a core on, just because they decide to declare war on the losing faction in the last second.
The auto-revolt supression system is completely broken if it involves islands. The units will constantly move between the islands, leaving the most of the land in a constant state of revolt.
The whole battle plan system, a key new element to IV, only works when used on a very small scale. It requires tiny border connection or using far more troops than necessary. In other words, work fine when you are in Europe, doesn't work at all anywhere else.  Troops will randomly move around instead of defending key position (positions that if undefended, will cause supply to be cut off). Just for transparency, I'll start off by saying that I was somebody who preordered this game. Furthermore, I posess a level of intelligence that allows me to (brace yourself) research something a bit more than what news articles say about a game. This allowed me to avoid frothing at the mouth and enjoy myself a ton when the game initially came out.
When this game first came out, there wasn't a ton wrong with it. Sure there were balance issues (and those still do exist today) but for the most part it was a fresh concept for a game with plenty of depth and complexity to reward people who wanted something to learn and get good at, and boy oh boy was it good when you understood a character. However, I'm guessing 2K didn't pay the Media Bill and, despite the "DLC" being all purely cosmetic at the time, the game was basically universally panned for having $60 worth of DLC and crap. See, to me, because I understand that skins are completely unimportant in a game like this where basically nobody will ever really pay attention to what you look like because it's a first person game where you don't have a moment to lose when chasing the monster, this wasn't really worth getting upset about. Alas, the various gaming news websites had done the damage. In addition to that, people who joined the game made by Left 4 Dead devs had bailed upon realizing this game required more working together than they were used to and, rather than adapt, gave up and moved on.
As a result, the game was dead within a few months, making it just another in the list of casualties of poor management decisions. To make matters worse, the geniuses at 2K games decided that, to recoup losses, when it came to actual content DLC, they made not one, but TWO season passes. Brilliant, right?
Basically, the story of Evolve is the tale of the developers wanting to create a more challenging and competitive experience while the publishers screwed them over from behind the scenes.
Since this nice revival, there've been a few major changes. First off, and probably best of all, they've significantly reduced the stress on the trapper by making the dome a universal ability by all characters. This in addition to the new Planet Scanner makes for more engaging gameplay rather than a 20 minute long match of hide and seek. In addition, the monster has been upgraded to be able to handle itself a bit better at stage 1 rather than being instantly destroyed upon being found.
Now, there were some modes removed, but I feel like that's not a permanent change. For now, while the game is back and the developers are getting a lot more data based on how people are playing, it's a good idea to keep the community all doing the same thing for now and slowly rerelease the game modes in time, ensuring they catch any balance issues as soon as possible, rather than having an uneven distribution of popularity between multiple game modes and yielding skewed data.
All in all, give it a shot and don't get disheartened if you do poorly. You'll learn, you'll improve and with you, so will the game as a whole for everyone who plays.
P.S. I'm not even slightly buthurt about my progress being reset. I'd rather everybody start off on a level playing field than have new players bail because all of the veterans have everything new and shiny all the time.

Oh man, the feels. I wasn't ready for this one. It really hit too close to home. It's a visual novel with an incredible aesthetic, it's just a beautiful way to spend a few hours. The sound design is great and immersive, the sound really adds to the pacing of the story. And remember to take the time to finish the epilogue too. It's cathartic after the emotional wringer you've just been put through.

Three Fourths Home is an interactive visual novel starring Kelly, a 24 year-old woman who has gone back to her estranged family after several problems in her life: her mother is worried about her but also still feels betrayed by Kelly's past actions, her father lost part of a leg in an accident at work and now drinks when the pain is unbearable while her brother Ben is a shut-in with who still blames her for leaving.
One morning Kelly decides to visit an old barn that belonged to her father and, on the way back, starts having an heart-to-heart phone conversation with her family about their life and her past: a storm starts brewing in and gets worse as you drive home.
-remarkable art style
-well-written and emotional story
-great dialogue
-interesting and deep characters
-good pacing, it starts a bit slow but soon things speed up as the weather gets worse
-great soundtrack
-solid sound design
-once you finish the game and epilogue you'll have an Extra section with the whole soundtrack, a few fiction stories written by Kelly's brother and a photo project: they're all very interesting (if you "complete" the whole Extras section you'll also be presented with an extra game scene that fleshes out the story)
-provides ample food for thought when played by its target audience
-the lack of voice acting slightly lessens the emotional impact
-short at 45ish minutes for the main game plus 15 for the epilogue
-limited replay value
Three Fourths Home was truly an outstanding experience for me, it started out a bit slow but as the minutes went by it was easy to connect with Kelly's problems and fears and here lies the game's greatest strength: through its impressive story and storytelling it not only tells a great tale but will also give you quite a few things to think about in regards to life choices, missed chances and how one deals with family relationships.
Even if you're not looking for some intellectual nourishment Three Fourths Home sports a story strong enough to be considered a good purchase even if you only take it at face value: the ending was pretty tense and somewhat of a punch in the gut with the powerful epilogue section being equally strong and emotional.
All things considered you might be, at first, slightly disappointed with the level of interactivity you're given since it all boils down to making a few choices during the dialogue but picking different answers will actually not only give the dialogue itself a different nuance but also shed light on different sides of a character's feelings or a life event. Having said this there's no denying that the dialogue will flow forward on the same path regardless of your choices so here's why the replay value is limited.
Three Fourths Home is a great visual novel with excellent story and writing: a cursory look at online reviews will show you that quite a few people were left pondering on how the story tied with their life long after they stopped playing and this should tell you plenty about its quality. Depending on how much you value "artsy" games and novels it might be overpriced for what it does but if you see it on sale or, like me, in a bundle pick it up, you won't be disappointed.

Вы любите тактические игры ? Любите посидеть и поразмышлять о своих действиях, придумать какой нибудь план для победы над врагами ? Если да -  эта игра не для вас. Бюро представляли как тактический экшен, но самой тактики там кот наплакал, да же на самой высшей сложности игра не заставляет тактически думать, всего по одной причине - тут самые идиотские напарники! Им плевать что вы отдаёте им приказы, им нужно лишь несколько вещей - Высовыватся из укрытия, когда по ним стреляет куча врагов; Стоять на одном месте и пялится в прилетевшую гранату; Выбегать на босса с криками "ВАААААГХ" и пасть смертью храбрых за несколько секунд. Если бы игра не позиционировалась как тактический экшен, я бы не так сильно обращал на это внимание. На удивление, враги действительно умно себя ведут, действуют сообща, закидывают гранатами (Ваши напарники даже этого делать не умеют) и обходят с фланга. Геймплейно игра превращается в обычный шутан, аля Gears of War, где всю каманду тащит на себе игрок. На тяжелом уровне сложности, пока не появятся мощные способности - это просто мука. Во всем остальном игра хороша - отличнейшая графика; хороший саундтрек; и отличнейший сюжет и атмосфера. Очень правильно разработчики выбрали время действия игры - редко нам дадут поубивать пришельцев в 60-е года. Что касается сюжета, он никак не удивлял практически до самого конца игры, но то что я увидел под конец, действительно очень и очень сильно порадовало.
Рекомендую всем ознакомиться с игрой, только не ждите тактики от неё и все будет хорошо ;)

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a great combination of XCOM and Mass Effect franchise. You play William Carter member of secret government organisation (The Bureau) which is fighting aginst the extraterrestrials threat in 1962. The game is a tactical TPS game and has also RPG elements. On missions the playable character has 2 AI controlled fellow agents. You and your agents get XP points by defeating enemies and completing missions; having enough XP ponits you level up and new perks become available to use in the combat. During mission you can obtain alien technology to improve your weapon and backpack arsenal. There are major and minor operations and you can unlock dispatch missions by completing investigations in the secret XCOM base. Williiam Carter has the special ability "Battle Focus" that slows time down and allow him to order other 2 agents to do actions like placing mine, deploying shiled sphere etc. At level 9 you can control your enemies' mind turning them against its race. You must use your enviroment for survival, and the enviroment can be your ally if you use it wisely! You can recruit new agents as well as retire max level agents. I recommend everybody who likes TPS games not gunblazing style. I really enjoyed playing it 8,3/10.

A cute and fun adventure game for someone looking for something a little different.
Graphics: 10/10. Everything looks absolutely gorgeous.
Sounds: 8/10. Solid sound effects, pleasant to listen to and add to the ambience.
Music: 10/10. Calm, relaxing, and fits the carefree adventerous spirit of the game.
Story: 9/10. A pretty good story overall; I don't want to spoil anything though. The characters have a good bit of personality, and you can find items with random bits of lore attached to them all over.
Gameplay: 8/10. A solid core of exploration, and the spirit wrangling minigame is pretty fun. Somewhat gameplay-light, but it fits the game well. My only real complaint is that the white flowers you collect don't really do all that much... you can turn them into keys (rendered obsolete as soon as you get the Skeleton Key, which you can do pretty early), sell them for money, or gamble them for a potentially larger amount of money. I was kind of hoping that they'd do more than that.
Overall: 10/10. A short game, but a really fun one.
A quick note: While the game is mostly kid-friendly, there are a few moments of subtly racy humor here and there. It's nothing a kid would really get though, so it's probably not a major worry.

All in all, a good game. Pick it up cheap if you can as once you've finished it, there's not much calling you back to play it again.

First off, I did get this on sale at $5, but I loved it so much I purchased a second copy for my sister.
Lili is a wonderful litle game, I gotta say. The art style is fantastic, everything looks so vibrant and full of life. That's actually the main reason I bought it. However, the fantastic scenery isn't the best part. Lili's cast of characters are quirky and unique, all with plenty of soul about them. There wasn't every a single time when I could say I was bored with this game.
Now, that being said, the developers did say it was originally going to be a tablet game, and you can tell. While that is by no means a bad thing, it may throw some people off.
Another thing is, holy moly, the music is fantastic. Each zone has its own original track that plays throughout that just sounds wonderful, in addition to a few other tracks you'll hear when fighting a boss or entering a room.
Each zone is crafted in such a way that is unique from the others, but still fits the over all feel of the game, filled with its own "Constructs" (the wooden robot like inhabitants of Geos) that all have things they need help with, and with malicious spirits that need a good clobbering.
One thing I will say, and this may be a negative to some, and a positive to others, but this game is incredibly easy, once you have the controls down. Like I said, it was originally supposed to be a mobile phone/tablet game, so it takes a bit of getting used to on keyboard and mouse, I'm not sure how it feels on controllers. It gets especially easy with the addition of power ups and items.
One final thing as well, the game can run very well even on older systems. I purchased a copy for my sister as well as myself, and her gameplay looked identical to mine, and she's using a 9 year old Nvidia GTS250 graphics card and an Intel G3258 processor, and she had no issues at max settings. So, props to the developers for optimizing their game so well.

The story is good and there are two endings you can trigger based on a moral decision (this is extremely obvious at the time).
I was also really impressed by the graphics and performance. A small title usually has a certain indie feel, but other than the length of this game I would totally believe it was from a AAA developer.
The puzzles are relatively simple, not getting any harder than what you'd find in Portal 1, and there's a few secrets to discover which expand on the story as well as giving you access to a couple of harder puzzles.
Overall, I would definitely recommend to anyone who is even a moderate fan of puzzlers and I think £14.99 is reasonably, but definitely work picking up in a sale.

This game is generally a great experience. It's a game about sneaking into your neighbor's house, and trying to figure out what's in his basement. Although it can be challenging at times, it's always fun planning your next move and hiding from the neighbor. The A.I. allows the neighbor to remember your moves, and he may board up a window or place a beartrap in your usual path. This keeps you on your toes at all times. In this game, there are 3 acts. The first one has a rather small house, but is still very fun. The basement has a large puzzle element to it. After completing that, you get into the second act, which is the same house with some extra things in it. You have 3 ways to complete Act 2: Finding the red key, bouncing on a trampoline, or getting a crowbar. Each escape ends in you running to your house, which triggers Act 3. The third act is very similar to the Beta 3 version of the game, but the major difference is the basement, which is similar to a broken-down version of the Act 1 basement. I won't spoil past then, but I must admit that this is one of the best games I have ever played!
