Ah Rift. A great game I actually loved playing until the horrible pings attacked. when the NA players go online, my connection goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥ But that was long ago.
But enough of that. Here's the crackdown.
Good:
- Fun. While being a F2P MMO, this can definitely be played at your own pace. The fun from portal and the invasions will keep you from getting bored.
- Great skill system. The skill system where you can have backups and just switch is very nifty. It's like having multiple characters without relogging. They can also be reset for cheap so experiment all you want.
- Less multiplayer pressure. One of the most frustrating part of an MMO is that at some parts, it wil require you to play with more people. While still existent, it is not a requirement.
- Great multiplayer system. In addition to fun, this game offers a lot of things to do! Free roam is definitely one of them but there are ones where you are teleported to random places with random people and given random quests. The dungeon system and party system are top notch so you will have no problems from the get-go.
- Easy to play. Without the end game technicalities and PvP considerations, this game is easy to learn and the system is designed to make it so.
- Good people.
Ugly:
- The servers. (that maybe fixed now)
- Ugly people.
Last words:
So if you just want to spend some free time and/or escape from stress, this is a good game to play.

A decent squad based third person shooter. Nothing more. The Bureau brings nothing new to the table but is still mostly enjoyable. The 60's style is done very well, even though the sci-fi elements detract from the experience at times making it feel like a 90's or even 00's game. It doesn't mix the settings properly I guess.
The graphics are solid, nothing special, but not bad either. They get the job done, like most games. Same goes for the voice acting. The effects on the other hand are done very well.
The gameplay itself is hit and miss. There's no research to be done, so if you pick up an alien's weapon you can fire it right away. It's something I missed, especially after playing last year's Xcom. There are mini missions to be completed and agents can be sent on different missions to level up and gather gear. Those missions can not be played so it basically comes down to selecting which agents you want to go.
Each agent has abilities that can be unlocked by leveling up. They're all fun to use and there's plenty of variation to mix things up during battle.
The battles play out in real time and with the press of a button time can be slowed down to make more tactical choices. Later on you'll have no choice but to use it as more and tougher enemies will be deployed. Without it you'll have a pretty hard time, let me tell you.
Also, If you're agents are down you'll have a certain amount of time to help them up. If you don't help them in time they'll die and you'll lose them forever. So it's important that you work together and manage them in the best way you can to prevent them from dying. Near the end of the game this becomes much less important because your other agents will be around level 4 or 5 already.
The Bureau is actually pretty lenghty. I finished it in about 14-15 hours on Veteran so I guess it can be completed in roughly 13 hours or so, if you stay alive the entire time. That's actually pretty decent in an age where most action (adventure) games can be completed within 7-8 hours.
If I had to rate The Bureau I'd give it a 7/10. It's frustrating at times, but fun enough to play and finish. The only issue here is the price, because even though there's plenty of content the game itself just isn't fun enough to pay full price.

Definitely the most fun strategy game I've ever played, and I don't even like strategy games.
Learning to play the game is a daunting process. The game spouts off a bunch of random fake mythical names, and throws you into the game with nothing but a tutorial that essentially does the first bit of the game for you.
Despite this, once you learn to play the game, it's really fun.
You play as a tribe in a country filled with a bunch of other tribes. The gameplay is mostly text-based, so don't expect an RTS or 4X game. It sounds fairly boring, and it would be, if the game didn't include a huge variety of gods, and loads of monsters and creatures to destroy/steal/cower in fear from.
The gods aren't the boring kind of gods, either. You can basically bribe them to do certain things, like create an earthquake, destroy another tribes farmland, and make your warriors stronger. There are also magical artifacts you can find, which usually help you hugely in battle.
The game does have a lot of reading involved, and the gameplay is overwhelming when you're starting off.

King of Dragon Pass is a text-heavy strategy and simulation game about leading your clan out of the Dark Ages, and into to fame and riches. If you don’t enjoy large blocks of text, this isn’t the game for you, but under that text there is a huge amount of lore to delve into including a whole pantheon of gods, and the scope of the actual game is equally deep. The primary form of currency is cattle, but because the game relies heavily on the barter system you will likely be trading quite a bit with neighboring clans. Will your leadership stand the test of time and bring prosperity? Or will the gods turn a blind eye to your efforts? For the clan’s consideration, I present: King of Dragon Pass.
As the game begins you will learn a fair bit about that lore of this world, as well as make decisions that will effect your disposition toward the different tribes and races. Do your ancestors believe in slavery? Free work is always nice, but if your slave pens are empty your clan magic will suffer. How did they feel towards dragons or trolls? Are they peaceful or warlike? The range of possibilities offering an extremely vast gaming experience that is fun to tinker with. Members of your council ring tend to remind you of your history, and keeping in line with your ancestors’ decisions will make more magic available to be spent during the Sacred Time on a number of buffs for war, trade, crops, and more.
In addition to what is spent during sacred time, cattle can be sacrificed in order to learn the blessings of the gods. Building a shrine will make the blessing permanent, but also require a number of goods and cattle for annual upkeep. Offering new temples will encourage other clans to visit, possibly forming new alliances. Once the alliance is strong enough, you might even begin negotiations to form a tribe. Approaching each clan and haggling agreeable terms is difficult, and you still might not be elected the king of the clan you created. Politics is a fantastically elaborate quilt of petty arguments and disagreements, and King of Dragon Pass showcases this beautifully.
King of Dragon Pass is an absolute pleasure to sit down with, easily absorbing me for hours at a time. The mouse-based controls and underwhelming sound effects seem to stain what is otherwise a fantastically constructed game, but both are easily overlooked for the variety of likeable music and superb writing. I understand this game is a phone port, but it translates much better than something more action-based. It took me about 6 or 7 hours of gameplay to ever see a random event twice. For a mobile port, I think the price is high but for the amount of content offered it isn’t a bad exchange for fantasy-lovers who appreciate a good read. I applaud A#(A-Sharp) and Herocraft, and hope to see more quite soon.

King of Dragon Pass is a great and very unique game, and I highly recommend it (but not the Steam version) to anyone. Hoping to replay it some more with the added bonus of achievements, and support for modern resolutions, I recently bought a second copy from Steam.
Unfortunately, I quickly realized that this version is in many ways a downgrade, based on a mobile port that was then ported back to PC. In the transition, some features and a lot of the charm of the original were sadly lost. This includes more superficial changes, such as the removal of the magic stone showing current blessings (which was replaced with boring tables) and the graphical village overview (replaced with dry text), but also the conversion of the UI to mobile conventions (e.g. no mousewheel scrolling). Even some gameplay features were also axed, such as manual control over your crafters, which limits available strategies.
Perhaps the most drastic change, though, is the removal of manual saving and loading of game states. While some may welcome this equivalent to other games' "hardcore" modes, losing the ability to switch between clans will be painful - especially as you are bound to grow fond of them after watching over their fates for many hours. This was in fact one of the first issues I noticed, as I intended to import some older saves into the game.
Ultimately, this purchase was a big disappointment for me, and I plan to refund it. I was hopeful for the new version of this classic, but it turns out that the original remains the unsurpassed Dragon Pass experience.

I actually first heard about this game by stumbling upon the devs Kickstarter for their second game, To Azimuth. I backed it just for the game because it looked interesting, but it didn't make it. After playing this game, it's a bigger shame that it failed.
Three Fourths Homes lies more on the interactive fiction side of the adventure game spectrum so if you need to shoot things or stick a rubber duck onto a fishing pole than this isn't for you. Interactive fiction/narrative games live and die on the quality of their writing and I'd say the game delivers. You play as a young woman named Kelly who's returning to her family's farmhouse in Nebraska after not being in contact for some time while a large storm is brewing. Gameplay is simple you just keep driving by holding down a button while you make dialogue choices. Having to hold down a button might be annoying for some but I have to admit I actually stopped noticing that I was doing it and it sort of helped a bit to immerse me more.
Like Kentucky Route Zero and Walking Dead Season 1, the choices you make in the main game are more about shaping who Kelly is and her relationship with her family. The writing is also low key and manages to bring some real humanity and character to the cast that a lot of games struggle with. You get a good feeling for Kelly and her family and you grow to care. The atmosphere is also really good and at some points it can be quite haunting. The ending isn't unpredictable but the epilogue greatly enhances it, really tying together the themes of regret and decay that the game has in a strong way. The Epilogue is the best part of the game because of this and really helps the game to stick with you after its done.
Overall Three Fourths Home is powerful and to the point, a really nice first outing for a fledging dev. I hope the best for them and I'd be willing to back them again if they give To Azimuth another shot. If you like interactive fiction and/or narrative driven games Three Fourths Home is well worth your time and money.

Three Fourths Home: Extended Edition isn’t a game, or a sim, or a visual novel. It isn’t any of the things usually required for an item to be offered by Steam. But it is (in my opinion) two things less commonly found on Steam: a totally inclusive artistic experience, and a detailed work by a writer bursting to express themselves through an emotional outlet involving the player.
It’s an account of a young woman, Kelly, early 20s, talking on the phone to her parents and younger brother, Ben, as she attempts to drive home in the midst of a Nebraska storm, tornado approaching. It’s a family, like any other, with a great deal of love, and lots of issues. It’s very difficult to say much without saying too much, so this will be an unusually short review, with fewer details.
This is the story of a search for self by all participants; characters, players and writer/developer, in no set priority that I can determine. The characters could be kinder toward each other, but in how many families is that generally the case? Everyone in this family has lost something, and throughout, they struggle to regain, or accept the changes that come with loss. Much is expressed through hints and subtle emotion and comments, since only the player is in the dark, and learns certain things through the dialog choices they select during the long conversation over the phone. The existing storm and the approaching tornado add a sense of inevitability, a feeling of the foolishness of man to focus on the minutia of our lives. This game is largely about aspects that may seem petty, but in reality are the very things that consume nearly every moment of our existence. Perhaps ultimately this is about the attempts all humans make to discover themselves through their attempts to discover each other.
One very simple choice I made in this game was so utterly tragic and heartbreaking that I nearly stopped “playing”, for fear continuing would taint the developers intent. I’m very glad I didn’t
Some hints to enjoy this game more completely
Examine the menu option for the game controls. Some are simply there to add a sense of heightened reality. One that I sorely wish I’d known of is the control for playing music in Kelly’s car. The music in this game is one of its strongest features (and that is saying a GREAT deal.) While the music would have added to my game enjoyment, I listen to the music by itself, and enjoy it immensely. Not just the music, but the sounds of the weather add much to the story. Headphones are a strong consideration. (The text is all silent, read from the screen.)
At no point assume this story is over (attempting to exit the game emphasizes this.) Perhaps the presence of achievements, ordinarily a distraction in such a game, may actually serve the purpose of indicating completeness more than accomplishment. Do NOT miss Kelly’s photo essay. And by NO means skip over Ben’s stories. I only hope that some day a game is developed based entirely on these, and similar, atmospheric short stories.
While comparisons to other games, such as Journal, To the Moon or Kentucky Route Zero might be made, this game is far more immersive and artistic than those. Perhaps more than any game that will come along any time soon. If you want to learn something about people and families, and perhaps even something about yourself with a game that does have some degree of replayability, Three Fourths Home is quite possibly the game for you.

Okay, so I made a short and sweet review on this before, but I now realize that doing so is very unfair to what this game is, what it means to be, and how it does it, so here's a proper review.
My overview will proceed incase you don't want to read the rest:
• Beautiful, captivating story that will make you genuinely feel for the main character, Niko.
• Amazing soundtrack that is oddly so good, that I didn't mind leaving the game idle and doing other things to listen to that background music.
• A cute art style for some cutscenes here and there that really fits the theme.
• Gameplay, while simplistic, is alluring enough to keep you ensnared into the rest of the game.
--------------------------------------------
Now though, for the nitty-gritty.
Story: 9/10
I don't believe many things should be considered perfect, and this game is surely no exception. While I really loved the story, and the direction it went in, there were a few predictable moments that you might see coming from a mile away. That's not to say the rest of the content suffers at all, though. In OneShot, the story feels like the driving force for the rest of the game. Being given a vague objective is one thing, but having the atmosphere, the surroundings about you dragging you in for the ride that is the rest of the game, is what OneShot accomplishes, and it accomplishes it way too well.
Gameplay: 8/10
Not much to say here, as it's pretty straight-forward. It's a simple, puzzle-driven type of game, and so the gameplay is hard to find flaw in, and with that, no flaws stuck out to me in the slightest. The game plays as you would expect a game such as this to play, and has occasional moments that will surprise you for sure. Expect to play in Windowed, Fullscreen will make things a bit harder to manage.
Soundtrack: 10/10
I will allow an exception to my prior comment about perfection, as this is where the game truly stands out. Every second, every moment that you play this game, the music- or lack thereof-- will set a lot of the mood. Feeling as you talk to someone and know something they don't, as the music suddenly goes quiet creates a mood that no other dialogue sequence ever could. Feeling the tension as music gets more dramatic, or at ease as you explore a peaceful meadow to relaxing music, OneShot never disappoints in this respect. I loved every second of every song placed into the game.
Art Style: 8/10
A majority of the game is played in the 2D space, where you can move up and down, left and right. Along with that, its art for most of that is pixels. While this isn't a bad thing by any stretch, the beautiful art is restricted to what such an art style can provide, so when cutscenes occur, and you can see the more detailed artwork, it stands out, and in nothing but a good way at that. You won't be disappointed in the slightest by this.

This was a very interesting interactive novel in my opinion. It handled the topic at hand with surprising delicacy. The main game is basically Kelly, the protagonist, basically visiting her grandfathers home in the country when the weather turns bad, so she heads home. She and her mom start talking on the phone, and in the midst of the conversation, it is revealed that one or more tornadoes are going to be touching down in the area. So, Kelly must try to get to the safety of home. All the while, she is chatting with her mom, and later with her dad and her brother Ben as well.
It is obvious that she has been estranged from her family and has recently come back to live with them, which has resulted in conflicted feelings and a lot of trying to regain the relationships she once shared.
I wont reveal the ending, but it was both ambiguous and obvious (funny how that works). Through the game, you are basically driving home as mentioned before, and the only knock I have is that you actually have to hold down the D key or (on a gamepad) and trigger.....the entire game, which is annoying. Outside of that however, I thought it was a fairly seamless experience. The dialogue was interesting and the interactions felt real.
There is an epilogue, and this is really where the variant choices and decision come into play (as was highlighted on the product page via the current first page curation (800+ variations). they all take place in the epilogue, and without revealing the actual content (as it would also serve as a spoiler for the main game), I will just say that this was at least as interesting as the main game.
The extras were all cool as well. Ben's stories were all well written and fun to read. Kelly's photo class final was fun to look at, and the soundtrack was excellent.
I give this eight snapshots of a tornado out of ten possible before getting sucked into it because you got waaaaayyyyy too close.

It's not *bad* but it's also not good enough to recommend, especially with so many significantly better story-driven games available (Kentucky Route Zero, 199X, To The Moon, and the Moon Sliver are the ones that come immediately to mind). The story is ultimately unsatisfying, as it leaves far too much left open to speculation and interpretation. A little ambiguity is nice, but this much just feels empty. Plus, as others have mentioned, having to hold the "d" key down is unnecessary and annoying, and the text in the main game is eye-straining. If you absolutely love artsy games and have already played all the other options, then it's worthwhile, but for most people it's likely to leave you unsatisfied.

Short but relatively sweet, The Turing Test offers 70+ puzzles and, in my opinion, quite an engaging and thought-provoking story. Although it might not bring as much challenge as other puzzlers out there, mostly due to a lack of variation between solutions to the game's puzzles, I didn't find it to be as boring as others have claimed.
The game looks visually stunning too but the sci-fi setting is really just reserved for the small areas in between chapters, the actual sectors (test chambers) themselves are quite plain but still keep with the overall aesthetic. I personally thought the story and its conclusion was quite satisfying, though nothing ground-breaking. There was also a lot of lore and additional story left up to the player to absorb, but I feel missing this could make the main story come off as a bit shallow.
Would I recommend this game? Yeah, sure. It might not be the best puzzler out there, but it's unique enough to be something most puzzle fans should enjoy. (I must admit £15 for a 5-6 hour game with little replay value is kinda steep however. Maybe wait for a sale if you're still on the fence.)

Visually, The Turing Test is stunning. The animations are smooth, the textures are high-quality, and the atmosphere is spot-on. The OST is absolutely perfect, and had me a little jumpy as a compliment to the atmosphere, though the game itself is not scary at all. It ran smooth as silk with no noticeable framerate drops. My only complaint is that the puzzles are too easy. A good portion of the levels feel like an extended tutorial with only a handful of options available which ultimately narrows down the solution to a simple step-by-step guide. Only a couple of puzzles really stumped me, but after sitting back to think for a couple of minutes, it was easy to solve them.
Where the game really shines though, is in the story department, and the lack of challenging puzzles do make it easier to experience the story. There's a semi-predictable twist, but the story makes you think, and perhaps question your judgement if you weren't 100% convinced before. I enjoyed the extra element added to the puzzles as a result of the story, and sorta wished there were more challenging puzzles to do with that dynamic. However, the game ends up being short and worth a playthrough if you're interested.
I think, if
first-person puzzle games (such as Portal, The Talos Principle, The Witness, etc) didn't exist, The Turing Test would shine, but don't discredit it without giving it a chance.

A moderately fun dogfighting and bombing game. Moderately recommended.
If you're playing with Mouse+KB, the game supposedly offers 3 types of control - Casual, Arcade and Simulation. In reality, Arcade and Simulation are completely worthless as they'll just have you spinning out of control the moment you try to turn towards the enemy. And even Casual is a bit too wonky. On the other hand, pure keyboard controls are decent, so I play with those.
You get to play a campaign with various types of missions. Despite the name, this game offers lots of different targets and objectives, not just dogfighting. You'll be shooting at bombers, submarines, boats, ships, anti-air emplacements, V-1 rockets, V-1 launch sites, tanks and other vehicles, fighters on the ground, fighters during takeoff, kamikazes, bridges, various other buildings, and mountain cannons. Well, you won't actually be shooting at most of those, you'll be launching rockets or dropping bombs or deploying torpedoes.
Bombing is actually the most fun part of the game. It's much more enjoyable to attack ground targets and ships than to dogfight. So it's a good thing that about half the campaign consists of not-dogfighting. There's also a stealth-ish mission and a bunch of times when you have to land, often in challenging conditions.
Now, as to why dogfighting isn't particularly fun. The controls. See, whenever you try to shoot at a target in the air, the game insists on trying to auto-aim. Except it always auto-aims you to the side of what you're shooting at. So you constantly have to fight the controls to actually aim at the target. It's not fun. At all. Shooting at ground and sea targets doesn't trigger the auto-aim, so it's fun. I think you can disable auto-aim by playing in Simulation mode, but that makes the plane near impossible to control anyway, so I can't tell.
This all culminates in an ultra annoying mission where you have to shoot V-1s flying towards London before they hit. Yeah, good luck with that.
Meanwhile, enemy planes aren't affected by this. They gracefully maneuver in a way the player can't replicate and don't have impaired aiming.
It's also slightly disappointing that this is YET ANOTHER game set in WW2 where you only get to play as the Allies. In the campaign, that is. You can play with a few German and Japanese planes outside of it, in Deathmatch and Survival modes. But even so, the campaign is the main part of the game. Also, even when you get to fly a non-Allied machine in the campaign, you're still playing an Anglo-American pilot who's flying a captured fighter.

Hello Neighbor is um…er…interesting to say the least, with much less emphasis on horror elements than would be expected from all the preview videos people have been watching on Steam/YouTube for a number of months now. If you picture Pixar remaking The Burbs and replacing Tom Hanks with a kid as the protagonist, you’ll have at least a slight idea of what this game is like. The art style is great and the cheery color scheme and cartoony graphics make for a whimsical take on the creepy-suburban-neighbor-up-to-no-good theme.
Is it worth the $30? Absolutely not! Well, at least not in its current state as there are definitely some bugs and glitchy gameplay mechanics that need to be fixed.
Examples: achievements are broken and don’t unlock, or perhaps you need to go with one of the alpha builds on the beta tab under properties when right-clicking on the game in your library to get them to work – I’m just speculating on that; sometimes if you get too close to a door you need to eventually go through but can’t open just yet, it’s possible to throw an object that you need to make use of through the door, making it impossible to progress further unless you restart the act, of course that’s assuming that you haven’t already made use of that object and that you tossed it rather than using it when at the door, such as a key that unlocks the padlock on the door – good news here is that this shouldn’t happen too often, if at all, if you’re careful; occasionally, when attempting to make use of stacked objects to solve one of the game’s many environmental-based puzzles, the objects will tip over, which is expected, but the unexpected part is that you fall all of 5 or 10 feet to your death which normally only happens from much higher up.
Now for the core gameplay elements. Stealth is kind of a factor but like the horror aspect, largely takes a backseat to simply running for your life and narrowly avoiding ‘The Neighbor’ by jumping/climbing like a total freak to avoid him. Works sometimes, other times it doesn’t (you have infinite stamina, so that works, plus you can oddly climb ladders at about 378 mph even while holding stuff…that, um, works too but is more comical than anything). Stealth definitely seems like it should be more of a factor and he’ll find you more often than he should. Also, it seems odd that he’ll break windows in his own house to more quickly come after you. Unique you say, hecks yes, but odd…absolutely! I think that aspect alone will have many gamers scratching their heads. Then there are the puzzles. Many puzzles. Sooooo many puzzles that I quickly lost count. They’re environmental/physics based and largely involve box stacking but the reason for doing so/the objective of this is so complex and obscure at times that sadly many gamers will end up getting stuck and likely give up. The tediousness of figuring all this stuff out and where to get objects you need to progress is ultimately going to turn many gamers off from wanting to put more time in this game, even if they normally love exploring and figuring out challenging things in games. I personally love this aspect of the game but I feel that the devs definitely need to turn it down a notch in a future build if they want to attract more casual gamers to it. That and the asking price. Also, the vast majority of things you encounter in the game, most notably the weird pseudo flashbacks or vision quests into the neighbor’s past, or whatever you want to call them, largely make absolutely no sense whatsoever, most notably old-timey, semi articulated mannequins pushing carts through a grocery store that looks like something out of Beetlejuice….don’t even ask.
Despite all of its quirks and a number of buggy issues, I can’t help but like this game and it will be interesting to see the direction the devs take it in, perhaps some DLC or holiday themed updates.
UPDATE (12/15/17):
Now that I've managed to get past the hellish puzzles and broken areas of this game, finally completing it, I can assuredly proclaim, as many others have indicated, that the ending truly makes no sense whatsoever. It will be nice once the achievements work, though I almost dread going through it again. Still, I can't help but look forward to doing so.

For instance (MINOR SPOILERS), character A says "No, wait, I don't want to kill everyone, so I won't!" and then there is a major plotpoint and a few sub-missions when Character B freaks out because they think "OMG CHARACTER A IS GONNA KILL EVERYONE!" I almost feel like I have to defend this game because it has taken a beating in some circles.  It is not pure X-COM...it is more like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of XCOM and Mass Effect.  I really enjoyed it - and while it took awhile to get used to, I enjoyed the third-person combat aspects as well.
I didn't really dig running around the base doing story stuff - mostly because I feel compelled to check the whole base after every mission for changes or new background info or side-quest-things (some of which led me to bonus minor operations.)   I *did* enjoy the combat, the pacing of the game during missions, and the scaling up of both weapons and enemies.
There are some minor flaky/buggy type things, but nothing that was a pain or gamebreaking.
The single most annoying thing for how I play is the lack of a save feature.  I need to be able to save when I want and then leave - since the game is auto-save only, I had to resort to checkpoint checking...but you don't know how long until your next checkpoint, and you have to pull up the "Load Game" menu to determine how long since your *last* checkpoint.  When missions can seriously run 30-60 minutes, and you can spend significant time between missions in the base running around for no good reason - the lack of a save system really hurt the game, in my opinion.  The autosave is robust, and the checkpoints are fairly frequent - but it did not substitute for the standard "save game" function for my needs.
All in all - if you like the XCOM world and enjoy conspiracy theories and cold war-era backgrounds - this can be a great game for you.  If you aren't into either - you'll find an above average game with some minor flaws.  What you won't find is something near the caliber of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, or other similarly-priced $50 AAA games.
Enjoyable and entertaining: Yes
Worth the time taken to play: Yes
Worth the money to buy at full price: Probably not.
Do I regret my purchase dollars or playtime: Definitely not.
All told, I got this game for around $15 - so I was very happy with my purchase.  I would not buy it at $50, but I would buy at $25-30 or lower.

I tried to keep this short but it didn't work. Sorry. There's actually a lot to say about this game in which potato sisters travel through space with their fluffy space cat.
I wanted this game because it looked cute, and I'm a sucker for a fat cat. I vaguely assumed, from the cutesy character art, that it was a game aimed at a young audience; but like I said, fat cat. 200 hours later, I would not let a kid anywhere near this, and it's become one of my favorite games of all time. I know potato people (and their vegetable brethren and sistren) in space sounds bizarre to say the least, but don't let that put you off. This game is hilarious, wonderfully crafted, endearing as heck, and even manages to deliver some pretty solid cosmic horror.
I could write another review, easily as long as this one, just talking about how much I love the characters. Instead I'll only say Cassie and Fay are both best girl and I can't think of a single major character who isn't at least mildly interesting. I wouldn't have expected robust character development in a game about space-faring potato girls, but here we are.
The devs paid ridiculously close attention to every part of this game. The scenery is gorgeous and sometimes pretty trippy. The music is fantastic, too, and there is tons of it. Every chapter has a different theme for its space hub, ship bridge, planet exploration, and boss fights, and some chapters have different music than they normally would if you play the story a particular way.
Which brings me to another neat thing about this game. There's the main story, which branches in small, predetermined ways as you progress (almost every chapter is actually two chapters, with the game picking one each playthrough), and one major branch that's up to player choice. You'll also have a couple chances throughout to make smaller choices, which don't affect gameplay but change how a particular event plays out.
There's no NG+ or anything, but there's loads of replay value. For one thing, you can't see every chapter in a single playthrough. After you've played the tutorial once, you have the option to skip it entirely in every subsequent game, a small touch that blew my mind and I wish other games would include. In addition, after completing the main story once,
When I stumbled over it I was thrilled, because I absolutely wanted more. It took me back to playing Pokemon Silver for the first time as a kid and discovering there was a whole other chunk of game to play post-Elite Four.
All that being said, Holy Potatoes is not gonna be for everyone. Some of the systems are a touch clunky, and it can actually spike in difficulty really quickly if you're not diligent about weapon crafting. (My first playthrough, I got stomped repeatedly in the second galaxy until I figured out that I was not going to make a dent in a level 4 planet with level 2 weapons.) If turn-based combat gets on your nerves, you're probably not going to enjoy this, because there's a lot of it and it gets very repetitive. A couple chapters are a little weak in terms of objectives, compared to most of the story, but that's mainly because they really nailed most of it.
Also, it's one of those currently ubiquitous games packed full of pop culture references. This one is also stuffed to the limit with puns. If you're not delighted by the concept of encountering, for example, a stalk of celery named Kale-o Ren and his potato companion Tarth Tater, you might find yourself annoyed rather than charmed.
One last thing: I don't recommend playing this if you're so thin-skinned that things like one throwaway joke about gender being a social construct gets your testes frothing. It's hardly an ess-jay-dubya game, but both protagonists are girls and the game makes no secret of that, which I personally feel is one of the greatest things about it. YMMV.
In summary: I f cking adore this game. I bet you will too.

Painkiller can best be described as a flawed series. The original Painkiller game remains fun to this day and the sequel, Painkiller Overdose, is, although not quite as good as the original, still quite fun. Unfortunately, after Overdose, the series took a dramatic downfall with one lackluster game after another. Each of these were, although officially endorsed, technically fan-made expansions that continued to milk the original game engine well past its due.
Hell and Damnation should, for all intents and purposes, be considered the next true Painkiller game after Overdose. The series makes a triumphant return in this exciting and fast-paced romp through purgatory.
Is Painkiller Hell & Damnation a sequel? A remake? Well it is sort of both. While the story progression in its relationship to the first game is... foggy... that does not keep you from enjoying it. As a remake, many of the original Painkiller levels are back and better-looking than ever, models and textures are all redone in gruesome HD glory. As a sequel, many bold new levels are presented. These all feel nicely done and stay true to the Painkiller style, unlike the levels of many Painkiller sequels.
As gameplay goes, well there is plenty to love. If you like your games fast, violent, and loud, then you will surely not be disappointed here. the weapons all feel powerful and all serve their own purpose. No one weapon is truly 'better' than another, and you will find yourself using each of them in specific situations. The enemies are all unique, and you will learn that although this is a fast shooter that revolves around your reflexes, 'shooting it until it dies' is not always the best strategy for dealing with every foe.
On the negative side, this game is disappointingly short. I managed to beat the main campaign in only four hours on the "Nightmare" difficulty on my first playthrough, and I was hardly rushing. This is definitely one of those games where if you do not buy the DLC (which adds about twice as many levels) you will feel like you don't have the whole game. This is disappointing, but hardly the end of the world. Besides, although story-wise there is no replay value in the campaign, gameplay-wise there is plenty, and a given level will not stop being fun just because you've done it once.
To conclude, Painkiller Hell & Damnation is a game I absolutely recommend. I would also recommend the original Painkiller, it's expansion (Battle out of Hell), and Painkiller Overdose, but advise that you ignore the others in the series. If you like Doom, Wolfenstein, Serious Sam, Duke Nukem, or any other old school fast-paced FPS games, then you will like this one.

Three Fourths Home: Extended Edition is a character study. You learn about Kelly, her family, and the trials that have led to this place and time. Kelly is trying to get in home in the middle of a summer storm in Nebraska. While driving she is talking to first her mother and then the other members of her family. The interactive comes in the form of selecting how Kelly responds during the conversation.
If you are looking for a game with a lot of interactivity, this game is not for you. But I suspect anyone reading this would know that already. If the general descriptions of the game have piqued your interest, then the game is worth your time and money. With that said, make sure you play the second scenario (Kelly waiting for the bus in Minnesota) to get the full sense of the game. Also, the stories that are included as extras are worth your time as well.

Three Fourths Home is an interactive short story of sorts. The main story, as far as I can see, has but one ending no matter which dialogue choices you make: the "interactivity" besides picking your words is holding down a button to drive...while you read. The graphics were simplistic and didn't work that well in terms of the main story. The epilogue was done quite a bit better: it had multiple endings - some bad that end it early, one "good" ending, all equally bleak - and the graphics actually fit the emotional tone of the narrative. Furthermore, at least the epilogue showed you the main character, as opposed to the main story where all you see is a car going along a background, and all the characters are merely heard, not seen. They're expressive enough but some facial expression would have been nice to go with it.
You'll notice I spent two and a half hours on this game. That was the main story once, the epilogue four times, going through the extras (including letting the soundtrack run all the way through for an achievement,) and then a final cutscene. So to do absolutely everything, less than three hours. Full disclosure: I did receive a free copy of this game from the developer. Do I think it was worth the time I invested? Only partly. Some of it was good, the rest I did not find a very engaging story - it IS a character study, do not assume plot of any kind. Will it be worth the time AND money that YOU invest in it? Sorry, in my opinion, no.

This is part one of my launch-day play through.  (Part 2 is available on my same Youtube channel if you want to spoil it)
I have several complaints about this game..
(Be aware that reading this review does have minor spoilers)
First off, understand that even with the initial 10% discount, $7 USD is too much money for this kind of game.
Secondly, a big complaint is that I honestly think the choices you make likely matter not in the end as it seems that everyone is going to get the same or a very similar ending.
Third, I dont understand the point of needing to drive, of having controls for lights and a horn.  The lights and horn and zoom controls included offer absolutely ZERO SIGNIFICANCE in the game.
Fourth, Whats the point of needing to hold "D" down the entire story to drive?  Why not just make the car drive automatically and offer a pause option to the player if needed?  It's not like holding down the D button on your keyboard gives the game some great gameplay mechanics.  There is nothing to dodge, no reason to stop driving, slow down.  It's just making sure you hold down the D key to keep the story flowing along!  FOR AN HOUR!
Fifth, parts of the story make no sense at all.  Ben's story he tells his sister is "a cool story bro" but offers nothing to the main story's plot, makes no sense in the situation at all.  There's a massive rainstorm, tornadoes are risking the lives of everyone in the story, but Ben is going to tell her a 15 minute fantasy story he wrote about a mystical beast in a fantasy land?!?  Uhh, okay.
Sixth problem is that parts of the story also are awkward.  Options to have your star 24 year old female obsessing over the masturbation of her younger 16 year old brother while driving in a rain storm talking to her mother feels out of place, awkward, and 'forced'.. not natural.
Seventh problem.. Unsatisfying ending to say the least.  Why build up this much tension and require the player to read and hold down a D key for an hour for "that"?  WTF.  Garbage.
I like the writing, parts of it.  I like the theme of the game just fine.  But for $7, or over $6 at the current 10% off when I bought it... ehhh.  I just think it could have been done much, much better and for the price, we should probably get something besides this completely random, unsensical mess of a story.
If the game is 80% off, it might be a good value for the people who tend to like this kind of game, including myself.  Anything over an 80% off sale will likely leave you shaking your head and thinking exactly what I thought at the end.. "WTF".
Two thumbs down, as much as I want to like it, for all the reasons above and the fact that the negatives outweigh the postives.

Game froze mid-match and ended with me being forced to hard-reset my computer, which I didn't appreciate, so perhaps some technical problems may still be present.
All in all. I'll give it a thumbs up but would prefer a middle-ground between thumbs-up and thumbs-down option for this one. It's pretty fun for a couple of hours but quickly gets stale after a while, although I'm sure playing with friends would extend how long the game can remain fun, but with a lot of grinding involved for the other monsters/hunters weighing down on the game's ability to stay fresh consistently, I'd have to say give it a try, but don't expect to stay interested for too long.

This is one of those times when I really dislike the Good/Bad rating system Steam has, as Turing Test is one of those games that is neither good nor bad- it's in the middle. There are aspects which I thoroughly enjoyed, but it fell short of reaching its potential. Let's start with...
...Cons
- Too short. There are lost of puzzles but many of them can be solved relatively quickly so what seems to be a longish game really isn't.
- Too many simple puzzles. Whenever they introduce a new element you go through a few puzzles that teach that element to you. Fair enough, but this teaching period goes for too long. No more than two puzzles are needed to teach a mechanic.
- It *almost* said something interesting about free will. Scripts needed more fleshing out, more discussion, more... more.
Pros
- Art and lighting are spot on.
- While there were some ovrly simple puzzles- the last five were astonishingly easy to solve when they should have been incredibly difficult- I did have fun solving a large number of them.
- Voice acting is well done, so good marks for the actors and director.
There's one thing that could make the game *much* better.
Community. Maps.
It will extend the life of the game immensely and give the fans a chance to create the devilishly difficult maps that they really wanted out of this game but didn't get. It is one improvement that shouldn't take a huge amount of time to program but will make the appeal of the game much greater than it currently has. It worked for Portal 2, and it should work for Turing Test. If the editor is relatively simple to use I would be tempted to throw a few maps together.

Title: Dogfight 1942

Genre: Arcade Flight
General Impression
Dogfight 1942 is an arcade combat flight sim that looks and controls fine, even after several years since its release. The “main” game focuses on the Pacific Theatre of operations and I was disappointed to find that it is such a short experience without the inclusion of the DLCs. These mission packs (containing the African and Russian fronts) are a clear cash grab and they should have been part of the full retail game, which costs enough as it is. If this wasn’t a fun experience, I wouldn’t have recommend it at all. But it can provide you with detailed and pleasantly easy to master, flight mechanics. I had no difficulty running it on the mouse and keyboard layout and the game has Achievements at least. Perhaps some Trading Cards in a future DLC?
Strong Points
+ Nice graphics and sounds.
+ Steam Achievements.
Weak Points
- No Steam Trading Cards.
- DLCs should have been part of the main game.
Rating 10/10

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is for me, the surprise of the year. It received a slew of mediocre review scores which painted a pretty bleak picture. However, upon playing it myself, I have found the game to be incredibly enjoyable.
You are thrust into the shoes of William Carter --  an agent with a troubled past -- in the midst of an alien invasion. With the military essentially being wiped out and all communications jammed, it falls to the XCOM organisation to deal with the alien threat.
As an XCOM agent, you will spend much of your time in the undergound base: delegating mission assignments (where your fellow XCOM agents can gain experience), exploring, completing side missions and talking to the various personalities within the facility. Many comparisons have been made between the XCOM base and the Mass Effect Citadel, which I would say are apt.
When you're done with the base activites, you can head out into the field. Most of the time you may choose between minor (side) and major (main) operations. The minor operations are fun little deviations, providing insight into what the people of that region have been through. You may happen upon individuals who have been infected by the aliens (this renders them basically catatonic) or dismembered bodies  scattered thoughout.
In terms of gameplay, you lead two squadmates into battle, stopping (well, nearly stopping) time in order to provide them with orders. To me, it feels like Enemy Unknown, except in third person. Along with providing them orders, you level them up, allowing them to use new and varied powers. If you play it as a straight up shooter, neglecting to order your AI squadmates around, you may have a bad time. I believe this is where a lot of the negative attitudes towards the gameplay comes from. The AI needs direction or they will get themselves killed.
A typical encounter would see you approach the enemy, getting yourself into cover and your allies. Pausing time, surveying the battlefield then deciding how to proceed. Perhaps you make your sniper cloak, move around to flank the enemy, then hit them with a critical strike? Perhaps you have your engineer throw down a rocket turret, which you then lift above cover to rain hell upon your enemies? Each battle is varied, giving you a lot of strategic options. This is something that I loved about The Bureau: XCOM Declassified.
The story goes from somewhat generic to "Wow, this is batshit insane!" As I made my way through, I became more and more engaged, to the point where I couldn't put it down.
The game does have its problems, but they are minor. If you have any interest in the XCOM universe and tactical shooters, I highly suggest you give this game a shot. It may surprise you.
+Outstanding graphics and atmosphere.
+The story takes some time to warm up, but once it gets going, it is captivating.
+Great tactical battle interface. Ordering your allies around is pleasant and easy.
+Good sense of progression. As you advance through the story, you and your allies level up, becoming powerhouses capable of taking on the most menacing of enemies.
+The XCOM base and its personnel are well designed. It's nice to walk around talking to each of them and completing their side quests.
-Lip syncing at times is woeful.
-Voice acting can be hit or miss.
-On higher difficulties, grenade spam can be a problem.
-The AI are bullet magnets. If you do not tell them what to do (constantly), they will die.

Here's Lili, your main character. What's she doing on Geos? Looking for flowers. How'd she get here? Shrug. Why is she not surprised by these talking constructs that are literally made out of wood that she did not expect to find? Seen stranger, I guess.
All your motivitation for this game is: I told you to. The enemies are jerks, and they're mean so go beat them up for us so that they can be less jerks and we the little people can stop being bullied around. I know I don't have the playtime of other people, and I didn't play this from the start, or even that long ago. I started this 2 days ago, and I thought I'd write a review which will help someone who's browsing this gamemake their final decision.
This plays very similar to World of Warcraft, in terms of hotbar casting and movement etc. Nothing particularly revolutionary in todays gaming, you move, the camera turns with you, and you can change the angle of the camera if you so choose but it pretty stays behind you.
BUT there are other things in this game that set it apart from other games. mainly the Rift mechanic. Rifts are tears around the world map from another world, and when you lure it out (basically opening it) you have the task of closing it usually killing certain amounts of enemies, for rewards. These Rifts can range from fire, to water, to earth, even darkness. At a certain level in the game with large amounts of people you can participate in Nightmare Rifts, much larger Rifts with much stronger enemies, as you can imagine, resulting in much better rewards. All in all, with the option of making public groups for Rifts, this game can be team based with people you've never met before, or you if you have the chance, you can solo a Rift, but it can be difficult. With this game come the soul tree, your way of making your own class, this game doesnt have your bog standard Mage, Warrior, Rogue, Cleric, you can be a DPS mage or Healer warrior, a Support rogue, or if they don't take your fancy for 10 levels use the least objectional class, and when you can unlock a new soul slot, you can change and customise your tree, in whichever you see fit. Lots of customisability in this game for anyone who's ever wanted to try certain mizes of things in games. What do you have to lose? It's free!
- Everything in the game can earned, bought or traded.
- Premium currency can bought from other players for a fee of in game money.
- Lot's of customisation with the soul tree.
- Accessible to newcomers and veteran MMO players alike.
- Deep lore.
- Very in depth game, lots to do, including PVP and minion quests.
- Quests caaaan be a little dragged out.
- In game currency can be slow to start with, it may feel like a lot but it isn't when you look at the big picture.
- The auction house is available to everybody, but to create a bid you need to have loyalty points which come from purchasing gems or REX (premium currency) which isn't a deal breaker, you can still sell on the world channel or to the Rift store.
There are other reasons why you should play this game, such as the community and that it's better than most games these days, but hey, try it for yourself, what have you got to lose? It's free! Legitimately free to play at that, I've seen no evidence of P2W at all as everything can be got in this game one way or another. See for yourself.

And unlike The Talos Principle or The Portal the protagonist is a real person, with a real voice and one you empathize with the more you progress ingame. If you can grab the game at a steam sale rates I definitely recommend it.

Great premise and pretty setting, but too short, far too easy and definitely way too silly.
The puzzle part of this game is fairly straightforward, you make things happen to progress in the story - which in itself is certainly fun, but:
* four hours to complete... including enjoying the scenery, reading pads, listening to audio logs
* way too easy and repetetive, most puzzles are so obvious that you know what to do immediately after entering the arena
* silliness - a grand beginning of a story that leads player through unrealistic environment (Europa has lower gravity, no atmosphere, space stations won't be made of corridors) full of dumb ideas (utterly stupid premise of an immortality? give me a break...) to a rotten and annoying ending (hardly any meaning, "choice" doesn't matter)
Basically, if you want a puzzle game then go play (or replay) any of the Portals, Talos Principle, Project Temporality, (...) - anything else, this is plainly disappointing.
I was lured by an overally very positive score and while it wasn't a complete waste of time and money... we should set the bar for a good game much higher than this.

contra

I voted this game a YES, but there's a caveat - it is an Early Access title and that needs to be considered when you look at buying in.  The $25 you pay to buy into the game's early access period is to help fund the developers and you need to be aware that you will be restarting every day or two (or possibly every few hours).  You should be willing to submit bug reports and feature and gameplay ideas to help improve the final product.
This is shaping up to be a fantasictally interesting game with first person, third person playability.  The end goal is multiple planets with different features, single or multi-player missions, survival, construction, fighting or domesticating alien wildlife, space flight, discovery and both PvE and PvP gameplay.
The graphics are getting better with each update and there are quite a few die-hard players around to answer questions through each phase of the game.
However, I'll say it again, if you're looking for a finished game or are going to spend more time whining about issues and yelling for a refund, then Early Access games are really not for you;  and Osiris: New Dawn is definitely an "Early Access" game.

Dogfight 1942... What a game!! Before playing this I checked out some of the reviews and there were some negative comments, mostly positive, but the negatives were mainly concerning the controls, lack of storyline, and unrealsim (one guy commented on how the game sucked due to the fact your bombs and torpedos reload whilst in mid air). So these are my opinions! This is game is FAR from a simulator, so if you're looking for a WW2 based flying simulator, this isn't your game! It's a fun, quick paced flight game based around WW2, from all different angles, Japan vs USA, UK vs Germany, and if you have the DLC, making the game a couple of hours longer, you can also play Russia vs Germany, and a mix of countries fighting in the Western Desert Campaign. The plane models are well made and look good, and the Ace camouflages are a good unlock feature and look amazing, and the graphics look and work perfectly fine, I even got some pretty tasty screenshots! The people who said this game is "too easy" must have played on the lowest difficulty, because the skill level between medium and hard levels are such a massive difference. If you like a challenge, then Hard is the difficulty for you, and the mission medals can sometimes be challenging to do aswell. The controls are easy on casual mode, but extremely difficult on the other 2 modes, and to get some medal unlocks and achievements, you NEED to use simulation mode. Really good game, graphics are nice, plays well, and would recommend it anyday, considering I got this from a bundle site, which I worked out that the game cost me 0.36p. (I got 8 games for £2.88p) 8/10

Many people hate this game, I look for reasons why, read forums, browse blogs, it seems most hatred comes from it introducing a new combat style, with a different sort of story.  The gameplay sure its different it uses a third person based squad command system.  Never saw this in a game before, looking at in videos looked complicated, and like I was micromanaging them like sims.  Its different, but comfortable, its not to complicated, so anyone can enjoy it without needing to spend hours learning a new way to play a game, introducing a new mechanic in gaming that isnt quite turn based and not quite an RTS hit the right spot.  People see this new thing, they go EW I HATE NEW THINGS!, but this "new" thing is easy to use, even dare I say FUN.  Other major complaint is the story changed, having no idea what the story was before I could care less really.  The story is terribad, corny, like Ed Wood from Planet 9 corny, there is a guy hunting sasquatches, there is no reaction at all to some big events, other things and lines are so bad, their sooOOOoooo bad, hahaha, but its still fun because their so bad.  Its not realistic at all, then again the game is called XCOM a game where you attack aliens, how would that ever be realistic?  Oh look im researching this gun, now I can use that gun 8 minutes later, this is so realistic!!! GTFO that isnt realistic, this game has no reasearch another big complaint, but who cares, the scientists are way more fun here, and you cant just look at something and figure out how ti works.  Go stare at an electrical socket, see if staring at it tells you how it works, it wont so those complaints are just silly.
Thoughts:
This game has INCREDIBLE attention to detail.  Just the audio alone is incredible, the footsteps are different on carpet than on floor.  People smoke in this game, the area around them and only them is smoky.  All the little things where other games cut corners or devs dont think of are included in this game.  Things such as animations not just for the main character but everyone else, useless dialog, oh there is tons, walking around there is alot of useless dialog, still fun to listen to.  useless animations are included to as scientists test weapons and new things blowing themselves up, all pretty fun to watch.  Those little things make the game feel alive!  One of the best things is in combat your hat can get shot off!  there is even an animation to pick your hat back up.  Hats were serious business in the 60's.  The game is fun though, going to space, and there seems to be multiple endings, well there must be since it has different paths.  Where other games use cut scenes to render scenes, in this game you can walk right through them, that was pretty amazing making this game stand out to me.
(-1 point because you lose your hat after a couple missions)
Rating:  9/10  Value:  49.99

Flawed game in almost every aspects. To put it bluntly, The Bureau is a Mass Effect clone, but done poorly. Think I would've preferred 2k Marin to keep up with the aledged XCOM FPS game in the works long ago before scrapping it all to give us this lame XCOM game.
PROS:
+The '60s environment is well done both in visual and audio styles.
+Character models are decent looking (in DX11 that is).
+Reminiscent of the Mass Effect tactical combat style.
+Story twist at a certain point.
+Tier 3 unlocked on the Steam preorder... meaning having all XCOM games w/ The Bureau.
CONS:
-Shoddy port running on POOR performance in DX11 (the game stutters A LOT).
-Weak combat system.
-Stiff character movement with bad controls.
-Weak friendly A.I. is one of the worst I have ever seen in gaming. Always need you to babysit them, constantly! VERY ANNOYING!
-Nonsense plot (you're handled new tech at certain points in the game without ANY explanation... just like some poor unlock excuse!).
-Permadeath on your companions is worst than just reloading your previous checkpoint. It seems to punish you more until you die, then reload checkpoint!
-Voice acting is forced. Lip synch is, out of synch!
OVERALL:
My final thoughts... the game does have more faults than positive aspects. I had some enjoyment at times but many frustrations too. Game is VERY UNSTABLE under DirectX 11. Can't take any screenshots in that DX11 and the game doesn't seem tested much on that mode. Worst, I had a few crashes and lots of stuttering, screen tearing, in DX11.
A gamebreaking bug I've experienced: At some minor mission (one where you see a massive "modified" satellite dish), I just couldn't continue my game unless I switched back to DX9; that way I could finish the mission then switchback to DX11 afterwards. Nasty bug I tell you!
RECOMMEND?
Only if you're an XCOM hardcore fan or if you're new to XCOM franchise, pick this game once its on a sweet deal. At 40$, its quite pricy for all the faults and cons this game have. So wait up for a drastic discount!
Sad that it took many years of development to get this result!

So I've had my eye on this game for a long time but never got around to buying/playing it since I have almost 600 games. I watched it's Kickstarter since its conception as a tablet/smart phone game. The one thing I really liked about this game was the art style, this was the one thing that drew me to it. I absolutely love the way it looks. And now I'm going to throw in my two cents about this title.
+Game is absolutely gorgeous, great art style, nice textures, some decent graphics, nice use of shaders and shadows especially.
+The worlds are very nicely detailed but not too detailed to keep with its somewhat cartoony/realistic style.
+Characters are all really nicely detailed, matches the style perfectly.
+Writing is very well done, some nice jokes that don't go over your head and just nicely done in general and each character has their own style of dialog. There are a ton of hidden adult jokes in the game, it feels almost like there was a conflict between writers, one was trying to put in all these clever little dirty jokes while the other wanted to keep it clean. And I love it, the jokes and gags are well done and not too silly or too adult. Example:
+Xbox 360 controller support with two control options, MMO and FPS with keybinding.
+Kid friendly for the most part but it's done in a way that it's friendly and interesting for everyone, even adults.
+QTE's are fun when they work properly.
+This game has hats that are not micro-transactions. You actually...dare I say it...UNLOCK THEM BY PLAYING.
+Pets that do absolutely nothing but look cool.
+Costumes.
+Really well done music, has a Wind Waker vibe.
+Get to explore the island after completing the game.
-Very basic game, there's really no depth to this game at all and the gameplay consists of running around, talking to people, doing some very limited side quests and then doing a QTE mini-game to defeat spirits.
-Controls are a bit confusing when using a gamepad, I personally use an Xbox 360 controller on 3rd person action games and racing games if I'm able to. Lili has some very confusing ideals for the controller. There is no pressure sensitivity for walking/running. I managed to get her to walk once by slightly pressing the stick to the side but that was it, only once. Controls for items on the UI are still showing keyboard inputs and NOT the X360 buttons. Double tapping A will make her run infinitely which is annoying when trying to click on something. Game auto locks onto items and people, I've had this happen to me a few times when trying to attack spirits and all of a sudden talk to a villager even though the cursor was showing on the spirit and NOT the villager. Also, for some reason while running, if you hold the camera left or right, your character then stays stuck running in the direction you were holding when the camera was first being turned, it's not a big deal but it makes the game feel a little clunky.
-QTE mini-game messes up, like a lot. I had the camera go into other characters, buildings and walls constantly during the mini-game. Sometimes the camera would look ABOVE the spirit and my character so I couldn't see anything at all. The QTE controls also mess up. You can press a button too early even though you saw it pop up and sometimes the buttons change around for no reason and a lot of the time the buttons won't show up or show on items you can't do anything with, like all four buttons will be highlighting the sharp weeds on the spirit's back and you have to just wait as a bomb is about to explode. I've had bombs explode because of this issue but I only ever had to retry the spirit fights twice, ever as the QTE's aren't hard, the hardest part is the bugs. I also never used an item during any of the spirit fights. And sometimes during a spirit fight, you'll pluck a flower and it will also trigger pulling a sharp weed as well, it can be very annoying at times.
-+Performance issues. The game runs fantastically for me and it looks great 99% of the time, but sometimes it'll just drop to 30-40FPS out of nowhere at the most random times, this happens in a lot of games, but there is literally no reason that a game this small in scale should tax a R9 270 2GB at 1080p, specially when there's no AA going on. This game also lacks a lot of video options, it has no advanced video options and no audio options. So a warning to those with lower specs.
-Costumes. This is my biggest gripe in whole with this game, it totes itself as having costumes but every single one aside from the secret costume at the end is just a re-colored version of her original outfit. The secret outfit is nice at first, but then you really get a look at it and it's very poorly put together, there are a lot of sharp angles, her legs are messed up and it's honestly just not that appealing. I really wish there was a costume pack or something with genuinely nice costumes.
-Bugged hat. I collected everything on my first run through the game without using any kind of walkthrough because I like to be surprised. Well, I found everything but one hat. The blue bird that you can get as a hat and a pet, I missed the hat, you get it from the cardboard axe dude, I missed it and now I cannot get it again unless I replay the game. That's annoying. I just wanted everything in a single playthrough.
-The devs try to push the game as a Legend of Zelda like title,
but it is most definitely not. It doesn't feel like a tablet title as it was born from, but it most certainly doesn't feel like a LoZ like game. And that's not a bad thing, the game is fine and isn't trying to be anything it's not but it's a bit misleading to potential buyers, especially since the art style is clearly inspired by Wind Waker minus the cell-shading.
-Game is super short, I beat it in a single sitting of only a few hours and got everything but a few achievements and a single hat that you can’t get if you missed the window to collect it.
-Music volume. It is so loud and no way to adjust in the menus, especially right in the beginning. Luckily, it's got some really nice music, sadly, there are very few songs.
-Annoyingly long achievements. Almost all the achievements for this game are just okay, I have no problems with them. But there are two I dislike; break 1000 vases and pick 1000 flowers. You'd have to beat the game a grand total of about 12 times if you were just casually smashing vases or picking up flowers and not purposely trying to get the achievement. I just don't have the patience or will power to play such a short game so many times to get two simple achievements specially since it takes a whole two seconds to break a vase when it should be instant for such a grindy achievement.
-Hats just don't fit right, they look really strange on Lili, like they're way too big and most of the hats are not very inspiring or "cool". I just feel nothing when I put a new hat on her. Masks are fine, the wings are really nice too, but the hats just do nothing for me.
Overall, I really dig this game. It’s not GOTY material or anything and it is a very well done port of a tablet game so don’t expect anything too crazy out of it, but it is a fun exploration game. Just know, you’re playing this game for the story, writing, art, music and characters and not the gameplay itself.
The game has some annoying issues that I addressed but ultimately, I still really liked this title and recommend it to anyone who likes exploration, story or puzzle games.

I'll start by saying that I'm surprised I played the game to the end.
Normally I'm not the adventure game type, and considering there isn't a huge amount of variety in the tasks required (nearly everything is a "find X of Y" hunt), the world as a whole is actually very well rounded and detailed both graphically and with optional flavor text and dialog. The characters are well personified with minimal (absolutely minimal) but well done voice acting.
It is also short, and I manged to beat it in ~3 hours. There is a choice to be made at a pivotal point in the story so I might actually go back and try to take another path. Plus there might be some things that subtly change the ending dialogs. I almost certainly missed some side quests/characterization too. For a relatively short game they managed to pack in quite a bit of content.
The story is simple but serves the purpose well, as does the crude level-up stats system. This is not an RPG to the extent that you need to consider min-maxing the few stats you have, and they seem to have minimal impact on gameplay. There are no dialog trees, but the dialog is at least partially context aware: If you encounter a character before you were meant to, often that encounter will be acknowledged during the dialog with other characters (eg: "Oh, I met (character) earlier...") which adds a nice bit of immersion.
The flower picking mechanic (flowers basically being used as a form of currency) is a bit tedious, and picking enough to get all of the extra items (keys, mostly) to unlock all of the optional doors and collect trinkets/flavor text is a daunting task. There is an achievement for picking 1000 flowers and boy howdy do I believe that could happen...
There's also an achievement for breaking 1000 pots - you basically walk into people's houses and break their pots for money Legend-of-Zelda style. That number seems to be a lie, though; The achievement counter advanced by 5 for every 2-3 pots broken, so I suspect the *real* number is 500. Still a lot though.
There is no health/death mechanic, and the consequence for failure is being teleported a small distance away.
The semi-optional mini game where you cling to the back of the "enemies" and pick flowers out of their heads is fun at first but gets annoyingly difficult. It is only required a handful of times, fortunately, and the reward for completing extras is merely extra masks that your character can wear.
The map consists of six areas - one of which is a single room you only deal with for an optional side quest - four of which are 99% of the game. These areas are fairly good sized, richly detailed, beautifully rendered but labyrinthine townscapes in which you meet the characters, collect the trinkets and find the switches which are the meat of the gameplay. The design and styling gives each area a very organic and "lived in" feel despite the cartoonish colors and proportions. It won't dazzle you with blooms and particle effects but it is very pretty. The mechanic by which you move from one "quarter" to the next is *nearly* seamless, with just a slight hiccup as you transition through an airlock-esque connecting area.
There is an abundance of invisible walls which gets a little annoying at times.
The protagonist character, which you play as, is notably not an annoying brat, moody or woefully inept. That wouldn't normally be something to mention... maybe I just have far to cynical a view of modern adventure games.
Finally, there is no foul language, sexually suggestive themes/dialog (not even a passing euphemism!) or meaningful violence - all "fighting" is the previously mentioned minigame where you sneak up on enemies and pluck flowers out of their head.
Overall a great game and I'd recommend it.

In Holy Potatoes! We’re in Space?! you take control of the space shuttle of two potatoes - the sisters Cassie and Fay. With them, you get to manage your ship, recruit more vegetables, research technology, manage your expenses, resources and travel from solar system to solar system, to stay ahead of the headhunters searching for you.
The gameplay happens in two stages - the management and the combat stage.
The management stage is choosing which planets to fly to, what to research, which weapons to use, what your crew should do etc. This part of the game takes a while to be fully understood, since there are so many things one should manage, and thus the HUD is quite extensive.
The most important part of this, is the travelling inbetween solar systems, the game seems to have countless random encounters, achieving the desired feeling of exploration.
The other stage of the game, is the fighting. The player can choose to go on exploration missions on a planet, which happens in the form of a queue of random encounters. Usually, one gets into a few battles on an exploration like this, and that's when the second half of the game begins:
Upon encountering an enemy ship, one gets into turn based combat.
Here, the player has to manage energy, hp, weapons and special moves to destroy the enemy's weapons and finally their ship.
Here, your crew's experience and your ships weapons combined with the players tactical brilliance are the key to victory.
Basically the player chooses how to spend the ship's energy, which weapons to use, what to target etc.
This fighting system, whilst original might feel stale after the first playthough, due to it's repetitive nature.
The game title should give away another big aspect of the game.
It is crammed with jokes, all the way, and whether you'll like this or not is obviously a personal question, and while it may annoy some, it does not get in the way of gameplay and makes the whole experience more Holy Poatoes-ish.
One last thing that I shall touch on:
Replayability.
Replayability is a very big aspect in this game, since most mechanics were specifically designed to make new playthoughs a new experience. Thanks to the variety in encounters, ships, actions etc. this was very well achieved.

+Replayable
+Humorous
+Rich in content
-Fighting can get stale after long gameplay
-HUD takes time to get used to
- Loved it
A very well polished, rich in content and clearly lovingly made game, by developers who like their Potato jokes.

Roguelike space exploration and crafting game. There are three primary storylines plus a ton of randomly-generated quests and events. If you don't like doofy pop culture puns, you won't like this. If you don't like choose-your-own-adventure events interspersed with objectively repetitive (but still super fun) turn-based battles, you won't like this. And if you're so incredibly fragile that exactly one throwaway line about gender being a social construct gets your nuts in a wad, you won't like this.
You will love it if you loved devoting yourself to games like Final Fantasy 8 as a kid, if a good grind session never scared you off, if gambling battle outcomes on your limit breaks was exciting rather than infuriating and if stubbornly reloading your saves when Triple Triad battles went way south is how you ended up with all those one-shot-only super rare cards. (Back before "save scumming" was a cardinal sin.) It doesn't walk or talk like Final Fantasy 8, but it has that
, you know? It's just a good time.
The scenery is incredibly beautiful, it's pretty quick to get an handle on the gameplay, and for being actual, literal potatoes, the characters are endearing as heck. Also, it's the only game that's ever made me string together the words "mermaid carrot boobs." And that counts for something. I'm not sure what that something is, but it counts for it.
P.S. Getting the rarer achievements for making weapons, by the way, entail doing what it asks in a
playthrough, not cumulatively. So if you're having issues with those achievements, especially the 20 SS-rank weapons one, that's why.

Rift is like WoW in many respects - a fantasy world divided into levelled regions, quests which drive a sort of general plot along, dailies and so on. The UI is pretty similar & you have many of the same classes too. That said Rift wins over WoW in many respects. First, it's free to play, and this really does mean free to play. There are very few things which you can buy from the Rift store which give you a genuine edge. Most are just vanity things - there's an armour & weapon set which helps a little but it's not absolutely required. You can play this game & have it be enjoyable & rewarding without spending any money - or equally you could spend a load on it & have a sweet "dimension" hideout & cool looking mount, and get your costume looking *just so*.
Secondly, Rift has these rift events whereby a rift opens between your world & a demon-infested hell dimension, and all manner of nasties come through. You can farm these if you like, or do the quests, or you can do the third thing which is:
Thirdly there's "Instant Adventures" where you join a raid group for a rampage across the countryside doing quests, grinding mobs & rifts, all kinds of stuff. These can be great fun.
Lastly the graphics make WoW look ugly & amateurish by comparison. Rift is *beautiful*.
On the bad side, well, it's an MMO so it suffers from the usual things MMOs suffer from like respawns killing you, and the fact that in the grand scheme of things whatever you do won't change anything long term, but that's all MMOs. Considering this one is free, and does pretty much anything WoW does only often enough better, I'm a convert. Rift rocks.
