Charming and beautiful, with some missteps in gameplay.
I don't remember exactly how I got this game (I think there was a Female Protagonists bundle?), so I didn't really know anything about it before it was in my library. I didn't know that it started out as a mobile/tablet game, but it makes sense considering much of the gameplay would probably be more approachable on a touchscreen.
You play as Lili, a sort of magic-botanist grad student who has traveled to an island to collect flower specimens. You navigate around a small number of interconnected maps, collecting flowers, smashing clay pots full of coins, and completing minor quests for townspeople. There is growing tension between the masked spirits of the island and their peaceful wooden servants, and your specimen hunt lands you right in the middle of the conflict.
While the exploration and character interaction is fun and engaging, the majority of the game seems to focus on one particular minigame, which is sort of a precision flower-plucking game. While clinging to the back of a masked spirit, you must accurately grab sprouting flowers while avoiding traps. The spirit bucks back and forth to create moving targets, and occasionally interrupts your progress with a "frenzy" of traps. This minigame is reasonably fun to play, although I don't think the instructions were very clear. You pick flowers while exploring by simply clicking them; to pick a flower in the minigame you have to click and pull away to uproot it. The more advanced stages get very chaotic, and it's unfortunately very easy to lose track of your cursor with all the bright objects flying across the screen.
The biggest issue I have with this minigame is that there are FIFTY separate instances for you to complete, and there's not enough variation between stages to justify more than, say, ten. Add the fact that each instance has a 3-star scoring meter, giving compulsive completionists like me cause to replay them, and it starts to get really grindy. Because of the emphasis on this particular part of the game, I assume this was the core concept that the rest of the game was built around.
Also grindy are the optional achievements for plucking flowers and smashing pots, which set the goal at 1000 (!) apiece. The flowers and the coins found in pots both function as types of currency, intended mostly for use in the item shop. The shop doesn't carry much; you can buy stat boosts, consumable items to make the plucking minigame easier, and a map upgrade (which I actually found pretty essential). There's a separate shop that sells single-use keys for locked doors. I don't quite understand why that wasn't just incorporated into the main shop, since the main shop also sells an expensive but reusable skeleton key. There's an achievement for maxing out each of your 3 stats, but for some reason they didn't make it possible to bring your 3rd stat all the way to max, so you can't 100% the game in a single playthrough.
The music is charming and pleasant, the designs and palettes are visually appealing, and there are some great particle effects. I had some trouble with the camera (mostly the FOV) when I first started the game, and it made me feel kind of queasy. It didn't help that the first area also has lots of lens flare and water spray, but once I got into town it became manageable.
The writing was more clever than I expected, considering how cute and all-ages the game apparently is. I don't mean the plot, although there are some dark touches here and there. The character dialogue and some of the menu descriptions have a lot of character and sometimes give teeny-tiny hints of being sort of not exactly all-ages. It's often self-aware, but never self-congratulatory. As an added bonus, the main character is allowed to be female without the writing needing to rely on "girl" tropes.
There are a couple bugs (sometimes the minimap toggles off when you decide to challenge a masked spirit again) and more typos than one would expect from an updated release. When you pass through a loading gate between maps, the camera and music both stutter and it's a bit jarring.
I would love to see either a remake or sequel with more areas and a greater emphasis on exploration & collection rather than chasing & plucking. Maybe all the functionless Lore Items need to be redistributed to the correct NPCs, etc., and find more reasons to reuse existing characters and give them more involvement.
Overall it's easily worth playing. It's fun and bright and engaging, and for me, the great one-liners make up for the grinding.

So somehow my review got lost, whether because of this "upgrade" to the complete edition, or some other reason, either way, here's my thoughts from back when I tried this abomination:
Really boring, and not my type of game.
First the options menu: It's horrible. Only a few resolution options, a few buttons for graphical options, which are preset according to setting like High, Highest, and so forth. No actual customising available. Keybindings cannot be changed. Basic mouse options of inverting, and mouse sensitivity buttons, rather than a bar or a number. All in all, the options menu needs a lot of work.
Game starts off talking to everyone, and walking into building to talk to more people. You can also add to your fun by breaking vases or opening chests. The chests contain items that have really unfunny descriptions. That is basically a recurring facet of this game. Unfunny dialogue, stale descriptions, and flat jokes.
During dialogue there is some voice work, but it doesn't match the text. Rather, it's your character saying hello multiple times in a conversation, and the constructs/spirit things making weird sounds.
Finally, the character design is pretty bad. The female doesn't have to be attractive, nor have large assets, but I'm going to have to say the haircut is pretty horrid. A tumblrina if you will. The whole look of her is unbecoming to me, other than the outfit, which is passable. I suppose she matches an explorer, although it feels like the designer wanted her to be Lara Croft, just without being attractive in a tradional sense. I suppose the word is, hipster. This is of course subjective, but will this present times inspired look work in the future, should someone find themselves playing it? Does it work in present times? I don't feel her look emphasizes 'geeky girl'. It's different, and I feel emphasizes tumblr, SJW, feminist, things of that sort. I personally don't fall into that camp, and as such, makes me worry that the game is designed by a development group that IS affected by those camps. Politics don't belong in a game, unless directly marketed as such, and creativity marred by such a thing is troubling. From what I played of the game, I don't necessarily think the game itself is an extension of SJW beliefs, but I believe the creation of the character you play as in a physical sense, IS affected by the creators political beliefs. Take that as you will.
The world is colorful, and the game is inoffensive, in terms of interactions, but it just seems aimed at a younger audience, or people with easily offended sensibilities. I like a wide range of games, whether shooters, puzzles, rpgs, or some adventure games. I'll even go back to games like legend of zelda, or super mario bros. This game, however, is not my cup of tea, and I cannot recommend it. It lacks depth, and your interactions with the world reflects that. I didn't feel engaged, and more like the game was a chore. Maybe I'll come back in the future, but as things stand, it's too boring to hold my interest.

First I would like to say this is by far my favorite grand strategy RTS game. I never get bored of it. No matter how many playthroughs I do nothing is ever the same, there are so many options for any nation you play, and there is always something to experience that didnt happen the last time. And the freedom to do what you want with the country you pick is great. You want to play as the USA and turn it communist and join the Soviet union, go for it. Nothing is going to stop you besides in game events that may make you change your mind. And even after you might get tired of the same world war 2 scenario after 200 hours of playing, there is no shortage of mods available that completely overhaul the game, giving you scenarios like the modern world, or even going back to the first world war. There is so much to do with this game, and it will be never ending fun. The multiplayer is also good too. you want to pick all the all the major nations with your friends and divy up the world, enjoy. Or turn on them and start the real war to end all wars. There is always a way to play.
The only cons to the game is it can take a long time, which for some is a good thing, and for those who havent played a grand strategy before, the mechanics can be a little overwhelming, but I think the tutorial does a great job of showing you the basics. And if you are playing the multiplayer with some people who do not have thousand dollar computers, it is hard to keep the game at a speed that isnt on the slower side of the speed up feature.

Purchasing this on a whim with the added benefit of 80% off, I feel like I was let-down by a series I've enjoyed in the past.
The first Painkiller and it's expansion Battle out of Hell were great exercises in classic FPS, wave-based destruction, that were as rewarding as they were simple. The plot was irrelevant, the levels looked great, and the variety in weapons and enemies made the game an enjoyable alternative to most contemporary first-person action.
Ignoring the DLC, this game has about a dozen levels with the bonus one's included. The updated graphics for the environments, effects, and enemies are excellent and the best part about this game.
The reptitive enemies (that is to say, the lack of variety) and limited missiosn destroy this game. Without the DLC you're essentially purchasing a stripped-down variant of the original game with a few levels from Battle out of Hell incorporated.  Co-op support is one highlight marred by the aformetnioned lack of level choice.
Having ponied up the $9 for all the DLC and buying a four-pack for $11, I can say the price is about right for what still amounts to a waste of potential.
Nit-picking details include: Changing the enemy sounds for reasons?? Rehashing the same enemy types again and again as oppossed to the unique encounters in almost every level in the original duo, nixing the Hell level from the original game (Personal Favorite) and finally adding only a single entry into the weapons arsenal.
TLDR: If you pay more than $10 for this you've been had.

tl;dr - This is a puzzle game with quality puzzles and a story that kept me interested and engaged the entire time.
Now to the really review:
This is a game that I bought because I'm a fan of puzzle games like Portal 2.  After finishing it, I honestly feel that it is an incredibly good game.  I found the puzzles to be interesting and pretty creative.  There were some really easy ones to begin with and throughout the game, but I think that is important for introducing new concepts within the puzzles and for allowing the player to get through the game without having to stop constantly due to being stuck.  There were few times when I was completely stumped for a while, but due to my past experience with puzzle games I kind of expected that, especially since Portal 2's puzzles were similar in that regard.  I think the tools used to solve the puzzles were interesting and the developers used what they had in some really good ways to truly make the puzzles engaging.  I also really enjoyed the optional rooms as those puzzles were quite different from the rest.

I greatly enjoyed the puzzles, but I also found the story to be very interesting as well.  I enjoyed the mystery that presents itself and how you slowly learn about it.  I enjoyed how in each sector the dialogue told a little bit more about what was going on so it was easy to listen while looking around the puzzle, but it would end after a bit so you could focus on the puzzle rather than sitting there waiting for it to end if you wanted to listen to the story.  The audiologs were fun to listen to (well "fun") while helping aid the player in figuring out what happened.  I liked all the references to turing tests and chinese rooms since I've heard of them before, and the other topics talked about and discussed by the characters.  I found the characters interesting.  Basically, I was engaged in this game the entire time I was playing it.
All in all, I really loved this game.  The story was interesting and puzzles were fun.  I really wish there was a system in place for users to create their own levels, but that is a small thing to me.  I personally think it was worth the money (granted I bought it when it was on sale).

I both liked and hated the game.  I dislike listening to the arrogant blather of "superior" machines.  I also dislike emotional responses to such blather.  The simple truth is that TOM has a lot of logical holes in his arguments, and Eva never pointed them out.  Tom says things like, "ISA has all the information they need" .   Who decides how much is enough?  TOM?  This sounds a lot like the HAL computer in 2001 A Space Odyssey, and it went crazy,   It decided humans were a threat to the mission, overlooking the fact that humans are the point of the expediton.  TOM is on the same path.  TOM's actions are based on "his" assumptions about the organism and its possible effects on humans and the Earth.  He doesn't know anything, he just follows his program. The fact, though, that he can make assumptions introduces the possibility of
errors in his thinking.  He categorically states that he is incapable of erroneous thoughts, but that statement is not true.
TOM assumes the overall effect of the organism will be a disaster, the crew think it could be the greatest event in human history.  They are the experts, not TOM.  Why should they be under his control?  It speaks volumes about corporate structure and ultimate responsibility.   Or liability.  Still, eternal life would seem to be worth pursuing from a corporate point of view.
The game, aside from philososphical meanderings, is smooth running and the puzzles are something that kept me busy for a while.  I ran into two small problems:  on several starts of the game, after a minute maybe of play, the game would freeze for several seconds, then continue normally; on one exit of the game, it froze on the menu when I pressed the escape key.  The menu displayed OK, but the program was frozen on the screen.  I used Task Manager to end it.  It did return to the proper spot on restart, so no harm done.
Others here have stated it is "no Portal".  A professional reviewer said "in a world without Portal or The Talos Principle"  this would be a much more significant game.  Well, I haven't played the other two, yet, so I haven't lost anything by playing this game.  I think it could have a more varied set of puzzles instead of similar ones.  The puzzles were clever enough, but seemed like variations on a theme.  Understandable in the context of the story and environment, but a little annoying.
Anyway, thumbs up on this review.  It was different and interesting.

Trying to find truly F2P titles that don't hide themselves behind a wall of cash shop consumables and "quick access", it's almost impossible. RIFT brings a nice background that can be played by the rulebook (PvP server), or set differences aside and team with the enemy in order to save the world (PvE servers). Progression is quite enjoyable, since class customization varies on what do you want to play, by mixing 3 main traits to create a class of your own, rather than being stuck on your classic "pre-mades".
The game does "block" a feature by default on new accounts (listing on the AH. CAN purchase items on sale, but CAN'T post items for sale), but it can be lifted by spending $5 worth of credits, turned into loyalty (sometimes, the credits can be earned for free!). Can't charge money into the game? No worries! With enough in-game currency, you could get a tradeable credit item (REX) from another player, use it, and charge your account with 1250 credits!
Apart from your regular "gachapon" items, everything can be obtained in-game, and exclusive mounts and costumes are obtained via Item Mall. Or by another player, if it's a tradeable item. Even boost consumables (EXP, drop, currency) can be obtained in-game, but at a lower rate. Also, if you enjoy the game, why not be a Patron and get a month of extra goodies!

The Typing of The Dead: Overkill is a game developed by Modern Dream and published by SEGA
In The Typing of the Dead: Overkill you play as a special agent who partners up with a potty-mouthed detective to track down the villain Papa Ceasar and save the county from a mutant outbreak. The story unfolds over nine episodes and combines horror with potentially disturbing, over-the-top comedy
The game is a reworked version of the first-person rail shooter The House of the Dead: Overkill - Extended Cut, in which the shooting mechanics of combat have been replaced by quickly and accurately typing words and phrases that appear on screen. Words are randomly chosen, so they are different every time you play, and multiple difficulty levels are available to provide a challenge for typists of varying skill levels
Movement and camera are on pre-determined paths so the experience feels like taking a ride through a haunted house at the fair, allowing you to focus on destroying zombies, picking up collectibles, rescuing civilians and racking up your high score. Boss fights at the end of each episode are well-designed and two-player co-op is a lot of fun, but it is possible to frequently encounter bugs in multiplayer that require you to restart the episode, such as words not appearing properly or the game desyncing and freezing
Since the game involves dialogue littered with profanity, plenty of gore, and touches on themes like incest and making fun of the handicapped, it’s not for the squeamish or those who may be offended by such things. If you don’t take your entertainment too seriously and can handle the outrageous content, it’s very much worth the quick, three to four hour playthrough, but no one would blame you if you couldn’t...

This is pretty much everything I wanted from the canceled XCom Alliance game that we never got. Yes, it apes Mass Effect, in more than a few ways. It has the third person cover-based shooting and pause-and-command system of Mass Effect, along with the mechanic of storyline choice steering your experience.
While it lacks the overwhelming scope of the Mass Effect games, it does offer a deeper tactical system than found in Bioware's games, allowing you to choose angles for cover, set up turrets down kill alleys and single out certain targets with your snipers.

The story is fun, even if you need to stretch your 'suspension of disbelief' a bit.  Honestly, considering that you had to do the same for the previous X-com games, it's not a surprise.  In the second half of the game, the stakes get raised and the plot twists in some interesting and unexpected ways.
The voice acting is pretty solid and the overall flavor of setting it in that weird time period of  the space race, yet before the hippie cultural revolution was a jolting and interesting choice.
It is 3rd best X-com game, past the first and the recent tactical remake

The game is not without it's flaws, of course.  The lip syncing and actor motion capture lacks polish. Also, the graphics are stylized and simplistic, yet run horribly on the highest graphic settings.  It's also rather brief, with very little in the way of fleshing out and side missions.
Also, it lacks the research, production, interception and base management of the previous games, so if that is what defines an Xcom game to you, you may be disappointed.
The horrible reviews have convinced me that this will be cult classic game, like Vampire: Bloodlines or Alpha Protocol (though not as broken as either of those) and that not everyone is meant to 'get it'.

Lili is a short, story heavy game with beautiful graphics and simple gameplay. Controlling Lili, a teen researching this colourful island for educational purposes, you find the island is full of slave like, wooden built, sentient robot humanoids run by evil spirits (who are in the form of creepy, mask wearing creatures). The plot is simple; stop the spirits and let the robot things be free and happy.
When it comes to gameplay, this game can get boring quickly, since there are a small amount of mechanics used to vary the gameplay up. Defeating spirits is fun at first, but after realising the amount of spirits there are to defeat in the game, I couldn't be bothered chasing them and accomplishing repeating quick time events over and over again. Sure, defeating them isn't wasted, as oyu are rewarded with their mask and character biography. Every character has a biography, which is nice, but not all characters are interesting. The main characters you meet in the story are charming, cute and even funny when reading their dialogue.
Overall, this game is colourful, happy and relaxing. Don't let the advertising image fool you, as this is far from a LoZ game. Buy this if you want a short, cheery story with a few giggles here and there, or really like to collect stuff.

There's something about the beautiful character designs, bright and colourful environment, simple yet challenging gameplay, and yes even the collectathon-ing that really makes this game special. The controls are a little clunky and the world feels a little 'UDK template'-ish, but there's a soul to this game that I rarely, rarely see.
You get a nice little selection of alternate costumes (mostly colour-swaps), a large selection of hats, and a few companion animals that float along-side you - all aesthetic goodies that serve no purpose, and that's how I'd want it. The dialogue in this game is solidly written, with some memorable characters; one in particular is a veritable stream of game references, which you will also find in hat collection. Will you be donning a plumber's hat, or perhaps a green hood with matching tunic and fairy? It's a little on the nose and slightly out of place, but all in good fun.
The game isn't 'huge'. You get four small areas of the island to explore, filled to the brim with unique characters and flower-picking 'combat'. You'll spend a few hours here, deep in the game's universe of wood-sprites and mask-wearing opressors. The only complaint I have about this game is its acheivements. Get ready for the long-haul, because the number of pots to break and flowers to pick requires 3-4 playthrough-lengths of grinding spawn points over and over.
In short, I can't recommend this game enough. It's the right balance of simple, fun gameplay, exploration, story, creative design and genuine heart you can't deny.

Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! is an indie sci-fi turn-based combat/management game brought to you by Daylight Studios, the same studio that developed Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?!. This time, unlike their previous game, Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! is set in... well... space.
Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! features very cartoonish visuals which fit the general goofiness of the game. As I mentioned before, Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! is set in the biggest unknown ever; space. One thing commonly attributed to space and sci-fi media of this nature are space ships. The spaceships in Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! are wacky, almost a bit too much. Some spaceships look rather neat and plausible while others are downright outrageous in nature. Sure, the game doesn't present itself as serious but tone it down a little. Every planet in Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! features differing backgrounds and even enemies. Seeing different locations really changes up the mood and is quite nice.
Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! features very nice music that has throwbacks to other famous movies/games in the past. I quite enjoy the main theme which resembles a mashup of The Legend of Zelda music as well as Indiana Jones, both calming and adventurous. Although the game is Science Fiction, you don't hear many common genres attributed to sci-fi, such as electronic. All of the audio that I've heard is orchestral, which, although it doesn't fit the theme, the music is very well done and inspiring.
Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! follows two sisters, Fay and Cassie, as they try to find their kidnapped Grandfather Jiji while getting sidetracked by things such as teleporting cats and space-Indiana Jones (NO, NOT HAN SOLO). In my opinion, there is too much exposition and cutscenes in Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! which seriously hurts the story aspect of the game because, in all honesty, it was kind of tiring reading all the many cutscenes. I do, however, enjoy the smaller cutscenes which are throwbacks to popular media, including, but not limited to, Nyancat, Indiana Jones, and The Legend of Zelda (I think). I like it when games have subtle-ish nods to other media (Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! is in no way subtle about it).
Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?!'s combat is very similar to the combat system in FTL: Faster than Light. You have an allocated amount of Charge which you have to use to your own discretion. There are multiple different types of weapon types which all have differing effects on spaceships, so the order of weapons you use and the order you use them in can have adverse changes in the flow of a battle. Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! is also a management game. In the time between battles, you can manage your ship and your crewmembers. Crewmembers that are in combat will sometimes have slight mental health problems such as unconfidence which can decrease their damage or quality in combat. Every crewmember has different strong points, such as proficiency with certain weapon types or proficiency in crafting.
Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! is overall a pretty fun game. The soundtrack is quite enjoyable, and it's graphics, although strange, aren't an eyesore. I really like the way the developers were able to twist the turn-based combat style of FTL: Faster than Light into their own original but not overly complicated combat system. If you take the time to really understand the story, you will find a comical story about 2 completely different and somehow related siblings on their journey to save their grandfather and escape the Eclipse.

Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! is a charming and cheeky exploration style game with management and random encounter aspects similar to FTL. However, this game incorporates a fun story-driven campaign with countless hat-tip references to Dr. Who, Harry Potter, Barbie & Ken, and so many others I gave up trying to keep track.
The game's controls are intuitive and it's core mechanics are well flshed out, using crew management, systems upgrades, tech research, and crew training to help you progress through the game's ever-increasing difficulty that does seem to be scaled well.
During my First Impressions review I found the game to be quite well done and judging from the amount of content available, well worth the asking price.
One complaint was due to the fact that the posted trailer for the game was voice acted whereas the game is not. This felt extremely misleading and I would be remiss in not mentioning it.

Having had ~7 hours in the game now, I think I can finally write a review.
The game reminds me of FTL a lot while not really being anything like FTL. It has the same base principle of "running away from the bad guys in a spaceship" with the added "this is our overarching quest" which – lacking in FTL – always motivates me to get going through the game.
Combat is moderately complex. You have weapons you can fire at the enemy (they need charge), you have shields that can either protect one weapon or your hull (so choose wisely). And you have pilot abilities which can turn around the fight quite quickly if you use them at the right times (they also don't need energy). There are a few strategies in combat that work really well, try to experiment around with weapon types, it might surprise you.
But the thing that gripped me the most is exploration and quests. In each zone you encounter someone will need your help and thus, you embark on a quest. It sort of gives you a guiding path through a sector, where to go, what to do. You are always running so there is only so much time before you need to make another galaxy jump.
With upgrades  to your ship, crafting weapons and more it makes you feel like part of the crew in a way that few games do. And it motivates you to keep going and kinda expand your abilities. You can also train your crew with new skills, research new upgrades and when a turret gets destroyed, the crewmember who used it at the time gets traumatised and afterwards needs therapy. Not sure if that's cute or scarring :P
The game also features the most adorable two sisters and banter in the universe :D
The negative list is pretty short.
- Random encounters aren't as random as they could be but  imo it's only a minor thing and hasn't stopped me from enjoying the game any less
- I wish there was a way to travel multiple planet hops at once which can make for very tedious jump-wait-jump-wait, scenarios
All in all I would call this game an 8.5/10. It's fun, it's surprisingly tactically deep, it's full of vegetable puns and pretty funny dialog between the two main characters.

Painkiller Hell & Damnation was made by Farm 51 and released in 2012. It's a remaster/remake of original Painkiller, Hell & Damnation stand for HD. A funny one at that - story-wise it's a sequel, gameplay-wise it's remake. Usually it opposite. It doesn't have so many single-player levels, quite few, developers payed more attention to multiplayer part instead. But hey, even such remake is great when the only things that Painkiller was getting for few years were awful expansion packs.
Technically, it's fine enough. As fine as Unreal 3 Engine allows. Loading time is good. Performance is good. Has nice amount of video options. Aside from having issue on my laptop where game will stutter more and more the longer it runs. But that's laptops for you.
Multiplayer is where developers payed more attention. There is a bunch of competive games. Even more, there is a survival mode for up to 8 players. And even better, you can play campaign with a friend. Coop mode is something always wanted in Painkiller Black Edition. So it's awesome even if it's 2-players only. So it all should give you a reason to buy this game despite owning Black Edition.
But community is dead. I see absolutely no servers online. So, I am afraid, multiplayer part isn't actual anymore. Well, competive part. Can always drag friend into coop.
Story follows Daniel after events of main game. Like, many ages after that. Or unknown time, but Eve isn't queen anymore. And it's all in the past. Well, I guess we can take it that all expansion packs after Overdose weren't canon. Daniel still travels around purgatory with no big reason, until he meets Death, who demands 7000 souls. Don't worry, this game is not sequel to Painkiller Redemption which had 1000 monsers per level, you don't actually have to do that in a game.
And well, you will see few cutscenes after that. And in these cutscenes you will be wondering why everybody is being so dumb. Actions don't make sense around motivations. Let's forget about it already.
So, what we are left with is a single-player portion of remake. Well, let's do numbers. This game has 9 main campaign levels plus 4 campaign boss levels. Plus it has one bonus level Factory. Plus 3 thematic small bonus levels. And you can get Christmas Trainstation bonus level DLC for free. And it also has two more bonus levels Labs and City on Water in "DLC Levels" for free, which makes no sense. So simple game purchase gets you 20 levels or so. But Black Edition had over 30 unique ones. So it's still feels like mini-version.
But if you care about DLC, then it should bring number close to Black Edition, also having some unique ones, like top-down DLC levels. I probably should be complaining about DLC milking, but damn, whole Painkiller Complete Pack goes on big sales sometimes where it becomes totally worth it.
And to be honest, I wish they wouldn't be afraid to remix levels to bring their own strenght. The way that levels in the game work, they are usually accurate with few lacking details. Like, it doesn't show off physics as much. But sometimes it also gives small improvements. Like, the lamp in Opera House doesn't crash down, which was impressive in Black Edition. But it has witches rocking on scene.
Sometimes it's clear improvement, both in graphics and small details. Trainstation is one of them. Small scene, additional types of enemies. Better looking. The train section itself even changed geometry slightly to allow monsters to chase you more effeciently, instead of using freaking stairs everytime you change spot in Black Edition.
And sometimes it's more on lacking side. Take orphanage as example. While outside it's slightly changed and even teases you at upcoming boss, which is nice detail seen few times in a game, once you get inside, it's pretty much copy-pasted geometry from original. Unreal 3 doesn't help to enhance noticeably. Actually, lighting feels a little off there, with overly bright flashlight and not enough darkness. And there is no small detail like a toy ball bouncing down the stairs. The different end of the map is nice in theory but ended up awkward on practise, due to not exactly knowing what to do next.
I didn't try DLC yet though, maybe they did it better there.
Gameplay-wide it pretty much stayed the same. Almost. This time around the hero drags along 8 weapons. 5 original and 2 from Battle Out Of Hell. And there is new additional Soulcatcher weapon, which shoots group-clearing saws and can catch soul and can even make enemies join your side, becoming powered-up as well. I will never get tired of watching fights between enemies in FPS games, really. And it helps to pull souls too. Not to mention that it's awesome to see leg of shielded crusader get cut out with a saw.
Yes, if there is one clear improvement then it got to be gore. Things still go flying from shotgun blasts. But this time you may also see a hand fly somewhere else, while the main body hits the wall and leaves blood all over it. So yes, it's quite satificatory if what you want from games is violence and guts.
Though it lacks some enemies, like those stereotypical "Woaaah!" bikers. But also brings new ones along. Mostly reusage of errr fat meat cutter. And those fast skeletons. Spooky. And it dares to use kids from Orphanage in other levels as well, which I don't approve so much.
Bosses stay pretty much same. Only feel easier. Mini-bosses are mostly cut down, in most cases replaced by group of mini-boss from the first level. But hey, at least those stupid "puzzle" bosses were cut too, save for one in Orphanage.
Balance pretty much stayes the same. Just small details. Like, stake gun can kill the flying undead with helmet in Cathedral from one shot, which I approve. Yet the gun that shoots 5 stakes feels worse than stakegun, somehow. Especially at distance. All while Battle Out Of Hell would tell you that it's sniper's dream.
In all honesty, gunplay here feels like having a bunch of toys. You just pick few favourites and stick to them. Because they all do fine. And there is a lot of ammo. So the game doesn't force you to switch guns much, you don't have to think about that. Which makes combat feel more repetetive. I, for one, completely forgot of existance of Shotgun and Stakegun. Well, okay, at least you can say that those two aren't as useful as others. Or I will forget about other weapons. Yea, too much.
Difficult is slightly different. The Normal was harder than Black Edition, it didn't forgive as much. But the whole gameplay didn't force too different approach for each sitatuion, so it also felt easier in repetiveness. Doesn't help that some bosses may end up being dumb.
On another good side, I loved tarot cards approach in this game more. This part is just more fun. Objectives are easier and don't require as much of grinding, so you can do some while concentrating on beating level. Like, sawing limbs of 50 enemies. It's not like "something bonus that hardcore people do after beating game and never use again due to beating game". Though, another small difference, is that HD doesn't open all doors in a level once exit appears. So, those who want to find secrets should do it during main gameplay. I even cared about souls more, due to powering up Soulcatcher with them and since you can drag them with this weapon.
But new music isn't all that good.
And they say that this game was made by developers to see if community still cares about Painkiller or not. And focused on multiplayer more than singleplayer, which is mistake, looking at it now. And well, judging by all DLCes, it probably was a success, hopefully we will get sequel soon. At very least it reminded people that Painkiller franchise wasn't always a terrible joke.

OneShot is a solid puzzle/adventure-focused RPG in just about every aspect, with good art, music, dialogue and characters. That alone is enough allow it to compete with other similar games, but what truly sets OneShot apart is in its impressive use of unconventional mechanics only possible for a PC game. It's not a horror game by any means, but you'll definitely feel some sense of unease in this strange world, that is when you're not laughing at the ridicilous jokes and impressively realistic nature of the characters and their awkward interactions.
I'm quite upset about the lack of popularity this game has, and the fact that I only randomly came across a comment mentioning it while skimming through a reddit AMA... But it was without a doubt a great ride and well worth its price. I wish I could play it for the first time again. Be right back, I need a box of tissues to deal with these rude ninjas cutting onions.

This game...this game is something very impressive.
Before starting, I had some idea of its unusual mechanics, and fourth-wall breaking style, but even so I was massively surprised by much of what it does.
I really want to keep from spoiling anything, because for me at least half the fun was in not expecting what was coming, so let me put it like this.
OneShot, at various times, is cute, scary, serious, charming, funny, thought-provoking, silly, strange, sweet, worrying... pretty much any type of emotion or atmosphere you can imagine in a game, OneShot made me feel.
The actual gameplay is high quality- largely talking to characters and exploring, but with well crafted puzzles and surprisingly interesting mechanics that work excellently. And the same mechanics show a lot of respect for the player's ability to figure out clues, while keeping from making anything particularly hard. Overall, just for the gameplay it was quite enjoyable.
But the story and characters are the main draw- the writing is excellent, the atmosphere is superb, the world is fascinating and gradually gets more and more interesting... OneShot managed to make me care about pretty much everyone in just a few short hours.
I think that's about as much as I can say without spoilers, so let me end by saying: trust your intuition when you are confronted by clues that seem strange. More often than not, you will have the right idea, even it seems odd.
Especially given that OneShot's on sale right now, I would highly recommend giving it a try. It's quite short, but provides an impact far out of proportion with the time it takes.

First I would like to say this is by far my favorite grand strategy RTS game. I never get bored of it. And even after you might get tired of the same world war 2 scenario after 200 hours of playing, there is no shortage of mods available that completely overhaul the game, giving you scenarios like the modern world, or even going back to the first world war. There is so much to do with this game, and it will be never ending fun. The multiplayer is also good too. you want to pick all the all the major nations with your friends and divy up the world, enjoy. Or turn on them and start the real war to end all wars. There is always a way to play.
The only cons to the game is it can take a long time, which for some is a good thing, and for those who havent played a grand strategy before, the mechanics can be a little overwhelming, but I think the tutorial does a great job of showing you the basics. And if you are playing the multiplayer with some people who do not have thousand dollar computers, it is hard to keep the game at a speed that isnt on the slower side of the speed up feature.

If you liked The Talos Principle or Portal, then you will probably like The Turing Test. If you haven't played Talos however, then you should grab that first, as it offers better puzzles, story, graphics and overall production quality.
Also I have a little nitpick/question to the writers (slight spoilers ahead):

It's basically a simpler version of Portal, but GLaDOS is replaced with HAL 9000. There's no actual portal teleporting; the gimmick involves holding and firing a set of energy nodes into wall slots that open and close pathways to the exit. I use the Portal comparison because of the overarching theme as well as the game pattern. I won't disclose any more of the storyline but if you understand the references made at the start, you have a good idea of what is going on in general. As with most levels of the Portal games, the puzzles place the player in a confined room. Once escaping the room, the player runs through a field that removes any spare nodes you may have. It's exactly like Portal's "reset" function between puzzles.
On its own merit, I found the game enjoyable and worth playing through. The story is still entertaining even if it is pieced together using themes and plots from other media. I also enjoyed the ending, which many people seem to be disappointed with.
In terms of difficulty, I found this game to be relatively easy, especially the final chapter. I expected the final chapter to be the most difficult, but I ended up breezing through many of the puzzles, and one in particular I am almost 100% sure I stumbled upon a cheese method without knowing it, as I didn't use half of the interactions in the room. In fact, there were only 3 puzzles that gave me difficulty: one was an optional puzzle that wasn't difficult once you paid attention to specific indicators; the second was a mandatory puzzle that tripped me up with order of operations, and lastly, I had difficulty with the final puzzle, but not because it was difficult. I had trouble because I overcomplicated it, and also overlooked one aspect of the game that was never used prior.
So all that said, if you want to try a puzzle game, I think this one is a good one to start. It's not difficult.

The Turing Test is a very well polished puzzler that I could barely put down until I beat it. It has a gripping story, polished visuals, and a fine-tuned array of puzzles to keep you on your toes. It's not completely flawless though. Some of the puzzles have very short time limits, and were almost impossible to get done fast enough, even when I switched from a controller to a keyboard and mouse. Also, it's pretty short. I beat it in 4 1/2 hours, but admittedly it is much better for a game to leave you wanting more than to drag on forever.

Having logged 700+ hours on my old account, I installed it on this one simply to write this review. And I can safely say this is the best F2P MMORPG you will ever play.
Pros:
1) Even though the combat is tab target, it manages to retain aq dynamic feel. All your skills work together in some way so finding the perfect rotation is always interesting. Combat is also incredibly smooth and is really quite enjoyable.
2) The Soul Tree system is perfect and will find a way to fit your play style effortlessly. You can even have custom classes unheard of in most any other game. A mage that doubles as a tank? If you want. A warrior with group healing? Go for it. A cleric with insane DpS? Hell yeah!
3) PvP is AMAZING. I really can't expand on this any more. Try it for yourself. There is very rarely two players using the same build as there are so many possibilities. Endless fun :D
4) The game has a solid storyline that really engages the players. You feel compelled to continue with the main quest line, although that shouldn't deter you from doing as many side quests as you wish. Quests have decent rewards, such as new equipment and a massive pile of cash.
5) Leveling up isn't a huge grind. Granted, there is some grinding to get new equipment or to get PvP gear. But unlike most, it isn't the same quest in the same area over and over again. The quests can be in different areas, and different objectives.
Cons:
1) Dungeons and monsters can get fairly tricky unless you keep on top of your equipment or have some fairly powerful friends. Join a guild for a group of regular party members.
2) You need a hell of a computer to run this game on anything over medium graphics. I currently have an Intel i5, 8 GB of RAM and a Nvidia 640 GT and I can only run it on high at 50-60 FPS. For max you will really need good components.
3) If you don't pay for subscription, it doesn't affect anything a huge amount but you have a few restrictions that are kinda irritating.
i) You can't buy or sell at the auction house.
ii) Pretty small bag space. Probably most annoying.
iii) It will take a LOT of grinding, however, to get a mount.
Overall, a very fun, addictive, and engaging game. Definitly one you should get. It's polished and feels like a paid game. The highest praise a free game could have.

Osiris: New Dawn will be familiar to anyone that has played any of the numerous survival games on steam recently (ARK, Rust, etc). OND still manages to provide you with a sense of awe that is different from other survival games due to its setting - Space! The visuals of this game will not disappoint you. However, at $27.99 (Canadian) the game does not offer enough content to keep a player engaged for long. That being said, the game is in early alpha so a lack of content is to be expected (as well as an abundance of bugs e.g. mainly your items disappearing).
The player cannot manipulate the world and all structures are pre-fabricated, meaning base building is incredibly limited - the pre-fabs do look fantastic though. I have only seen 2 weapons in the game in my play through, a pistol and an assault rifle. I had the pleasure of riding around in some vehicles on one of the servers I was on and I have to say that was the best part of the game for me - they maneuver beautifully. There are a number of different types of aliens and you will encounter some during the day and some during night (fun surprise). Resource gathering the game delivers quite well and even differently from other survival titles (e.g. gas collecting). Crafting in the game, however, is average.
Given the history of early access games I would suggest that anyone who does not like to waste money to hold on to their wallet - give it time, and if the game is heading in the right direction, purchase it. If you are like me and are ok with dishing out some cash to support this early access title then I encourage you to do so, as this game does have potential and you will be entertained (if only for a short while). Verdict- Graphics: 9/10 -  Gameplay: 8/10 - Content: 6/10 -Roleplaying any space movie ever: 10/10
I hope this review finds you (the reader) well. My apologies for the length of this review. One love, Cheers!

When I read the reviews for this game, I didn't think their descriptions and score matched up. I had to see for myself, to form my own opinion and try to make out what they were talking about. So, here we go...
Aliens are invading, and contrary to the trailers the gameplay is absolutely nothing about concealing their presence. It's about shooting them.
On the surface it's a 3rd person action game in a Mass Effect style but with a much heavier emphasis on tactics.
However, in reality, the tactics aren't that important. You'll need to use the tactic interface a lot, for sure, but any flanking manouvers or other fancy movement will just get people needlessly killed. It's much more efficient (and easy) to just sit as far back as possible while spamming abilities and take potshots at the evemy, while keeping a secondary heavy weapon on hand for the occasional close encounters.
And this is a bit unfortunate.
The game seems designed for all this tactical depth, but it never encourages you to actively use it. I played on Veteran (2nd highest difficulty) and the above listed method worked great for pretty much every fight in the game. The story elements, while functional, don't really serve any other purpose other than to ferry you from one mission to the next. There's audiologs and a few minor puzzles to solve if you want to, but ultimately much of the game feels like a missed opportunity.
But despite that, and some inconsistencies/glitches I stumbled across, I still don't regret playing it. It's nowhere near as great as the turn based XCOM:Enemy Unknown, but it's still a fun romp while it lasts.
This is a decent game, and if you like the Mass Effect combat style you'll find plenty of entertainment here. There's not enough variety in it to warrant a purchase at full price, but on a sale? Definitely.
Just keep an open mind and enjoy it for what it is.

Metacritic score (~67) is not that far off. Not impressed so far, although I'll update my recommendation if my opinion changes. It's not that the game is terrible, but it gives lots of hints about the game that it wishes it could be, but fails to be. And I think I would like THAT game more than I like this cover-based third-person real-time-strategy shooter hybrid that can't make up its mind on what it wants to be and ends up second rate at either.
The things that the devs put a lot of effort and care into look/work great. Unfortunately, those things don't seem to encompass quite enough, and not in the most key areas. Examples: When you go into the AI-teammate command mode, time doesn't stop, it only slows down to something like 25% speed. The writing is... um, not the worst, but I'm bored of these people already and I only just met them. AI's kind of dumb early on, although supposedly later on in the game it stops feeling like escort missions and they actually hold their own.
It's not without its good elements. I like the setting itself; care definitely went into that, if not necessarily the dialogue. Where it's not a dark corner with fog and darkness covering up the extremely flat and featureless textures in unimportant corners and other corner-cutting measures, the world looks decent. The promise of what it could be/could have been is still a significant part, however.
It'd probably be a fun multiplayer co-op game, to be honest. Ditch the AI and just choose different classes and run through a campaign with 2-3 of your friends.

Recommended, with caveats
Problems before playing:
I had a lot of initial trouble getting the game to run. (This is going to get a little technical) A month ago, or so I formatted my computer, so working from a fresh install. The other day I had some computer issues, so I ran an SFC scan, which fixed whatever errors there were. Then the next day received the comment to run the game in compatibility mode.
I decided to give it a go and installed the game. It worked, and I didn't even have to mess with any settings.
Review:
So far, I've only played through the first stage. This appears to be a bit of remake of The House of the Dead Overkill, which I played on the Wii.
The story is going for more of a parody style (Think Black Dynamite, the movie)
The fighting style is typing the words that appear next to the zombies, this varies significantly in difficulty and style (and allows you to add words via a custom dictionary). Sometimes it's a simple word like, "cut" and sometimes it's making fun of another movie such as, "fly you fools". I'm not quite sure how the bullet system works, it seems that as you're typing, you're shooting the zombie, effectively knocking them back. It appears you can also use the mouse as a gun, should you choose.
There were pick-ups and power ups scattered through the stage, but were often hard to spot. Pressing tab would pick these up, but it seems there's no penalty for repeatedly pressing tab, so I turned to the habit of just pressing it every few seconds while not attacking enemies.
The background music fit for the action, but I had no audio for the bullets that I was shooting, leaving it feeling a bit odd.
Playing on the normal difficulty, I had no trouble getting past the first stage, and was only hit twice.
Overall:
Not a bad game, if you can get it to work. If you’ve played House of the Dead and any typing games, you know what to expect from this hybrid.

This game is a very interesting game in my personal opinion. Some people that have played this game may argue that this game ISN'T "basically another portal". However, the bottom line is: yes, it basically is another portal. The game mechanics are a bit different from portal, but the concepts are basically the same; go through puzzles to the end of the game.
The story is somewhat interesting, but it's hard to pay attention to unless you choose to stop and read everything. Another big issue is that you're so focused on solving puzzles, you may be unable to pay attention to dialogue unless, like previously mentioned, you stop and pay attention to what they're saying.
One small issue I had is that the game is a bit too easy. Don't get me wrong, some parts were headscratchers, but I was able to finish this game with relative ease (7 hours if you include the time where I paused the game and left to go grab some food). I'm not sure if my age has to do with this, but I played portal 1 when I was very young, and portal 2 when it came out, and I just felt that compared to both portal 1 and 2, The Turing Test was too easy for me (I completed The Turing Test the same day I wrote this review, July 2017).
On a more positive side, I found some dialogue to be very fascinating. The talk of tests such as the Turing test and the Chinese room test interested me mainly because the movie 'The Imitation Game' taught me of the Imitation game itself (just saying, I highly recommend the movie).
A cool fun fact is that one of the optional rooms actually requires you to have some knowledge of logical math. I took discrete math two semesters ago and I was very surprised to see something I learned in school was actually necessary to solve a part of a video game (yeah, I never thought I'd ever hear myself say that either).
I feel that the game is worth it for $20, but if you can, wait for it to go on sale to make it a bit more worth it for you.

One Shot has three types of reviews.
1)SPEACHLESS/EVADING/HONEST type:
Saying that it is an amazing experience that is not intersubjective, and cannot be described with words, well... without spoiling all of it, so "trust me, play it, and you won't regret". And those actually tell nothing about the game by definition.
After playing the game you will realise that those gave you nothing, but at least those were honest about it.
2)POSITIVE/TECHNICAL/REDUCTIVE type:
Contrary to (1), reviews that are trying to describe the game, the gameplay, the graphics, the music, the story or meaning, without spoiling anything, and this task is doomed to fail. Those reviews also, despite all the good intentions of helping potential buyers, are very reductive and missinformative, becasue they pretend to decribe what is undescribable.
After playing the game you will realise, that those gave you nothing, just like like informing a piano buyer that it is black and have keys.
3)STATISTICAL/CYNICAL/ARBITRARY
"Just look at the statistics, would a bad game have so many positive reviews?"
After playing the game you will realise that those gave you close to nothing. This is much better than nothing, becasue satisfaction of so many people have to mean at least something and statistically, the risk that you won't like the game is much lower, than with games with mixed reviews.
So - maybe counterintuitive - the last type of "anti-review" is actually the best.
I will not be the one that tries to convince you, without spoiling.
I will just add another positive review to the pool.
Please do the math, play the game, and write another positive review, just like all not-trolls did.

They have puzzles, some are easy, and others are not so easy to pull off. The game gives you hints, though not all the time so you need to think "outside the box" if you come up with particular....puzzles. By particular puzzles I mean that remember I said is a surreal game? Well this game can throw you some puzzles that are actually solved by doing stuff
so this is what I mean by this game being surreal and I have to say it is very clever. I always appreciate the soundtrack and art style indie developers use in these games, because you don't see these types of qualities outside of videogames anymore.
The scenes that play out or the different location syncs in the music are really nice, whether it is the upbeat tune playing or something ominous being presented. The art style is the same thing especially how it looks. The scenes are nicely presented which make Niko and the world with its characters more memorable. It's a short game if you put the time toward it and solve puzzles with ease, it should be a 6-9 hour long game until completion. This game deserves a 10/10 Game of the Year stamp, if you are not into slow journeys I can understand why; just letting you know that there is no fighting mechanic and the gameplay is just you and Niko on your own.
Now, if you still want to hear what this game really about and how I perceive it I thank you and hope the next section makes you think as I do. This next part is really for people who completed it and have the same thoughts as I do, or just people who still want to be more convinced in buying it but don't mind some spoilers.
This includes the satisfaction of completing it that satisfies our curiosity to explore. Niko on the other hand does not have a choice in the matter when doing this. Niko is a special...case because you got to realize that this game is self-aware and I know other surreal games do the same thing when breaking the 4th wall, but is not really a laughing matter. What other games usually follow is the standard formula when it comes to 4th wall breaking and the protagonist is a blank of a shell, you are the one that fills in that shell and you are the one guiding the protagonist through the journey, you are the one influencing the person to do as you are told, you are essentially god from their world view.
What makes this game different from the rest is that yes you do influence Niko the protagonist to follow this path and that, but Niko has a mind of his own. He has his own personality, his wishes his own goal and you are here to follow along with him. You are not simply there to follow a simple goal and the protagonist just stays quiet, acknowledging your existence but without doing do much about it. He will interact with you same as you do with him. What you must understand, and trust me it took me a long while to get off my usual mindset of videogames, is that you must treat their world as if it is real and your reality as real as you are playing on your screen with Niko. You will have a connection with Niko whether you care or not you will have some sort of bond between the two of you. This almost never happens in video games where the protagonist acknowledges your existence and you acknowledge his existence and go on a journey together to this world he lives in. You felt like you are actually travelling with Niko along the entire journey the two of you go, meeting fascinating people and the world in its current state. Keep in mind that you are a god in their view but even gods have to follow some rules in certain types of areas you explore, and Oneshot is one of these rules you must follow.
I find this new set of mind...interesting, like I never felt the weight of an actual "literal" god playing with an entire civilization, everything depending on this kid to save the world, yet Niko only wants is to go home, but you are the one deciding the fate of the world. I like how this game sort of acknowledges the ‘’prophecy saves the world’’ trope and it addresses itself beautifully. The choices that are made are one of the most difficult choices ever, yet the game does not punish you for it, it is just a decision about what’s best for them. Not to mention it is a discussion for people who want to view it as "is this the right choice". Remember, you get Oneshot.
This game makes you feel like asking you questions such as. "Is this how a god perceives our world?", "Is our ultimate purpose in life predetermined or do we have free will?" Maybe I am just rambling but for people that have the excuse "it is just a game", they should consider that the Atari era is long gone, games have become a form of art and now they’re becoming a form of thinking. I thought it is good to express it here for any future discussions in my review so if you are into this stuff just leave a clean comment here and hope this review opened your mind even more about these kinds of things. At the end let me ask you this; what do you see Niko as?

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! is the second potato-themed game from Daylight Studios, published by Daedalic.
Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! follows spud space pilots, Cassie and Fay, as they search the universe at random for their legendary space pilot grandfather and try to escape from the Eclipse, an intergalactic federation intent on removing our heroines from the potato gene pool.
The graphics are colourful and charming. For the most part the potato caricatures resemble the celebrities upon whom they are based. Animations are good, and the expressions of the main characters in particular are fun to watch.
The game is split into two different viewpoints: an isometric view for the management screens, and a 2D side-on view for the exploration and combat screens. Your space ship looks suitably 'techy' on the ship management screens, and although I found the interface a little bit cumbersome in places, it's simple and very nicely presented. In battles the ships have a good cartoon-like feel to them, which is continued through the 2D cut scenes at various points in the game.
Graphics options are limited, but it's not a graphics-intensive game; I wouldn't expect any reasonably modern PC to have any performance issues.
Sound effects are okay: nothing special, really, but they're appropriate and fit the game well. Music is excellent, with obvious influences from popular culture. The music for the second galaxy's mission, in particular, made me laugh. Unfortunately there are no voices, but the dialogue text is mostly well written, with only a few consistent mistakes.
Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! plays like a humorous potato-themed FTL, that's simpler in many ways, but more complex in others.
After a mostly pretty informative tutorial, which also sets the scene for the game's story, you're given control of a small space ship with two pilots and a crew of three (always the same spuds, but with some variation in starting skills), some starting cash, and basic weapons. The game gives you a mission immediately -- always the same one, unfortunately -- and your immediate task is to explore the starting galaxy to find a space cat.
Each galaxy has a hub, where your hull and weapons are repaired for free and your ship is refuelled on arrival, and you can purchase resources, hire crew, upgrade your ship, and buy and sell weapon designs and weapons. The hub also houses the warp gate, which is used to jump to the next galaxy, which will have a new hub and a new mission given to you on arrival. From the hub you can travel to other planets to explore your current galaxy, too.
Once you arrive at another planet, you're then given the option to 'explore' it. This presents you with a sequence of semi-random encounters, which typically offer you decisions that may earn you cash or resources, or damage your ship, or throw you into battle with an enemy ship. Battles have simple options, but can be surprisingly tactical, especially once you've played enough to gain another pilot skill or two, and have more than the couple of basic weapons available at the start. It's also strictly turn based, as opposed to FTL's real-time combat.
Travelling to planets and exploring each use one unit of time, or 'Sol'. When you arrive at a new galaxy you're given a certain number of Sols before the Eclipse goons who are following you find you, and then, in the early game at least, it's game over: you'll have no hope of winning that battle!
So the basic model is a lot like FTL: progress through a sequence of galaxies, with a certain amount of 'moves' available in each before an overpowered enemy catches up to you, hoping for random encounters that strengthen rather than weaken your position. But Holy Potatoes! gives you a bit more control, with a central hub in each galaxy where you can always count on getting free fuel, fixing your hull, selling stuff, and hiring crew. It also takes away FTL's randomness in ship upgrades and replaces it with a simple, if somewhat bland, level-based upgrade system that's solely based around how much cash you have available to spend at the hub. It also adds weapon crafting, research, crew training, and an interesting psychology mechanic for crew members caught out when the weapons they are manning are destroyed. Similarly to FTL, there's a strong random element to the game, and a couple of bad virtual dice rolls can see your game wiped out, although it does seem to let you restart from your last save position if you want to, rather than starting a new game.
The biggest let down for me, though, when compared to FTL, is that Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! just doesn't have that much to do. Random encounters repeat often and are largely not very interesting. Missions occur in a set order and are always the same, increasing repetition and decreasing replayability, which to me is a poor design decision given the other rogue-like elements in the game. There also doesn't appear to be any permanent improvements that last across games, as everything you do in Holy Potatoes! is reset when you start a new game. That makes playing through each time from the start feel more like a chore, rather than an opportunity. (Although it's possible I just haven't made enough progress to see any 'new game benefits'.)
The writing in the game is mostly very good, and I suspect you'll either love or hate the humour, which is full of popular culture references and potato-based puns.
Pros:
+ Creative and silly potato-based humour
+ Charming graphics
+ Good weapon crafting, crew management, and research options
+ Combat is a good blend of simple and tactical
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- More repetitive than it should be, and thus less fun to replay
- Not enough variation in random encounters
Some questionable design decisions that make the game much more repetitive than it could have been mar what would otherwise have been an excellent game. Even so, I don't hesitate to recommend Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! It has lots of silly humour and some genuinely good ideas, and it's great fun to play for a while.

An excellent third person tactical shooter where there's a lot of emphasis on giving the right orders at the right time to your agents.
You play as William Carter who at the start of the game is delivering a very important briefcase to the director of the Bureau of Operations and Command, Myron Faulke, at Groom Range when he is suddenly attacked in the room he was given while waiting to go inside the facility by a female officer who starts discharging a strange black substance from her eyes before she turns her attention to the briefcase that then explodes in a blinding white light that completely and utterly incinerates the infected female officer and knocks Carter out, who later wakes up with the gun wound he sustained inexplicably healed.
But that is only the start of Carter's problems as an unknown enemy force has attacked the facility and now he must try and get to Faulke and find out just what is going on.
This game doesn't go easy on you, even on the easiest setting, as the enemies are extremely relentless and cunning as they will attempt to flank you, toss grenades to flush you out of cover and many other tactics to eliminate you.
You can also send your agents out on dispatch missions that can give you access to new technology, a new recruit and other things that can turn the tide of this secret war in your favor.
There's also several documents and photos scattered about the base and mission areas that can provide a bit more backstory aside from talking to the agents and personal.
The Bureau borrows a lot of elements from the Mass Effect games, especially when it comes to how you give orders to the agents, the various powers that you will unlock and many others, but I feel like its done a bit better here then in the Mass Effect games, especially considering the setting of the game itself.
This is without a doubt one of the most interesting and fun tactical shooters for quite sometime to be released on home computers and consoles alike and I highly recommend it, especially to those who are fans of the XCOM series.

I don't really remember when I bought this game but I've been sick the last few days and been trying to find something to kill time so I installed it. Not gonna lie, was not expecting much when Lili's character model loaded on the beach and then walking towards walls pushed me forward. However, I got something that was really fantastic. I really miss this genre of games that were popular in the N64 era, and don't understand why they died out.
Basically, you're going around collecting flowers off the heads of "Spirits" which are tyrants of wood people called Contructs in order to further your studies as a ...flowerologist? (they made up some name for it don't remember anymore.)
Anyways, if you miss these open world collecting games you'll love this. It could do with a lot of fine tuning, especially with Lili. She doesn't have any idle animation except for her fingers twitching and her clothes/hair are constantly being wind blown even inside buildings. Sometimes they zoom in on her face and she's totally expressionless in the few cutscenes they have and I feel like there's more that could be done with it. Also, I don't like how she halts when she picks up flowers from the ground or breaks pots. Kills the flow and makes collecting even more tedious.
Upside, the writing is well done and a lot of the characters are extremely likeable and goofy. I actually had a good laugh at a couple of the Spirits and I don't often when I'm playing games by myself. Constructs can be kind of adorable too but many of them sit around crying about being slaves like it's even that hard on them. You got ping pong, guys. Lighten' up.
They don't hide the games influences (Legend of Zelda, Mario, Fruit Ninja are all referenced heavy handedly) so if you enjoy those games you'll have fun.

The Typing of the Dead: Overkill is a great game to add to your library because it brings a lot to the table, in a seemingly small package. At first glance it seems like a boring typing conditioner, but once you actually play the game you experience a deliciously mediocre storyline riddle with tons of humor written as an homage to old exploitation horror films. Besides the hilarious in game dialogue, the dictionary the game uses by default offers a lot of words or phrases that will keep you smiling or snickering throughout your playtime. If you spend the few extra dollars to purchase the DLC dictionaries as well, you can introduce a whole new level of silliness into the game that only adds to the humor and ridiculousness. If you ever got tired of the typing experience as well, the game comes with the House of the Dead: Overkill engine as well, so you can instead just traditionally shoot some infected.
Overall, this is the perfect kind of game to have around if you are looking for a typing trainer, or to have around just to start up on a boring night when you are looking for some brainless gameplay. It can give you some cheap thrills, some cheap laughs, and has plenty of features to keep you busy and coming back when you are bored. I imagine there are better tools out there for conditioning your typing, but I feel that I can safely say, none will be as fun as this one.

All in all this is a military training simulator designed to prepare submarine  and anti-submarine personel in the use of their stations, and Sonalysts did not care much to expand it  anywhere beyond that.
3/10

Despite having developped several videogames, Sonalysts is originaly a provider of professionnal softwares and simulators, aimed at training US Navy officers. This is clearly visible, as the gaming experience in Dangerous Waters feels a bit outdated, even for its time of release (2006). The graphics, sound effects, and gameplay possibilities are quite limited, at least compared to Silent Hunter 3, which was released a year before. On these aspects, the game is closer to Silent Hunter 2 (released 6 years prior to Dangerous Waters !), and we feel like commanding a submarine from a distance, rather than fill the shoes of a real navy officer.
That being said, the simulation part is meticulous, and has a great level of depth. We are able to command submarines (and a few other vehicles) with a high degree of realism. The game gives access to many weaponry, instrumentation (namely sonars), and takes into account a lot of physical parameters (force instance, thermal layers in the ocean having an effect on sound speed).
It takes a bit of time to fully master the operating of ships/planes/submarines, but the gaming experience is worth the effort.
Nota : apparently, DW is NOT Windows 8 compatible, and Sonalysts have stopped supporting the game. Therefore no official compatibility patch will be provided. Yet, some unoffical patches found on the subsim website may help resolve theses issue.

I was pleased with The Turing Test. It's a first-person puzzler, in the vein of Portal or Quantum Condundrum, but it also has some genes spliced from 'walking simulators' like Gone Home or Firewatch.
While some people find the puzzles too easy, I think they're about on par with the other puzzlers I mentioned, and the plot is better, making it an overall better game than other walking simulators hands-down, in my opinion. From my layman perspective, I feel like The Turing Test has one of the most convincing science fiction plots in videogames, in regards to the science. I wish they would've cleaned up some of the other plot-holes and inconsistencies, but I personally didn't find them too distracting and the game really fed my interest subject matter with a bunch of optional reading. If you're interested in transhumanism, you will get more out of The Turing Test.
The art ranges from excellent to serviceable-but-repetitive, and the music is sometimes hauntingly appropriate, and other times a little out of place.
So while The Turing Test isn't a perfect game, if you like heavy science-fiction and methodical puzzle solving, it's easy to recommend The Turing Test.

[Edit]I noticed, that some people seem to love this game, while others pretty much hate it. As you propably know by now, I'm the latter one. One word for this little game: enchanting. From the art and character design, story, the metagaming nature, and the cute protagonist named Niko. Don't be fooled by its simplicity, this game is fascinated about morbid stuff and throw some exhausting puzzles and apparently some attention to detail as well.
Despite the game mainly uses the old-school RPG game style, it manages to incorporate some gorgeous pictures which are candy eyes and endearing. Then the narratives are simply pretty life-like, not too stoic nor boring, which makes the game flows really fluid. Then the puzzles really want us to make both Niko and ourselves 'excercise'.
The metagaming and 'organic' responses are used pretty well in this game, especially in the game's narratives and when solving the puzzles. For some people this might be creepy, but in some circumstances, e.g. when the main character tries to 'talk' to the player it makes us more sympathised and even touched, which establishes the bond between the game and the player and for me it is absolutely astonishing.
Storywise, I have to say it's pretty dark and morbid. When everyone in it are just hopeless but you're as the savior have to carry a big resposibility on your shoulder to try save them despite the despair atmosphere.
In terms of design, it is absolutely gorgeous. The environment and characters are just brilliant to look at and the simplicity reminds us that beauty doesn't always come from sophisticated or complicated things. The colours are also pretty neat; the colour theme really divides each of section pretty well and it manages to create the suited atmosphere for each circumstances. Plus there are some paintings incorporated in some scenes which makes the game even more appealing.
Even though I'm only a casual gamer, this game for me a bit too short. But it doesn't mean the devs weren't doing a brilliant job. I wish more games in the future can be this adorable and facinating. This game brings both sadness, creepy and cute into one package and I'm really excited about it. I have to admit this is the very first time that actually a game could be really this engaging and I won't hide the fact that in the ending I just burst into tears, and you got to see it for yourself.
In the end, a gorgeous design, depressing but heart-warming story, a clever implementation of metagaming, heart-breaking ending(s) and obviously Niko, One Shot absolutely won my heart and this game is one of the best to stir your feelings and challenge yourself a bit.
