The Bureau is a solid tactical shooter that had an intresting twist in the story and played out rather well overall. My impressions are based on a playthrough at the highest difficulty level so I don't know how easy it gets if you crank it down.
Combat in the Bureau is not your typical shooter gameplay at all - if you run and gun you will very quickly get murdered by even the most basic of encounters. Most of your combat time is spent in a slow motion tactical menu where you can utilize soldier skills and designate targets and where to move.  Your soldiers level up as you use them in missions and gain skills based off what class they are and what you choose for them. While playing on the harder difficulties if they bleed out they will die for good adding an extra level of tension but if you stabilize them before they bleed out they will come back to life after you've killed everything in the area.
I really did feel like the commander because of the combat system and how it is very strictly defined by what you tell each soldier to do - they aren't AI's that will do everything on their own, if that's what you want this isn't the game for you at all and you will hate the combat. I felt combat was very fun and was the strong point of the game.
The story.. I have to admit after like 5 hours in I just started skipping all the dialog I really didn't care about the story at all in this particular game for some reason. Even skipping through it though it did yield a cool twist towards the end of the game that very likely causes different endings, though how different I don't know.
I recommend giving this game a shot, atleast at a discount maybe. On the hardest settings and doing every side mission I came across the game was not even 20 hours and it has no multiplayer - you could very likely cut that in half rather easily on lower settings and skipping side missions.

Rarely have I ever been so moved by a game that I've been driven to actually write a review positive or negative, the turing test is one such game. This game angers me a lot because I think it could have been much better if the writing/direction was better.
First you have Ava Turing who is probably the stupidist character I've ever played in a game (that wasn't intentionally so) she is supposed to be an astronaut specifically trained for a mission but seems to know nothing of that mission, (mainly important things that are spoilers) and also has never considered basic moral/philosophic questions. Your able to listen to audio logs that clearly explain what has happened but your characters acts complemtely shocked about what is said in them later when it is brought up in story. She will object to things that she had to have know about and trained for for literally years before going on this mission, its simply absurd.
Than there is title, the idea of the turing test is brought up a lot in the story so I hesistate to say the creates don't know what it is, but they clearly are not that well versed in the idea, the ideas presented are basically equivalent to a long youtube philosphy summary in quaility and sometimes dipping below that. Like for example there is a moment which I believe is supposed to be joking and remind you of glados, Ava askes TOM how he would sovle a puzzle and he suggests cutting off her arm or throwing her through a window. It's sort of funny but if you think about it for even a second its stupid, he has seen her solve enough of these puzzles and should also urely not want to injure her as a solution (if not least because he needs her).
Aside from those major complants the game has a real problem with flow. So the dialouge only happens when you complete a puzzle meaning if it takes you longer to solve the puzzle than it does for the dialouge to happen you just sit in silence til you're done (except for the music). The problem is this always happens, is basically impossible not too even if youre really good at the puzzles, so you end up having this conversation which will be somewhat heated at times, which is arbitarly cut off, only to finally pick up when you move forward. It feels very stiff.
Finally for my complaints I hope you like the BZZT sound effect because you hear it everytime you can't do something with the tool and despite being a sound effect isn't effect by the SFX slider or any slider except the master volume,
The puzzle overall are fine if uninspired generally it definitely wishes it was portal a lot of the time, there are a good number of references/similar elements. And the voice acting is good which is about all I can say that is really positive about it.

The game is decent for what is it, but not for the full price.
The story. I believe the story could've been conveyed in a better way, some of the dialogues felt simply void-of-life and a bit too chatty about philosophical stuff (which isn't a bad thing given the focus of the game, but some balance is needed and it wasn't quite there), while most of us would hope for being given more info about the crew and more - didn't quite happen. The main focus of the game is on puzzle solving and given the execution of the game, these two (story and the puzzle/environment) doesn't feel well connected. The very endings were executed a bit too fast and felt rushed altogether, and left me feeling rather bitter about the whole experience.
The levels. The difficulty wasn't always progressive, it could feel to easy and sometimes it could try to challenge you with something new out of nowhere. Thanks to this, finishing the levels rarely felt satisfactionary.
Some of the annoyance was about certain elements and how they worked.
Mainly the mechanics of boxes and pressing-pads. Sometimes you'd use another tool to make the box fall down on top of it to press it, but even with careful placement the gravity would sometimes get messy and make it roll elsewhere.
Visibility of the elements. The game didn't make it clear it was possible to control certain elements with the others (by such ways as highlighting), or worse scenario, some of the important elements weren't always clearly visible (on the wall in a shadow, or if placed close to each other, they had same colours - which in my opinion should be better avoided).
There were a couple of other stuff as how tedious it felt the time it took from switching from one device to another, the time between the camera changes, ...
(Oh and I absolutely hated the ladders. Please don't make me climb ladders in a puzzle game.)
I give them that esp. the bonus rooms had some clever take on puzzle solving. But at the same time I really hated how easy it sometimes was to simply walk past by them. It shoudn't be Hidden Rooms.
I believe that this game wasn't that far from a seeming perfection; it's a shame given these stuff could've been worked out with little bit more effort.

I look forward to seeing where the game developers take Osiris and hope that they will stick with it to fully flesh out what it can do.  One could argue that $25 (US) is a bit much for so little game-play at this point.  But, I also tend to look at these things from a longer look with the hope that the game will see a good long life.  I paid the $25 because I really like what the game could eventually become...sort of "paying it forward" kind of thinking.

I'm amazed. Absolutely amazed. I CAN NOT believe that a game THIS GOOD has slipped under my radar (and a lot of other people's) for SO LONG. As of writing this review on December 11th, 2017, I have completed my second playthrough about 30 minutes ago. After owning this game for only 36 hours I have logged 10 hours, and it is my favorite story-rich Steam game of all time. Maybe even flat-out favorite story-rich game of ALL TIME.
You have just woken up in a dimly lit house, as what appears to be a cat-like humanoid. You quickly learn this characters name is Niko. As you walk around and begin the gameplay, you slowly realize that OneShot is NOT your average Puzzle/Adventure game. It does an excellent job of letting you know this before you even leave the first room, less than two minutes into the game. Just wait, this game goes to extreme levels with its puzzles. Let’s just say that some things are done that are absolutely phenomenal.
The more you play through the first 20 minutes of the game the more you will draw comparisons to Undertale. Let me assure you. This game is significantly better than Undertale in every way.
Whether you hate Undertale and want to stop playing because you think it’s the same old game, or you love Undertale and don't want to play a rip-off, do not quit this game. You will miss out on a hell of a lot.
The main gimmick of this game is the meta-ness and the fourth wall breaking being a part of the actual story. On top of this, each puzzle is meticulously thought out so every single thing you do in-game makes sense. Nothing is too difficult, nothing is too easy. It’s difficult to describe how well this is done in a review without spoilers. Just trust me, you will see things you have likely never seen in a game. It can and will amaze you in more ways than one.
This game is a masterpiece the likes of which I have never seen before. I have never been so instantly immersed in a world and stayed so until all the story was exhausted a whole 10 hours later. I do not know if I’ve ever felt so emotionally attached to a fictional character, ever, in my life. If you have never seen gameplay of this, or hell, even heard of it, don’t spoil yourself, experience it first-hand and buy this gem. You will not be disappointed.

One word for this game, beautiful. I purchased this game on a whim purely because the graphics looked interesting but it was so much more than that. Amazing graphics, incredible soundtrack, loveable characters and interesting gameplay mechanics - OneShot has it all. I would highly recommend this game to anyone and everyone purely for its amazing storyline. 10/10

This is the jankiest, most sluggish online shooter I've ever played.

Aside from the game's setting appealing to the part of my lizard brain that love cowboys and shoot-bang, I'm constantly drawn back in by the feeling of accomplishment you get from adapting to the jank and becoming decent at cowboy-ing it up, and the experiences you can have while playing this game.

team was outside spamming dynamite into the building.

You don't actually fall, you were really just kicked
.
This game is god damn magical.  Once you get past the weird jankiness of everything, you can enter a whole new world of memorable video game moments.  I can't wait to spend another almost 100 hours on this.

This is my game of the year.
I love the idea of picking any country in the world from 1936 and seeing the impact I have on the war; for example, turning Brazil fascist, dominating South America and causing Britain to go ballistic and launch constant naval invasions against me.
The game has three difficulties plus an iron-man setting to challenge more skilled players, playing as Germany on normal setting is a near-guaranteed win, while playing on a tough setting as a minor nation is near-impossible to win yet it's fun to try and impact the war. The game itself is very fun. Also, the focus tree and research trees are very well balanced and in-depth, with some bespoke to specific nations.
However, I do understand critical points made from other reviewers and there is room for improvement, but to pay in excess of £10 for each expansion seems very unfair considering the game itself is £34.99 as I type. Even then, this game seems slightly neglected in comparison to past installments including EU4. Paradox should take a leaf out of Valve's book, where CSGO is only £11.99 and is usually always undergoing TLC.
Overall, I think the game is amazing. If you want to try what Hitler failed to do, go ahead. Likewise, if you want to turn America into the Communist States of America and rule alongside the Soviets, do that too. The game allows you to have fun and presents so many opportunities for you to dictate the war. Personally for me the game was worth the money, but if in doubt watch a playthrough or two of the game on YouTube. It's challenging at first glance but don't let that put you off what is a great game.

Its hard for me to say but DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!!!!!!!!!!!!.
Its a broken piece of garbage and at its current state is only suited for multiplayer matches cause then you do not have to get frustrated by the veryveryvery stupid AI.
Does this game has any plussides? Yes and no. It has good ideas but the execution of those ideas is lacking and amateurisch at least. We always get the promise from paradox that the problems will get fixed in the next patch or paid dlc. But I have had enough. The base game is just not good and badly developed. Its just to dumbed down and buggy.
A few examples.
1)
If you can avoid a war long enough you can steamroll the AI. This because troopupkeep is non existent (all the sliders from HOI II and III are gone). Because of that flaw the AI will continue to produce troops (until he used up all of his manpower) and place them at the borders. Then attrition kicks in so he starts losing preciously build equipment. So after a few years you have AI countries that have massively huge armies with hardly any equipment left. In previous games you had to stop building units at a certain point because you economy could not keep them up anymore.
2)
Armycreation is so dumbed down that I have the feeling that paradox was just plain lazy and then made a pissjob doing it.
In HOI III you could create divisions (some had unique names like ss units etc), armycorps, armies, armygroups and theaters with an entire commander tree in place. Mj General, Lt General, General, Field Marshall
In IV you build a division jam them in an army and assign them to a commander and theater. Theaters are useless they are just in place so that your lower toolbar doesnt get crammed with army portraits. Then they implemented a nice feature called the frontlines and defensive lines etc. Its nice but you have to assign each army with its own frontline and on a large front becomes very tedious. And the AI isnt helping either. Once you start gaining ground to lines shift so irraticly that you are managing more the frontlines then your armies cause overextending happens a lot. So something nice done horribly wrong.
3)
Aircombat and Naval Warfare are broken as hell.
The creation of aireal units with officers is gone. Just jam a number of units on an airstrip and have at it. Or get ready to get frustrated.
The mechanic of an airplane in my book is that is flies from point A to B. In HOI IV thats not the case. Here the airplanes pop up at the sector you assign them to attack for instance. German bombers are bombing the crap out of london. They are stationed in France so they have to pass through a zone called the english channel. Logic dictates that if I put interceptors up in the skies of the channel I will intercept the bombers before they reach the target right? Not in this game. In Paradoxes WWII simulator the people of the world use wormholes or warptechnology to reach the target area.
And again due to a lack of any normal resource usage in the game airplanes dont consume fuel. So build 20000 planes you can let them fly for ever and ever without any problem. Never knew people in the 40's were that advanced.
The same goes for ships. In HOI III at a certain point you had to stop building ships due to their constant need of fuel. Dont worry here givin enough time Belgium can build 50 carriers without breaking a sweat.

I had doubts when I bought the game, burnt by the many cookie cutter 4x clones out in the market.  However, Stellar Monarch surprises with a novel approach to the 4x genre.  It cuts away a large amount of micromanagement present in 4x games while maintaining the feel of a game with complex underlying mechanics.  The drawn graphics actually make the game more charming and immersive unlike other titles that have opted for souless 3D assets.
The best comparison to Stellar Monarch is if a simple cell strategy game like SolarMax is designed to be in the 4x genre; turn-based, massively expanded in scope with advanced resource and colony resource management, research, diplomacy and combat.
The right level of abstraction is needed and I believe Stellar Monarch comes close to making the perfect balance between the simple 4x phone games and more complex 4x games like MOO, Galactic Civilizations or Stellaris.  The design direction is great and will be appreciated by people who enjoyed the 4x classics.
If you're looking for something fresh, this game doesn't disappoint.

I've played Rift since, I think, a week after it's initial release and I cannot recommend it highly enough.  It's only gotten better.  I would honestly say it is a BETTER game overall than World of Warcraft AND it's free-to-play.  It was largely glitch-free even upon initial release and it has only improved.  (I can't even say that about Elder Scrolls Online, my favorite MMORPG.)  The graphics are stellar (probably the best for MMORPG next to ESO), gameplay is engrossing, and the lore is gripping.  From the very beginning, I felt committed to this cause and involved in the game.  I love that the game brings mini-instances to you by dropping rifts and implementing zone events on a regular basis.  There are only 6 races (all humanoid), but there is a wide range of customization available straight off when making your character and then again once in-game with armor dyes and the barber.  And I absolutely cannot praise enough the soul tree system of skill advancement they use.  It is a really great idea and allows for a lot of customization when it comes to your class.
There's only two things I can really say AGAINST the game: 1) since it is free-to-play, a lot of the cooler items are available only through the in-game store.  However, they are not items necessary to "win" the game.  You can still easily succeed at the game with crafted items made of materials you farmed yourself.  The store available for sell is largely just collectible items like mounts, costumes, and companions and the prices they are sold at verge on extortion.  2) Dimensions, while a cool concept, seem kinda like a pointless addendum to the game.  I just have a bunch of dimension items taking up space in my bank and bags.  They tend to accumulate quickly.
Other than that, if you love fantasy MMORPG's, you cannot miss Rift.  If you give it a try, I don't think you'll be disappointed.  It is a cool steampunk-ish  spin on your standard fantasy MMORPG.  It has grit and polish at the same time.  I find that pretty impressive.

4.5/5 RIFT is a free to play MMO with a familiar (Warcraft) feel to it, that does enough to distinguish itself from all the other f2p MMOs out there.
- The class system has been designed with flexibility in mind. Every class has the ability to switch roles, so you could be tanking in a dungeon one minute and doing solo quests as a DPS the next. MMO newbies can play with preset skill-trees to avoid being overwhelmed, whilst MMO veterans can tinker away with custom builds to their heart's content.
- Dynamic zone events. You can be quietly questing in a zone, when suddenly, rifts open up spawning mobs and eventually, the event boss.  This encourages everyone in a zone to band together to close rifts and take down the boss, which is great fun.
- How you choose to level up is really flexible. Do quests, instant adventures (kill/fetch quests with other players), zone events or dungeons.
- RIFT is still actively being developed. Version 3.0 is due soon (end of Otober 2014)
- Once you hit lvl 50, a new skill tree system (planar attunement) opens up, offering more customisation. A special set of dungeons (Chronicles) designed for 1-2 playes also becomes accessible from lvl 50+.
- If want to try dungeons (designed for 5 players) but haven't got guild friends to join with, you can join a dungeon queue that will automatically match 5 random players together. (Note: the wait time depends on your role, it seems that tanks are in short supply, followed by healers)

- Quests can get a bit grindy sometimes; many are of the "collect 20 of .."  or "kill 12 of ..." variety. However, occasionally you do come across more fun/unusual/interesting/innovative quests, lifting the game above your standard MMO.
- Some zones are not well optimized and FPS will suddenly drop from a smooth 60fps down to 20fps.
- Free players can buy stuff from the auction house but can't sell (although there is a trade chat channel available). It is possible however to use in-game currency (plat) to buy something called REX that another player has paid for using real cash. The REX can be used to unlock the ability to sell in the auction house.
Recommendation: If you want to experience the fun and familiarity of an MMO like Warcraft, but don't want to pay a monthly subscription, then RIFT will provide exactly what you are looking for. It is a well-designed, flexible game ... and did I mention it was free?

Oh, Lili, where have you been all my life? It's hard to argue with anyone that might label this as a port of a casual, mobile, kid's game; you'll play as a young woman on a field trip wandering around an island, picking flowers, making friends and not really being challenged all that much. But while all that may be true, to be so reductive is to a do a great disservice to an amazing hidden gem of a game.
The most obvious strength of Lili: Child of Geos is its visuals, as there's a glowing radiance emitting from every individual pore of the world along with everything that populates it. But what's less obvious is the writing that backs it up. I feel like the dialogue in a lot of games is there merely to facilitate moving the player to the next objective or set piece, and I guess that's fair enough since actual game play is typically going to be the feature that gets top billing while the story is little more than connective tissue to form vague context for your actions. However, I think people sometimes forget gaming is an entertainment medium, and there's lots of other ways to entertain besides pure play, a fact this game thankfully does remember and arguably makes its greatest triumph.
The story is a strange mix of being playfully throw-away and surprisingly thoughtful and philosophical. Lili travels to the island of Geos in search of its unique floral life as part of a final school exam, but once there finds it is inhabited by Spirits and their workforce of slave Constructs. These large, wooden homunculi must tolerate the bullying whims of their masters lest they cease to exist upon failure to serve their purpose. I probably make it sound much heavier than it really is, but it does at least dabble with notions of free will and life choices and prioritising the things that are really important to us, which are bigger issues than most titles will ever dare to approach. As it transpires, these Spirits have the most exotic flowers, which also gives them their power over the Constructs, setting the scene for several hours of roaming Geos searching for Constructs to help and Spirits to deflower.
Geos is made up for four medium sized districts that are unlocked sequentially as you rid each one of its Spirits. The game and its world may not be huge, but that just allows them to focus on populating it with beauty as every inch of the environments are lovingly crafted with a wondrous level of detail. In many games you'll find yourself wandering into some stranger's house and find the entirety of their personal dwelling is made up of a table and a few chairs, or maybe a bunk bed and a fireplace if they're lucky, that sort of thing. I love how every single house in this game looks properly lived-in, with bedrooms, kitchens and even bathrooms, which really sells the illusion that this is a real world being inhabited by real people... or wooden slaves and freaky tree spirit things, in this case. I really wish more games would take the same effort to make the peripheries of the world just as interesting as its core like this one does.
Unfortunately, when it comes to game play, that's where I'd probably have to admit the game is at its weakest. You'll spend the majority of your time here either picking flowers, smashing vases, looting chests, talking to people or ambushing Spirits, with the amount of time you spend on each of these things pretty much depending on the type of player you are and what you decide to make your goals for this game. There's no combat as such, and you can't die, the only real challenge being trying to jump on the backs of the game's 50 Spirits and playing rodeo with them as you pluck their flowers off. Otherwise it's all a very leisurely affair, the only other complication being upgrades to help make your plucking experience a little easier.
So, yes, it's kinda short, it's arguably shallow in some areas, and it isn't massively challenging, but there really is so much warmth and charm and personality exuding from every part of this game that I feel like it more than makes up for any other shortcomings. Lili herself in particular is the very embodiment of this as she's an incredibly lovable foil to the rest of the cast and a perfect example of a well-balanced female lead that's entirely capable in her own right rather than lazy developers falling back on sexuality to sell a character. I think there's still great depths of enjoyment to be drawn from Geos, and especially from Lili herself, and I can't wait to join her again on her next adventure.

Lili: Child of Geos is a beautiful and relaxing action adventure. When I saw screens of it I first thought this is probably some kind of highly polished hidden object game. What “sold” me was when I discovered you can actually walk this marvellous world.
Item hint:
+ Beautiful somehow cuddly graphics
+ Mostly relaxing atmosphere
+ Okay story, hints to a possible prequel
+ References
+ Moderate length
+ Game advises to visit the options menu and asks to automatically determine graphics settings
+ Basically no grinding
+ Good controls
0 Unfortunately no voice acting
0 Different camera modes
- Some advertising for another BitMonster game
- Level cap, making it impossible to max out all skills with the same avatar
- Flowers sometimes in places that are simply unreachable
I started playing this game in the hope it would provide a counterpoint to Dead Island which had become exhausting and bullseye. After playing like 15 minutes I felt pretty relaxed. The game still has tense moments but all in all it's a pretty tranquil experience.
Although the game's world is not too big it has an expansive feel to it, maybe because it looks lived-in or alive.
The back story is rather light, maybe owed to the mobile origins of the game. You control Lili who has come to Geos as a Vegi-Magical student from the Gildern Magis College (with a deadline) but is quickly entangled in in the conflicts of a two-class society. Most NPCs have some depth to them which you learn by interacting with them, i.e. fighting the bad ones (Spirits) and talking to the good ones (Constructs). There is usually a reward for exhausting interaction.
There are some indicators to a story that happened before so there may be a prequel.
The Constructs are wood-based being making a disturbingly wood-based living in wooden houses with wooden furniture and wooden toilets, even toilet paper
.
There are a number of pop-references in the game and there is a mock pop-quiz where Lili can show off here extensive knowledge of games.
There is also occasional, not too much, advertisement for another game by BitMonster.
The game is of moderate length and may take you two evenings to complete. You can explore the world some more after you beat it. There are a number of achievements that may make you play some more and the “max out skill” achievements actually require you to stature at least one additional game – it took me not quite an hour to max out a single stat. Besides that there is almost no grinding.
Unfortunately, there is no voice-acting. Instead there are a few generic sounds or words, e.g. “Hello”, and Lili's feelings are well-done by stances and facial expressions.
With so many games not actually having any actual options, I found it interesting that the game starts out with advising you to go to the options menu and offers to automatically determine your machine's graphic settings.
The controls work fine with the world's topology and are pretty tight with few exceptions. When chasing a Spirit it happened at times that instead of jumping onto them I suddenly found myself in conversation with a Construct or picking a flower because the game decided that was more likely what I wanted. Then you're supposed to collect flowers set around the world but a few of them are simply set in places Lili can never reach, e.g under bridges.
There is a number of different camera modes that aren't listed in the games help - I didn't find any use for them. Activated them with keys Insert, Delete, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown, then move around a bit to see their effect.
Lili: Child of Geos was a lot of fun and I recommend it. I bought the game as part of a bundle and probably wouldn't buy it for the full price (currently 10 Euros) but wait for 50% off. I'd be delighted  to see another game of this kidney, maybe a sequel or Orchid prequel.

MY REVIEW OF PAINKILLER BLACK (RECOMMEDED) (since it won't let me post it and it keeps saying that I need to play it for five minutes when I've played 17.4 hours of it)
Painkiller is a fully old school shooter from 2004.
The story is about a man called Daniel who dies in a car crash with his wife, his wife goes to heaven and he is stuck in purgatory, he is assigned to kill Satan’s generals, he is also aided by a woman named Eve. The story is stupid and crappy and takes itself too seriously and just like every other old school shooter it is almost forgotten during gameplay and really doesn’t matter at all.
Since this is an old school shooter you do what you’d expect you would do which is going from point A to B killing everything along the way. You go through these large and well-designed levels killing all of the enemies to activate the exit point, the enemies spawn in and each area is locked off until all of the enemies in the area are killed, and each new area you’ll go to will have a save point. In painkiller you have some fun and interesting weapons such as: the painkiller which is basically a propeller blade on the end of a stick, a shotgun crossed with a gun that can freeze enemies, a stake gun that also fires grenades, a rocket launcher that’s also a mini-gun, and a gun that shoots shurikens and lightning. You also move fairly slowly but you can gain momentum by bunny hopping.
The music is one of the best soundtracks I’ve ever heard in a game, all of the music is all rock that is really good and really fits the gameplay, the soundtrack is so good that there have been times where I have killed all of the enemies and wished that the music didn’t stop playing.
Battle out of hell
Battle out of hell is the first expansion pack for painkiller and there’s only one chapter but it lasts for ten levels and it adds in a multi- stake gun that also shoots explosive balls, and a machinegun crossed with a flamethrower.
Problems:
Strict health system: since painkiller is an old school shooter you’d be playing it on a high difficulty, but is where this problem happens the most, the health system is really strict since there are very few health pick-ups lying around a level and they only give back 25 health and a lot of the health you’ll collect comes from the souls of the enemies and one soul=one health and the souls take quite a small while to appear and once you’ve killed everyone in the area a lot of them will have disappeared.
Very small hit boxes on enemies: the hit boxes in this game are so small that if you fire a rocket into a group of enemies, unless you are aiming directly at one of them the rocket will just fly right through a whole group of enemies, this also applies for the stake gun.
The haze effect: when you get hit by a melee weapon in this game it does this annoying haze effect where everything will be blurry for a second which causes the framerate to tank to maybe ten frames a second.
The enemy AI: the enemy AI isn’t very smart which is fine since in every other old school shooter the AI isn’t very smart and its meant to be like that but in painkiller its much worse to the point where they will get stuck on objects or you’ll just be searching for one enemy who’s stuck in a corner somewhere when you’ve killed everyone else.
The boss fights: the boss fights in painkiller are probably the worst part about the game, since during the boss fights there are large destructible physics objects such as pillars that will constantly get stuck in your way making you a sitting duck, there are also unnecessary design choices such as this one boss where after you’ll take all of his health away he’ll destroy the floor putting you and him to the next floor below which keeps killing you because of the fall damage.
Sadly the music in battle out of hell is nowhere near as good is it is in the original game.
Despite these problems Painkiller is a very good game with entertaining gunplay and combat but will fall a little short due to these problems, it’s not as good as DOOM or serious Sam but you should play this if you like old school shooters.

Evolve is clearly a passion project for this team, otherwise they would have abandoned the game rather than rework it. A lot of concepts in Evolve's previous incarnation sounded great on paper, but didn't work so well in practice. Many of these aspects have been re-worked, others have been outright removed, all to give the players a better, more fun, more engaging experience. I never played the original evolve, but I think the people who are upset for spending so much money sight unseen are unfairly criticizing the fact that their shinies have been reset to the same level as the reset of the peons. This complaint might be fair were the Legacy version of Evolve not still accessable to the people who bought it.
Evolve Stage 2 is a different beast (no pun intended) from its original incarnation, and as such having everyone start off on a level playing field makes sense. The barrier to entry of cost is no longer a factor, a smart move on Turtlerock's part, so the only other real barrier would have been people with an unfair advantage from having spent money when there is currently (July 18th 2016) no functioning cash shop in the game.
The developers seem to have taken criticism to heart in how they've re-tooled everything, making the matches shorter and more action packed, which in turn amps up the tension and the overall fun.
Be aware, though, that monsters are at a disadvantage in the early game and you may as well be playing Dark Souls until you fully evolve.
There are still a few things here and there that need to be fine-tuned and balanced, but they're definitely on the right track.
At the current price of $0.00 you can grab your friends and have a good time. Particularly entertaining when you're all in a third-party voice program and one of you is the monster and there's pick-up player with bad manners on the hunter team.

If you are familiar with
style tabletop games, then the abstractions and economic focus (vice military control) will feel very familiar to you. The game's pillars are not based on American-style wargames.
Many devs who make 4X games seem to have the souls of engineers; Aurora 4x being the archetype. In those games micromanagement focuses on design, production, and use of
like ships. Mastery of those concepts leads to victory.
This game requires micromanagement and is numerically obtuse as well, but it focuses on the qualitative values of game elements (i.e. cards) instead of design, production and use of things.
Like Eurogame board games, the elements in Stellar Monarch are driven and controlled by complex sets of rules and their interactions. Also like a board or card game, many of the rules seem arbitrary and unreasonable. In a board game this is required for simplicity and balance, but modern PC games are usually more refined.
(Better) PC games usually give players a better illusion of control and keep their rules meaningful, but subtle. The player's actions are more independent and positive and negative feedback loops are more sophisticated.
I'll highlight by using an example of Stellar Monarch's military officers.
At first blush this would seem to be an interesting and detailed mini-game. In Stellar Monarch, like a card game, the player is
officers and can see all the detailed information about them. However, when presented with clearly bad officers, the player is very overtly constrained from taking action by the game rules. Instead of the player feeling in control and being immersed, the rules dictate an arbitrary discard system which results in the deal of yet another random officer card.
For example, despite perfect knowledge of their Commodores' issues, the player is unable to act on that information effectively and suspension of disbelief is broken. There are no subtle consequences or positive/negative feedback loops -- just a hard and fast rule, "You cannot discard a commodore card." It's ironic that less numerical precision about a Commodore's qualitative value might have been better for the player's overall game experience.
If you don't like card or board games, particularly Eurogames, you will find these kinds of weaknesses pervasive in the game's design.
EDIT: Previously known as Pocket Space Empire, the dev changed its name to Stellar Monarch.

I'm not particularly happy about this game for its price point. It should be $15 or less, ideally $10 for what you get.
While it's a good idea and a relatively polished execution, the game is somewhat less than what is promised in terms of grand strategy FUN, rather than implementation.
The game essentially distances you too far BACK from being invested in it, alongside a very unclear (if ultimately relatively simple) learning curve (the fleets especially).
Combat is essentially positioning forces near planets you want, then pushing a squadron one by one onto the enemy planet. It's not so much hard as it is very unclear why you're winning or losing and almost RNG-esque if not for just spamming larger fleets on enemy planets.
Diplomacy is largely a wash; there's no real differentiation fluff-wise with other civilizations aside from a blurb and their racial character art. In fact, fluff is very weak in this game and makes it hard to role-play if you were looking for that in an empire-builder. You barely emotionally care about whatever's going on beyond taking more territory and balancing out various gewgaws of imperialism (from your Courtiers to what fleets are where to the annoying as hell Hive universal enemy).
What takes the cake is the eventual Rebel era which essentially stole all of my frontier-expanding invasion fleets in one "well F you, player" swoop with very little explanation other than "the Era changed and now all the previously pretty loyal planets and the fleets on them now HATE you and will fight to the utter death against you."
THE BIG tl;dr:
5-6 out of 10 (Not worth the current price, but bless the developers for trying)
I really want to like this game, because I feel it could ultimately be very charming, but it ends up being a sadly mediocre (if valiant) attempt to build a great empire builder that takes out the micromanagement of other games like CK2 or the Total War military series. There was a lot of potential here.
You just want to be invested in your empire, but are carried along by momentum of "one more turn" hoping you'll find enjoyment. The game however doesn't really give a damn about you similarly, sadly.

I was quite hesitant to buy this game because it looked quite simplistic from the pictures, but having spent nearly 20 hours with it I've definitely had a full on romance with it.
The game definitely lives up to its description as a game that is about leading an empire, it's extremely strategic and you really do feel like you're in charge of a sprawling empire amongst the stars rather than a game player manipulating a spread sheet with graphics. There are quite a lot of moving parts to the games' mechanics and it means there is always something to be thinking about and doing. I've played it on the easier levels so far to get the hang of it and am really excited about making use of some of the other parts of the game that haven't featured so heavily for me on the higher levels (at the easier levels you can ignore the diplomacy as you steamroll over everyone, I suspect that won't be the case at the 5 higher levels I've yet to play!).
Be aware that at date of writing (December 2016) it's only just launched and there are a few kinks that need to be ironed out, however the developer is very engaged with the community and responds to posts and questions in the steam forum, so I have every confidence it will get even better over time.
If I have one criticism of the game it is, like many strategy games, that the tutorial doesn't tell you many of the things that you wish you'd known hours into the game. That said, this game possibly is the best I've ever played for informative tool tips - every single facet of the game's mechanics are explained if you take the time to read the tool tips over the numerous screens. Yes it's a little overwhelming to start with, but it absolutely isn't a black box, you can learn to play it well.
I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a good 4x strategy, particulary if you don't like micromanagement, and if you just want to play one... more... turn...

Surprisingly enjoyable.
Despite its low end graphics and un-storied developer, this title is worth your time especially if you are into Paradox strategy games.
It's a quick, hands off, space based 4x, the conceit being that you are the immortal emperor of the Terran race, ruling from the centre of the galaxy, naturally superior to all. To win you must be prestigious enough, blood-thirsty enough or valorous enough to claim the title of "Ruler of all Galaxy" (developer is not a native English speaker, cut them a little slack). Anyone familiar with the Warhammer 40K licence should find some common ground here, but it also calls on classic sci-fi such as Asimov and Clarke.
There is almost no micro-management in this title, that's what you have courtiers and councillors for, instead you are concerned with balancing political power, addressing the court and dictating the fleets. It is, as the name might suggest, like crusader kings for a pocket-able device.
Despite it's low-fi feel, it does a good job of depicting what it would be to be the immortal emperor of Terra, dictating the growth of your people and seeing off the mewling, un-evolved alien races of the galaxy.
For people who want to be space emperor.

Hello Neighbor is the most scariest stealth horror game I have played, and can bring some jump scares just through audio. It has a very nice gameplay but has been ruined by the latest ‘Alpha 3’ (of this review). I am hoping this will be improved. Want to find out what I think of this game? Watching this game throughout development has been amazing. Alpha 1 was a blast but had some very stupid bugs. Luckily, it was replaced with Alpha 2 which is so far, the best alpha played and personally, should replace Alpha 3. Beta 1 was very buggy as well as Beta 2 but was saved with the final beta before release. All the issues I had with previous builds were listened to by tinyBuild and all fixed, ready for release.
Audio - The audio is very realistic and scary. Hearing thumping when the Neighbor sees you does bring a bit of frightfulness to the game experince. Hearing objects break are pretty amazing and sounds like real life. I really do like the audio and it is pretty nice for a cool 'indie' game.
Gameplay - [Alpha 3] The goal of the game is to reach the door to the basement. Although it sounds easy enough, it’s not. There are traps (bear traps) and obstacles in your way (i.e the fence / gate upstairs). Most importantly, there is your neighbour. You need to keep an eye on him and if you see him, you’re screwed. You can find items such as a flashlight, crowbar and more throughout the house that can help you get to the end.
Graphics / Visuals - This game has incredible / smooth graphics that look very ‘cartoonish’. The item graphics are very overwhelming. Unlike most indie games, this game includes a thorough settings which allows you to change the most important features which impacts your performance a lot. You can change anti-aliasing, post-processing, shadows, view distance, textures and another one. This game brings very tense gameplay and having the nice visuals give you a bit of the horror genre. This game is also amazingly optimised for computers and seeming I have a slightly worse graphics card and an older processor (i3) than the minimum specs, this game runs perfect on medium settings. It is definetly worth picking up if you have 6GB RAM or more.

Evolve is clearly a passion project for this team, otherwise they would have abandoned the game rather than rework it. A lot of concepts in Evolve's previous incarnation sounded great on paper, but didn't work so well in practice. Many of these aspects have been re-worked, others have been outright removed, all to give the players a better, more fun, more engaging experience. I never played the original evolve, but I think the people who are upset for spending so much money sight unseen are unfairly criticizing the fact that their shinies have been reset to the same level as the reset of the peons. This complaint might be fair were the Legacy version of Evolve not still accessable to the people who bought it.
Evolve Stage 2 is a different beast (no pun intended) from its original incarnation, and as such having everyone start off on a level playing field makes sense. The barrier to entry of cost is no longer a factor, a smart move on Turtlerock's part, so the only other real barrier would have been people with an unfair advantage from having spent money when there is currently (July 18th 2016) no functioning cash shop in the game.
The developers seem to have taken criticism to heart in how they've re-tooled everything, making the matches shorter and more action packed, which in turn amps up the tension and the overall fun.
Be aware, though, that monsters are at a disadvantage in the early game and you may as well be playing Dark Souls until you fully evolve.
There are still a few things here and there that need to be fine-tuned and balanced, but they're definitely on the right track.

If you're a fan of First Person Puzzlers that skillfully manage to intertwine its narrative and puzzles (Portal 2, Talos Principle) or ones that force you to think outside the box and slowly build up your own understanding of the world's rules and boundaries (The Witness, Antichamber) then you might want to steer clear of this one... Unless you're completely starved for your next first person puzzle gaming fix and simply don't mind it being tedious, repetitive, overly simplistic, repetitive and, bafflingly enough, both highly derivative and uninspired at the same time. It's also really rather repetitive.
In my opinion the most important element, the puzzle design, is woefully undercooked. Few of the puzzles require any real thought and most of them simply involve laboriously executing that one obvious solution that immediately jumps out at you after looking at all the available elements in any given puzzle - It feels like it never goes far beyond the introductory stage for its individual elements and rarely, if ever, tries to do anything interesting with them, which leads to the everpresent feeling that pretty much everything overstays its welcome - Which, in itself, is a feat, considering that the game is only about 4-6 Hours long.
Now I'm not entirely opposed to sacrificing puzzle difficulty/complexity for the sake of a strong narrative, but sadly this isn't the case here, either. While I can't say that I hated the story it sadly was about as underdeveloped and simplistic as the puzzles. There simply isn't much to it, much of it, and what little plot developement there is is constantly sabotaged by the bizarre, stilted and disconnected pacing of it all. The story and the puzzling simply never mesh together, the game never attempts to use downtime within puzzles to move the plot along and instead harshly seperates the two elements. There is an unintentional, to me often comedic feeling of artificiality to everything and even the admittedly occasionally fantastic voice acting doesn't help to change that.
The somewhat unpolished feel that permeates the technical presentation also doesn't help - The game consistently feels clunky and sometimes downright unpleasant to control (ie activatable panels that require overly long presses and camera focus to activate, the unwieldy feeling of the remote bot and cameras and so on) and zone transitions and loading screens feel abrupt and often jarring. It's not a bad looking game, though, and visually there's subjectively very little to complain about.
Long story short, this sits somewhere between "ehhch, maybe with a deep, deep discount" and "avoid".

I'm sick and tired of seeing reviews saying "just play this or that game" without actually telling me anything about the game for fear of "spoiling" it. Let this review of mine serve as an example of how you can still let people know whether or not they'll be likely to enjoy a game WITHOUT spoiling anything important.
Gameplay-wise, OneShot is just a series of puzzles. It has "puzzle" puzzles such as a light sokoban puzzle in one place, "adventure game" puzzles like "go find the code and type it in" or "combine item A with item B and use it on object C". The puzzles are all pretty good, the adventure game ones are logical and/or very well hinted, and basically every item serves some purpose. Generally speaking, if you look everywhere and talk to everyone you'll probably know exactly what to do when you get to where you need to do something. The "puzzle" puzzles vary in difficulty from extremely easy to maybe moderately hard; I had to get a notepad file out and actually think a bit for a couple of them, but nothing had me tearing my hair out in frustration or giving up and looking up the solution, which is a very good sign.
The game plays with its medium a bit. Some puzzles involve going and looking at/messing with files on your computer instead of things inside the game proper. I don't consider this a spoiler considering it's something you start to see within the first five minutes of the game, and it's not really even an especially exceptional feature these days, as far as I'm concerned. But it is a well-used feature, even if the "go do things with your files" puzzles are among the easiest the game has, and it ties in well with the game's overall story and themes.
The game's visuals are all original and very nice, a good several steps above your typical RPG maker fare. The music is all good, not a lot of actual melodies present but it does the job of setting the tone for each part of the story very well. The story is good and does have a happy ending to find, which I personally consider a must for any story-driven game whatsoever. There is a good sense of humor and a lot of heart here, and enough charm right from the start for a person like me who doesn't usually like "adventure games" as a genre to not just press on, but actually enjoy it.
As one final note, you will see a few reviews saying something about getting a permanent game over if you close the game instead of saving when it basically forces you to save. I was originally going to say something about the game not respecting the player's time as a result of this, but thankfully this is no longer true in the latest patch. You don't have to worry about digging up your save files and deleting them and starting all over if your computer has a power outage or the game crashes or you have to close it and leave for some reason. Good on the developers for that.
Generally I would say that if your first impressions of this game are good, you're likely to enjoy it. It's quality stuff. If you don't like any of what I've just described then this might not be for you.

It's a first-person puzzler, a short game, and its strengths are in the level design and concept, not the visuals. Honestly it feels like a game that should have been built in a different engine other than Unreal. I'm guessing it's Unreal because every indie game made in Unreal has to have the shiniest metal surfaces and bloom that feels like you're sitting in a dentist's chair and someone knocked off your sunglasses. I got Talos Principle to run on a laptop with 4 GB of on-board RAM perfectly. My PC has 16 GB just on the board and I had problems. (I realize RAM is just one possible aspect but it's the only specification I can recall from memory rn.)
That may be a source of all the negative reviews, because the types of people who have PCs that can manage to play this game are the type of people who want the high-end games. Maybe I'm stereotyping, but I don't care. If it ran better on lower-end PCs and looked like something for the indie crowd too maybe that would help. Right now it looks like a game marketed toward CoD players. I'm not that guy. I like stuffy, pretentious art games. This is the perfect game for me and I wouldn't have known it if I hadn't just randomly found it one day.

Lili: Child of Geos is a 3rd person casual adventure game about picking flowers and exploring a strange, colorful and cartoony island. Said island is under the tyrannical ruler of the Mayor of the wood spirits. So, what's a girl to do? Pick flowers off of their heads until she viva la revolutions the entire island. Duh. I mean, using a sword/gun is so 2012 anyway. Well, the non-voice acted characters in this game are happy enough to greet you upon your arrival. Some have side quests and others just want to chat. The side quests are amusing (and sometimes eye-raising) but are pretty much busy work fetch quests. The exploration is reasonable but a bog standard affair of finding keys and opening locked doors/chests to locate the multitude of artifacts in the game. What’s rather interesting about the key system is that you can buy a skeleton key pretty early on and it makes a key vendor completely pointless before you even get the chance to encounter him. That wasn’t well thought out. Otherwise, this is a fairly standard and mechanically light adventure game. So, let’s talk about the flower picking.

The main mechanic to fight the wood spirits is picking a certain amount of white flowers plus the final red flower from their heads within the time limit that Lili can hold onto the spirits. You have to sneak up to them or catch them in a run in order to start the flower-picking mini-game and this isn't very difficult to accomplish. Picking flowers is done by click and holding a flower and then dragging them away from a spirit’s weaving head as they run around. Lili must do this while avoiding accidental clicks on thorns or allowing bombs to explode. There are also green flowers that extend's her grip time and gold-coin flowers that give Lili, well, more gold. There are also “bonus rounds” where the head may be covered with bombs, gold coin flowers or thorns. Upon completing the level, the game will rate your score, giving you one to three stars for how well you did. You can then replay each spirit to get a better score, if you wish. This is repeated for every wood spirit “fight” and the only thing that really changes is the difficulty and amount of grip time Lili has.
This mechanic isn’t the most interesting I’ve stumbled across. It definitely feels like it was designed for touch screens first and it doesn’t make the best transition to the mouse. Its passable when using the mouse but I think you’d find it more entertaining on a tablet. The flower picking is certain different from what I normally see. However, I will say that It’s good that the campaign is as short as it is. Since it really starts to run out of steam towards the end. I can’t imagine a longer campaign sustaining itself on the back of this idea.
While Lili claims it’s a RPG hybrid, it’s an extremely bare-boned one. The only things you can customize when you level up are your running speed, time under stealth and grip aka how long you can hold onto forest spirits. Which are certainly helpful to progress through the game, there’s not a lot of in-depth choice to any of these stats. The other things you can customize are Lili’s clothing, floating companion and hat she wears while running around the island. There’s a decent amount of selection but they only affect how Lili looks.
The story is pretty straightforward. You’re Lili, a student at some school who’s on assignment to this island to find flowers for some research project. Upon arriving to the island, she sees how the wood constructs are being oppressed by the wood spirits and their mayor. Though he’s not very good at stopping you from achieving your goals. The wooden constructs request that she helps them out. So, she does. What follows is an amusing, light-hearted exploration of the island. Littered with references, jokes and quirky characters. The script is pretty well done, especially when it comes to some of the descriptions of artifacts she’ll find along the way. Though some of the character growth dialogue that Lili has feels forced or out of place. The whole subplot of Lili being unsure whether she wants to continue her degree at the college or if she wants to do something else. It just kind of comes out of left-field.
Originally developed for mobile devices, Lili was ported to PC later on to mixed results. Lili’s settings menu is horrendous and lacking a lot of features that should be here. There’s a casual-normal-hardcore difficulty slider. Graphics can be changed but only with a quality slider low-medium-high that gives you very limited control on how the game looks. For resolutions, I could only select 1280x800 and 1680x1050 (my native resolution), with full or borderless window. Windowed mode doesn’t seem to exist. It's very inadequate for a third person title even if it does run rather well. Music can be turned on and off but there’s no slider to adjust the volume of the music or sounds.
It does get worse with the keybindings. You can’t change them. The game simply displays a keyboard showing you what they are and that’s it. This is where Lili shows her mobile roots the worst. You can get by with what it has and the game is short enough to prevent it from being annoying. However, I'd prefer to see the devs make the settings menu more comprehensive and customizable in the future.
Probably the biggest problem I had with Lili was the control scheme. Lili has two different input schemes: “FPS” and “MMO”. It seems that the MMO style was designed for touch screens while the FPS style was intended for regular PC gamers. The difference between the two is mainly how the camera can be changed in regards to your moment. MMO has you click and dragging to move the camera while FPS’ camera stays with your mouse. Regardless of which style I picked, I was never entirely satisfied with how Lili controlled. She felt largely unwieldy to move around the island. Especially as you started getting movement speed items. It took playing around with my mouse’s DPI setting, the in-game mouse sensitivity and input scheme before I could get it to a place where I was reasonably ok with it.
I liked my short time with Lili. However, I’m having a hard time deciding whether I should recommend this to anyone else. With the main mechanic being just about picking flowers, there’s really not much to this title. Even the flower picking is only really fun at first, then it loses its appeal towards the mid-to-late end of the game. There aren’t any puzzles or platforming or any other ideas to sink your teeth into. So, it’s a bit lacking. I’m also aware that this is a more casual adventure game. As such, I’m willing to let a lot of this slide because I knew what I was getting into. Additionally, there are control and PC settings menus that are just...extremely lacking. That all said, if you’re just looking for a casual adventure experience to break things up, Lili is a title to give a look. Otherwise, I’d recommend looking somewhere else for something that has a little more depth and content. Do not expect something on the level of Legend of Zelda or a more involved RPG because it will disappoint.

I say this because he is clearly meant to be shown as the antagonist, but his motives are understandable and, to some, even agreeable. His choices are ethical or harmful depending on how you look at it and from who's point of view.

The graphics are very good, with pretty lighting and shiny textures. The animations are also decent enough, really the only complaint I have is the walking animations of the humans at the end, but that is a very, very minor complaint, and not at degrades my opinion of this game.
Over all, this is a must play if you are a Portal or The Talos Principal fan that is looking for some puzzling to do.

I have not yet finished the game, but I have played a good chunk of it to get a taste of what it is like. I should also note that I received this game for free.
I will start off by saying that this experience certainly is interesting. You look for your grandfather's journal entries, and you seemingly warp from memory to memory to read up on, or even partially experience what he was involved in.
My feelings for this game are mixed because, as many others have pointed out, often it feels like an unpolished project. It did at times feel like I was playing an early alpha project to the point that it weighs the game down quite a bit. In this game, a menu and save system is absent, and overall the gameplay feels a bit sluggish. There were also jump scares which seemed to come out of nowhere, and I am not a fan of random jump scares, but I have to admit that some were quite clever, like a shadow running past you without sound or warning, seemingly uninterested in harming you.
, I did not play this solely to pick on technical aspects. A fan of horror has great love for mystery and eeriness, and with that in mind, I was enjoying myself. The setting was interesting. The village outdoors looked weird at first, but then I started feeling that it fit the setting quite well, as if the village had been swallowed whole by darkness that was some forsaken occult dimension. It felt like a dream, no, like a nightmare. There were two occasions I remember particularly well where the sheer atmosphere and environment kept me on my toes. The original author said that this was inspired by Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and while I am unsure how much that reflects on Fireflies, I can tell that efforts were made to make the environment your greatest fear and enemy.
If this game receives an overhaul (a game menu, a save system, improvements etc,) I think more players would be into it. Would I recommend this game? Yes and no. It depends entirely on the player. For most players, I would not recommend this game.
, I had some good moments in this game which personally I feel makes up for the bad. If you are able to put gameplay and bugs aside, and if you enjoy short horror stories where you keep looking around you, and as if you just stumbled upon the forsaken aftermath of satanic rituals, then go for it, you will be startled!
If you would like to see what the game looks like, there are currently two video previews on this store site. The preview with commentary is me playing the game.

Fireflies claims to be a game inspired by what some would consider one of the greatest horror experiences of all time - Amnesia: The Dark Descent. While there are some very mild resemblances to that game (you carry a light source, solve puzzles and collect notes while encountering the odd scare) Fireflies is essentially an asset flip, bargain basement horror experience, one riddled with glitches and bugs (some game breaking). The graphics are poor and the framerate (even running on a GTX 1070) dire. Sound design is hit and miss but isn't as bad as some other indie titles out there, it's servicable but can be awful at times. A horror game should pride itself on well produced audio. This game fails at delivering anything remotely creepy. Instead it relies on a number of well placed jump scares which I will admit got me and my friend a few times as we played through it for our Youtube channel.
The rest of the game resorts to shock value with tastless diary entries detailing horrific subject matter that even far more mature games like The Last of Us and The Walking Dead wouldn't dare touch. Puzzles are obtuse and made more difficult by some of the worse controls I've experience in recent memory.
Below is a video of myself and my friend playing the game, we weigh in more detail than this review and you'll get a sense of what you're buying should you decide to pick this particular game up.

This game tries to merge two different genres of gaming, Realistic Survival and Survival Shooter. Before you play this game, its important to know that you can choose to remove all monsters from your server/play session.

Once you have enough to build the starting building, first then the game tells you that you need additional resourses as you need to build its walls too. Back to finding resourses. Once your first starter base is up, you'll quickly need Hydrogen Gas. An enormous amount. You'll make about 8 trips with 7 gas canisters to have enough to build your first advanced structure. Still no signs of vehichels, as ALL VEHICLES are endgame.

The game have huge potential, and the devs seem alright, though also overambitious with plans for several moons and many more things which right now seem unreachable in the games current state. I wish they would fix the current flaws/bugs and THEN focus on exspansions.

RIFT is the perfect World of Warcraft clone. It has everything WoW has:
Same interface, mechanics, professions, auction house, instances, raids, BGs, item naming, controls, addons on Curse, talents, etc,
It also has the additions that WoW has always needed:
- Random Zone Events (constant, running all the time)
- Rifts (which appear randomly and massively accros the map)
- 1 and 2 players dungeons (Chronicles)
- Built-in mechanics that in WoW you need addons (sell grey items, quest guides, etc)
- Instant Adventures, which randomly matches you with a bunch of players and then you keep doing infinitely chosen grinding quests in a zone, giving massive EXP and rewards (the best way to level).
But mostly important it has AN AWESOME CHARACTER CLASS AND ROLE CUSTOMIZATION. It's something like "make your own class and roles":
- Caster DPS-Tank-Healer
- Pure caster DPS
- Caster and Melee DPS
- Caster with Pet DPS and Healer (or just DPS)
- Melee Tank with Healing habilities
And a LOT MOOOOOOORE.
Regarding the Free to Play aspect of it: you can completely play the game without ever spending a penny, but a few restrictions:
- You can't sell on the Auction House
- Limited bags (very annoying)
- You will have to grind a lot in order to buy mounts
But I was so hooked the first day that I bought the Classic Collector's Pack, unlocking a lot of extras, plus giving 1 month of Patron, which means 40% additional exp = faster leveling. Also, I WANTED to pay, because I was willing to help Trion. This game DESERVES money. It's polished, addicting and well crafted.
If you want to play WoW but aren't willing for a comeback, RIFT is your game!

Okay, this one needs some work.
GoI Online is an excellent game. Alliance adds, on top of the PvP mode, a PvE play option. It adds some new content, in the form of new missions and Special Abilities, but the base gameplay is the same -- but the opponents are bots. And if you've played Online, you know that fighting bot captains isn't fun because they are dumb. It doesn't matter how many you have to fight at once, or if they add boss fights. The captains are still bots.
On top of that, playing PvE matches is a near necessity for advancing in the "overgame" (as I will call it; it has no official name as far as I know). On the surface, this third mode of play is the coolest mechanic ever -- a global, risk-style map that makes every game worthwhile, and adds a depth of strategy above the round-to-round combat. In practice, this discourages playing the better gamemode -- PvP -- in favor of MMO style grinding. Competitive MMO style grinding.
Consider what would happen if we replaced all the progress made by playing PvE with just a meter that automatically filled depending on what you targetted. The overgame now appears vividly hollow. Go back to how it is, and it is that, but with incentive to grind.
Only buy this version if you absolutely love the base game and are craving for more content or want to support the developers. GoIO deserves it.

Pocket Space Empire is to most space 4X games what Unity of Command is to Gary Grigsby's War in the East: a straightforward experience stripped of a lot of cruft.
As the description says, you don't concern yourself with minutiae like planning out each planet's production, or organizing your fleet in detail. Planetary governors take care of the former, and the game takes care of the latter by a handy system for assigning certain fleets to certain directions, and by building squadrons to match a desired composition.
As the emperor, your time is divided between three main pursuits: managing your wars (which are likely to be more or less permanent) by directing fleets from your headquarters on Terra, deciding research priorities, and ruling over your court.
War management is fairly traditional strategy game fare: point and click to move your fleets. Some of your fleets will likely be autonomous; autonomous fleets always station a squadron on each border world in a certain direction or directions, which generally takes care of defense. You get to manage the more interesting offensive half of things. Although there isn't a great deal of depth to the moment-to-moment maneuvering, especially as your empire grows more powerful and your enemies fall behind, there is a good bit of strategy at play. It takes a long time to move fleets across your empire, so changing fronts should not be undertaken lightly, and you'll find yourself careful in committing your mobile fleets. Rarely will you attack for the sole purpose of taking territory: the random galaxy generator seems to do a good job of scattering features of interest so that you're usually aiming for one of those, with supporting offensives to secure your flanks.
Research is research; it progresses more or less linearly in five separate areas, and you can choose one area for primary and one area for secondary focus, at the expense of research speed in other areas.
Finally, personnel management. Your Imperial court has six departments, each providing bonuses or penalties to your empire's functioning. You must balance the presence of factions in the court to prevent rebellious sentiment from growing, but this (along with less-interesting management of planetary governors and fleet commanders, neither of which can be easily shuffled around or relieved of duty) is not Crusader Kings 2. Your courtiers, governors, and admirals are mostly interchangeable, and they don't have personal motives or bear personal grudges. Court management is mainly shuffling cards around.
In the end, though, I like it. This is a beer-and-pretzels 4X to go with my beer-and-pretzels wargame collection. It isn't especially deep, and I don't know how well the gameplay would hold up if you were to sink 100 hours into it, but it's worth the price of admission, and it presents you with a unique take on managing your space empire.

I played through the main game on console, and have just finished replaying through it (along with all the DLC) before I jump into Dishonored 2. I honestly have to say, this is without a doubt, one of the best games I have ever played. Not only is it fresh and imaginative, but it is also creatively charged and extremely absorbing. You will find yourself fully immersed within the ruined city of Dunwall in a matter of minutes, and whether you choose the path of a vicious killer, the unseen shadow, or somewhere in between, you will finish this game feeling fulfilled and wishing that it were longer. If you are on the fence about this game because of its age, don't be. You will not regret opening up Dishonored, as the experience you will have with this game is unmatched by any other.

Dishonored is a fine show of how gameplay and setting can come together to support eachother. The gameplay is quite varied with both stealthy and combat oriented styles avaliable. You can strike from the shadows at long or short range, or go toe to toe with the enemy, or even complete the game without killing anyone. The supernatural powers you have are innovative and made to interact with the world and eachother. A short range dash called blink forms the foundation of your supernatural abilities, and combines well with the combat and stealth. It can also be helped by a double jump or by an ability to slow time. The other powers try to get away from straight "shoot beam/ globs of status effect." Instead you can posses animals and people and move around in their skin. Or stop time to pick projectiles out of the air. Arkane has made a commitment to simulation based systems which allows the systems they make to be combined in unique ways. Summoning a swarm of rats will allow you to get rid of corpses or give you something to possess.
In addition Dishonored has a world that breaks the mold of fantasy. The Empire of the Isles is based on Victorian era Britain, with a twist of being based on refined whale oil. Indeed the Isles are minor compared to a massive, mysterious continent called Pandyssia. As the name implies all human expeditions have discovered a menagirie of deadly flora and fauna. The main religion actively despises the main god entity and hunts his followers. The main god entity in turn seems little concerned with morality. The cosmic forces seem to think of humans less as incredibly important deciders of the great war of good and evil and more as a source of amusement.
The story itself is a pretty standard tale of revenge. The empress of the isles is killed, you're blamed for her murder, yadda yadda. However the world and gameplay are worth the tepid story. If you like stealth, or want to see how to use different powers in unique ways, or want a world that isn't based on Warcraft buy this game.

OneShot is an adventure game where you, as a God, guides a cat-like child named Niko on her quest to save a doomed world by placing the sun on the top of the world's pillar, in order to return her back to her home. Sounds simplistic, right? Well, that's where I was wrong at first. Soon enough, you'll notice that the game is self-conscious and its obstacles will make you think outside the box (even literally, sometimes) in order to advance Niko's quest. By the end of the game, I'm counting back on the times I've been blown away and learned to adore most, if not all, of the major characters you meet up with. And it all takes after a single playthrough, much to its namesake...
For its lovely charm contrasted by the world's darker overtones, the mechanics and its immense, clever plot twists, OneShot has won its place in my heart. Warmly recommended!

It's short, but very engaging. It's definitely on the easier side, but you'll definitely get a few hours of enjoyment out of The Turing Test, because the story is very well made. I hope to see more from this development team in the future with more complex puzzle mechanics.

One of the reviews for this game describes it in terms of Portal and The Talos Principle, and they're not far off - The Turing Test is exactly that type of story-based first-person sci-fi puzzle game.
Expect 2-3 hours of gameplay if you take it easy and don't go tearing through at light speed. The puzzles do gradually get more and more complex and challenging as the game progresses (as you would expect), with new gameplay elements being introduced regularly to keep challenges fresh. I wouldn't describe any of the puzzles as particularly challenging however, and only the last one provided more than a few minutes of difficulty.
Story-wise, I'd describe the plot as 'sufficient', but there was a lot more potential there than was actually explored. The ending felt a little abrupt and unsatisfying, though this didn't stop the puzzles from being fun, and there was at least enough plot to tie together what the character is required to do.
Graphically the game looks pretty good, though some physical elements within the game could do with a little bit of a physics adjustment, but that's a very minor detail.
All told I enjoyed playing through The Turing Test, and if you enjoyed the aforementioned games you'll probably like this too.
