I would recommend this game for those who like puzzle games. I would definitely not recommend this to someone who likes a nuanced story about artificial intelligence and the meaning of consciousness.
But that's sort of the problem: the game is
to be about that nuanced story. It's in the title, it's in every single puzzle room with Ava and TOM chatting, every optional puzzle, and a good majority of the audio logs. The game does a fantastic job of opening questions about the differences between an AI and a real human, contrasting its philosophical concepts against a Turing robot, a mind-controlled human, and an immortal human. I just wish that it actually used them, like SOMA did.
Spoilers ahead for the story, but in my opinion it's not complex enough to really warrant a spoiler warning, so make of that what you will.
Ava Turing is awoken from cryogenic sleep to investigate why the ground team on her mission to Europa have stopped responding. They discovered an organism that repairs DNA and halts aging effects, and are now infected with it. When this finding is reported, HQ says they can't leave Europa due to the unpredictable effect it could have on humanity and the Earth as a whole and TOM, the station's AI, is authorized to use deadly force to keep them there, so they destroyed the communications array to stop the AI from doing that. This is where the story gets really murky for me, and I can't figure out anyone's motivations. So I'll explain the components of the story, and how they kind of interact.
The crew have biometric implants to allow the AI and by extension HQ to monitor their vitals. This seems quite reasonable but they apparently are not told about this when they signed up. The AI tells them that removing the implants is a breach of their contract. This means that consent to having them was in the contract, and apparently none of the crew ever read that part, because the AI cannot lie. Nobody ever mentioned it to them in their entire career or had to repair them? Similarly, none of the crew ever questioned why their biometrics could be read by anyone else on the station at all times, even when they're not wearing a suit?
Apparently, this implant which is "woven into every nerve fiber in the hand" can also control a human's mind in ways that are never explained and are just used to give the crew a reason to act irrationally and mistrust TOM. He implies at one point that it influences the subconscious. It also can see what that person sees, somehow. We are never told or shown the effects of this control on a person either in narrative or directly, because even when characters drug themselves or stand in Faraday cages to avoid control they don't act any differently. In fact if not for TOM's implications, I would have no reason to believe that anyone is being controlled at all. It looks quite a lot like people are just being paranoid and irrational to the point of chopping off their hand (which is also inconsistent, because the two characters you see that undergo this process actually still have their hands and apparently have the implant in different hands: Sarah in the left, Ava in the right). However, the game doesn't allow this ambiguity in interpretation to exist, because when Ava's implant is removed, your control over her is permanently severed.
The organism that the crew found apparently repairs DNA, but there's a disconnect between what the game says about it and what it shows us. Realistically nobody knows anything about it because it was researched for maybe a month before it was concluded "it's the solution to death!" by people who are apparently scientists. It's shown keeping some plants alive for a few weeks, preventing some cells from dying to an unknown amount of radiation, and somehow killing a fetus. There's a bunch of potential untested problems with it too that are actually brought up, like its effects on existing cancer, growing children, the Earth's ecosystem, diseases, possible overpopulation and starvation. It doesn't mention the potential mental effects of living forever, which has been explored enough in fiction that I think I can say it would be bad. But nevermind all that, we have to share this potentially apocalyptic bounty!
So, here's why all of this matters, and why I'm confused. The crew wants to return to Earth. They aren't allowed to because they're infected by the organism. There's no room for discussion in the plot here, no "research it for a few decades" or "send more people" or "let's try to avoid the bad effects", the crew wants to return to Earth
to the exclusion of any rational thought. The story presents this as humans being sentimental and having survival instincts, but when TOM starts to use his lethal force nobody tries to compromise with the all-powerful AI in the interest of staying alive. Someone also independently discovers the implants, causing a mutiny with the goal of...killing TOM? Getting to Earth? I really don't know, but the implants end up being the impetus of the plot with Ava giving weak arguments on how they're bad and eventually defecting to the mutiny.
At the end, everything falls apart to present you with the binary choice of shooting the humans to protect TOM or just letting TOM be destroyed. There's no conclusion to anything the game posed as a question. The moral ambiguity of an AI's humanity, killing the few to save the many, potential immortality, all of that is just washed away because being controlled is bad, even though it doesn't make sense that people were being controlled. Whatever, the game has to end now! In the face of an existential threat, the super-powerful AI can't disable them with a leg shot, be forced into a compromise, or have any kind of negotiation. In fact, the humans act more robotic than the AI does throughout the whole game, insisting repeatedly that TOM just can't understand humanity without ever admitting any kind of fuzziness or kinship with him, never changing their views or opinions and never offering any meaningful retort to the AI's attempts to equalize consciousness and neural nets. I would normally concede that that's an interesting point, but the problem is that that "irony" undermines the entire narrative and blows all of the philosophy out the window by treating it so poorly.
The puzzles were actually pretty enjoyable up until the end, but even that's spoiled a little bit by the story. If your perspective is really as TOM through Ava, why do you have to jump to a camera or a robot to control some things? Whatever. Turn the voice volume all the way down and quit the game at the end.

Recommended for casual play or those wanting to pick up something that will take them back to the older days of FPS.

Early access review, 19 hours in game.
This game plays fairly well and there's a lot of potential.  Yes, there are some bugs, clipping issues, etc, but the game succeeds in reaching the imagination.  I don't mind tough games, so enjoyed the challenge of figuring out how to play.  It took me about three hours to realize the jet pack works tons better if tools/weapons are holstered.  Some resources are tough to find and you aren't able to make beacons ahead of time (game's version of map waypoints, but actual items you stick in the ground).  I learned landmarks instead (eg: go to the O2 vents and the hydrogen vents are visible, magnesium can be found near there, follow indicator back to base).
Needs a lot of fleshing out, but I like the starting point and am looking forward to future updates.
edit:  One month and 57 hours of game time...  Game is slowly evolving.  Some bugs corrected, some game mechanics changed and plenty more to be changed on the horizon.  Still recommend, though first play through new players may want to select "no aliens" when configuring the game and adjust after learning the basics.
Update:  91 hours in game....  Not a fan of some recent changes.  Don't mind the map changes as much as the resource changes.  Very difficult to find what you need now.  Don't get me started on now being required to make "primitive" structures before you can build regular structures.  Game still has promise, but dev's are taking the scenic route getting there.

If you are looking for a casual game that has a unique combat system, this is a good game to get.
First off some of the most notable bad features:
1. The controls starting off suck. If you are using a controller. The game does not tell you what buttons do what. All the key maps are for the keyboard. That is until you start playing and enter combat. Then they show up as the controller keys.
2. The resolution cannot be adjusted in the game. You will need to edit the config file if you are not happy with the settings. (FYI that file is filled with junk you will need to sort through).
3. The storyline starts off very pathetic and Lili just decided to do whatever everyone wants,
With those out of the way, you have a short, lighthearted adventure game. You play Lili who ends up on the island looking for flowers for her Vegi-magic college assignment. There are 3 types of inhabitants on the island. The constructs are the ones you will interact with for quests. The fish will give you general information and the spirits are the guys you need to battle to get the special flowers. The story starts off slow and progresses more about Lili's life and the freedom of the constructs. The enphasis on flowers starts to slowly go away as the quest to defeat the evil mayor takes full stage.
The combat system in this game is a bit different. Both good and annoying. You must jump on the back of the spirit and collect flowers. Once you jump on them, thorns, flowers, and bombs pop up on their backs. It is your job to hit the right button coresponding to the flowers and bombs. Get enough flowers in the timeframe and you defeat it. Fail and you just fall off and have to run back up to it and try again. There is no dying in this game so you can keep trying all you want.
The graphics are beautifully done. The locations are vivd with life. For the most part, all with the exception of a few constructs look uniquely different. The spirits look almost exactly the same but with different masks. Each location although foresty has its individual look and feel. Definitely a good looking game. I played it on my 4K tv and the resolution defaulted to that. (When you first log in the game sets the resolution to your systems max even if you do not want it to.)
The game is definitely not hard to beat and ranges from 4 to 9 hours to play depending on how many achievements you want. One thing to note is the abundance of game references and items from other games throughout the island. The dialong is quirky and not meant to be taken seriously.
If you want a simple game that does require a little bit of action, this is a good game to get.

Other reviewers complain about a lack of games to join and a horrible playerbase, but honestly I can't say I've had the same experience.  There are always games to join, even during off-hours, and after some 50+ or so games I've only had two people complain in a match (to be fair, they were mostly co-op matches, maybe the pvp matches are worse).
The game's strength is in how well it balances first-person action with strategy elements, though I could see that being a con for some, as you really have to be good at both in this game.  The learning curve might be a bit high for people who just want to shoot things, and the action might be a little too fast-paced for those who only care about tactical battles.  For those who like both, however, the game is amazing, and best of all it's wrapped up in a wonderfully detailed steampunk setting.
Overall, I've had a great time in the game, and after 30 hours or so I still feel like I'm only scratching the surface of strategies and techniques.  Between the different roles/ships/loadouts there are a lot of possibilities for customizing your playstyle.  There are some problems with the game (obtuse UI, and a lack of an easy way to coordinate with your faction), but the core gameplay is solid and definitely worth the asking price if you are new to the game.

What a great casual game of hitting tennis balls and knocking people out which make the game humorous. Like a super hero with the power of the tennis raquet he will vanquish his foes one ball at a time!

Tennis in the Face:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

You know, Tennis is one of those games that I am not…. let’s say, built for. Well, try to visualize a frog with a tennis racket in his hand… It is a bit hard to imagine, isn’t it?  Well, don’t! I have the answer for you. Just play Tennis in the face.
Tennis in the Face is an action/puzzle game with great physics. You will be playing Pete Pagassi, who will attempt to save the city from Explodz, an evil energy drink company. You will start your quest, as all good Tennis players, in a metro. You will have at your fingertips the Oddingtong Metro map and all you have to do is to get all the necessary golden crowns to unlock the next metro station.
Armed with your sensational and precise serve (hopefully, you make an ace), you will have to hit all characters in the level with your tennis ball or a can of the energy drink from Explodz. Achieve a chain reaction and knock out all your enemies with a single ball (sometime 2) and you will score the perfect game, set and match!
A well-executed game which offers over 100 levels with nice graphics and catchy music. Very easy to play, fun and the difficulty increases with each level.
Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Fun Graphics
-	Easy to play
-	Over 100 levels
-	Great physics
-	Achievements & trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	This type of game will always be a bit repetitive
Well, I know what I am going to play during each Grand Slam - Tennis in the Face!

House of the Dead: Overkill is a rail shooter, and I've never played a rail shooter. Apparently I'm not particularly good at them, either, according to my performance in this game. Not 'bad', exactly, but not quite 'decent' either. It can't be all my fault, though, because sometimes the game is really bad at telling you things, and sometimes it's hard to precision shoot when the camera is whipping all over the place without warning to get to the next location. Overall, the gameplay gets a halfhearted 'pass' for being functional, if a chore at times.
On the writing side of things, HotD:O is a Grindhouse-style comedy game. The jokes are hit-or-miss, but the 70s parody is spot-on so far as I can tell, and the two main characters are well-written and have wonderful chemistry. The cutscenes also go out of their way to shock, which is quite amusing. I'll never forget one character digging a ringing phone out of a corpse, holding it to his ear, and then handing it to his blanching counterpart, saying, "It's for you."
Oh, and I haven't actually played the typing tutor part yet. Maybe I will at some point. It seems like a one-time kind of joke, not the kind that will last a whole game.

You're probably hearing this for the umpteenth time, but here I say it again, if you liked
you'll like The Turing Test as well.
The gameplay is very similar, yes. You have a special gun and you solve puzzles with it and go from one room to the next.
But what is interesting about this game is its premise.
You're on Jupiter's moon, Europa, and the ground team is missing. You wake up from your cryogenic sleep as Ava and you're sent by T.O.M. (the AI) to the ground station to find the team. As you pass through each room, you get more and more information about what happened there.
Right from the start, the game presents you with a question - If we build machines with an advanced AI that can mimic human behavior, would that mean they can think and feel just like us? Would they be considered alive or conscious just like us?
And whether machines could have consciousness or not, how would that affect our human society? And how do we even determine if something has consciousness or not?
The game presents many points on either side of the argument throughout.
It somewhat reminded me of the anime
.
(I believe you will have to read all the notes and stuff in the game to really appreciate this)
Now yes, this game isn't as big as Portal.
It's not as long as Portal. The puzzles are easier. And GLaDOS could eat TOM for her breakfast.
But as a standalone game, I did not find it lacking. I enjoyed it in fact.
My friend calls it 'Portal Lite' and I feel that's pretty accurate.
Also, you get 100% achievements when you complete the story plus 7 optional levels (which aren't that difficult either).
PS. I received this as a gift from a friend.

"Do you recommend this game?"
Eh, slightly recommended?
The Turing Test is definitely a refreshing experience to the FPS puzzle genre. Although, the principles of gameplay and story is closer to The Talos Principle and a little of Portal.
Puzzles similarity: The Talos Principle
The puzzles are often about juggling your resourses with timing and some logic and observation, and much like the other games, there is only one textbook solution to each puzzle. However, my personal opinion is that its difficulty is between Portal and TLP. If you're looking for a challenge, try Road to Gehenna DLC instead if you haven't.
Progression similarity: Portal
One way in, one way out. A corridor or loading screen before the next room, and no backtracking. So if you want to revisit the few 'hubs' there are or retry the optional rooms, you have to reload.
Story similarity: The Talos Principle
Simply put, both are philosophuical in nature. However, while TLP engages the player in the question of existentialism and the transcendence between AI and human, and you may arrive at an objective answer, The Turing Test is more about moral dilemmas. Nevermind the twists you may find at the beginning and or end, you may find yourself thinking differently from Ava despite her debate with TOM.
Conclusion: Play it for the story (and atmospheric music).
Bit boring compared to Portal 2. Stick with that.

As other reviews note, the game doesn't offer anything challenging or unique, given that Portal series and Talos Principle exist. In the end, even the music sounds like it was just taken from Talos Principle.

Lili is out sailing to find the island of Geos which is for whatever reason super rare to find. She finds the island and plans on collecting flower samples from the island. The island consists of wooden constructs and spirits. The constructs are essentially ill treated slaves and only Lili can help because your a human. Thus your goal is finish your school project by grabbing onto the mean spirits and... deflower them. As Lili runs around grabbing and deflowering male/female spirits she also collects things. You can buy stuff at the shop as well. You also level up your grab, stealth, and speed skills.
The art style is amazingly fun and colorful. The pull flowers mini game is actually quite fun considering how simple it is. The music and characters are quite lovely as well. More then anything this game just has that casual goofy fun vibe going for it.
It doesn't have actual speech in the conversations. It advertises itself as a Legend of Zelda when it play more like a Animal Crossing slash flower picking similulator. I would also say that the game suffers from being to simple. You'll be left feeling that the game could have been a legend of zelda if they would have tried for it. The game tends to shove video game references and trivia down your throat.
Its a casual fun game. Don't go in expecting a grand 3D platformer because this is just a phone game on steroids.
As beautiful and playful as this game is it really isn't a huge value. I can only suggest paying around $4.

Never in my life have I seen a worse UI than the one in Alliance. It's busy, it's confusing, and has absolutely no flow or hierarchy of information. There are far too many menus to find what you want, and the buttons are all over the place. The terrible part of this UI is that it must be MUSE's 4th or 5th attempt at designing the UI. I have never seen a company try and fail so many times at something most college level graphic designers can master.
Alliance still uses the matchmaker for it's multiplayer matches. This thing has been a terrible inconvenience (at best) since it's introduction a few years ago in the original Icarus game. It is in fact so useless that many devs and interns at MUSE recommend using an in-game work around to it. The community has never been large enough for it to work, and it's been a detriment to the game for years.
The ships in Alliance are a disaster, which is in stark contrast to the beautiful ships from the original Icarus game. In the original Icarus game every ship looked plausible. Every ship looked like it was designed from either a need for functionality, or put together to be as functionable as it could be (the junker). In the original Icarus, gun positions and arcs seemed to have a thought out purpose for their locations. If you look over every ship with your eyes, you'll see that every piece of those ships is there for a reason.
Run your eyes over the ships in Alliance. Not one of them makes sense. They are jarringly erratic in design, and most seem to lack any reason for their designs. Take for example the Judgement ship. It has smokestacks on top of it's balloon. Why are they there? What are they connected to? What purpose do they serve? Or look at the Magnate; it has walkways with rail guards for some of the way, but then those railings just stop, and that walkway continues, with nothing stopping you from a fall. Who realistically would design a ship like that? Would you walk around on something like that? These are just some of the many design "WTF's?!" that every ship in this g ame has. Just design for design's sake, with zero thought for functionality. Whoever designed these Alliance ships needs to have a long talk with the designer of the original Icarus ships.
The issue with the Alliance ships isn't just functionality or design, it's actual mechanics as well. Going back to the original Icarus ships, each has a distinct play style, tactical uses, and configuration of gun placements that make sense to each ship's overall design. In Alliance, not so much. I couldn't describe to you the unique role for each ship in Alliance because every ship functions, handles, turns, and flies very similiar to each other. There is no variety in styles or tactics. The gun placements on every Alliance ship is the worst part of the whole design! The placement and arcs of these guns seems erratic, as if someone just chose at random the placement for each gun on each ship. There is no advantage I can see for using any of the Alliance ships over thir much older, and much better designed original Icarus ships.
In short, the key feature of this airship game- the airships, are a mess. A terribly designed, insipid, candy-coated disaster. If there is any reason to not play this game, it's because they key feature of it fails to deliver across the board.
I have 44 friends on my steam list that own Alliance, and 77 friends who own the original Icarus game. Of that number, only 2 of my friends recommend this game throuh Steam (one of them is a MUSE employee). I cannot in any capacity recommend Alliance to anyone. This game fails to deliver in even the most basic aspects, such as UI, and is simply not worth it.

This is not a remake of the story from the first Painkiller (Black Edition) but a remake of the levels from that first Painkiller game. You play again as Daniel who has to collect 7000 souls to finaly get back to his wife in the real world. The gameplay is the same as allways: Kill enemies, "search" secrets and go to the next checkpoint. At the end of each act, you'll have to fight a huge boss. You have one new weapon which shoots saw blades and collects souls (not only from dead enemies). The other weapons are the known ones from Black Edition and its addon.
There are just a few levels of the first Painkiller game and its addon. (my favorites like Alcatras, The Forest, The Bridge and many others are NOT included.) In the last chapter, you play a level from another Painkiller game. (I believe it's from Overdose.)
Pros:
+ Levels are almost exactly copies of the Black Edition but you walk a bit different ways.
+ Co-op mode could be very fun. (I've not tested it yet)
+ Multiplaye is okaye since there are different game mods
+ Workshop
Cons:

In case you weren't aware: the original Painkiller (Black Edition) was the only one developed by People Can Fly, and widely considered to be the only one worth playing, as the license has jumped from developer to developer since, with pretty consistent nonsuccess. With that out of the way, Hell & Damnation, despite being made by yet another studio, is an HD remake of the original game -- and while perhaps an inferior experience to the purists, is the first release since the original to at least stand on its own. It's a frantic oldschool-inspired shooter experience with genuinely insane weapons, and you'd better learn to bunnyhop if you want to keep your skin on.
The knocks against it are mostly that it's missing a good handful of levels from the original game, it feels a bit different because of the new engine, the plot is still stupid, corpses still linger before giving up their all-important souls, and the reinvented final boss is still a poorly designed hassle that no longer has the benefit of at least being thematically interesting.
On the upside, it still plays just as well, generally looks better, has an additional weapon, adds a pretty good selection of achievements, uses a better save system, actually has acceptable loading times, rebalances enemy distribution to mostly do away with the annoying hitscan attacks, inserts a few new levels of its own to make up for the ones cut; and the levels that were cut, despite being aesthetically memorable, were really kind of an♥♥♥♥♥to play. There are also co-op campaign and survival horde modes that I haven't had a chance to dive into yet.
Really, the biggest problem with it is that it costs twice as much as the original at this point while ultimately having less content, but if you can grab it on sale it's a perfectly worthwhile remake that doesn't overstay its welcome. The bosses are still kind of awful, though.

What to make of The Turing Test... Well, for starters, it's very similar to Portal, that much is obvious, both in gameplay nad design. It does, however, take itself more seriously than Portal ever did and tries to raise some interesting points (and given the name of the game, it should be quite obvious what they are) through it's rather short course. These are, however, only hinted at rather than explored in depth and fall short of my expectations. The story is painfully cliché, and you almost exactly what went on before the first chapter is done.
The puzzles themselves are remarkably easy during the whole game, and not even the few extra hidden ones offer any semblance of challenge. This doesn't mean their flat out bad or poorly designed, there's a few interesting toys to play arround with, but quite a bit of the fun of a puzzle game goes out the window when you solve them all in a couple of minutes on the fly without even having to stop and think or assess your present situation. Workshop integration and custom puzzles would be a good addition and I'm frankly surprised it didn't ship with them. Seems standard for this genre...
It does however look very pretty, runs incredibly well and it's very polished. During the less than 4 hours I spent to get through the game (do take into account the INCREDIBLY long loading times) i never came across a bug or any sort of problem.
At the end of the day, if you're looking to take up most of an afternoon and have an itch to play something along the same lines as Portal or The Talos Principle, The Turing Test will work, but you won't be able to avoid comparing it to those games and feeling a little bit underwhelmed byt the similarities and unexplored potential of The Turing Test. While i wouldn't really recommend paying a whole 20€ for it, it does enough right to be worth a cautious thumbs up in a "get it during a sale" sort of way.
The ending is also a bit♥♥♥♥♥♥frankly.

There is nothing happy about this empire apart from some cute graphics: it is just a dull, repetitive, and bug-riddled attempt at a time management game.
Happy Empire almost feels like a game developing course project. It has some vague grasps on what parts make up a time management game, it also has some nice-looking backgrounds and 3D model animations (although it kinda looks like as if some assets are bought), but it cannot work as a whole.
The issues with Happy Empire are numerous. The command queue function only works when it feels like it. The background and the (invisible) level path often do not match up, which means many resources are blocked, despite a seemingly unobstructed route to them. There is also zero variety: the first level displays almost all gameplay mechanics, and from that point on, it is the exact same repetitive, boring level every time, sometimes with excruciatingly terrible design. As a cherry on top, the achievement system does not work at all.
If you hoped to get a decent little time management game because it looks good, then I am sorry; if you bought this, you only got a time-waster, nothing more.

3/10 TL;DR click/time management; poorly layed out
I enjoyed 12 Labours of Hercules(7/10) series.  Happy Empire game mechanics are the same.  Unfortunately, "clearing the path" of items is nonsensical.  There are items completely off the path that block continuation.  Figuring out the order is baffling.  The game does not properly que worker (ignoring blue que marks) and does not indicate if a worker has already been assigned to a task.
Worse, you must pay to activate a trader, before you can trade with him.  This hides his trade requirements, making it impossible to plan a tactical route for finishing.
The function of buildings is not explained.  The developer does not understand the critical words "trades" and "income."  On several levels, a trader falsely lists an income, while only paying off in trade.  On level 23, the goals are WRONG.
The developers had no desire to create a meaningful challenge.  Pass on this one and go play Hercules (any in the series, I like the 1st one better.)
BUGS: Several times, a worker gets stuck on a task.  Black screen finale.

Hello Neighbor is a mixed bag for me. I have been following this game for an extremely long time and I truly wanted to love the final product. I found the central idea very compelling and I absolutely adore the asthetic of the game world. However, I am really sad to say this game does not deliver well enough to the point where it is worth the $30.00 asking price. In the game's current state I would say it is worth about $15.00 if we are being generous.
For the sake of time I am going to make this very simple and write down a list of pros and cons of this game
Pros:
+ Extremely charming graphics.
+ Some occassional "Wow" moments.
+ The aspect of a horror game without jump scares is very appealing and this game has a base from which it could do this very well. Sadly it does not deliver on this very well.
That is honestly about it for pros. I really wish there was more I could list that I really liked about this game. Now onto the cons.
Cons:
- The game is riddled with glitches in its current state.
- As you learn more about the game the sense of any replayability starts to wear off as you learn how everything works.
- Not very scary in all honesty. I have not finished the game, so I don't know if it suddenly picks up towards the end, but at my current point in the game its not that scary.
- The neighbor kinda just stands there when he catches you. It only adds to the game feeling very not scary. It would be  better if there was AT LEAST some sort of animation or something at all.
- The "Advanced AI" which is one of the game's main selling points is not anything really special. It can be downright dumb at times honestly.
- The controls in this game are overly clunky and at times just do not work correctly.
-Game gets slightly repetitve after only about 3-5 hours of play.
- Game treads a line between fun and frusturating quite often.
- MANY MANY MORE.
In closing, I wish this game would have simply entered early access with a $15.00 asking price and the promise of more content and further development. I love the idea, but the execution is nowhere good enough to warrant the asking price of this game. I actually changed my review from positive to negative after investing more time into the game and realizing how many faults it truly had. I really hope I can eventually change this review back to positive at some point if the game improves.

So first of all as of now I have 113 hours in the early access and 48 hours in the full game. I have played all of the versions of hello neighbor and seen it as it went through pre-alpha, alpha 1, alpha 2, alpha 3, alpha 4, beta 1&2, Beta 3, Hello Bendy  and final release. When I first looked at the game, I loved the idea. The idea of sneaking into your creepy neighbor's house to find what he's hiding is a genius idea. I always wondered as a kid what was in my creepy neighbor's house. For me, the prototype and pre alpha looked better than the full game, and that says a lot. It seemed for me that every update made the game worse and worse. The pre alpha which was the first ever release was more scary and more stealth than the full game. It had realistic graphics, the neighbor was very scary, and the chase music was the best. Next came alpha 1 which was super easy to beat. It literally takes me 5 minutes. You just have to get a hammer and lockpick and boom easily beaten. I didn't like the layout and the neighbor wasn't as good. Than came alpha 2. The original alpha 2 (alpha 1.5) looked way better than this cartoonish mess we got. The game actually has a basement which is what the game is all about, but its 5 seconds long. The game isn't scary whatsoever, but there is a bit of stealth. Alpha 2 is where it started going downhill. Next came alpha 3. Alpha 3 was this gigantic house, half of it was unexplorable. It was extremely hard and buggy and the neighbor was very annoying. It was scary however, and I liked it being only night. The chase music is still a weird ghost banjo and its not that good. Alpha 3 was a good build, but it could've been better. Next came alpha 4. Alpha 4 was SO BAD. The fear rooms where a good idea, but they aren't fun. They give you weird powerups which doesn't fit in a game like this. There were so many unfinished rooms and half baked puzzles and it was just a big mess. The basement was cool though. I dont have many good things to say about alpha 4. Than the betas. Oh the betas. Beta 1 and 2 were SO BAD. The game was broken to the point it was unplayable. It was basically alpha 4, but broken and without a basement. I liked the intro though. Too buggy. Next came beta 3. Really... Beta 3 was just... bad. It consisted of puzzles that made no logical sense, and wasn't fun to play. The basement was short, and the boss battle was cool. Beta 3 wasn't that good other than the boss battle. Really, using a GRAMAPHONE TO GROW TOMATO BUSHES? I hate how they did the tomato bushes, I literally could've walked through them IRL. Beta 3, wasn't that good. Next came the full release. I think the full release was a massive let down. It was so hyped up to be awesome, but it fell flat on its face. The only cool parts of the game were story elements. The gameplay is not fun the neighbor is SO glitchy. The supposedly SUPER SMART AI is broken. The AI is so bad and stupid and it really isnt fun. If you go in the front door ONCE expect there to be 10000000 cameras and bear traps. The neighbor throws glue and tomatos from god knows where and he has an unlimited supply. The gameplay is very glitchy, the physics suck and I always go flying even with the latest patches. I liked act 1, despite it being glitchy. The basement wasn't that exciting and then it ended. Act 2 was really hard, but I liked seeing the shark again. In the first build I discovered you could literally beat act 2 by stacking 4 boxes and jumping into the trampoline. Act 2 was super glitchy and the neighbor, once again was stupid. He would continuously go right back to where i spawned and I couldn't do anything becasue as soon as I spawned he would run back and catch me, moving me back 2 feet. Act 3 was literally beta 3, and dissapointing. The puzzles are dumb, and you hardly ever run into the neighbor except for once or twice and HES ANNOYING. The game isnt fun, the "boss" battles are literally just you trying to get on a giant neighbors back and running in front of yourself. Than it turns out to just be a dream. Really. This game was a great concept, terrible execution. 3/10. if I am generous, 4. I have played this since the beginning and I really wanted this game to be good.

Forenote: I've been playing Alliance since launch, just not via the actual Alliance launcher, so the hours are misleading.
While not quite as "open world" as originally discussed on Kickstarter, Alliance mode forges forward with a whole new vibe of teamwork and gameplay. I know a lot of people are very concerned that it hasn't "lived up to its hype", but what we have now is a stable, fun system that the devs can now expand on as we go.
Alliance brings some -much- needed PvE to the game, which finally ends the unfortunately imbalanced PvP matches for new players. I know a huge amount of people who refused to play, or stopped playing, because of many of the PvP matches being reputably hit-and-miss. A new player who loses 0-5 in their first ten matches because of stacked teams is basically just going to walk out the door and not look back. I almost did the same when I was new.
PvE allows new players to learn the ropes in games with reliable difficulty options. They can explore the ships, try all the weapons, experience the player tools, and practice their tactics with friends before trying out PvP.
I think with a dedicated PvE mode (and considering how often GOI has been included in sale bundles), we'll see a steady increase in players, and less people will be put off by the PvP since they'll have something else to try out instead.
Spread the word! Get your friends interested. Show them the game, get them to buy it. The more support the devs can get, the more they can improve Alliance mode to be like the dream we had for it!

This game is absolutely worth the price if you enjoyed the original. Ignore the other reviews, seriously. Let me break it down easily for you:
LEVELS:
There's less levels, yes. But the included ones are EXTREMELY pretty. Everything was touched up, but not much has changed, except for a few surprises on some of the maps :)
The game is better to buy if you are going to get the dlc's, which add the other maps and a few new ones that actually live up to the painkiller style! (nazi bunker and coastal level).
They also made changes on dlc versions of other old levels, such as new areas for the Asylum and cool changes to Snowy bridge.
I REALLY enjoyed this and it was so SO satisfying to see these amazing levels in full HD. It didn't feel as nice playing painkiller in the original graphics as the years went by. It DID get dated, it's still a classic.. but Nordic Games has done a terrific job.
CO-OP:
This was not as fun or functional on release, but after the mega-patch it's functional and FUN. You now CAN unlock tarot cards on your playthrough with your friend, so playing trauma together on a playthrough is exciting and fun, and progression can happen.
SURVIVAL: These are GREAT challenge levels brought into the game. Even for veterans. Some of the difficulties are quite hard even for good players and it's fun to see how well you can do. It's fun!
STORY: Sub-par unfortunately. It IS a (maybe?) canonical sequel, but the concept is kind of crappy and the voice-acting for Eve is bad (you can hear her microphone buzzing a tiny bit). But Painkiller doesn't need too much story!
CONCLUSION: This is a lovely game if you buy the DLC's. I dunno about Heavens Above because it's some gimmicky 3rd person mode but I imagine it might be fun too. The rest is spectacular. <3

tl;dr
Short & Sweet
Decent puzzles for 20 bucks, music is great, some of the voice acting is atrocious.
Any fan of Portal will find The Turing Test a nice stroll through a familiar park.

Short and sweet, The Turing Test is on the easier side of the FPS puzzler spectrum.
Taking clear lessons from Portal and The Talos Principle (this game includes explicit reference to the latter's namesake, buried amongst notes) you're tasked to solve some 70 odd puzzles of increasing complexity. Along the way you get to meet T.O.M., this game's GladOS, who commences each puzzle chamber with either some story-related dialogue or thought experimentation (a couple of recurring commentaries and intepretations on Searle's Chinese Room were pretty cool, there's something serene about an apathetic professorial voice guiding your thought).
Eventually your relationship with T.O.M. starts to change, and the gameplay with it: you move from confident single player to what (to me) felt like watching a Portal 2 solo co-op speedrun, moving around a secondary figure. This is one of my issues with this game: the transitions are slow, you either have to point at the target you wish to control and hit 'E'
run your hand over your keyboard to hit 'backspace' (obviously you can rebind it but it's a super small game, and you only use the feature for the latter half or so), only then to wait for some mock-static to let you have the new character. There were a few incidents where I'd have the solution and just be impatiently transitioning through setups and characters as I applied it; a few more than normal.
I also found that the pacing was a bit off: the game is broken down into 7 chapters, each (generally) introducing a new element to the puzzles. Of the 10 levels allotted to each chapter, around three will be dedicated to simple solutions that explain how it is and can be used. The game sorely needed an explanation for some of these instances, because they often didn't prepare me for what was to come -- for example, who the hell would've expected that you could've taken the orb the robot was holding in his arm-mounted gun
? There's no visual cues for this, no explanation, it's just a "Gotcha!" moment that dragged out a few extra minutes of irritation.
The difficult ramp is awkward. No puzzle solutions come out of the blue, and unlike Portal/Talos, I don't think there was an instant where I was driven away from my computer in search of thought-space. It's up to you whether you consider that an integral part of the subgenre. What difficulty I did find towards the end seemed to be largely in relation to criss-crossing wires, where one simultaneously has to assess the physical space in which they can move along with the logic gates that traverse it. If you want a challenge, I think Infinifactory or some of the harder scenes in Talos are preferable.
Complaints aside, the game's pretty attractive. They don't do much with the set design beyond an extended dialogue at the end of each chapter, but I never got bored of picking up and rotating the scattered models throughout the levels. The voice acting's pretty alright, though I think if the crew's audio logs weren't entirely optional then I'd be marking this down, as T.O.M. is (as mentioned above) super-sensually-sounding :). I had a bit of a laugh at some of the artistic liberties taken; there's a scene where you can see the crew manifest and there's some four male characters with photographed heads (I assume, developers) and two female characters with digital features (the protagonist and a later appearance), which screamed lazy uniformity. Thankfully, what little, bothersome quirks there are take a backseat to the scatterings of prose and conversations that show an engaging command of a lot of sciency stuff that I didn't care about (given that the premise is explained laconically by the narration) along with extended factoidal quotes(?) of Searle and others.
I received this in the Humble Monthly and can't say if I believe $20 is a reasonable price for my recommendation; I think it's a bit too short, but if you take it slow and soak in the atmosphere it'd probably pass muster. Conclusion:
A nice and enjoyable game but 20 euros is too much for such a short game. I really prefer Portal 2, or Quern - Undying Thoughts which are in the same price category. Way longer and way more challenging games. It's not really comparable to The Talos Principle.

Alright, as you can tell I have played this game for a chunk of time now. Did training, caught on very quickly, went to multiplayer and was doing pretty well right off the bat. Still need to work on my sneaking, but I've got combos, movement, dodge, abilities, ect mastered with both the Goliath and Elder Kraken. These are your two starting monsters. I prefer monsters. Now, a few issues I have.. Monsters need more time in the beginning to feed. It's bad enough that taking the wrong path can liimit your food, as there are small creatures there. That combined with having maybe 15 second headstart, kinda poses a huge negative on us monsters, as stage one monsters being destroyed by the hunters. Another concern I have is respawn. Several times now, I have nearly wiped the hunters, and they respawn and before I know it I'm back up to having 4 hunters on me again. I understand having a respawn, I suppose I won't argue with it, but there should be a manual 30 second delay for all respawns. Not a deployment timer in which reinforcements come in waves. It blows♥♥♥♥♥ That being said, this game does have me hooked. I love the concept, as basic as it is, but I love the race to evolve quickly and destroy your opponets once domed. Oh, yeah, that too. If the survivors are withing like 100yds they can dome your♥♥♥♥♥and keep you stuck with them for a fairly long♥♥♥♥♥time. Your only choice is to fight, because severely hurting a hunter can shorten the time the dome is up, allowing you to break free quickly, and go feed so you may evolve, regain your armor, regain some of that hp you lost, and go back with a more powerful monster. All this being said now, again, I would reccomend this game. The combat is intense, I LOVE hitting people in air. If you hit somebody in mid air, it will slam them down to the ground. It's hilarious. Pros and cons aside, it's a good game. 3.7 stars*

I'll be quick in this review. This is a First Person Puzzle game, similar to Portal or The Talos Principle but unlike those it isn't as memorable. This doesn't mean it's not good or worth playing, far from it, it just has a lot to live up to if being compared to those two games, both in the narrative department and the originality of the puzzles.
Comparisons aside, this game does have a nice story but even it being easy to predict, especially with the hints you get when completing opcional puzzles, it does stay a nice tale to follow through to the end.
Technically I think this games sound and looks pretty nice. The sound is not the front of the show but it helps create the mood the game goes for. As for the graphics, while not special are still beautiful and the game runs at a good framerate.
The game took me about 6 hours to beat and it was fun to play. I think most of my time spent were on some of the optional puzzles but even the regular ones have some which are very enjoyable to solve and give you sense of accomplishment.
Overall, for puzzle fans this is an easy recommendation. For people that are interested but are not sure, I suggest giving Portal a try first and if after playing The Turing Test you want something more challeging and with a much more meaningful story, I recommend The Talos Principle.

I really enjoyed the game, so I would suggest to try this game out for yourself. Yes, it resembles portal alot.
But even with that the game is really enjoyable and it draws you into the story, making you miss it after finishing the game.
Voice acting is top notch. But there are moments I wished it was a bit more emotional. As counter argument to myself - if you think about it - protagonist going through story finds out pretty tense stuff. And that would explain her being a bit stunned and not very talkative at times. Trying to process it all.
All in all, it feels very real. Natural emotions. The story is written so it makes you think. Giving you psychological problems through dialogue. And then reading in notes stuff Tom has learned from the crew. Basically - human and AI interaction.
Story - could have been a bit thought over. At the beginning going in optional levels you find out stuff from story from down the road and it kind of ruines that realistic feeling. It doesn`t give away key elements of the story, but you kind of sense what could happen. That does build up intrigue, but dialogues in main story doesnt follow up. Ava can talk with Tom about stuff she has already read on tablet or in notes and her dialogue is written as she doesn`t now it at that point.
Levels - easy. I finished the game in under 6 hours. There were levels I did resort to walkthrough (only two or three in the whole game). And some made me go through trial and error to find out the real solution. Could have been more of them. Most of the levels were walk in the park.
To recap : If you enjoy games with great story - this one is for you.If you are looking for a challenge - not so much. You could just be disappointed.

This game is unplayable. The balance issues are still a major problem. When playing as a Monster, you will be lucky to win 1 out of every 40/50 fights, and that will be only because you're paired with underleveled players or players that are just horrible at the game.
Planetary Scan takes away any kind of stealth gameplay that the original may have had, as it recharges fairly quickly, allowing the hunters to basically home in on you within a minute or two of the round starting. Once you're spotted, you have little chance to win. Your only hope is to pray you reach Stage 2 before the Hunters find you, and that in and of itself is particularly impossible, given some team set-ups.
You can haul scaly backside across the map as fast as you want, but with some of the perks available to hunters of higher levels (did I mention that yet? Chances are you are two times as likely to get paired with a player 5 to 10 levels above you with access to much better perks as you are to match against someone your own level) it will never be enough. Quick-Charge jetpacks, optimal fuel consumption and jump height modifiers make escape impossible as they can keep up with you better than you can out-maneuver them.
If you want to have any kind of success, your best bet is to forget that Evolve has any Monster characters at all and stick with the Hunters. Then you can sit back and laugh in glee and giddy excitement as you wipe the floor with a Monster player who, let's face it, never had a chance to begin with.
All in all, I had exceedingly high hopes for this release. To date, it is nothing but a supreme let-down. I may edit this if improvements are made in the balancing area, but for now this is my opinion, and this is where it stands.
Edit: Updated. Even with what is considered one of the most OP Monsters and maxed out skills, there is still no way to avoid hunters long enough to reach Stage 2 most of the time.. I have played over 100 matches to this point, and have 12 wins to my name, mostly in lieu of terrible hunters. All of my Levels have effectively been gained from Sympathy XP for losing matches, outside of the 12 wins I have, and I'm sitting at Level 25.
Not to mention that match-ups are still horribly screwed up. I just faced a Lvl. 40 and Lvl. 50 player at the same time. One is double my level, the other is 1.6x my level. Both undoubtedly had access to the BEST skills of their chosen characters, while I'm stuck here, bogged down with skills that I either unlocked and maxed out, or managed to scrape together the measily 10 silver keys I get per most matches to power up. How the F**K is that fair?
On top of that: Jack has TWO Scan abilities that he can spam back and forth for endless pinpointing AND a Repulsor Beam that you really can't get past no matter how hard you try? And they say the Monsters are OP. Hah. I laugh at your infantile cries of unfair balancing.
Planetary Scan needs to GO. NOW. If that's not possible for whatever idiotic pretenses people have for keeping it, then it needs a MASSIVE cooldown timer. This is just ridiculous.

Well, time to give it my own review!
Sincerely I’m not sure about how to start. Lili: Child of Geos is simple. Wonderfully beatiful but simple. It’s a short adventure that only enters by the eyes. I think the best way to structure this review is with the classical order: Graphics, Gameplay, etcccccccccc.
Already clear, right? They are astonishing. If you can play the game at it’s fullest you will enjoy more than I can express. I remember taking an insane amount of screenshots because I just loved everything so hard. The environtments are very well done too, I could feel like I wouldn’t mind to live when the game happens (yep, I know that sounds cringy but come on).
Doesn’t shine much. You’re the teacher’s daughter going into a mysterious island to gather rare flowers. You find weirdos that can talk and are cursed and you don’t even ask why. It’s like the game itself is rolling and saying come on just play you don’t need a history behind everything, right?
It isn’t bad, but repetitive. Run, gather flower, run, kick jar, “fight” enemy. Repeat x999. There are no real combats in the game so it’s perfect for a child (and for 20+ years old weirdos like myself huehue). Lili: Child of Geos forces you to grind a lot. To defeat a lot of enemies is the main task of the game, because rarely you find puzzles that need some kind of “research” to success (more like talking to the NPC that helps you every single time).
If going straight to the point, the game is extremely short. And that’s the main reason because I don’t recommend buying it at full price.
Well, it depends of the target of the game. The main character, Lili, only can say things like “Hi” or “Oh” and has only a few animations. As the game is an indie itself I won’t blame that, because I’m sure the company spend most of the time in developing the wonderful environtment.
I’m a sick lover of achievements, and although I got them all in this one. I’m gonna blame that. Most of them are grinding at it’s finest: scare 500 birds, break 1000 jars, etc. Just an excuse to play some time more, and that’s a very negative point. But whatever, they had to supply the lack of content.
Amazing environment and atmosphere. Perfect for kids with the non-violence and there’s no hurry to finish the game. Also has a lot of references to other games and if the player is not a kid will get most of them. Consider to buy when at sale.

The things you're typing can be pretty funny too, and I was constantly finding myself chuckling at the stupid things I was being forced to type.
As for those concernd about the difficulty, I breezed through it on normal difficulty. I type at around 50 wpm, and I was rarely challenged in this game, because I was mostly in it for the dialogue and dumb set-pieces. I cannot comment on how easy the easy mode is, but it might be an issue if you type agonizingly slowly.
My only real complaint is that the boss fights are extremely lame and uninspired. They're extremely repititive, and are normally easier than the game.  This is a shame, because the boss designs themselves are somewhat interesting.
It's not a super long game, so take that how you will. I finished the main story in exactly the time that my counter reads, and I thought it was the perfect length, I could feel the typing gimmick becoming slightly old at the end. But, there is a little bit more if you're looking for replay value. You can play co-op, or play the original game without the typing.  For me, the short length is almost a plus because I find myself swamped with amounts of games, and can appreciate a self-contained game that knows when to know to end. That being said, for gamers on a budget, you may want to wait for a sale when it drops to $5.

Schacht is a procedurally generated platformer focused on speedrun format . I am not a huge fan of games that are designed around leaderboards because not everyone wants the pressure of competition. The game itself is pretty decent but do to lack of progression it won't appeal to everyone. There is no "single-player content" beside beating high scores and doing achievements.
You may experience infrequent crashes and glitches along the platform edges. Nothing too serious but it is not perfectly fluid experience. Basic video options and controls are there. I like that you can toggle a shadow of people who played the map if you want to do a race against it. When you actually playing the game you can use several hotkeys like restart the level or checkpoint ( small thing but it makes speedruns more intuitive )
As far as I can tell there are around 60 preset platforming sections while maps are made from a random pattern of those. This system can actually create some weird levels because I think the pattern can repeat itself. Still, once you play about 30 maps you will probably know how to solve any issue that game can throw at you. So after about 4 hours, you will explore the actual unique content of the game.
4.2 Billion maps? Well, we all know how these games that promise the universe go. At least this game has good variety of backgrounds and combinations of platforms which are worth low asking price. I will have to complement developer on making platforming sections a risk vs reward . You will find that almost every preset section has a better way to approach it if you got some guts.
There is a map editor if you love playing with it but It seems limited to using preset sections.
Platforming tools are pretty easy to pick up but hard to master. There are four basic mechanics that you can learn in 4 tutorial maps. I have been craving a bit of Spider-Man experience and this game kinda gives you that feeling of extreme agility. A very fast-paced game that you can play for 20 minutes on a break and still enjoy it. Overall very self-explanatory.
The game looks very slick. Bright colors and surreal looking platforming give it a nice aesthetic edge. Sometimes Sun is too bright (hopefully a glitch and not design choice) Music is also nice but it is not as up-tempo as I would like for a game this quick. Audio is a bit too relaxing. You can also do some character customization with couple items and colors.
For a speedrun focused game it is pretty darn good but you will mostly compete against your own best score. I really wish there was an arcade-like option with preset maps and maybe bosses that you would have to race. As it stands this game is focused on leaderboards and competition when there is no real community. I can see myself coming back to this game for a quick rush but replay value is limited.

A solid and really fun running game in the same vein as T.E.C 3001 and some others. Schacht has you make your way through procedurally generated sci-fi levels where the goal is to get to the end whilst avoiding obstacles. The manoeuvres available are similar to other running games such as jumping, air dashing, wall-running, swinging from grapple points, and using jump pads. At times there are force fields that require the player to use their EMP ability, which disables some force fields and enables others.
The controls are very slick and everything works really smoothly, though there is a bit of a learning curve at the start. I've particularly found jumping between multiple wall-running platforms to be a bit fiddly if you're not used to it, but with time you get a hang of it.
There are daily, weekly, and monthly challenges provided with highscore charts for a bit of a competitive element for those who really dig it, as well as an option to simply pick a randomly generated level.
There is a very easy-to-use level editor available in the game too, which provides a large variety of platforming pieces. It takes literally a few minutes to construct a level, which you can then submit to the workshop and have other people play it. Having this kind of community support feature can greatly prolong the lifetime of the game.
One minor problem though, I've found trying to access Workshop from in-game causes it to freeze and become unresponsive. Not sure if it's a problem with my computer or with the game in general. So the only way I found to get community-made levels was by exiting the game first.
Generally a really fun game and highly recommended for anyone who likes running games full of challenges.

There is one thing that sets Dishonored above the rest: level design.
Throughout the 9 levels, there are tons of ways to play: you can sneak through the sewers and come up through the kitchens, get on the roof and jump through an open window, posess a rat and sneak through a tunnel, find a guard house and rewire the traps, or even charge in with a sword and pistol, flinging wind and rats at any who oppose you. If you take your time to look, there is always another way to approach a mission, with both slaughtering everything in your path and leaving no trace of your presence being equally viable options, with the game even encouraging two playthroughs to accomodate both playstyles.
Aside from level design, the implementation of a simple ability, Blink, is fantastic. You have it by default after the prologue sections, and it just completely opens up the gameplay and adding a lot of depth to the level design. You can go up, over, and around obstacles quickly and efficiently and, if ever spotted, can get out of dodge with a little bit of foresight to backtrack quickly.
Another strong aspect to the game is the atmosphere. Dishonored takes place in the city of Dunwall, the heart of an empire in a steampunk era running off of whale oil. A rat plague has engulfed the city, killing or displacing most of the population. The entire game has a sense of dread, with homes abandoned, corpses everywhere, and the City Watch enforcing martial law to "keep the peace" (read: slaughter anybody infected with the plague and blackmail everybody else to line their pockets). There is no hope, yet you are fighting for a better future by toppling the corrupt government that stole the throne -- just kidding, you're just trying to get revenge for your friends with benefits Empress getting murdered and clearing your name so her (and possibly your) daugher can take the throne.
It's the little things throughout the game that really make the game come to life. The letters to loved ones, the street gangs trying to scrape together a living, locked chests and hidden compartments that send you scrambling to find little scraps of information in order to pop open a secret area. The potions that heal your health and mana are competing elixirs designed to fight the plague. Multiple factions exist, trying to survive in the rat-infested city.
Collectibles in Dishonored are better overall than most games, as they actually have a function. Runes allow you to unlock more abilities granted by the Outsider, Bone Charms add small little boosts to make life a little easier, and gold and ammo are everywhere, allowing you to purchase a crapload of upgrades that are overall pretty terrible (almost every monetary upgrade improves your fighting capabilities, which means that stealth be damned).
The graphics are extremely dated, feeling like a mid to late 2000s game. It definitely feels like it was made with consoles in mind, including controls. Speaking of, controls work fantastically for both keyboard + mouse as well as controller.
Overall, Dishonored is one of my favorite games from this decade and spurred my interest in stealth-first action games. I plowed through to a platinum on the playstation, and it's even better a second time on PC. I give it a 9.5/10, and highly recommend it for both the casual and hardcore stealth players, whether you want to assassinate everybody in the city or make the entire government disappear without a trace.

An excellent first-person puzzle game with strong ties to past genre-defining titles. With the familiar setting of a potentially sole survivor waking up to a friendly A.I with demands, it is easily recommended to sci-fi fans, as the game juggles the themes of humanity, fate and free will, freely.
The game rewards creative thinking over muscle memory, and, after introducing the basics of gameplay, leaves the player to build on previous lessons while introducing new concepts at a moderate pace.
Because of how well the overall plot, gameplay mechanics, the general challenge level and attention to details come together, it's even more easily recommended if the player isn't yet used to thinking with portals.
Content-wise, the game features a good number of mandatory puzzles as well as a few optional ones that all grant some minor insight into the overarching plot (and the brief release of seratonin as you watch those achievements unlock).
It offers no replay value outside of watching different endings and solving the optional puzzles you may have missed. Special mentions goes to the outstanding voice acting! I dunno, can you end a review like that?

It’s been a while since I’ve played a game that I felt strongly enough to write a review, I’ve been stuck in indie land for some time playing games that just made me feel… meh – simply aiming for achievements rather than enjoying the gameplay.  That changed with The Turing Test.  Simply put, its a wonderful puzzle game.
Fans of Portal or Attratico will find the gameplay familiar.  You’ll play as Ava Turing, an astronaut on Jupiter’s moon Europa, and without going into detail you will be traveling through puzzles created by your crew members in order to prove that you are in fact “human” – the aim of which would be a spoiler.  You’re only companion during these challenges is the base’s AI – T.O.M.  While these challenges story wise are a bit of a stretch, it is the core aspect of the game, and are quite fun to solve.  The main story is provided in snippets as you progress both in dialog with the AI, but also in audio recordings which are worth listening to.  At the climax of the game, you are presented with a moral dilemma of sorts, and the audio recordings help add extra drama to your final decision.  I found the story line to be the best part of this game.
My largest gripe is that the game is short, 6 hours without rushing, completing all challenges and secrets without the aid of YouTube or walkthroughs.  The puzzles while initially seeming daunting, are easily solved with a little patience, making Portal and some Attratico puzzles look downright impossible in comparison. Due to it's short length, I'd recommend holding off a purchase of this game until you can get it on sale.
The game is very atmospheric and reminiscent of Alien Isolation (without the horror) and Event[0] (without all the text), movie-wise it would compare well to 2001:A Space Odyssey.  Without sounding silly it does an excellent job transporting you to Europa, feeling the isolation, exploring the base, and being part of an unfolding discovery.  I found the graphics themselves (max settings) to be sharp, although when picking up objects there is a delay for them to come into clear focus.
There is no multiplayer, and no option to build and upload your own challenge creations to the workshop – somewhat of a disappointment that could have extended the interest.  The DLC, I got as part of a package, I can’t recommend buying, its an upgrade pack that really isn’t work your time (includes artwork, soundtrack, and an alpha demo).
Final Recommendation:  The disappointments in length and DLC are easily overlooked due to the engrossing story, smooth gameplay, and atmosphere.  The moral choice you are presented with at the end is a difficult one to make, and I’d be interested in hearing in the comments section the choice you personally made after completing the game.

Definitely a fun puzzle game akin to Portal or Talos Principle, though with less elements the player needs to work with. The puzzles revolve mostly around providing power to various objects like doors, light bridges, or lifts. Apart from an added ability halfway through the game, that's pretty much it. A lot of the puzzles felt rather easy, the only exceptions being some of the optional side ones which required a bit of lateral thinking to solve.
The game's plot is driven almost exclusively by dialogue. At the start of each puzzle room the player and the AI have a little chat, sometimes carrying a conversation between multiple rooms. This becomes a problem if you get stuck and have to take time solving one room, because theres awkward silence while the game waits for you to move on before continuing the drip feed of exposition. After each set of puzzles you arrive in a room to explore with emails to read, audiologs to listen to, and photographs to pick up and squint at. The only problem here is that there's apparently no subtitles for audiologs, and it can be a pain at times to read all the different pieces of paper lying around. This was most prevalent in the report notes in the Bio lab.
Apart from just two secrets that require you to go back to a previous chapter from the menu to get to, there's no real replayability to the game. You can easily find everything else in your first run, and the only thing I've seen that changes the ending is your choice right at the very, very end of the game.
All in all its a fun game if you like puzzles and light philosophical musings. Snag it on sale or in a humble bundle.

This is your cup of tea if you like Portal or, i hear, The Talos Principle (which I haven't played). However, don't expect the same brilliance or polish. I enjoyed the voice acting immensely, but most other elements of the game had flaws that I couldn't quite ignore. I'll be using Portal as a basis for comparison. If you haven't played Portal, you don't need this review. Go play Portal instead. It's better.
Let's start with the puzzles. They are based around a few simple elements (buttons, power conduits and light bridges mostly) put together in a large variety of ways, much like Portal. Unlike Portal, the puzzles don't escalate much in difficulty. The later puzzles are simply larger, with more doors and buttons, but without any more thinking involved. I don't remember feeling challenged even once, and I'm fairly certain I finished a few of the puzzles in ways not indended by the developers, such as running and jumping onto a platform from an odd angle without activating the light bridge I was obviously supposed to use. Other places, the intended solution didn't work every time, because it relied on boxes landing on buttons, and they would stubbornly roll off the button because they didn't land just right.
There are a few optional puzzles (related to achievements), but the hardest one in my opinion is the very first one, and solving it relies more on luck than skill (as it requires finding an item later in the game, and then returning to it). At least the AI helpfully lets you know that you should probably be returning to it, rather than randomly trying everything.
Next is the story (spoiler free review, don't worry). This, like Portal, involves an AI with an agenda. This is a game with a much more serious tone, though. The whimsical tone of Portal meant that puzzle elements could be added as needed, and their existence explained with a joke. In The Turing Test, the puzzles seem forced, and the explanation given for why they exist is not at all convincing. They are apparently designed to be solvable only by a human (hence the name of the game), since the AI is "incapable of creativity". The AI itself comments that it would have to resort to brute force to solve the puzzles. Ironically, I'm sure that is exactly what a lot of players are doing, and I suspect it works just fine. Also, from the audio logs I got the distinct impression that the AI is absolutely capable of creativity (the subtle, manipulative kind).
And how did a few crew members build all this? If they had saved some energy and built only half of it, the game would have had a suitable length puzzle-wise.
Conclusion: If you like Portal, and you get this game for cheap, it's worth an hour of your time. If you
like this type of game, it may be worth all of 5 hours. There is close to nil replay value.

Flight of Icarus was about a suicidal airship pilot named Gabriel in a dystopian steampunk world. Which was ravaged by plagues, wars and greed of humanity. Then came the Guns of Icarus Online, which was about airship pilots following the footsteps of the protagonist of first game. It was a PvP game and an interesting comcept in its own right. But wasn't advertised too much and known to a small, loyal player-base only.
Then a wild creative idea appeared: A PvE extension! It was a welcome addition for the existing players and also a valid reason to return for me (I'm not a hardcore PvP player).
GoI Alliance, simply puts you on an airship, gives you a wrench and few other things (varies) and wants you to keep that airship afloat and destroying AI controlled airships at the same time.
One of the four players aboard becomes a pilot, who -apparently- pilots the thing. Rest of the crew picks one of the two roles: gunner or engineer. Gunners operate the guns and destroy other things. Engineers repair & maintain everything and keep the giant scrap of metal afloat for others to continue doing their jobs.
Interesting teamwork game for anyone that likes fast paced action. You should try... yes you.

A long awaited new adition to guns of Icarus! Alliance offers new factions, ships, guns and of course, snazzy steampunk outfits! If your faction manages to take victory in the war period, the top players will be embodied in the lore. after almost 1,000 hours in the base game and about 100 in alliance (including beta and alpha testing releases) I feel that It is definatley worth picking up. If you dont want to pick up alliance for 20.00 at least grab the base game for 5.00. its well worth it. See you in the skies!

what is the game:
PvE expansion to "guns of icarus online." guns of icarus is an online team based airship combat simulator. you pick from 3 classes pilot, gunner, or engineer. each ship carries 4 crew typically 1 pilot 1 gunner 2 engineers. pilot spends almost all his time flying except on a select few ships where he can sometimes shoot or repair one item. gunner spends most time shooting and fixing the guns he shoots, tho helping engineers repair is not uncommon. engineers spend most of their time running around the ship repairing everything, and depending on the ship shooting as well.
the "alliance" expansion to "guns of icarus online" creates a less competative varient of guns of icarus that is more noob friendly. at the same time the expansion adds unlockable pve ships and guns (test ships/guns that will eventually be balanced and thrown into pvp). the alliance mode is not just for new players dificullty settings, it allows for older players to have a challenge as well.
"guns of icarus alliance" also adds a faction war system to the game where multable factions fight for control of a risk style map based off decisions made by players in that faction. currently there are 4 factions eventually there will be more.
Pros:
1. comunity is much more polite in pve (pvp varient some experienced players had zero tolarence for new players)
2. grind factor in this game is so low it almost doesnt exzist (only the pve class specails, guns, and ships are unlockables)
3. game is 100% skill based minimal grind means all players are on equal footing (minus the games learning curve)
4. guns/ weapons are unique to eachother and require various amounts of skill to use (praise hades... best gun IMO)
5. pve engineer equipment makes engineering even without shooting more interactive (ship parcore ftw)
6. each ship is unique and its weapons are fully customizeable (putting the right weapons on a ship is key to winning)
7. team based combat makes game great to play with friends (even noobs are deadly when they are cordinated)
Cons:
1. current lack of map variety (only one map per PvE gamemode as far as i can tell)
2. faction conquest/risk feels vert disconnected from the actual combat in game (just click where you want to help fight)
3. lore is awsome but game doesnt do anything to make you feel like your in the world (mostly because lack of maps)
4. very high learning curve (this could be a pro or a con depending on who you are)
5. occasional toxic people (its a 100% multiplayer game even tho pve is more chill than pvp some people are just toxic)
6. forced to fight on blue team in PvE (I HATE BLUE TEAM)
7. no RED ship ornament (also i can only paint bloon Red not hull)
What i think is missing: (some for current build others i expect would require another expansion)
1. to add to map varity and immersion... make climate / background and some models change texture and color to reflect where you are deployed in world map
2. virtual lobby / overlay lobby with the town you are deploying from (make it a default shape similar to map variation idea so you can see other shipmates / crew
3. ground targets / battles (even in modern warfare people dont just fight in the skies)
4. open world to fly in with merchant/pirate style missions with pve and pvp elements (and towns to visit / walk around)
5. ability to create your own airship (limited enough that said ships will stay roughly balanced)
6. ability to paint ship hull (and Red hull paint)
7. more ship ornament (not just a Red one... but i want a RED one)

The game fools you at lower lvl monsters, making you believe it was actually fun and letting you win against newbies. In the case of unfair matchmaking, instead of improving the system the game no longer show's players level so you have no idea what your up against, whether they're noobs or veterans and it gives you no clear path of exit. It also seems that the update either shortened respawn time or it's been this way the past few updates, but killing defeating hunters is extremely difficult because of short respawn intervals. For example, recently i fought a well balanced match against seasoned veterans. I killed 2 out of the 4, and went to keep battling the rest. i quickly gave up when i realized that in the time it took me to kill the two, the respawn timer had gone down for my match and both players were respawned instantly.
The problem for the latest issue is the fact that players don't have individual respawn timers, the team respawns at once, and the timer isn't started when players die. the respawn counter or whatever triggers respawns could be counting down while a player is still alive. This makes it extremely stupid when you kill someone, and they come back 10 seconds later
