Rift is a great game, but has some drawbacks, which can discourage people after some point to continue or even try this game.
Lets start from character creation. Rift offers you a quite big variety of character customization options and you can come up with many many different possibilities... if you have paid for additional colors, hair styles etc. From here you begin to see it's free to play features. At very beggining you can have maximum of 2 characters, unless you buy additional character slots later in-game. But despite these restrictions character creation still gives you plenty of options, but just like in any other game.
At the very beggining you are introduced to Rift's story at different perspective (depending on which side you are playing). Intro movie and low-level quests explains, why these two factions are fighting together, but it's f****ed up a bit (that's what i liked), because there is no good or bad guys. Just big misunderstanding.
After playing a while some people will get that feeling, that Rift is kind of similar to WoW. Character control is very similar, just like other features I will mention later. You can choose from 4 different classes and each class has 6 ar 8 (I don't remember exact number) different Soul trees. It's like talent tree system, but you can customize it completely by choosing 3 different soul trees for you character. At first it might be a little tricky, but that's why you can choose from already created patterns. You can have several different soul tree combinations which you can switch almost any time. So, for example, cleric can be tank, DPS and Healer whenever he want. UI can be completely customized as you wish. UI is so flexible, that you don't need any add-ons (okay, maybe one or two).
Crafting system is neat. Also somewhat similar to WoW's. You don't to buy additional mats every time you want to craft something. Also, some daily quests will help you level up fast, if you are stuck, since they give you all required mats on the plate. It might be pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when you reach lvl 295.
Dungeon group system is very nice. (I'll just stop saying "similar to WoW"). Choose a dungeon, choose a role, wait a bit and presto! Didn't get any loot? Here, do these daily quests and have some equipment. Bosses are very dynamic and each has it's own tactic. Those, who don't know them yet, can follow in-game intructions what to avoid and when.
PvP system offers you PvP stuff, which you can buy for killing others. You can choose participate in one of several battlegrounds (here called warfronts). It has balance system so there wont be 10 guys pulverizing 5, but can be tricky sometimes. As you kill others in PvP, you also gain exp. It's a good thing, if you're PvP person. That way you can level up all the way to max lvl only doing PvP, but you can't level up to X9 lvl and stay in battlegrounds forever. After hitting max lvl be prepared to get wrecked a lot. Try saving up your Favor for 60lvl PvP gear to avoid some of the wrecking. But still you'll be nuked all the way until you get end-game gear. It's not like other games doesn't have that thing, it's just this gap is very very big and it will take quite some time untill you'll overcome it.
Be prepared for "some" achievements. Like every little step you take, you get an achievement. Something happened? Achievement!
It's buyable content is mostly vanity items and boosts, but some essential functions are taken away from you, as a free user. Such a auction house. You have to spend some money to gain permision to post auctions. This might suck, but you can buy REX packs, for game coins, so you don't have to spend real money. One REX is enough to get you back those features. It's price varies from 1,2k to 1,5k platinum (back in 2013 end and beggining of 2014). It's not dramatically much, but it takes some time to get that kind of money. As you reach level 60, you'll notice that you can buy mid-end-game gear for money OR you can begin griding dungeons for PvE currency. Dungeons and Chronicles can be fun first 20 times, but that only give you some cheesy boots from tier-whatever. Anyway early 60 griding is what hit me, personaly. Same chronicles and dungeons over and over and over again. But I guess I just don't have patience for that.
So basicly Rift is really fun to play, much content to explore and many hours to play. It has some flaws as f2p game, but they don't make such a big impact to your gameplay. Many players will find similarities to WoW and despite high-level griding it's definitely woth a shot.

The Turing Test is essentially The Talos Principle cosplaying as Portal. Or maybe the G-rated Sunday matinee of SOMA.
If you've played any of those, you know what to expect.
If not, TTT is a decent first-person physics puzzler with an angsty future-space-exploration storyline hinting at the dangers of AI, which most of us have been aware of since 2001. It doesn't do anything particularly well, nor does it do anything particularly bad. It's a thoroughly average, enjoyably middle of the road knockoff; interesting without being compelling, challenging without being difficult, meeting expectations for a solid afternoon playthrough without underwhelming or exceeding either way.
Level design is reasonably good. There are a few puzzles that get fairly tricky and force you to think, but even the most difficult pale compared to the latter levels of Talos. Some of the mechanics are not well explained, if at all, and occasionally only used once, forcing you to sit there banging rocks together until you discover the intended nuance. The biggest complication for me was the reliance on object physics to solve some of the puzzles, which can go horribly awry at times, turning a simple solution into a frustrating and repetitive trial-and-error until you get the Rube Goldberg result you want. You know, those "Ugh, REALLY?" moments.
Music and audio are satisfactory and functional; nothing terribly exciting. Adequate. Some of the exposition recordings are quiet, muffled, or indistinct -- make sure you turn on subtitles. The worst complaint I can offer about TTT is that the ending credits scroll in as if being typed out, one loud, slow, click-clacking letter at a time. Between that and the splash screen's obnoxious foghorn, I suspect someone at Bulkhead has a fetish for annoying sounds. But if that's the most heinous crime this game commits, that's pretty good.
If you have the itch for some additional generic store-brand Talos or Portal puzzles, this will scratch it, just don't expect (or pay) too much.

The Turing Test tries way too hard to be thought-provoking and clever, and ends up feeling overly simplistic and flat in both its analysis and puzzles. The puzzles are designed to make you "think outside the box", but they often are obvious to anyone that has played a bit of puzzle games.
I'm a big fan of both scifi and puzzle games, so maybe I've just seen the ideas presented here too many times, but it was a shame to see that this game didn't really explore them in any new way.
On the positive hand, there
some interesting ideas and puzzles here, it's just that they are way too few and way too short. The exploration bits are pretty nice, but they are short and not really the selling point of the game.
Go play some other first person puzzler if you want good puzzles (Antichamber is a favorite of mine, both Portal games are great and Talos Principle and QUBE seem to be great although I haven't play them yet), and read about AIs if you want a better exploration of the themes present here  ("Humans Need Not Apply", a short documentary by CGPGrey, and "The AI Revolution", a 2-part post by Tim Urban of WaitButWhy, are both an accesible but pretty thorough introduction to the topic). If you just want good puzzles, play Hexcells or Squarecells or (if you're up for a big challenge) Stephen's Sausage Roll.

Two games in one, Typing of the Dead: Overkill is House of the Dead: Overkill lightgun railshooter converted to a typing game where you have to type words to kill the mutants (zombies, whatever). And as a bonus, you can still play the original game as an alt mode, plus three minigames to keep your skills honed. In case you haven't played railshooters, here's the deal. Your characters move in first person automatically. Your job is simply to put the cursor on whatever it is you need to kill, and shoot, with periodically reload. In typing mode, each target has a word or phrase you must type to kill it, and on easy mode, capitalization and spacing doesn't matter. Ammo, medpacks, and collectibles are grabbed via the TAB key in the typing mode (and must be "shot" in the lightgun mode). As the enemy gets close to striking you their "word" will turn from green, to yellow to red, to flashing red. Occasionally enemies will throw objects at you which must be taken out first, but you can't switch targets mid-typing. So if the enemies aren't getting closer, try to intercept their projectiles THEN attack.
This game makes even my decent typist hands cramp up. I can do 85 wpm with 99% accuracy, but I can only get 92-95% accuracy in this game, which means I can't get the big bonuses. :D   And it's really "pretty" in a sick sort of way, as it relies on jump scares, enemies popping up left and right, even right next to you. After all, you are dealing with mutants / zombies that simply starts walking, and often, it's just when you get up to it.
Every level has a boss, which requires a bit different attack, as often it will launch projectiles that you have to deflect (with your shots), while attack the boss, and type certain words to get out of the way of their charge attack. Sometimes minions may join in. The only exception is the final boss where the game seems to suggest you must enter relevant keywords, but in reality you can just spam the keyboard (enter as many random characters as you can).
There were tons of collectibles including soundtracks for the jukebox, 3D art models, pages of a comic book for this game, and concept art. And there are separate collectibles (and achievements) for the typing portions as well as the shooting portion.
The game was apparently the 2nd most profane game ever sold, with the m*****f***** phrase dropped virtually EVERY sentence when Isaac Washington, one of the player characters, speak up. It seems the record was only broken by Mafia II. So if you don't want to assault young ears, wear headphone or don't play this game. Not to mention this game has tons of adult situations, including a biker strip bar (and undead strippers), among other things.
The game also relies heavily on B-movie grindhouse style exploitation, where NONE of the female characters met a good end (is that a spoiler?)  The PC version also brought you the DLCs and extra levels that have you play 2 of the 10 levels as Varla Guns and Candi Stryper, instead of Isaac Washington and Agent G for the other levels. And they have their own challenges.
All in all, Typing of the Dead: Overkill is a load of fun that will surely challenge your typing skills, and there are word packs you can purchase that will expand the vocabulary if you think the words are starting to repeat on you. And if you got tired of typing you can always use the mouse and play the actual rail shooter game. Buy it, if just for the novelty, and it may even improve your typing... if you can get past the purile humor and mature theme.

Dishonored is an amazing stealth based FPS where you have several different tools to get through each level in your own way.
For example, group of 4 guards. You can blink past them and rewire their electric turret to kill each of them in less than a second. Or you can throw a grenade, freeze time and shoot the grenade out of the air with a crossbow. Or you can spawn a pile of flesh eating rats that will eat them alive. Or you can freeze time and shoot each of them with each invididual projectile, which is the normal gun, a normal dart, a sleep dart, and an exploding dart. Or you can lob a tank of exploding whale oil at them. Or you can summon an incredibly strong whirlwind and knock them off a cliff. Or you can simply run up and stab each of them old fasioned style.
The possiblities with this game are nearly endless, and it has such a rich story with different endings, that one playthrough is simply not enough. To anyone who wants to be a ghost, a ninja, a warrior or anything in between, play this.
10/10. Cheers.

Weeks ago, I found this game by accident on the Steam store. I shared a link to it with a friend just to joke about how weird it f#cking looks. He joked about gifting it to me as a joke, and at the end days of the Summer sale, he actually did it. And holy f#ck, what a let-down this thing is. Now sure, I wasn't exactly sure what to expect from it, but the whole game falls flat on my opinion. And as I usually do, I'll start by talking about it's negative points.
First and foremost, the gameplay. It's f#cking boring. Have you ever played Arkanoid? Then this is it. The bulk of the gameplay is the exact same f#cking thing. And the worst part is, it's easy as hell until you reach higher levels, however to reach higher levels you gotta keep playing for 10 minutes in a game where even when you try to get yourself killed, it doesn't seem to happen.
Second, is the gimmick with the LSD-like effects. Sure they look cool, but the novelty of them wears off stupidly fast. Here's the thing: the game on itself is boring and easy, adding those effects makes it nearly impossible to see what's happening... But it won't matter because of you hold the trigger and move in one direction while spamming A, you'll still last for 15 minutes despite not knowing what in the actual f#ck is happening. What's the point of the effects? To make it harder? To look cool? Who knows, but it really doesn't do much to enhance the gameplay, it's just there as a selling point.
Third, the price. 3€ ain't too bad but you'll expect a game this kind of average to get some sort of good deal during big sales such as the Summer sale, which might I add, for most people it's the biggest one in Steam. Well, not for this game. All it got was a miserable 15% discount with is nearly unnoticable. I even though of buying the game myself before the sale if it did get a good discount but 15%? Even games that got released months ago got better discounts. And honestly, the game isn't worth neither 3€ or 2,40€. Maybe 1.
Lastly, the game looks... Kinda bland. Not talking about the seizure-inducing effects, those look cool, but the rest of the game? All enemies are a variation of smiley faces either straight or turned upside down, the backgrounds rarely change the balls are those same MS-Paint-looking smiley faces but green and at times with hats, most of it looks bland as hell, like something straight out from the deepest parts of the Steam Greenlight.
Does the game have anything good though? Well...
The game works well with controllers. It's to be expected though, since as far as I'm aware, it was released first on Xbox360 and then re-released on Steam.
The dev/s did put a lot of effort on the LSD-like effects and the sounds. And for that they should be deeply commended.
...But I honestly can't think of anything else. I haven't played this game much, yeah. But there isn't really much to see before you've seen it all. The whole game is all about some amazingly looking effects that don't really add up much to the whole experience. Maybe it's fun to play this while high, who knows. But you gotta be high as hell on my oppinion to play too much of it. I sure as hell though, gonna tell my friend to look if he can refund gifts.
TL;DR Edition: Cool effects and sounds on an underwhelming pong game that's not even pong, IT'S F#CKING ARKANOID with smiley faces all over the place. The whole game is based around the novelty of having seizure-inducing effects that won't let you see sh#t. It's a cool concept but executed poorly. Couldn't even stand an hour of this thing before I got sick and bored of it.

I was a big fan of the original Painkiller back when it came out. It was fresh, and most importantly, it brought the old school modern shooter style back into the modern era, i got fond memories of me and my friends playing till 2am in the morning just trying to reach to the next chapter.
That beign said, i just need to point out that this games straves as far as possible from the original, without loosing it's old good painkiller feel to it.
The entire Painkiller franchise has always had three main things that make it great, the aesthetics (both on the levels as well as the monsters and creatures you fight), the gameplay, and the "longetivity". Whenever i get asked what i liked the most about the old Painkiller, i always have the same answer, "Lenght", the lenght of this game doesn't even come close to the first one, the levels are stripped down and often times the new chapters just doen't made it in time for the beauty in design that was the first one. However the game adds new weapons and keeps it's old mechanics new, it does this by never betraying the fast paced formula and as an end result it just manages to share fantastic things with the player, the downloadable content was sadly where the game shined, in terms of it's level design, they add more weapons, enemies, levels, and all of this while sticking to a subject at hand, i could be fighting soldairs in bunkers, or maybe roman imperials, this startling absurdity and insanity just creates a fantastical, delusional experience that embraces the player and welcomes it to this sequel, because it is a sequel, the vast majority of bosses have changed, as well as the levels (as i mentioned before), heck it even gives you different guns as you progress through the game.
The bottom line it's that this is not a remake, it's a sequel, a sequel to a fantastic gem that gave birth to thousands of bad sequels, but luckily this is not one of them. It's not as good, but neither bad, and that's fine by me.

Painkiller Hell & Damnation (a clever title instead of Painkiller HD) is a remake of a classic retro first-person shooter and carries over the gameplay mechanics that we're used to from way back in the day when bunnyhopping and massacre were the recipies for success instead of the pathetic hand-holding mechanics seen commonly in modern shooters.
You take the role of Daniel Garner, a soul taken into purgatory after a fatal car crash some time ago and permanently separated from his lover as a result. Daniel is your run of the mill badass character with a dark past and a penchant for causing incredulous amounts of pain in a short time, Daniel is offered a chance to reunite with his love in exchange for collecting seven legions of souls for the Grim Reaper himself; thus begins your thousand mile marathon of blood.
Gameplay, as mentioned previously, is absolute retro FPS goodness. You can carry as many giant and powerful weapons as you can get your hands on which you use to impale, dismember, decapitate and gib all the varied waves of foes foolish enough to get their ugly mugs in the way of your crosshairs. As you massacre foes by the bulk they drop souls in the shape of glowing green orbs, collecting them heals the player for 1HP and can overheal you to well above 100%, and to encourage players to collect dropped souls the player can enter "Demon Mode" when they gather 66 souls. Demon Mode grants the player damage immunity for a short time all the while replacing your weapons with an instant-kill pulse that shreds all enemies nearby. When your screen starts pulsing in grayscale that means you've almost collected enough souls, so you have a chance to line yourself up with a large amount of foes in order to maximize it's effect. The player can also collect gold in the levels in order to cover the cost of "Tarot Cards" that provide a powerful buff for a short duration, these buffs include improved damage resistance and slowed time, among many others that can be unlocked as the player progresses. Enemies in Painkiller have a wide variety of capabilities, from being simple mindless cannon fodder to hefty tank enemies and sometimes enemies that can use special abilities to slow or disarm you for a short period.
Level design is extremely straightforward, but easy to navigate so you can kite the waves of ghouls into bottle-necked corridors for easier clean-up. There are also secrets and hidden areas to find, making level exploration a rewarding and worthwhile experience.
In terms of graphics: There isn't much to mention. Graphics are sub-par at best despite the well animated opening cinematic, and character animation is at best laughable as Daniel and everyone else in the cutscenes move stiffly and robotic. Enemy animations are pretty well done, and much more aesthetically pleasing than cutscene animations.
A negative aspect of Painkiller is the physics system: Jumping or otherwise interacting with physics objects in the world is clumsy and awkward, and cleary remains unfinished. This is especially bad when you are trying to kite enemies and you get hung up on a stray object that's laying in your path.
But the worst part is the glitchy coop mode. Several times in the coop campaign I have been unable to move, access the menu or do anything after re-loading a level, not to mention the horrible server issues and terrible lag compensation.
Now, another note for all newcomers: It is HIGHLY recommended that when reaching the first boss of the game, known as the "Necrogiant" that you PAUSE the game and search up a strategy guide. Because no word of a lie, this boss will sh*t all over unprepared players on any difficulty.
So in conclustion, Painkiller Hell & Damnation is a retro FPS targeted towards players looking for a blast-from-the-past with no limited weapon inventory, health regeneration or cover systems seen in all these newer shooter titles, and instead focuses on everything that made the genre a success to begin with.

This game tries to work your brains like Portal or the Talos Principle with great puzzles and an interesting thoughtprovoking story, but is sadly failing in the end. Firstly, the puzzles are mostly way too simple. It's just connecting the stuff in the right sequence: barely any out of the box thinking is needed, except for the optional puzzles, but they too are very simple.
The story could be good in another game, however in the context of a 3D puzzle game it simply feels a little bit out of place. Every time you enter a room, you get another bit of dialog, and at the end of the main chapters there are nice "vignettes" in the form of rooms with items your can pick up, audio logs you can listen to and text you can read. However, since this is all "interrupted" constantly by bad to mediocre puzzles, the pazing of the story (and thus also the emotional build up) seems off. I think this story would have fitted better with an adventure game or walking simulator. It also doesn't help that the main character you play, Ava, is clueless as hell, which further strengthens the disconnect I had with the story. It's just not believable a person as dumb as this would ever be able to become an astronaut!
There is some good however: the UE4 engine is glorious (especially the lighting), and the voice acting and music are also pretty decent. However, overall I was quickly bored by this game, and only finished it because it was so short.

As a fan of Metroid Prime's puzzles, Nabacular Drop, Tag: The Power of Paint (those games were the inspiration for Portal 1 and 2) The Ball, Garry's Mod Puzzle Maps, Portal 1 &2 (especially the user generated levels), Minecraft Puzzle maps, The Puzzle Mirror's Edge maps, QUBE, Antichamber, Quantum Conundrum, The Unfinished Swan, The Room, FRACT OSC, MIND: Path to Thalamus, The Witness, and most recently The Talos Principle and its dlc, I came into this game looking for another game to challenge me in the way those past games have. When compared to its contemporaries I would recomend first checking all of them out before trying this game, since they are all much less expensive and with more content per dollars than this game. However,  I'd say if you're like me and have already played all the other games in this unfortunately small genre you'll get a kick out of it all the same and that for fans of the genre this is not one you'll want to miss.
In terms of story, the game delivers. Taking its queue from talos principle Qube and portal, the narrator is an untrustworthy ai who seems to have alternative motives. What makes it interesting is that, like Qube, not all is what it appears. Won't go into spoilers but definetely was a solid twist of some of the tropes found in other games in the genre.
But in terms of gameplay, the puzzles are often lacking up until the last third of the game when the usual mechanics  are pushed aside to make way for the more original ideas at the core of the gameplay's design, complementing the shift in story that happens at that point.
Overall I'd recomend getting this game on sale, and only if you have already played the other games in the series, particularly the witness, both portal games, and The Talos Principle + dlc since they all have much more engaging puzzles than this game and longer lengths to match.
I hope the developer will release more challenging dlc that applies the later mechanics in the game in new and interesting ways, and promise to review that dlc if/when it ever gets released. Here's to hoping!

Dishonored is an amazing game, it is stealth gameplay at its absolute finest.  You play the role of a bodyguard who has been framed for murder, and you take revenge and clear your name.  How you achieve this is up to you however, you can use brute force, killing everyone and leaving a trail of bodies, or you can use cunning and stealth, and finish the game without so much as harming a single person.  It is this dichotomy that may be Dishonored biggest appeal to me; the combat is so fun and satisfying, using your movement skill to zip around and kill unaware guards with one-shot finishers.  At the same time, by taking this route, you are taking an active role in increasing the death and plague of the city; if you want to leave it a better place than the beginning of the game, you must take stealthier approach, putting your blade away and taking mercy on those who have wronged you.  The graphics are amazing, it is well-optimized, and the grim, dark Victorian-England Steampunk setting implores you to search every alley and turn over every stone, which you should be doing because of all the goodies hidden throughout each level.  The DLCs are interesting and well designed as well, even the City Trials are fun and I have sunk many many hours into improving my scores on each trial.  No matter how you play dishonored, you will not be disappointed by the experience at all.

Some cons:
- Gameplay ends up being somewhat repetative.
- Soundtrack is dull (and it's the same thing on loop for every mission)
- The physics are unrealistic. The planes don't stall, I've gotten into mid air collisions and somehow still managed to keep on flying with only minor damage.

I got this game on sale for absolute peanuts, so I can hardly complain about the faults. If you enjoy flying, you'll most likely enjoy this game.

I don't doubt many people remember the good old days of House of the Dead 2 and its hilariously bad voice acting.  ("Suffer, like G did?").  I expect slightly less will remember the bizarre spinoff 'Typing of the Dead' that made just a few subtle changes and one huge one.  Shoot the enemy by hitting the right keys on your keyboard.  It sounded silly - it WAS silly - but had a fantastic charm about it.
Typing of the Dead: Overkill is the same premise, but with vastly more polish. As you would expect from a classic arcade game, there's nothing to write home about when it comes to narrative, but killing all your gory foes with finger blistering typing skills fits the game style in a way that would probably surprise most people.
Whether or not you played the original TotD, if you can type without looking at the keyboard, then this game is good for a laugh.  It comes with a hearty recommendation, but don't get mad when you can't find the ^ key just as you really need it!

When I first got this game, I kinda knew what to expect.  I'd played House of the Dead in the arcades, and I liked the idea of incorporating typing into the popular rail shooter.  I played it for a while, had fun, laughed at the stupid jokes and extreme over-acting of it all, and then pretty much shelved it for awhile.
A few days ago, I got my first mechanical keyboard (Corsair K65 RGB, Cherry MX Reds).  Then I remembered I owned this game, so I redownloaded it and I can honestly say that this game went from kinda fun to EXTREMELY fun.
With mechanical keys, my average score in the game is around 91%.  Definitely a different experience.  I almost wanna say you won't have any real fun in this unless 1) You love typing, and 2) You have a badass mechanical keyboard to play it.
As for the game itself, if you've ever played a rail shooter before, it's pretty standard.  Game moves on its own, zombies come at you and instead of using a light gun, you use your keyboard and type the words, terms, or sentences below the zombies.  Type it out correctly, and you kill the zombie.  Do it quick enough and you'll get a headshot.
If there are multiple zombies on screen, it'll use red arrows and a flashing border around the word to let you know you should dispatch THIS zombie first, or you'll get slapped.
The game mixes it up a lot.  Some zombies will throw stuff at you, and rather than concentrate on the word below them, you wanna shoot the single letter attached to the object flying at your face, and THEN take the zombie out.
Some words, terms, and sentences are longer than others, especially if you have some of the dictionary DLCs installed.  Also, get in the habit of hitting TAB periodically, as there are various green health packs, slow-mo power ups, game music tracks, and game artwork that can be collected.
The jokes are over-the-top, the monsters are disgustingly awesome, and my typing score is getting better and better.  Grab it up.

Combat in this game is one of the best that I have seen in all Paradox games. I especially like the battle plan system in which you can give orders to your troops and decide where you want them to attack, and then the AI starts all of the attacks, instead of in Hearts of Iron 3 and other Paradox games in which you have to assign units one by one to provinces or give them all over to the AI. One critiscism that I have is that they removed the system in whcih you would have to place your HQ divisions, but I can see why they did this as it would make the game a lot harder to learn.
In my opinion, this is where the game lacks a lot. In Hearts of Iron 3, there were 11 ideologies (National Socialist, Fascist, Paternal Autocrat, Social Conservative, Market Liberal, Social Liberal, Social Democrat, Left Wing Radical, Leninist, Stalinist and Non Aligned) which by no means represents real life, but it is better than Hearts of Iron 4's political ideologies (Democratic, Fascist, Communist, and Non Aligned). Also in Hearts of Iron 3 you could decide on a lot of laws, such as your Civil Society Law, Conscription Law, Economic Law, Education Law, Industrial Law, Press Law, and Training Law. But in Hearts of Iron 4 you can only decide on your Conscription Law, and Economic Law. There is also some vital information that is hidden from you such as the drift of a country to the Allies, Axis, or Comintern. The new national focus system is amazing, and it is one of my favourite features in the game.
When it comes to research you get a metric button of choices at the start of a game and during earlygame, a lot of catching up during midgame, and then in the lategame you almost finish everything (and then install a mod that gives you even more stuff to research). Overall the techs explain themselves very well and are for the time they are set in excluding the tanks. Sometimes you reach lategame tanks too quickly. In a lot of my matches as Germany I could skip Panthers and Panzer 4´s and go straight for the E-50.
You need Civillian Factories to repair oher factories that were destroyed by plane bombings and battles. And you can use Civilian Factories to build new stuff like more factories, more factories or more factories. You could go for nothing but factories but if you did that then you would fail; a good amount of factories - military or civillian - is needed but you also need to construct other structures aswell, such as: Anti Air guns to gun out bombers and fighters that want to destroy your cities, infastructure which you will need lots of when you invade Siberia, huge parts of Asia, South America, and Africa, and Radar which you will need to scout out your enemies before you attack. Hearts of Iron 4 excels in this area.

This is by far my favorite WWII game I've ever played, as well as my favorite strategy game overall. Compared to other PDX games, HOI4 is still in its infancy, so don't expect it to have the level of polish of EU4 or CK2 in terms of the national flavor or AI, but it's an amazing game in its own right.
I think they've done an amazing job on coming to a compromise on depth vs. micro-management. Playing it you feel like you're really the "big guy in charge", you tell everyone what to do on a big level, and they figure out the details on their own. The way they've used strategic areas for air and naval makes it so that you can focus mostly on your army, while still making the other two areas very interesting.
The amount and quality of mods for this game is tremendous as well. I especially love the total conversion mods like "The Great War" and "Kaiserreich", and it's fun to sit back and play them when you need a break from the historical WWII setting.

The Turing Test is a linear puzzle game, much in the style of portal, where you are fed new dialog and information after every puzzle. It differs from portal in that rather than clever, passive agressive remarks, you get thrown concepts that make you think about what makes us human, and whether an A.I. could ever become concious and if we could even figure out if it had.
The puzzles arn't very challenging until the very end, though the game keeps you interested by making you want to find out what happened to the crew members, and whether or not the A.I., Tom, may be responsible.  The Turing Test is a blend of both The Talos Principle and Portal, but fails to be as good as either.  Nonetheless, it is still a very solid game that will make you think about your existence while you solve some fun puzzles.

Lili: Child of Geos is a very peculiar and unique game. It is a game that children and adults (channel your inner child adults!) can play and enjoy.
: When the graphics are set on 'Fantastic', which is the highest value, the game is gorgeous. The view of the island itself is magnificent and the lighting in-game makes the entire game seem somehow enchanted and magical.
: The storyline is pretty simplistic and one should not expect a complex and in-depth storyline from this game. The plot itself is that you are Lili, a botanist and student sent to the supposedly 'uninhabited' island of Geos to collect samples of flowers to bring back home for your research project. However, you find that the island is not empty and that there are creatures (constructs and spirits and many others) of a different variety.
: As you read in the upper section that Lili is a botanist, you may assume that you will pick flowers throughout the game. Yes, you are correct! You will be picking countless of flowers, breaking vases, talking to goofy individuals, scaring birds, finding items, and fighting spirits (yes, you will pick the flowers off of their backs!). You should not expect a hack-and-slash style or a difficult puzzle from this game.
: This game is hilarious. If you actually take your time (like I did) and talk to everyone and read everything, it turns out that our heroine is a gamer! And there are Zelda and Super Mario references (and many more) throughout the game as well as things and topics that would be considered 'inappropriate' are slightly implied so that if your children are playing it, they will not understand. If you are playing it (an adult), you will laugh your butt off!
Overall, I truly enjoyed this game. No, it is not difficult but it is hilarious. It is a relatively short game (I would say approximately 3-5 hours if you don't take time to look at anything, read anything at all, explore, or do side quests), and the only reason I have 9 hours game-time is because I wanted to receive every single achievement (and I also kept going afk while in-game). This game is a good way to unwind after playing a scary game or having a bad day. The hilarity of this game is what kept me coming back!

I don't often post reviews, but I think this game deserves one.
Like many other gamers out there I've fallen foul of the whole Early Access promises and been bitterly disappointed several times. Some early access games I bought years ago are still... early access, which doesn't fill me with any confidence that they will ever be finished. So with a lot of money already wasted on these games, why did I take a chance with this one?
A couple of reasons if I'm honest. Firstly, and I think most importantly, there are regular updates being uploaded by the devs, so it shows that there is actually someone working on it. This gives me hope that the game is actually going to progress beyond a fancy looking sandbox, which is basically what it is. This is not necessarily a bad thing - an early access has to start somewhere and getting the basics working correctly and receiving feedback is important. No sense in building an entire solar system of planets if the first one doesn't convince the players to bother exploring.
Secondly, the game looks beautiful. The lighting is great and the weather and night time effects are very atmospheric. The day/night cycles might be a little quick, but that might be adjustable at full release. The creatures are pretty cool, although random spawning would be preferable to them always respawning in the same locations. Plus some pack attacks would be cool instead of single creatures which are an annoyance rather than a threat.
I thought I would add a short list of immediate pros and cons. I've only played 13 hours so far, but have experienced most of what the current game has to offer.
Pros.
1. Looks great and is very atmospheric.
2. Co-op works - definitely helps to have a mate share in the collecting of resources.
3. Smooth, easy movement and combat. Not too many controls - arcade feel rather than simulation.
4. Believable tech tree - unlike Life is Feudal where you can build a bow but not use it!
5. Vehicles! Only built the G.A.V. so far but it drives well and has a gun turret. Sweet.
6. Planned expansion. The game is going to evolve with player feedback.
Cons.
1. A little bit grindy. BUT... you can task your robot to automine and this does help.
2. The current build has a game area that feels big while you're walking, but once you build a vehicle you're in a tiny sandbox world. I really hope the game environment grows massively otherwise vehicles are pointless.
3. For a game with stunning graphics, the resources are... cartoony. They look more in keeping with World of Warcraft - large, bright objects on the surface that you can see from miles away. Would prefer a system like Planet Explorers where you need to scan for them.
In summary - I think the price is a little steep at the moment for the amount of content in the early access build, but with the proposed new content (including extra planets) and the beautiful way it looks and feels, it's definitely a game you should own if you like exploring and building. And being able to play with your mates on a private server gets a huge thumbs up.
:-)
Here's hoping that the updates come thick and fast. I want to explore the rest of the solar system! :-P

Dark Souls 4 is the latest installment in one of the most critically praised video game franchises of all time. Strangely, however, with this entry in the series the devs seem to have taken a very different approach, departing completely from certain elements of the previous Dark Souls games. For one, the dark and gritty art style and atmosphere of the previous entries have been replaced with what appears to be a mch happier, almost cartoony air of nostalgic joy. The story, as well, makes no mention of any of the characters previously introduced in any Dark Souls game (aside from the Capra Demon, who seems to be playing the part of the primary antagonist). While the gameplay is certainly just as challenging - and rewarding - as it has been in most other Souls games, most of the mechanics function drastically differently. The equipment system has been simplified drastically, melee attacks are almost completely nonexistant, the parry mechanic now only works on attacks of a specific color (an odd choice, but I'm optimistic), and rolling has seen a massive nerf.
While others may see these drastic changes as a bad thing, or even grounds to question the validity of this game as a Dark Souls game at all, I personally embrace the new direction the devs have taken the franchise. It's bold, it's fresh, and it certainly helps ad some cheer to an otherwise rather down-beat game.
As for where this fits into the DS timeline, the jury still seems to be out on that one, but my personal theory is that this is but one in a series of prequels that will help flesh out the story already established. Who knows. Maybe the devs will go all George Lucas and start calling the original DS trilogy "Dark Souls 4-6". Only time will tell.
All in all, I give it a 9/10. Fantastic gameplay, fantastic soundtrack, fantastic art, fantastic lore. Sadly, though, I had to deduct a point for a startling overabundance of water.
Game strongly recommended.

Rift is a beautiful game, the look and feel of it is extremely polished and allows for you to just jump in and play. It doesnt reinvent the genre but no MMO's do as it is an over-saturated market and pretty much everything has been done. It does add a few new things such rifts and hunt rifts (Raid Rifts), which are nice as you dont have to be in an organized guild raid team to just jump in. The community is good and are willing to help new players. Ill summarize the important points into pros and cons below.
Pros.
-Indepth crafting system with option to purchase more crafts (Real Money) means you dont need to roll 4 Alts to cover all trades.
-Ability to trade REX which when activated grants you real money credits to spend in the store, the going rate fluctuates between 900 and 1000 in game money for 1125 Credits (roughly) and it is easily acheivable at late level.
-The graphics are beautiful, i play in Ultra so i cant say anything for below that.
-The skill system is brilliant, you select from 3 souls which have different passive and active skills so you can create your character how you want and if you are not sure what your are doing then there are preset builds and guides to follow
-The soul system is changable at anytime so you are not limited to playing a DPS toon unless you roll an alt you can create a tank soul or a healing soul and switch between.
-The developers are activly evolving the game, hosting events and adding new content which draws in new players and keeps the game fresh.
Cons
-Cash shop could be seen as pay 2 win as you can buy end game equipment with real money (This doesnt really bother me as i have friends who i play with and they dont have time to grind as much as i do.
-The game does not require money to play, unlike alot of other F2P games they restrict you so much that the game feels like a demo, in RIFT the game is open and completley playable despite the 2 points below.
- To use the auction house you need s credit to your name, this can be done by spending as little amount as possible on the cash store or spending a REX although earning enough in game money to buy a rex is hard without the auction house.
-My biggest bug bare is bag slots, they are only purchasable via premium credits and they are character bound so if you do roll an alt you have to buy them again, It makes it really slow to get going if you dont have a gold farm to trade rex over between toons.

My boyfriend and I played this game together and greatly enjoyed it (overall).
Overall rating: 8/10
Objectionable Content: Mild? (bordering on 'some'?). There is some "humor" that is questionable both in taste and apropriateness for younger audiences. *See end of review for details, including trigger warnings and warnings for parents.
As far as the rest of the game goes, the atmosphere and evironments are absolutely stunning and worthy of screenshots. and the music is varied and well-suited. There is a bit of a Zelda-esque atmosphere which comes as no surprising seeing all the little Zelda references sprinkled throughout the game. It was refreshing to play a game that was not violent, yet still involved "beating the bad guys." So many of the characters you meet are adorable and hilarious, and have succeeded in getting laughs out of both of us. It is worth talking to all of them; they say some of the most ridiculous things. The gameplay centered around a very simple concept: pick flowers, though it was a pleasant surprise to find that it could be still be challenging sometimes. I would easily recommend this game to most of my friends.
Pros:
+ Fun, non-violent gameplay
+ Gorgeous visuals
+ World worth exploring (not overwhelming like big sandbox games)
+ NPCs worth interacting with
+ Nice soundtrack
Cons:
- The aforementioned tasteless jokes (why it is 8/10 and not 10/10. they were pretty gross.)
- Unexpected spike in difficulty between areas/levels.
- Does not clearly state its save mechanism (it's autosave, btw) and does not indicate what triggers a save
- Bit pricey for the length. I wouldn't pay more than ~$12.
- No replay value (one achievement needs ~half a 2nd playthrough but that's it.)
*There are a small handful of instances in which sexual harassment is normalized or made into a joke. Fortunately, they are few and far between, and most are easy enough to ignore and move past, but I can see a couple of the jokes being potentially triggering - especially since you would not see it coming from a game like this (we were very surprised ourselves). None of these jokes are a big piece of the game, but it's enough to make it not an 100% all-ages friendly game. To be more specific,
TRIGGER & PARENT WARNING: Stalking (creepy photos of Lili and her butt in one NPC's place), Sexual harassment (abuse of power/authority), Sexual abuse (1 joke).

Lili is a decent a reasonably creative collectathon that I can't imagine getting more than 6 hours out of. It's worth picking up on sale, but not for the full price of $20.
Pros:
- Looks great, especially considering it started on mobile. A lot of that probably comes down to the fact that most levels are cleverly designed to avoid needing to draw more than 20 feet in any direction, but the game does run on Unreal.
- Usually clever writing. Not perfect by any means, but it's generally entertaining.
- Strong world design. The descriptions comparison to Tim Schafer's work is pretty accurate in the world and character design.
- The main mini-game is fun. It involves trying to pick flowers off the head of a spirit as it runs around and sprouts bombs and thorns to make you miss. It's reasonably challenging to win the later rounds with a perfect rating, but you're going to breeze through it if just passing is enough for you. Mileage will vary heavily here.
- Lots of hats. Every spirit (52) and most quests (something like 12?) will give you a hat. There are also at least two pets to find, but the costume changes are limited to palette swaps, unfortunately.
Cons:
- Very limited graphics options. You get a few presets with no descriptions of what any of them actually do. I don't think many people are going to have trouble running the game, but Highest turns on an incredible level of depth of field. I'd have liked to be able to turn that off.
- Short. I finished it in 3 hours. That was enough to defeat all 52 spirits (most with 3/3 stars), complete nearly all of the quests, and find around 60-70% of the collectibles.
- Controls are a bit wonky. Particularly the camera.
Notes:
- Achievement hunters beware! Lili has a ton of achievements and *most* are near enough to completable in a sane person's playthrough. Then there's "Break 1,000 vases." I only got to 120 despite making an effort to break any I came across. You could probably get an extra 100 or so by going out of your way to look for them, but the full 1K is going to take some serious grinding.
- Trying to play it on a standard touchpad would be a nightmare.
- The description compares this to Zelda, but the only similarities I can find are some of the humor, Wind Waker's art direction, and the fact that money is completely and utterly useless in both games. Don't buy it hoping for puzzles or Zelda-like combat.

Pretty great game, althought it may seem unbalanced when you start out this is only for a few rounds as the game is a bit more difficult to learn than others. Hunters seem to be the hardest to learn due to it being a team based game to where 1 person can bring down the entire team. Monsters are easy at first but gets more difficult when people are more coordinated. Because of this many new players don't even bother and just call monsters op. Personally I was on a 6 losing streak as a hunter but I learned my roles and soon I went on a winning streak. After playing a bit of monster I found it way harder to learn because of the teamwork of others. Give this game a go and learn how to play and you will have a blast with this. Not all games are meant to be won sometimes you must face defeat.
So far I have encountered no bugs although others seem to be having troubles with the game.
I do not like how we do not start with starter perks making it unbalanced if a founder player has a lot of perks, although you can still unlock perks through specific hunter levels. So far there are no real currency items in the game and almost everyone has a fair chance at this game.
The gameplay is great and runs smoothly, going around as a hunter and a wrong turn and you will become the hunted. Although chasing fast monsters are annoying it is still fun while being the monster is actually scary because of the hunters ability to drain you if you do something wrong. But the monster's fear is replaced with hunter's fear fleeing at the sight of you which is what I love of this game.
I wish the tutorial and the characters were more explained as the only way to know what your abilities do is to press esc ingame. The singleplayer should allow all characters to allow you to see if you like them or not, although I do not know if custom allows all of them. It is also quite dumb to only allow AI charcaters to be ones you own.  The shop is pretty horrible with limited options but this may change as I saw a new shop in one of their dev videos.
Here are some tips: Manage your jetpack fuel wisely and use them to dodge attacks, you are a dead man if you keep panicking with your jetpack. Position yourself well in high grounds and such and make the monster go through all the trouble to get to you. Know who to target as monster, force the medic to waste his fuel and then focus him and if the support is shielding everyone focus him. Try to knock down one hunter as this will give you a huge advantage and use him as bait. There are many more tips out there, try the reddit evolve subreddit as this is where I learned some great tips.

Rift is a great game for MMO players. Great graphics and beautiful landscapes. Progression is very smooth, even at the beginning of the game, and every minute spent in the game is rewarding. I will admit that traveling can be a bit slow unless you have a mount, which only takes a little bit of grinding. Very good game.

It's a nearly perfect clone of WoW, only it's free to play, and it won't simultaneously give you eye-cancer and eye-AIDS the way WoW will. Here's what's going to happen. You'll get some guests. You'll go click on some world model. You'll hit some hotkeys. You'll get some more quests. Next thing you know you've got 3 level 50 characters.
There's nothing wrong with this game if this is what you want from it. Personally, I like to interact with game worlds, not game menus. I don't enjoy this, but since I know lots of people like WoW, I'm recommending this because it's basically the same thing only a lot less ugly and cartoon-ey.

RIFT - a great option for MMO players. Great graphics, beautiful and detailed landscapes. You can customize your character the way you want to by using different souls available within your selected class. For example, take a bit of Pyromancer for offense, a lot of Elementalist for some serious pet capability, and some Chloromancer to heal the party. Rift also has several pre-built options for those who like to get in and play quickly. Beyond all of the systems in the game, the standard things about the game are also very well done. The audio is phenomenal, and the controls are pretty intuitive. Glitches are very infrequent, and minor anyway. Besides, the game is still fairly new so such things are to be expected. Leveling up in this game is not grindy at all. The game frequently keeps you on quests (storyline and otherwise) which level you up as you play the game, rarely (if ever) forcing you to pull off to the side for some time to just level up. The solo-play material is well-handled, as is the group-play material. Gameplay is mostly solid, and the freedom to progress however you wish is definitely a bonus. The quests could benefit from more variety – something Trion should keep in mind for future content updates – and the overarching story is easily lost beneath the endless strings of ‘Collect this!’ and ‘Kill those!’ If you go in expecting total originality, immediate disappointment is sure to follow, but spend some time with the game, and you’ll be impressed with what Trion has to offer. Rift breathes new life into the genre, restoring otherwise tired old concepts and proves success isn’t always built on originality.

Adorable and with a beautiful art style, Lili: Child of Geos is a refreshing and imaginative game packed with fun humor, quirky characters and wonderfully crafted areas to explore.
Gameplay is simple: you're Lili, a young student visiting the island picking flowers for a school project. As you stroll around collecting, you'll bump into lots of interesting folks with fun things to say, little quests for you to do and treasure to find.
The game has no combat involved. Instead, you encounter evil spirits to be purged by picking flowers from their backs. It's a mini game that was intended for tablets and phones, but still translates decently to mouse controls and is easy to pick up. Various challenges are thrown in when picking the flowers, like prickly thorns to avoid and timed bombs to fling off. It can be a bit repetitive though as it's the same minigame for each spirit.
All in all, Lili is a charming adventure in a beautiful and creative world. Great for kids, casual gamers, and anyone needing a nice dose of childlike wonder and joy.

When I saw Sierra's name on this game I had to play it.  I mean this is Sierra.  King's Quest, Police Quest, and Quest for Glory! This is one of the great publishers of the old time.
Well I guess things change.  Granted this is mostly just a publishing job, but Shiftlings starts with an interesting premise that seems to rush to an uninteresting game.
The thing is nothing in the game is mechanically unsound, there's an interesting mechanic where one of the two characters are "big" and heavy.  They are connected by a cord and can switch which is which.  In game there's a story about "Black Hola Cola" that made them heavy, but... well it's just a weird reasoning for this mechanic.
The idea is the heavy character can be bounced on and drag the other character up.   All in all, this is an interesting concept, and in fact I liked it for a couple levels.  But that's kind of the problem.  I liked it until I felt like I was doing the same thing each level.  Each level is different and most will take some time to think about and consideration but... ultimately it's often very similar.
The one thing I'm confused on is the controls.  I have two control sticks, why couldn't I play with two characters at the same time?  Would that have made the game better?  Probably not  but it would have been a preferred method of control.  Instead I'm able to play as one character, or both characters using one control.  I could switch characters, but with out a second controller I wasn't offered the ability to control both characters at once, and I felt that left the game lacking quite a bit, maybe a little more excitement would have been possible.   Then again maybe this was tried and it wasn't fun for the developer.  But the control scheme they did find is a bit dull.
The real problem with the game is the graphics.  Now the graphics are gorgeous and look great.   But the thing is that every 10 levels has the same graphics.  They wear on you a bit.   However the game does change them every 10 levels (out of 50)
The problem comes in that the visual languages the graphics takes to show the level isn't really all there.  Objects look ok, but there's really not much at a glance to tell you how to proceed to through a level, most of the game is just walking around to see what you can see in each location.  When you pull the map back (through a press of the right bumper) it becomes a colorful mess.  Good graphics, but a puzzler needs something other than just colors.
The fact is the lack of this graphic language and the similarity between levels is why I stopped playing after just 14 levels.   It's not that the game was too hard (though there's a few hard challenges to figure out).  It's that it wasn't that interesting nor rewarding.   I think of something like braid where I played through it to beat the puzzles, figure out the story, and see what mechanic was coming next.  I forced myself to beat some puzzles because I wanted more.
Fez had a great visual language.  While I think there's flaws, I just wanted to see what else Fez would challenge me with.
Limbo had two colors but easily made it clear what the player was doing and kept the player interested for it's short run time.
Each of these games found a reason to make the player play these games.
The real problem with Shiftlings is it doesn't have this reason.  After I hit the second set of levels I decided I didn't want to go through 10 levels more to see something new.   There's some voice lines but they didn't keep me invested in the story.  My characters were 100 percent silent, and much of the jokes fell flat in the "This would be funny if you knew what these words meant."  But they were just alien words trying to play off the futuristic feel.
That's not to say there's nothing here.  Far from that.  I liked the other half of the humor attempts.  The game play mechanic was good, it's just the variety that was missing. There's a good set of levels in the game, but too much filler in my opinion (And probably not enough levels to really sustain a full game if you remove the filler).  But ultimately I stopped playing well short of the goal and that's a shame.
But that's the thing, the game didn't grip me at all, I didn't feel like I was having a good time, and so in the end I put the game aside, and can't recommend it.  At 15 bucks it's kind of expensive, and even cheaper, there's so many other games.
I mentioned Braid, Fez, and Limbo, all are fantastic games.   There's Thomas Was Alone that tells a fantastic story.  There's also Ibb & Obb that have a better couch co-op feel (and a better controller feel) there's probably thousands of games on Steam that do puzzle platforming, and that's kind of the issue.  Shiftlings doesn't do anything that makes it able to be recommended over all of those games but even without those games, I don't know if I could recommend Shiftlings because it doesn't do that much special on it's own.
A shame, but I hope for better from Sierra, because I'd love to see that great name and logo back on top games.  The thing is, this isn't one of them that will put up there with the Quest series.

The "balance" for the game is to give targets ridiculous levels of health, and hitting those targets with rockets or bombs is like winning the lottery.

Combat is fun, but is repetitive and the same every level. Because aiming and hitboxes are inconsistent trying to use rockets is a complete waste, so you just use machine guns every level. The turret levels are the worst I've every played, because you can be shot from guys that are too far away to hit or are over your head and you cant look up high enough to see them, which seems like a huge design flaw and ruins many levels. On these levels the hitboxes and aiming are the worst. Sometimes you need to be directly on a plane to hit them, sometimes you need to be way over their head. You think you get an idea on how aiming works and then you try it again on another plane and none hit. On some planes I moved the aimer on top, slighty in front, way in front, and all around them, and none of the positions registered hitting, which showed lack of polish. No wonder this was a budget title.

Welcome to
, a short Atari-like adventure game about playing as a man (described in the game as a "zombie") that moves slowly with jerky movements.  Controls are simple:  Left, Right, Up (Jump), and Space to fire.  Essentially, you're lost and want to get home...but you lost your key, so you quest for your key...but along the way you fight an idle grim reaper (1 HP), a fire reaper (3 HP), and a large skull-headed stone serpant (Approx. 10 HP).
As you progress on this adventure, you'll find your character sprite changing.  First his skin falls off to become more skeletal with his bones exposed, but soon you turn a bit more corrupted...more demonic as you become more imp-like and your head grows horns.
Overall, this experience was about 15 minutes long, though some people may breeze through faster or slower.  Please be warned that you only have 1 HP, so if you get hit once, it's game over.  At least you have only 3 enemies to kill, so it doesn't feel like it's such a chore.   Be careful around the boss, though.
I recommend
.  It's a free game with a single achievement.  Though the story is almost non-existant (and negligible), the gameplay is okay.  The jerky movements take a little getting used to, though.

I rolled a character and played him up to level ten. Then I just couldn't take it anymore. Rift is a WoW clone - as stale as that tired MMO experience and not nearly as interesting in terms of story and lore. Rift's vaunted features - the periodic rifts (which get boring because they're more "more of the same"), the soul tree, etc. - don't help the game, nor do they save it from being a WoW clone. That, and the choppy character motions and slow response times are just disheartening.
More of the same. More "get me ten of this" or "kill a few of these things that take far too long to kill, and that you're tired of killing after 2" or "use this thingy on that shrine" quests. More tedious grinds followed by other tedious grinds etc etc etc. Same bags, same gear system, same control/motion/action apparatus, same topographic features, same town layouts, same feel, yadda yadda.
Why does a company make a game that FEELS and acts so much like WoW that you might as well be playing WoW?? When this game came out, the tagline read "You're Not in Azeroth Anymore". That's true, you're in a drab, tiresome imitation of Azeroth. Blatant plagiarism lauded as a fresh experience. A game that claims to be different and yet feebly tries to out-Wow Wow. Fail.
Save your time. Find a better game, even one you want to act as a placeholder. Life is just too short to play second-rate WoW when you already got tired of WoW years ago.

One of the most stellar and personal experiences you will ever have.
OneShot is a fourth-wall breaking puzzle game with a mechanic of exactly what it says on the tin: You only have one shot. The characters you meet, the world you immerse yourself, and, most importantly, the main character Niko - their fates are ultimately up to you as a player and what you value.
Yes, you as the player are a seperate entity from the character, and the game makes sure you know that. In fact, there are many things that you can only do as a player that Niko cannot. The game takes the fourth wall, says, "That's very nice, but how about we don't have one," and sets you on a personal quest where you, the player, are an actor in the world just as much as Niko is, and your relationship with Niko is a uniquely personal one. It's an incredible storytelling and game mechanic that works tremendously with the game's ultimate premise - You only have one shot.
The puzzles do well to fit within the context of the game without taking you out of the immersion and don't feel like they're impeding your progress. That being said, the puzzles are extremely simple - so if you were looking for a logic challenge, you won't get that. Instead, you'll get an incredible story interweaving both the world presented and our own world in an extremely personal and emotional rollercoaster.
Absolutely one of the best singleplayer experiences I've had; I highly recommend this game!

The 'fights' consist in getting close enough to the enemy, and triggering the QTE (with the mouse cursor, or with ABXY buttons of the 360 controller). It is a nice QTE, compared to the average QTE in other games. During the fight you also can choose whether to use or not some powers (flash bombs).
The Character can be upgraded and customized (although the outfits are different almost only in colors). The flower picking is not tedious, comes spontaneous while you walk around enjoying the scenery.
When I saw the achievements....picking up 1000 flowers....I thought it was crazy. But no, in fact in only a few hours I did everything in the game and it really was no hassle. I enjoyed every part of it. It is the exact game I was looking for: it is nice, fun enough, and not complicated at all. It is a perfect game for children, or for grownups that want to relax from all the other FPS and action games, and dedicate themselves to this relaxing game. You don't have to reflect, you don't have to plan anything or else, just sit back and enjoy this little game. 80/100

Although I do recommend this title, I do so for specific reasons. Specifically from a design aspect, I find the mechanics to be a fascinating way to have a non-combat oriented game that still proves to be challenging, interesting, and altogether very different.
The mechanics are pretty simple as far as a concept goes: you are a student botenist, and are collecting rare plants to study for a report, and thus go to an island. However, when you get there, trickster spirits get in your way and steal whatever flowers you have collected. To get them back, you must ride them like an unbroken bronco, plucking them while trying to hang on. All in all, very different, and definitely worth studying, especially if you have any interest in game design. Outside of this main gameplay trope, shall we say, there's a fair amount to explore in this world, with flowers showing up around every corner, plenty of people with well fleshed out personalities to talk with, and an interesting stat system to learn to make future, more difficult spirits more manageable.
Then there are the aesthetics. This game is absolutely gorgeous for the few resources it takes. The textures are well placed and the models are incredible. The animations are so carefully crafted, that it draws you into the magical island you have entered. I haven't found anything that feels out of place, or that jars me from the experience of the game, even with all of the collectable hats you can find for your main character.
Now the story is why I recommend this game with caution. Although it is fairly well written, it definitely is aimed towards a target audience that I am just not a part of. I believe this game to be designed with players younger than me in mind, older children into the preteen age. I feel like most children could get something out of this game, although I'm not completely sure how young too young would be for this particular title. However, being in my early 20s, this story simply doesn't compell me personally.
Now even with the somewhat childish atmosphere and story, I still found myself truly enjoying the game. It's not my favorite game, by a long shot, but for what it is, it does offer some decent entertainment for when I just want to relax and play a game that reminds me of the titles that got me into gaming almost 20 years ago.

It's a short, adorable, absolutely beautiful game about collecting flowers and making friends. It's exploratory and challenging, just enough to keep you interested in what new, spiffy thing is waiting to be discovered. The story is simplistic but comes with an interesting choice around the midpoint, and it's always good to see an intelligent female protagonist who dresses like an actual person.
Then you take a break to get a pop, and realize that the inhabitants of the game are only capable of eating each other. That the cute little artifacts you've been finding are remnants left by people who have died here and been trapped in slave-bodies, bereft of the memories of their former lives. That the disassembled man giving you advice can't really die. That the vibrant landscape is a beautiful prison. That smiling, clever Lili is one bad fall away from waking up with a barrel for a chest and no memory of who she was.
Kids' game, folks. For kids.

I'm going to keep it simple and say that I found Lili: Child of Geos to be a lovely indie title. The graphics are beautiful, the soundtrack is excellent, the characters are cute and entertaining and the gameplay is simple yet enjoyable. I'd love to see more games like Lili!

In Shiftlings you control two aliens in spacesuits, one purple and one green, which are connected by a hose, sort of like an umbilical cord. If the hose is cut you can't breathe and you die. The hose is used to pass air between the two, making one of them fat and heavy, and the other one small and light. The lighter one is able to jump higher, fit into smaller areas, and bounce on his fat Shiftling buddy to reach higher grounds. The fatter one can be used as an anchor, preventing the other one from falling down laser pits or dropping down into fire. He is also able to pull the smaller one up ledges.
The object of the game is to activate a teleporter which takes you to the next stage. To activate the teleporter you first have to get to some sort of console and repair it, which is simply done by the press of a button. Of course there are things hindering you from reaching these consoles and teleporters. You have to figure out how to get to them by using the Shiftlings' two different sizes and weights, putting a lot of focus on puzzle solving, making this a puzzle platformer. The game is in 3D, but is played from a 2D side-scrolling perspective.
Shiftlings can be played as a co-op game, and offers both online and local co-op, but works just fine playing on your own, which I did. I can imagine the game being a lot harder playing with someone else actually as you would have to time certain jumps and reactions quite perfectly. Controlling the game is fairly simple, and I have no complaints about the responsiveness. The hard thing is to keep track of which button you shift size with and which one you change character with.
Graphically it's crisp, bright and rather colorful. It can be a little too much on the eyes sometimes, but it's no real bother. The overall theme of the game is a bit quirky, with a TV host making silly jokes when you die or when you do something good. He actually reminds me of a teacher I had who always told jokes in class. Most students hated him for it, but I could actually appreciate his attempts, perhaps because of how silly the puns were.
The game is a good challenge, though I must admit I got stuck a few times and had to resort to using a walkthrough. It feels somewhat repetitive and could use more varied levels and goals. A decent game that is worth playing for those who like puzzle platformers.

Sorry...I want to, but I sadly can't recommend.
The good news is in the theming and originality. It certainly looks interesting, with a wacky startopia-kind of visuals and humour. And with a pitch like "you play two people joined together by rope; one of them is small, the other large...and you can switch them around"...what's not to like?
Unfortunately, this game is seriously hindered by what I think is a lack of playtesting. Controlling isn't very tight, but it does requires it. The result is that a misstep can ruin a carefully laid out plan, and missteps are quite common. You can't jump on top of the large player as the little player, leaving you to set them both up for a harder construction than it needs to be (meaning: using the environment). Being able to climb the rope as the smaller janitor and/or a braid-like "rewind a bit"-button would have been much needed improvements as well.
Unfortunately, it has none of that. And the thing with humour is that it can make or break a game. If the gameplay was better, I'm sure the live commentary of the host would've been received better. Now I just quit the game before it got on my nerves, but it was getting there.
Finally...the originality. As I said, I SADLY cannot recommend. It absolutely has potential as a puzzle platformer. In fact, if these were the SNES or N64 days, it may have become a classic (games were more rare, and thus more forgiving to a game's errors). The premise is good...perhaps even great. "Brothers, a tale of two sons", proved that gameplay with two characters can work. However, it isn't executed to its full potential. Having to switch between them isn't optimal (why do I have twin sticks on this controller?), and the aforementioned lack of precision hurts things. And for this type of game, where you have to do things by trial-and-error, this hurts even more. At one point I was at a "okay...this should work"-situation. All I had to do was land on my fat janitor and bounce of to the platform. I missed...and had to do the whole setup to that situation all over again. That's the problem: these errors can happen, but the fail-state (this set me back entire MINUTES of setting up) is just too much.
So...again: I unfortunately can't recommend. I wish it was, and I feel that with mods (see the suggestions in paragraph 3) things would seriously become better. Alas...I can't but rate it how I see it. :-(

I have a fond memory for the Monkey Island games that first drew me into the puzzle-adventure game genre (or whatever the genre is called). I am always comparing the gameplay to those games. This game includes some of the humor in the game (although the characters you control don't talk).
What drew me in and has done so on subsequent play-throughs is the ability to select a different combination of characters which not only leads to different ways to solve the same puzzles but also opens up new levels. It has a high degree of replayability, which is quite unique for a puzzle game.

I love this game so much.
Before I go on about how good it is, I will say that the controls are a little weird (you get used to them after a while) and there's a lot of backtracking. But that's all the stuff in the game that I would consider to be negative. The rest of my opinion on it is very positive.
I think what really sells it for me is the writing and characters. The playable characters don't talk but they do make little sounds. It's quite charming and I like that their stories are told mostly through pictures. The Cave itself is a riot. I loved listening to this guy talk and I would play the game over and over to get every shred of dialogue. It's so well written and the actor sells it. The game's dark and yet oddly goofy sense of humor is also extremely enjoyable. It's definitely not for the easily offended, as it does poke fun at death and murder, but it never crosses into legitimately inappropriate territory either. It's a nice and refreshing balance.

The game starts up as a pretty much survival horror puzzle game, with the atmposhere densing with each title card and opened doors. But - as there always is in this kind of situations - there is a very thin line between fun and half fun.
Greeting us with pretty flashy and not-eye-unpleasing graphics with lots of bloom and post-processing effects and slightly above mediocre animations, the game makes a very good first impression. User interface is rather clear and futuristically simple, making itself easy to read and easy to understand, without lots of popup windows explaining things on screen. Even in game, you don't need any sort of tutorials to get in with the needed knowledge. There is not much story to it, not even clues from the horror movie The Cube, which Half dead is clearly inspired by. And as much flavoured stuff there is, it lies upon walls and floors of the procedurally generated maze-maps with couple of modifiers set by general gametype rules. And there are plenty of them, fortunately.
You are some guy or gal entrapped in this "horrific" environment learning the laws of the survival of the fittest. Or, if there are more of you, you can cooperate, whatever.
The map itself is not making anything scarier, if there are any elements plausible to be considered as such. It does not create any tension, urge or feel of intimidation. It doesn't create any sort of sense of danger. It just is. Good thing it's pretty.
And then there're traps. Some of them more sophisticated than other, some of them just not really fit to this type of sci-fi creation. They're mostly deadly, but as anyone could've guessed by now, the player has a way of checking the surroundings. Opening a door could already set off a trap, but the hazard could not be so imminent, lying inside another chamber. So, throw something inside and find out! Got nothing to throw? Throw your shoe! Got no shoes left? Well, you better have a way to come back for them or find some more from other deadly-or-not fellows entrapped with you. And did I mention minesweeper experience? Well, that's not really minesweep-y, now is it? But the thing is, the floors of each room have a color coded stamp, indicating how many traps are in the neighboring chambers. Just like in ye olde classic.
And that pretty much sums up the game. There is nothing less and nothing more to it - solid, repetitive, randomly generated experience, pretty much the same across all lands and connections. It's fun with and without friends for a couple of hours, and served with a pretty smile and a price of a bad hot-dog, it is a considerate green light for a buy. And you'd not really expect anything more, as you'd already be half dead.
