Cry of Fear itself was one of the best horror game I have ever played. Now, I haven't dived deep into horror, but this game has given me a strong impression on what horror should be about. Not to see what a character is going through, but to bind with him, and to feel what he feels throughout. The music, monsters, and people in the game are all metaphores into Simon's own life, and what he has to battle. And the end to me was quite ♥♥♥♥ing insane as well. At least 1-3. For ending 4, I feel doesn't give a strong empression, since it was a proper, good ending. Even after 4 playthroughs, Co-op campaign, and Doctor mode, I still get scared from the man Simon is at the end, and what he has created.
The soundtrack itself is quite meh. But the 3-4 major songs, playing after finishing a few objectives are really good. They show the emotion Simon has. His dissapointment, guilt, or triumph. All of them fit well, but some are just annoying after hearing them for the 40th time, with the same bombastic beat, (which is the train station).
You should try this game anyway, it's free, and has quite a lot of content for such a game. Well, that is if you want to spend the time trying to get it all, which is quite long, but always fun. I'm glad with the 28 hours I spent on this game, and I wish to spend more, not only on the story of Simon, or the Co-op campaign, but instead on the custom campaigns. Like MGSV, it has given me insight onto a genre that I never thought I would like, since I personally play Battlefield, Fallout, and Dying Light. I'd give it an 7-8/10, and for anyone who hasn't played horror, I found this to be a good start, and wish to get other games like this. I have mixed feelings about this game.  I thought I was getting a full "Zelda"-like game with a female protagonist and a unique combat mechanism, but this was just "Flower-Picking: The Game," with occasional optional fetch quests.
I'm not even sure what demographic this was meant for; the dialogues, humor, and videogame references are older-teenager appropriate, whereas the gameplay is simplified enough for an elementary student to master.  Likewise, The main character looks like she's 15 and acts like she's 12, but is supposed to be a graduate student, and has apparently played every old school videogame on the planet except for Zero Wing... even the other characters in the game couldn't place her age.
What I liked about this game:
- The visuals and character designs were interesting, creative, and well-crafted.  I really enjoyed the overall look and atmosphere of the game, and the attention to detail of the artists.
- The game's frequent references to other videogames and movies, the dark humor, and the sassy side comments.  It was worth it to keep talking to characters and to read all the Mayor's signs.
- The balanced learning curve.
- The ability to pick up wearable items like ridiculous masks, videogame hats, and flying pets.
What was okay:
- The core game mechanic of picking flowers off spirits' backs.  While there was an increase in difficulty as the game went on (the introduction of thorns and bombs, the movement patterns of the spirit, the need to score higher combos of non-thorn flowers), there was not enough variation for it to feel appreciably different after about the 8th enemy.  The only real distinguishing factor from that point on was how long of a combo you needed in order to win 3 stars; early enemies only need 8-12 flowers in a row, whereas the final boss takes a chain of 30-40 flowers.  As you can imagine, by the 52nd spirit this minigame had worn out its welcome.
- Sometimes you will be able to complete optional side quests instead of fighting, which fall into one of four categories: "find all the hidden things," "visit that place you just visited," "fetch an item from the chest you just opened," or "fight that spirit you just fought"... O.o
- Four Hand Monty's "if you are short on cash and don't want to break vases" bonus ball-and-cup minigame.
- The oversimplified inventory system that consists of three tiers of armor for each of your three stats, three one-use items that I rarely ever used, two kinds of currency, two levels of keys, a cheater's map, and a bottle that summons butterflies for no reason.  That's it, unless you count the treasure trophies that only exist for flavour.
What I didn't like:
- Being constantly interrupted by either Mailbox, or the Mayor, or the fish, with long blocks of dialogue that you can't really skip.  I'm all about witty banter and story progression, but considering you need to play through the game twice to get all the achievements, it would have been nice to be able to bypass the excessive chatter.
- The big mid-game "choice."  I played through the game a third time, just to see what would happen if I chose the alternate path, and it was totally not worth it.  I was expecting at least a cutscene with the Professor.
- The rainbow bird poo.  Seriously?  That needed to be a thing?
- The achievements.  Some of them made sense, like the ones for beating the spirits, but some of them were needlessly tedious such as the "break 1000 vases" or "scare 500 birds." Additionally, these achievements are not cumulative across multiple playthroughs, you must break all 1000 vases using the same save file.
There is also one broken achievement for this game: "unlock all doors."  It seems there was a discrepancy between the PC version and other ports, with the PC release only having 22/28 unlockable doors programmed in.  Thus, the achievement cannot be unlocked without manually altering the game code (you can find instructions for this online, but I personally didn't want to risk irreparably damaging my game data just for 100% completion).  [Edit 12/19/14: The broken achievement has been removed from Steam, so you can now get 100% completion!]
Overall, I would give this game a 7/10.  I liked the setting and the humor, but the core gameplay and the achievements were tiresome and boring by the end.

Lili: Child of Geos is a game with massive potential that would've been excellent if it were actually made for the PC, and worst of all it's not even the developer's fault.
Seeing this game in the Steam Store, the first thoughts to come to mind were "This looks fantastic" and "Why haven't I heard of this before"? Unfortunately the answer was evident in about 10 minutes. This is a mobile port - a fantastic looking one that trumps most indie games made for the PC proper in terms of looks, but a mobile port nonetheless and that permeates the game to its core.
This game is obviously a labour of love and it shows. But that it's also a mobile game utterly annihilates all of its positives - there's a "but" for each and every one.
•Every inch of the world looks fantastic, but you can't interact with it beyond walking around it.
•All of the levels are utterly distinct, but there's only four of them and they take 20 minutes to beat.
•The characters are well written and distinctly funny, but you never get more than half a dozen lines out of even the most prominent ones.
•There's sidequests and optional content, but they're all threadbare.
•Design is solid all around, but assets are reused to a comical degree - I had trouble telling NPCs apart.
Threadbare describes the game as a whole. Combat altering inventory items? Great idea. There's three of them and they're thrown at you, though. Stat increase system? Great idea. Shallow as a puddle, though. Climactic mid-sequence about abandoning previous life choices? Great idea. It consists of three and a half lines of dialogue either way and falls completely flat though.
Worst case is the combat (or "combat", but there's enough high-octane explosives involved that I think you can safely ignore the whole nonviolent billing) - you perform the same unchanging minigame twenty or so times and then the game is over. Fifty-five if you're aiming for completionist.
For a mobile game these are all more than excusable. Hell, I've no doubt that had I played this on a mobile device it would rank up there with the best; Dead Space iOS and Infinity Blade. But I didn't, and for a PC game, to put it lightly, it kicks it straight in the balls. Right in there. And it isn't the developers' fault. But that's just how it is.
At it's best Lili: Child of Geos is an exercise in frustration at lost potential the likes of which I haven't felt since Crash Twinsanity.
Even though I wouldn't actually recommend this to anyone, maybe just buy it anyway. Support the developers. I want to see another game from them. Built from the ground up for PC this time.
Also, gamepad support is kind of lacking and the video game references get a little shoehorned at times.

So this is a puzzle platformer game.  It's not very long, but I've played it a few times.  You start by picking a team of three characters and lead them ever deeper into this cave.  Each guy has a special ability.  Now, the unfortunate part is instead of letting people solve puzzles in different ways, these abilities only really come into play for each character's personal area of the game.  In between these personal areas, you play generic areas that appear no matter who you've picked, and as such, they need to be navigatable with every character.  Puzzles involve finding items and putting them where they go.  Baiting a trap with a hotdog, powering something with a battery...  It's not exactly rocket science.  Oh, and it's Co-op feature is little more than a timesaver, letting you move characters around at the same time, instead of having to lead everyone through one by one.
Did I enjoy it though?  Yeah, else I wouldn't have replayed it.  It's quick and easy and pretty to look at.  Different characters and ending art give it some replayability.  Fun for a few hours at a time earns it a recommendation.

This game impresses me. Pure and simple. The F2P model is fair. Thats rare enough. Items are still a bit pricey, but the free content is MORE than enough to keep you busy while you decide if you like this game is good enough to put money in to it. The questing is basic kill and retreive. Boss quests. Collect materials quests. This is an mmo... im hoping you arent expecting a myriad of choices here. I will say the questing is good, tho. The dungeon content in this game is good for mmo's. Tank and healer and dps archtypes mean everyone fills a purpose and the INSANE flexibility of the character creation often allows more flexibility allowed past the cookie cutter archer/warrior/priest most mmo's hand you. A very nice addition to this game is also the Rifts (as the name implys) are a big part of overworld adventuring. They are a welcome addition to the normal questing/dungeoning/pvp route i follow to level cap in games. Oftentimes at lower levels you can spend entire playsessions just closing Rifts and pushing back the opposition that flows from them.
I mentioned the flexibility of the character building? Yup. THeres that too. Across 4 classic categories: Rogue, Warrior, Priest and Mage, you have many different sub classes to plug into your "soul" to create just the kind of character you want. If your sick of cookie cutter mmo classes this game should be on your list for that reason alone.  The healer classes can be customized to heal passively, or do more healing with casted spells or instant casts. Tank classes can be customized to pour out AOE damage to hold aggro better, at a cost of surviveability or to heal and buff and be more sturdy. Dps classes can be customized to do just about anything you want. Heal a little, buff a little, or just melt faces. WHatever suits you. O and you can save many different soul builds to your character too, so you can switch between them quickly. Rogues and priests can tank with the right builds. I know there is a class for rogue healing as well, but i am not sure if you have to buy it. If you do feel like paying the actual money, you can also heal with Warriors and tank with Mages in addition to all ive mentioned. Coupled with a few soul builds and suddenly you are capable of filling several different roles out of one archtype. Different in the mmo world to have such versatility.
Pvp in this game was probably the weakest point for me, but that too was fleshed out enough to keep me playing, even if it isnt quite as flashy as say... WOW or something. My different builds performed differently in pvp as well, making me look forward to trying different specs in the unforgiving battlegrounds.
Consider this game a 90/100. I am very impressed with the overall content available, the F2P model, as well as most any of the other facets of this game. I will call them all at or above my baseline expectations for Mmo's, whether F2P or not. I dislike the mmo grind but the Rifts make it seem less... idk... grindy. Lili: Child of Geos is a wonderful casual adventure game. You follow Lili on her quest to free the citizens of Geos from the Spirits by gathering items and collectibles. There's really no point in the game than to immerse yourself with the wonderful cartoon fantasy world while discovering hidden items and collecting flowers - white ones which you can get anywhere and red ones which you need to fight some spirits to get it.
I really enjoyed this game despite of the lack of gameplay and the linear story line. What makes this game so much fun is the great art style and the graphics, this runs smoothly on my 3 yr old gpu, and I can appreciate that.  There are collectable items in the game like hats, pets, and masks. It's a nice addition, but the dresses are just a change in color. It would've nice to see something different.
The music is perfect for a game like this but sometimes it gets a little annoying, I would have liked it to be a little subtle while im exploring and want to hear more of those ambient sounds.
I can highly recommend this to someone bored of the usual games and just want to chill out and enjoy the fantasy world. But if your an average gamer who wants more gameplay and some serious satisfaction out of a game, this isn't for you. I'd say it's great for a collectible, but honestly not worth the price, since the game is too short and replay value is very low.
Graphics: 7 - I like the graphics of the game and the the world of Geos is beautiful.
Gameplay: 4 - There isn't really anything to do here aside from collecting flowers to proceed with quests and maybe collecting  masks and hats.
Music: 7 - The music is above average and will keep you feeling like you are in a cartoon fantasy world, but it gets repetitive. I woud've enjoyed more if I was hearing a more soothing music and more ambient sounds.
Replayability: 3 - The game doesn't offer anything more after you've beaten it once, maybe just to pick up more flowers and vases for achievements, or maybe get those missable hats or masks.
Overall Impression: 7 - I still give it a 7 despite of all the negatives, there is a certain charm to this game the you can only experience once you start adventuring with Lili=)

It's very cute, and simple. If you're looking for a short distraction, it's a great choice.
I picked it up on a whim during the Autumn sale, sat down, and blasted through it in one sitting.
I looked at it because of the visuals. For an indie game, it's beautiful. Stylistic without abandoning realism. Bright and colorful. Great lighting. The character models are also really good, and well animated for the most part. The NPCs do seem to have one or two looping animations that they run through, but there's a lot of different NPCs, each with their own thing going on, so you never spend too much time looking at the single animations.
There is a story in there. It's nothing fantastic, but it isn't horrible. Its a sort of basic hero story; you show up on this island for a school project, and are introduced to a class struggle between the spirits, who own the island. and the constructs, who were created to serve the spirits. It moves along pretty quick, and the "big bad" of sorts is pretty entertaining to deal with.
The gameplay is almost a QTE sort of thing. You run around the island, picking up collectables. Flowers, which can be traded for money, chests that have money and quest or cosmetic items, and vases that you kick open for money and achievement score. Then you come across spirits roaming the quarters, and jump on their back for the main gameplay, where you are shown flowers you have to pick. You pick the good flowers and avoid the bad flowers, and pick bombs to throw off as you progress. You can upgrade your Speed (movement, helps you keep up with the spirits), Grip (gives you more time to hang on to their backs), and Stealth (makes you harder for them to notice, allowing you to get closer to them before they see you and start running away). I upgraded Speed to max, and Grip about halfway, and never had much trouble. You also get scored on how well you did. Picking more bad flowers or letting bombs explode in your face take points away, and for every 3 star score you get, you get the spirit's mask to wear.
There are also quests to do for the constructs. Simple stuff, like find me an item (in a chest somewhere nearby), go take down a specific spirit, go find and talk to another construct. They give cosmetic items, hats mostly.
You get a lot of hats to choose from, mostly masks from the spirits, but a fair amount of regular hats or headwear.
TL;DR - It's fun, really short, and really pretty. I bought it for less than $5 and I feel really happy with it. I don't know if I'd agree with $20, but for $10 or less, its definitely something to pick up

I found myself only really using 2 of the 10 power-ups available to me (Blink & Dark Vision aka. wallhack) as the rest would be lethal to targets and other support powers like time-freeze and possession took up too much mana (in the game, you want to minimize killing if you want the "good" ending).

You pluck flowers off your target and the difficulty increases by increasing the required number of flowers needed to be picked and the introduction of dangerous objects that mix in with the object. Despite this simplicity the game is fairly enjoyable because it comes in combination with a fairly enjoyable setting and atmosphere.  If I were to compare it, it would have to be with the atmosphere of the first city you wonder through in JRPG games like Final Fantasy IX and Kingdom Hearts.  It has a joyous, adventerous feel that warms your heart.  Maybe not at full price, but I would certainly recommend this game if you want to play around in a happy setting with surprisingly well polished graphics and lighting.  I feel like this game is worthy enough for the developers to turn this into a series starring Lili in more adventures but with more RPG elements, more puzzle elements, and a larger world.

It is hard not to like this game simply due to its strong sense of personality, sadly while it has style in abundance the variety of content is simply not there. There is a bit of a plot here but ultimately the desire to return to the game isn't strong enough and the reply value is almost zero.
This brings me to the issue of, "Should I recommend this game to others?"
That is really a very conditional thing because there is money involved.
Had this been a F2P game then I would wholeheartedly recommend it due to the fact that, in short sessions, the game is really very enjoyable and is a pleasure to look at. The visuals and style of the game just scream quality from the rooftops and there is enough tongue-in-cheek humour here to put a smile on even the most cynical of faces. If you enjoy games you will come across such a large number of references to other titles it is almost wrong to call them Easter Eggs since the game is saturated with them rather than having them hidden away. The developers clearly love Legend of Zelda and other Nintendo games because they not only attempted to create an Nintendo-esque art style but they also added music to the game which is clearly inspired by games such as Wind Waker. They achieved that goal with such success that you could drop Mario or Link into the game world and they'd look perfectly at home.
Unfortunately when it comes to paying money for this and wanting value for money from your purchase, Child of Geos has very little to offer. It reminds me of something that would work well as a casual game for a rainy afternoon but nothing more, as such I wouldn't recommend this game unless it was on sale for maybe £2-3 at most.
What the developers have created here is really something which deserves a sequel though, while they missed the mark on gameplay they have set a new benchmark for style and quality for the visuals, music and presentation for an indie game. I sincerely hope that this isn't the last we'll see of Lili.

This game is adorable, and is providing some surprisingly difficult timing, progression, and reflex puzzles.
Its a relatively simple concept; needing to control 2 inept alien maintenance workers, permanently connected by a tether hose to each other, with a forced size shifting, One must always be fwoomped up large with a weak jump ability, and the other small, more agile, and able to bounce off the head of it's puffed up partner. Switches move platforms and doors, blocks can be shoved around by the larger alien, instant-death traps are littered all over the 50+ levels and the level designs make excellent use of providing limitations for movement with a reasonable progression of difficulty as you learn new tricks to get around areas.
There's an interesting little meta story that goes along with your progression, allowing for an announcer to give commentary as you play through the levels... and there are times that gets a bit irritating, particularly if you're struggling through a difficult section where there'll be a quick quip every time you make a mistake and die, but overall it's pleasant enough.
As a solo-plyer game, you get to alternate control of each alien, or you can control both simultaneously, both following the same directions and jumping at the same time, and though that makes the timing tricky for some puzzles, its very workable. There is also the option to play co-op, and have each player control a single alien, which makes some things faster, but also more confusing.
Limited replayability for time-attacks or item collection (3 semi-hidden collections per level that you can go back at any time and try to grab if you miss them on the first run-through, They are all findable, but some will require some brain-work to snag), but it's a fairly reasonable length game if you're only planning on a single run-through.

This game tries hard to be a humorous puzzle-platformer. The puzzles are a bit obvious at times, but not too bad. It's just a shame the rest of the game doesn't let you enjoy them. The platforming is especially broken, and the game finds itself incredibly amusing.
The movement of the characters is either very slow, or somewhat slow and extremely floaty. Floaty movement by itself is bad enough as it is in a 2.5D platforming game, but it's especially worse in The Cave: any falling damage instantly kills a character, and it's very easy to fall between a ledge and an immediately adjacent ladder or rope (you know, where you expect to latch on immediately if you walk off the ledge). There's no way to look before you leap, which may result in some extra cheap deaths. The fact that the game features a "zero deaths" achievement is just insulting to its players.
For a game that's only five years old, the animations are much too clunky. If a character is climbing a rope while holding an item, they'll float for about half of the animation loop. If a character jumps in a corridor with little headroom, they'll get stuck to the ceiling while the disembodied mass of the character follows an imaginary parabolic path above that ceiling. There are some moments where the game is too eager in optimising a jump ("I just wanted to get out of the mine cart, not jump immediately onto a ledge"), and some moments where the game just doesn't ("why can't you grab that ledge? oh, I get it, I'm just two pixels too far to the right").
I'm not sure why other reviewers praise The Cave's story. The tiny bits of story in this game are shouted down by the narrator, who takes his sense of humour very seriously. On paper, the humour is somewhat similar to other games directed/written by Ron Gilbert, but the execution simply doesn't compare.

Great platformer / puzzle game. There are 7 characters based on the seven deadly sins, and you can discover their dark pasts by descending into the Cave for a "tour". You can control 3 at a time, so if you want to know the story of all characters, it's 3 playthroughs already. And there are bad (succumbing to the sins) and good (overcoming the sins) endings too, so it has quite the replay value. The puzzles are smart and funny, except for a few mildly annoying ones. All characters have their dedicated level, where you can discover their secrets and the mistakes they've made, accompanied with the dark and sarcastic humour of the Cave itself. These levels connected with other levels, which are the same for all characters. All characters have their special ability (for example the Time Traveller can phase through non-solid obstacles, or the Knight has invincibility), which is mandatory to use in their level, but they can come quite handy in the other levels too.
Once you figured out the puzzles, the game can be finished under 2-3 hours, but it's quite enjoyable, so I definitely recommend playing this.

After playing this game twice, I had a lot of different impressions of the game. I've played the collectors edition with artbook, soundtracks and some ingame power ups.
Painkiller is a FPS were the protagonist is always mooving in maps and has to clear them from enemies. After each area or room the game saves automaticly.
To the gameplay: First of all there is no auto heal. You have to collect souls and armours to survive. Between the rooms you can look for secrets to get power ups or extra munition. The last big diference between this game and other FPS is, that there is no possibillity to scope.
All this things sound quite harsh in the beginning, especially the missing of auto heal, but the game get's never unfair and there are a ot of armours and lives placed in the levels.
An other positive aspect of the game are the good designed and powerfull weapons. There are nearly a dozen af them, they are all compleatly different and none of them is OP or useless. And they all have an epic impact. Eaven the first shotgun blows weaker enemies away, eaven in the endgame. The missing of an iron sight or scope isn't so bad, because they are 100% acurate. This point may sounds bad, but especially in the endgame the speed is so high, that it wouldn't make any sense to scope.
But there are negative points too. The game is extreamly monotonous. Mayby I wasn't motivated enough to get all the secrets and achivments, but for me the game was only doing room cleaning stage after stage. Nothing against the stages, there were nearly all good designed like cemetries, oriental castles or creepy adventure parks with roler coasters. But it was still room cleaning.
An other weak point is the enemy design. Especially after the cool level and the extraordinary weapon design I could not belive how lame most of the enemies are. They have all only melee attaks (exept one or two enemy types) and all lok like skeletons, nights or ..... clowns. There are some bigger enemies to, but you can handle them like the small ones
(bunny hop away--turn around--shoot like hell--restart this untill all enemies are down).
But the worst are the bosses with own(!) stages. They look bad, and apart from the dragon boss they are all boring to defeat. I was  not even shure if they attaked me or I was just gliching around.
Last but not least the soundtrack. During the game I really liked the aggressive rock musik while shooting around. But I remarked that the sngs were repeating. A look to the special soundtrack CD made even everything worse. There were only 14 songs. ( Tony hawk for Nintendo DS has much more) and when I say they sounded all equal it isn't eaven wrong, because there are songs wich are  double on this CD.(And the others still all sound identic)
So can I recomand you the game. ( Hint: There is the tag at yes upwards)
I have to say YES and NO. When you like nonsense violence in arcadic shooter than yes. (I got the collector edition for   15 €     with artbook and soundtrack CD)
Or when you want to try games like this one AND if it is on sale than ok, try it.
To the rest of you who don't like monotonous games or are interested in an good storry: it's mayby better not buy this game. There are other ones for aeven less mony.

If by some miracle you did manage to get your weekly cap, you are looking at 5 entire weeks of INTENSE grinding, just to open these two simple features. By that time you will probably already be topped out in levels, and at end game content anyway - so what's the point at even trying.
The server(s) population is dwindling, The new expansion has pushed away players instead of bringing new ones in.

If you loved Half-Life: 2 then you'd probably enjoy Dishonored in a similar fashion. Both games drive a great story and mini-puzzle mechanics. You could just blaze through the story in Dishonored and skip a lot of the optional quests but as a stealth player I enjoyed taking the side-quests - which aren't solely "side quests" because they do affect some major changes in the game (eg.
.
If there are two things that made me give this a  9/10, it's probably the power-up mechanics. Over the course of the game, you can source for Runes to buy special powers and find Bone Charms as passive effects. I found myself only really using 2 of the 10 power-ups available to me (Blink & Dark Vision aka. wallhack) as the rest would be lethal to targets and other support powers like time-freeze and possession took up too much mana (in the game, you want to minimize killing if you want the "good" ending).
The next major point that made me solidify my decision for this missing point was the random passives from Bone Charms. Yes, their locations to be found are always the same but the passives they give you are random. It might not seem as a bother to most but I found out the hard way because I only found the faster choking speed charm at one of the very last missions in the game (and for 95% of the game I was pretty much choking everyone). After I got it I realized the game had auto-saved over a choice I wanted to change so I went back to my previous manual save (which was before I got the bone charm) and IT WASN'T THE FASTER CHOKING. I went on to finish the game with my crushed soul, not being able to find anymore bone charms (and without faster choking). Most of the bone charm effects are pretty bad too so finding faster choking is a BIG GAME CHANGER for stealth players.
Other than these points, the game was a truly fullfilling experience which you don't get from many games these days. I'd definitely recommend picking this up and giving it a good play through while taking time to appreciate the rich story (and flip through all those random excerpts from books if you like).

Lili: Child of Geos is a game I'd kept my eye on ever since it first appeared on steam. It's colorful and unique art style and character designs interested me enough to put it on my watchlist. Having had the chance to finally give the game a playthrough I can see it both met my expectations and also took them in a different direction. This isn't your typical RPG by a longshot. You won't really be level grinding or anything like that as there really is no battle mechanic. You play as a botanist and your typical task on the island is to pick flowers. The best flowers happen to grow on the backs of creatures known as spirits. Picking them off their backs as they try to shake you off takes the form of a mini-game. I hadn't known going in that the game was a revisioned port of an iOS game, but it by far feels like one. That isn't a bad thing however as this game is beautiful to look at and the 'battles' can get quite challenging when thorny flowers and bombs are thrown into the mix. The game is also quite charming with a very unique art style I greatly enjoyed.
I do have a few issues with the game however, the camera has a bit of a wabble motion to it that is noticeable which can't be turned off in the options. If you easily get motion sick, this may get to you at first as it almost did with me, but as you're moving around it becomes less noticable. The game is also dull in parts and repetitive. Especially at first but once the game gains momentum it becomes far more interesting. The game even has a fairly dark undertone which I enjoyed but doesn't ever drown out it's charming and humerous nature. The writing is a bit odd at times though with occasional typos oddly phrased sentences and punctuation errors that hardly ruin the gameplay. Dialog is easy to read and understand even for children, though item descriptions can use words a bit out of reach for younger players. The game also features an auto-save feature which can get annoying towards the end of the game when you're given two choices. I would have liked to have saved at that point manually to reload later and take the other path instead of having to play through again.
All in all, I enjoyed myself while I was playing and genuinely felt myself drawn into the world this game created. This game isn't for everyone and I wouldn't consider it an RPG as it's closer to a modern day point and click adventure. I'd recommend it to ages 10-15, especially to female audiences or Miyazaki anime fans as it has a similar world feel. It won't be a length sit. I finished the game in 5.5 hours, but it does have a branching path towards the end.

This a nice game of constructing your own hob-powered destruction engine, but bear in mind that it is essentially a physics trial&error puzzle game. There are 37 levels in total, and the ships you build are only to specifically fight the enemy(s) of each particular level. Nothing is carried over besides unlockable (over various) parts for your ship.
For me, it was interesting at first, but grew tedious as I had to reinvent my ship for every stage, and was left in severe want of a free-form/sandbox stage to build an all-purpose mega-ship or an inpractical behemoth of my own.
Once you finish the stage, there is little left to do except to replay old stages to get a higher rating (done by using less materials and guns). It took me 7 hours to finish this game, and while it was an initially fun experiment/distraction, I wouldn't recommend that you pay full price for this.

Expecting (and hoping) to change this review someday from a negative to a positive, but right now this simply isn't ready even for Early Access.
TLDR: If you've enjoyed ARK: Survival Evolved, you'll be severly disappointed by Osiris: New Dawn - at least in its current stage of development.
The game looks really interesting. The game sounds really interesting. But as early as this into Early Access, the game simply isn't.
Official servers are limited to 12 players. For real.
Unless you play single-player or a private server, you can't progress through the tutorial (or do anything remotely useful) because the servers have reach their (severely limited) structure count capacity, which doesn't resolve itself by destroying other people's structure.
The map goes on and on for what seems like forever (if you feel like wasting an hour walking in one direction you'll still be wondering where the map ends - if it ends at all?), but there's definitely nothing bar empty canvass beyond 1km from the spawn location. Hand-crafted map not really. It's all the same beyond that 1km radius.
I suppose there's a few hours of gameplay on single-player to be had, which is totally worth the US $25. Or not. This should be a $2 Early Access.
Suggesting this game to be early-beta rather than early-alpha (as the developers have done), is basically criminal.

Hell and Damnation is the remake of the original Painkiller game and its first expansion pack released 10 years ago. As it is a remake it offers better graphics and better sound effects and music. And of course we now have achievements! This I would normally say is a really good thing as you can practically relive the experience you had with the vanilla game. This is good, right? We should bow before Farm 51 and Nordic Games for making this possible, am I right?
Unfortunately, no. I do not really have anything against DLCs but when DLCs are required to have the full gaming experience I consider it a mistake. What happen here is that Hell and Damnation offers only half of the campaign. In fact, while these had a theme in the original game and were divided up properly into chapters we now have a mess. A rather weird mix of levels and as half of them are missing you can spend more money to obtain all the missing stages. They did create some new levels and boss battles and weapons and also enemy types but these I believe were completely unnecessary.
If Farm 51 had just remade all levels and released them at once without having to stick with DLCs I would have easily recommended this game. If you do not mind spending some extra money then perhaps you may find the remake interesting. Otherwise, pick up the Black Edition of the vanilla game and complete it once more and leave this version to those who are new to the franchise so they may not be deterred by this version.

There are three common levels you have to play through in each play of the game and in addition to this, each character has a unique level. Thus if you want to see all levels (they are worth it) you have a decent amount of repetition ahead of you. While repetition in some games may be fun, I think it is less fun in a puzzle game. I'm surprised the developers didn't give the player a mechanism to skip these levels if you had already completed them. There is already a mechanism to skip the levels of characters that you're not playing with.
That's a minor criticism. It only matters if you enjoyed your first playthrough so much that you're ready to go back for more.

Lili is a short but sweet game by Bitmonster, inc. It's a wonderful first impression for the studio and I honestly cannot wait for them to release more games. The game reminds me a lot of Zelda and Kingdom Hearts in its design which I enjoyed and I thought the goofy story line was cute as well. The cast will steal your heart by the end of the game and you won't really have a problem with that. There a few different areas on the island to explore which is surprising for such a small game. It's quite fun to unlock all the doors and see what's hiding inside. The combat system is interesting. Instead of hitting them or shooting at them you jump on their backs and steal their flowers. I thought this was a very unique take on fighting systems. Lili is beautifully designed and lots of fun to play though it is only about 8 hours long so I would suggest waiting for it to go on sale. If you're looking to blow off some steam this is certainly your game. One of the best games I've played in a long time! 8/10

Lili: Child of Geos tells the story of a young botanist, Lili, set on a quest to the supposedly uninhabited island of Geos as part of a school research project, but as the stories never tell the whole truth until you live them, you will soon find out that the island is actually inhabited by creatures called the Spirits and their creations meant to serve them, the Constructs. It won't be long before your arrival will alert the Spirits as your presence starts to influence the lives of the Constructs and make them question their existence as servants, so you will soon be caught up in the affairs of Geos’ locals. As much of a premise for a serious plot there is, the game chooses tell its story in a satirical way, adding jokes and references to other games every now and then, some which fail to deliver, making the entire story feel irrelevant after you realize most quests are there to fill in the space without an actual outcome in the storyline. As a game that focuses on exploration and the landscape it creates with it, it was disappointing to see how limited that exploration really is; it was exciting to find new items, meet new Constructs and see where else their quests will take me, but after a few minutes you will soon realize that there are only around eight additional sidequests, most which take no longer than ten minutes to complete and as for everything you see in the distance, you will never actually get there.
As for how the game plays, well it certainly is different from anything you have experienced before, as your main objective is to defeat Spirits by jumping onto their back and picking the flowers that spurt from their heads. This is where the game shows its true nature, as it was originally made for tablets and picking flowers by dragging them with your finger across the screen feels natural and easy, but doing the same thing with a mouse can be a little bit tricky. Using a controller makes the whole thing a little bit easier as you can select the flower you want to pull using the action button, but at the same time it creates another problem, as you can only select from a range of four flowers, mapped to their respective action button, so later on in the game when you'll have to deal with up to eight different flowers, weeds and bombs at the same time, the controller will prove to be more of a burden than a helpful tool. Outside the battle the game works much better, using the keyboard and mouse or the controller to move around, collect flowers, look around for treasures and meet Geos' finest, but then again for an open world experience, there is a really small number of things that you can do outside the main story, which isn't that long either and the first glance at Geos will soon be shattered by exploration limits and the lack of new things to keep you going for longer or distract you from your main objective.
Looking back at the iOS version of the game, it's clear that the visual upgrade worked out for the best and Lili: Child of Geos looks amazing on PC, but the real beauty when playing the game comes from the art style itself, taking you somewhere between what a gnome village would look like and combining it with a good Pixar movie. The landscapes are simply amazing and as for the characters, even if the Spirits look the same except for their masks, the Constructs each have a unique touch to help you recognize them whenever you see them around Geos. The bad part in all this is that you never get to explore everything that you actually see ahead of you and the five different locations of the island can be completed within minutes as there is nothing else to do besides the main objective and a few chests scattered around.
The soundtrack complements the visual art style, probably not in the best way possible but its better with it there playing the background as you move on than without it. The worst part on the audio side is the absence of voice acting, which is understandable since most mobile titles lack such things, but as a PC port it's hard not to complain about how great the dialogue could've been voiced by the right actors, and on the same note it could've made some of those lame jokes funny just by using the right voice. The sound effects are okay, but since there is a limited number of items and objects that interact with the environment and your character, it will soon feel like a repetitive and monotone experience.
It takes around four hours to finish Lili: Child of Geos, which isn't nearly enough to justify a 20€ price tag, and aside from that and a few achievements that you'll miss on your first playthrough there really is nothing else to keep you around, no matter how beautiful the island of Geos is.
Judging by the first look, Lili: Child of Geos is beautiful and unique, but in this case the first look is deceiving, as the game won't last more than a few hours and as for the time in which it actually is entertaining, that's probably less than 30 minutes, but if that time is enough for you and you're just looking for a great view, Lili: Child of Geos delivers flawlessly on that side.

Oooh boy, this is an odd one...
When I came along to see this game on sale, I thought what would await me was a cheesy, but pretty RPG with puzzles to solve and battles to win, much like the advertised likeness to Zelda and Psychonauts. What greeted me instead was an almost childish flower-picking simulator with the most gorgeous artstyle I ever saw.
And I didn't mind.
I bought this game, like some other people, because of the screenshots, and the promise of reliving some of the charm of the games of my childhood. I'm not normally a person who cares much for graphical fidelity in games so long as the gameplay is fun, however in this case? Quite the opposite. Something about the graphics style just makes me innately happy whenever I look at it. It puts my mind to rest for a while, which as a person with depression and anxiety attacks is a bloody godsend. The entire game is very colorful, vivid and nicely stylized, with very fluent animation, adorable little details and an overall just... happy feeling to it. It's easily one of the best-looking games I've played in my life, and it does so not through polygon count, but clever, passionate stylization. Don't get me wrong, though, the models are still pretty high quality.
With the graphics out of the way, though, let's address gameplay. This is where I initially felt cheated by the storepage claiming such close resemblance to the Zelda and Psychonauts games. I imagined adventuring, clever puzzles and dangerous trials. What I got was "Flower Picking - Collector's Edition", with the 'Collector' being quite literal. This is a game about collecting things and smashing pots. Collect flowers. Collect money. Collect conversation. Collect Collectibles. Every so often you'll fight a spirit, where the term 'fighting' is used much in the same way the term 'Discussion' is used for having a 12-year-old squeak into their microphone online in your FPS of choice. The spirits run away from you, because apparently a 16 year-old hipster florist apprentice is more dangerous than a mystical, 7 feet tall nature spirit with magic powers. Once you've caught up to the spirits, the fighting is technically a long, randomized QTE. They grow flowers from their backs. Sometimes they're good flowers, sometimes they're bad flowers, sometimes they're bombs. A button hovers over them and the game wants you to press the button that hovers over the thing which won't harm you like a parent presenting three hot stove plates and a plushie to their three-year-old and telling them to think fast.
Occasionally the gameplay is broken up through quests you get from talking carpentry accidents that more often than not involve walking to a specific place or talking to a specific person. Sometimes you need to defeat a certain spirit, which you would probably do anyway sooner or later.
What makes the quests, and the game in general interesting are the conversations. Despite the childish flair of the game, the writing is actually enjoyable for the most part, offering some casual humor around every corner. The characters are all quirky enough, and while not exactly believable, are enjoyable to interact with and had me talking to them over and over again to see more conversational options. Whether that was because I actually enjoyed the quirkyness of it all or simply because there's not much else to do I'm not quite sure, but it's lead me to finishing the game and doing so with a smile, so whatever it was, it worked!
On account of the writing, however, and the general presentation, in this case of the main character, I'll have to give a bit of a cringe-warning:
The game likes its references. Which is all fine and dandy, many games do it, and to great effect, usually in the form of little trinkets hidden here or there, or a quest resembling the story of a classic. Lili has a slightly different approach to that in some points, "slightly different" meaning "IN YOUR FACE". The game enjoys repeating how much of a gamer the main protagonist is, and how much she knows about casual video game trivia to the point where it had me sit in my chair, squeeze my legs together and groan.
"Look at us!", the game keeps saying, "We're gamers just like you, haha! See? We played some video games!"
"Alright, that's cool!", I replied with a smile and went on with my business.
"Oh hey, did we mention how much we love gaming? Hey, we're just like you! Gamer bro fist, haha!"
Alright, game, I get it. You guys made a video game, I kind of figured you'd probably have played one or two before.
"Hey look at how much we know about games! Man, games, am I right? We love games so much. We should hang out now because you play games, too!"
One last thing to consider before a purchase is the length of the game. I've completed the game with all sidequests in about 4 hours. It's not a terribly long game by any stretch of the imagination. You can beat it in a single afternoon if you're so inclined, and there's little reason to go back to it afterwards unless you just need a breather from grey reality and want to delve into a colorful, gorgeous fantasy island again.
All in all, however, it's a minor itch and completely ignorable. The game, while about as casual as a stroll through the park on a sunny spring day, was still enjoyable and while I would not recommend it for the full price, it's certainly worth a look on sale. Whether you're feeling down or just long for something lax to play while listening to a podcast or letting the day fade out, it's sure to put a smile on your face if you don't mind an experience that's more focussed on presentation than gameplay. It's an immensely impressive starting project for BitMonster and I'm looking forward to their next games already.
PS: BitMonster, if you guys could make another game with the same art style but more engaging gameplay, I would love you forever.

Red Trigger doesn't do anything special. But maybe that's the charm of it.
Red Trigger plays in first person and gives you a pretty nifty laser rifle. This rifle isn't used for killing, however. It's used for activating red pieces of the landscape, which are key to your completion and survival in the Red Trigger world. A puzzle game at heart, Red Trigger features no story to bog you down. Complete the puzzle using your rifle and knowledge of your past mistakes. In a sense, it plays a lot like Portal. No direct combat, just lots of critical thinking skills. Enjoyable, and simple. Easy to digest, even.
Negligable, but it's nice on the eyes and not very impressive. It definitely doesn't try to look pretty, but it's simplistic animations and creative presentation gives it some points.
To make it short and sweet, if you like puzzle games, you should play Red Trigger. It's a short but easy to understand game that'll give you a nice 30+ minutes of gameplay. For something free, that's very difficult to say, since the F2P market is ridiculously watered down these days. Red Trigger is, therefore, commendable for it's efforts.

This game is a bit like Chinese food, you know, with the sweet and the sour?
Its a gloriously sleazy, ultra-violent 80's B-Movie cheese-fest as expected from the House of the Dead series, it can help you or your children learn how to type, provided you're okay with them looking at undead mammaries and hearing a multitude of... unpleasantries, and if typing isn't your thing, you can play it with a crosshair in an alternative mode that uses your mouse similar to that of the arcade light gun cabinets! That's the sweet.
The sour? This might be something that might only effect me, but for whatever reason, I can't enjoy the game for prolonged periods of time. So far, my time in game has been spent playing just one level at a time every time I boot it up. The main draw of the game is the typing, of course, and while it is so very satisfying to pull off a long phrase in the short amount of time you might be given to react, the satisfaction just doesn't seem to stay very long for me. Again, might just be a personal thing. I feel like when played in short chunks, like one or two levels at a time, it stays fun and satisfying without overstaying it's welcome. Don't get me wrong, while the B-Movie cheese tastes great, there can be so much of it to the point of it being overwhelming.
But, after all that, I still say give this a go. If you're looking for something a little dumb or tasteless this Halloween, this might be a fantastic pickup.

An OK puzzle game. You have to "think like a developer" to solve item-grab combinations, but you can figure out the rhythm and logic easily enough. Tons of backtracking and not much replayability, unless you want to complete special levels for certain characters.
Not much in the way of spoilers here, but there are no real "moral" choices. You just follow the stories, discovering the dark hearts of the characters. In my case, the hillbilly (who burns down a carnival since he can't have the one he loves), the scientist (who launches a nuke due to her greed), and the twins (who dabble in using rat poison to get their way).

Video Version of this review:
You have your choice of seven different characters to play as in this game, but you can only choose three. You can choose between the Knight, the Hillbilly, the Time Traveler, the Scientist, the Adventurer, the Twins, and the Monk.

Each character has their own unique abilities, but seeing as I’ve only played as the Knight, Hillbilly, and Time Traveler, I’ll only explain theirs. The Knight can create some kind of magic shield to protect himself from all kinds of danger, like fall damage, fire, and being shot by enemies. The Hillbilly creates a bubble around his head. This helps him to stay underwater for a long time and not run out of air. And the Time Traveler, can sort of teleport herself a few feet ahead, so you can get past barred gates.

I could have looked to see what everyone else does at the beginning of the game, but I didn’t even know the characters had abilities at the time, so I can’t go back now.

Basically, you are supposed to explore a cave, which apparently can talk, since it acts as the narrator. Each character is looking for something, and has their own little area of the cave that sort of tells their story. The Knight, for example, involves kings, princesses, and dragons. That’s all I’m gonna say about that. I don’t like to spoil anything.

There are also these markings on the wall that show you images of the characters, giving them a bit of backstory. Each of these characters seems to have some sort of troubled past. Is Double Fine known for making games about characters like this? Because they did the same thing in Psychonauts.

There was a part of the game where I have to flip three switches, but the gate closes when you let go, so I didn’t know what to do about that part. It turns out that was actually for the Twins to go through. I thought I was unable to progress, until I found out online that you can actually bypass this area by taking a side path straight into the Time Traveler’s area. So at least that’s a thing.

There are a lot of puzzles in this game, some that require multiple people. Some are easy, and some I had to constantly leave the game to look up a solution for. Some of the solutions seemed kinda ridiculous to me at first, but then again, I guess I should have paid attention to the way the camera moves when I get near a certain puzzle. So I guess I’m just stupid sometimes. Big surprise.

You can move your character by clicking anywhere on the screen, using WASD, or the arrow keys. The only time I use the arrow keys is when I’m swimming as the Hillbilly, because it’s not easy using WASD when you have to hold “Q” to keep the bubble around your head.

If there’s anything I really don’t like about this game, its when you need to solve a puzzle with 2 or 3 characters, and the other two characters are all the way on the other side of the area, so you have to move each character individually. This is rather slow and a bit boring. I don’t know if this is a co-op game, but if is, I think I’d recommend playing it with someone because of this.

It’s not really that easy for me to judge this game, because of the puzzles, seeing as I am absolutely terrible at puzzles. But I think that the game is worth a look, if anyone is better at puzzles than I am, and I’m sure everyone is.

In my humble opinion I suggest this is a game worthy of your money. I highly recommend this game if you are into a stealth game or if you like to use brute tactics and force in order to achieve your goal.
Introduction:
The game introduces you as the "Royal Protector" Corvo Attano, which is returning back to Dunwall to meet with Jessamine Kaldwin; the empress of Gristol, to tell her that he has not succeeded in finding a solution to the rat plague currently infesting Dunwall. His reunion with Jessamine is made short however, since she is assasinated right infront of him. Corvo tries to battle the assasins, he is however knocked out, giving the assasins an oppertunity of escaping. Shortly after "the royal spymaster" shows up blaming Corvo for the murder of the empress. You then have to find out who murdered the empress, and reclaim your honor.
Gameplay:
This game offers diversity in terms of strategy. I personally found myself discovering new ways of infiltrating target objectives on my third and fourth playthrough. This game also allows you to choose how you want to play. You can choose if you want to kill someone, or if you want to complete the entire game without killing anyone. The way you play the game also affects how the ending will turn out. You are also able to use certain powers, some of these powers can be used for a stealthy approach, some can be used to kill.
This game has some glitches and bugs which I find a bit frustrating. Dialogue between NPC is cut whenever you are being detected by them. The dialogue does not countinue from where it stopped once they return back to their un-alerted state. There are also situations where something you haven not done is count as a kill, which is frustrating if you are trying to achieve a playthrough without killing anyone. It is also hard to recognize some of the NPCs' who will be alerted by your presence, and those who will not.
To conclude this short review: I believe this game is a good investment, since it offers great diversity in playstyle and player based choices. The story is also very good. The things I found negative about the game are minor. As a side note I want to mention that I have not experienced any major problems with this game (only very few crashes, as expected).

As usual with my reviews, let me start with the TL;DR version for those who don't have time to read a wall of text,
"Lilli: Child of Geos" is an astoundingly charming indie game full of colour and character. The gameplay is addictive but can get a bit samey, but, thankfully doesn't overstay it's welcome. While the $20 price tag is a bit high for a 5 hour long game, it's well worth a shot when on sale if you are into casual, colourful experiences.
Now for the meat:
Lilli is one charming title. There is so much colour in this game to help make the island of Geos feel alive, making each of the characters you meet another interesting addition to the game. Just starting off this review, if I have to say what this game's strong suit is, it is definitely the art direction it took with aesthetics, I couldn't ask for it any other way.
The gameplay, while somewhat reminiscent of "Zelda" games, lacks any sort of true combat mechanic. Even the game remarks at one point, acknowledging the fact that you will not "kill" anything on this island, even the bad guys. The idea predmoninantly is based around the idea of exploring the town (divided into 4 seperate sections) on the island of Geos. While in each section of the town there are various tasks to be completed: from independant exploration to find treasures, flowers, and pots to smash; to completing quests the various towns people have - most of these ranging in a form of a fetch quest, disappointingly.
The game also features RPG-esque stat building. These stat points are there to help aid you in the core mechanic of the game, which is finding, capturing, and defeating "spirits". This involves using the mouse to click on flowers and plants to pluck from the head of the spirit while trying to maintain your grip on said spirit by not plucking thorny plants or getting hit by...-bomb flowers-....
This mechanic works well enough to do the job, but is certainly not the highlight in quality for this game. The mechanic itself tends to get a bit monotonous after a lengthy playthrough with this game, as well as the 3-star rating system that seems to be unclear as to how to obtain a rank. Often times I found a well executed "plucking" of a Spirit would only reward 2 stars, while other times I was fumbling over thorny plants and mis-clicking, I still got 3 stars.
When it comes to the controls of this game, this is probably the worst part, sadly. There are NO REBINDABLE KEYS. while the game doesn't use a lot of keys to begin with, I had many frustration that the "Interact" and the "mount Spirit" function were mapped to the same key, leading often to me talking to an NPC, rather than mounting the spirit I was chasing. Additionally there is some of the ABSOLUTE WORST mouse acceleration in this game. Even set to the "highest" mouse sensitivity, the game seems to have "camera smoothing" which results in the games camera and character feeling very, very floaty. I figured perhaps a controller would feel more comfortable for this type of thing, but surprisingly it was even more uncomfortable for me to play with a controller than a mouse. This is something that I hope the Developer will fix in later patches. Unfortunately, if you gathered with the 3-star rating system, addictive game play, colourful graphics, and wonky controls: Yes, this game seems to be intended for mobile platforms, and I think is quite a blemish on this game to have to comprimise competent, and proper PC graphics and control settings to aid with the underpowered mobile devices.
Before concluding I would like to mention a HUD bug this game seems to have, which is most apparent on 4:3 panels. This game does not feature proper word wrapping or font-size adjustments. Often text will bleed off of the on-screen button or prompt - this looks unattractive and very amatuerish.
Additionally I want to make 1 side note: While I am not a professor of law, I think this game borders dangerously close to infringing some copyright, with blatant use of Nintendo IP titles and names, additionally a music track in Mill Hill is dangerously close to a track in the Sims 3.

Lilli, with it's blemishes aside, is still a fun and addicting game to play. While the price tag is hard to justify for it's 5 hour campaign, if you find it on sale, I can't recommend it enough that you play this game. Give it a go if you want a happy, and very casual experience!

First, let's talk about game length... I heard this was pretty short so I held out for a good sale and finally picked it up for about $4. After almost 3 hours I'm maybe halfway through the game. I figure it should give me at least 5-6 hours of gameplay which is decent for that price but at full price you may want to hold off.
Anyway, about the game itself... The characters and the world are totes adorable. You'll find humorous writing, both light and even a little dark, video game references and great art direction. It's a good looking game with it's own style.
It's not without flaws, though. The biggest one which may even make it difficult for some people to play this is the barfy mouse-look. I can't even call it mouse acceleration. It's way worse than that. The mouse-look lags way behind and then suddenly snaps into position. It's very awkward and even though I never get motion sickness playing games, this had my stomache rolling sometimes.
Also, this game does not allow you set your game up via launcher or main menu. It dumps you into the game right away and you can fiddle with some minor graphics options once you get into it. The game did an adequate job of detecting my hardware and the game ran fine for me but for some others this may end up being a problem. Every game should allow you to configure your settings before rendering more than a menu just for safety's sake.
Another minor thing is the lack of voice acting. There are some voice clips, from Lili saying "hi" in 3 or 4 different ways to the other characters having their own little intros/outros to some grunts/barks during combat but aside from that none of the dialog is voiced which is weird since the voice acting that is there isn't bad. It would have been nice for a game this short to be fully voiced, at least the main characters.
Overall, though, it's a fun, cute little game involving smashing vases, stealing people's belongings out of thier homes, picking flowers and completing quests in good ol' RPG fashion. Pick it up on sale!

I bought this game almost entirely because it looked really cute from the screenshots. After playing through the first two areas (so far), I must say I am very pleasantly surprised! The art is very nice, as I expected, but the detail is far greater than I expected. Such a lovely atmosphere! The world they've created is one that I am thoroughly enjoying exploring. You can tell a lot of love went into this game just from looking around.
But enough about the wonderful art. If I had to classify this game I'd say it's a point-and-click with some (very limited) RPG elements and quick time events.
The game's story is... well, it's silly, but it's interesting enough. The humor is where it really shines. From conversations to item descriptions, this game has a lot of laughs packed in.
Gameplay is a bit rough. I feel confident in saying that this game was made with touch screens in mind, so the controls are a little clunky and the "battles" can be tricky--after all, you only have one mouse instead of a handfull of fingers. Still, you'll get used to it pretty fast. I'm playing on the hardest difficulty and I can usually get 3 stars (the max number) on my first try, and I am by no means a hardcore gamer. I've only played the first two areas, though, as I said, so it will presumably get harder. Still, I'm sure this will be a turn-off to some, so I feel the need to mention it.
No major glitches so far, just some camera twitchiness when you talk to people as it switches from "world view" to "conversation view", and once where I could read a sign through a wall.
Music is adequate. Nothing to write home about, but works well with the atmosphere and isn't irritating.
Sound effects are good, but the random dialogue bits (the game isn't fully voice acted, but sometimes people will say a few words of their text) are sometimes odd. Such as Lili saying "Hello!" when she's actually saying goodbye in her text... or just randomly in the middle of a conversation. What up with that, Lili?
All in all, I am pleasantly surprised and really enjoying the game. Do recommend.

If you have played Portal, it is impossible not to compare this to it; I was actually disappointed by how similar this game was to Portal.  I in fact wanted to stop playing this game and go play Portal, but the tidbits of story I was dropped in this game had me stick it out.
Pros:
- Some clever puzzle mechanics
- Engaging AI companion
- Being able to play as the AI a little bit was a welcome addition I did not expect
Cons:
- Too many different puzzle elements
- Story that builds and builds but ultimately fails to deliver in favour of leaving the player wondering
- Spends a lot of time telling the player to think over philosophical questions, which the player ultimately is not allowed to answer for themselves
- The end quite frankly was disappointing
Overall, I'd still recommend the game - it's entertaining for what it is, and since it's not that long it's an alright way to spend a couple afternoons - but you can't go into this expecting the next Portal, and you would in fact be benefitted by never having played that before.

Cuphead's art and music style is the big draw of the game, and it shows. There's a ton of detail visible in the animation for even a single character, and it's clear they put a lot of effort into it. Gameplay-wise, it's a pretty fun mix of boss rushing and platforming that's considerably more boss rush than platformer, with most of the game being bosses and only 6 relatively short platforming stages. It's noteworthy for being difficult, and for the most part it earns that title, though it can also be a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t sometimes. It's fine if you're just going through it for the same of finishing the game, but once you get into replaying stages for high grades you start to notice things like the bosses sometimes not throwing enough parryable attacks at you for you to actually possibly get both the parrying and time bonuses for the stage without just restarting, and other similar issues arrising from the attack patterns being slightly random each time that lead to getting an A rank sometimes just being a matter of chance. Or how some mechanics are more of a curse than a blessing, like how the first super move becomes worthless pretty quickly because of how vulnerable it leaves you at the end of it, essentially giving the enemy a free hit most of the time, but if you let your meter fill up you don't have any choice to use it since you can't just use the smaller, cheaper special attacks instead once it's full.
If you aren't going for grades then you don't have to worry about any of that, but then you have to worry about the game being fairly short; it doesn't take long to finish each stage once, and each time I reopened the game I was always surprised with how much my completion percentage had grown because it didn't feel long at all. The $20 price tag is paying more for the style than the amount of content, though, so it's really up to you if you think it's worth it or not.

This game is very fun, with singular graphics.
It's like playing an episode of the Twilight Zone. Dark themes, and the puzzles can get repetitive if you are going for 100% on this one, but overall, The Cave is a fantastic adventure game.
Well designed levels, witty writing, and fulfilling puzzles.  A solid pick-up if you are looking for a game to play one hour at a time.

The Cave is a puzzle platformer where you get to control 3 out of 7 possible characters at a time, leading them through the mystical "Cave", a place of mystery and desires.
The Cave consists of several unique "layers", some belonging to the cave itself and some unique to the characters you chose each playthrough that gives you a peek on the moment in their lives that turned them either evil or virtuous.
The levels themselves are not particularly hard, in most cases it's pretty clear what you have to do, although there are a few instances you might have to look up online to find how to proceed(damn parrot!). But for one they're all beautifully designed, each with its own theme and feeling.
Your roster makes up an interesting bunch, anything from a medieval Knight to a Time Traveller from the future, each with their own unique ability that helps you complete some parts of the game(besides their unique level faster). And for mute protagonists they certainly have a lot to say!
And speaking of voices extra props to the "Cave". Yes, it's a talking Cave. Only he doesn't talk to your spelunkers but to you. And he's absolutely hilarious!
Now for the bad.
The biggest issue I had with The Cave was the fact that even though it requires multiple playthroughs to fully complete it, it also forces you to replay the "regular" levels every single time. There's no "shortcut" even if you've already completed it 5 times before. So every time you go back to see the story of another hero or a different conclusion to one you've already seen you HAVE to go through the 4 "Cave" stages(getting the treasure, the Mines, the Zoo and the Hermit). And even knowing exactly what you have to do some of those can take a good chunk of time.
Also there were several cases where I really, REALLY, missed a button to call your other heroes to the location of the one you're controlling. As it is now even if everyone has to go to the same room you have to take them there one by one.
Even with those two minor annoyances though The Cave remains a very enjoyable game. Highly Recommended!

In my humble opinion I suggest this is a game worthy of your money. I highly recommend this game if you are into a stealth game or if you like to use brute tactics and force in order to achieve your goal.
Introduction:
The game introduces you as the "Royal Protector" Corvo Attano, which is returning back to Dunwall to meet with Jessamine Kaldwin; the empress of Gristol, to tell her that he has not succeeded in finding a solution to the rat plague currently infesting Dunwall. His reunion with Jessamine is made short however, since she is assasinated right infront of him. Corvo tries to battle the assasins, he is however knocked out, giving the assasins an oppertunity of escaping. Shortly after "the royal spymaster" shows up blaming Corvo for the murder of the empress. You then have to find out who murdered the empress, and reclaim your honor.
Gameplay:
This game offers diversity in terms of strategy. I personally found myself discovering new ways of infiltrating target objectives on my third and fourth playthrough. This game also allows you to choose how you want to play. You can choose if you want to kill someone, or if you want to complete the entire game without killing anyone. The way you play the game also affects how the ending will turn out. You are also able to use certain powers, some of these powers can be used for a stealthy approach, some can be used to kill.
This game has some glitches and bugs which I find a bit frustrating. Dialogue between NPC is cut whenever you are being detected by them. The dialogue does not countinue from where it stopped once they return back to their un-alerted state. There are also situations where something you haven not done is count as a kill, which is frustrating if you are trying to achieve a playthrough without killing anyone. It is also hard to recognize some of the NPCs' who will be alerted by your presence, and those who will not.
To conclude this short review: I believe this game is a good investment, since it offers great diversity in playstyle and player based choices. The story is also very good. The things I found negative about the game are minor. As a side note I want to mention that I have not experienced any major problems with this game (only very few crashes, as expected).
(I'm sorry for any grammatical mistakes made, as I am not a native english speaker. Hope this review is readable)

1. Game is extremely similar to World of Warcraft. This is a pro and a con. It's a pro because World of Warcraft is awesome, who wouldn't want to play a similar game. 4. game is advertised as free. is it? NO! if you've ever played tf2 when it went f2p you'll understand this. in rift as a free player you get a couple bag slots, a couple character slots and a couple other restrictions such as not being able to make auctions in the auction house until you spend 5 bucks of real money to make it otherwise. there is no way to get bag slots besides real money or getting to max level and selling a lot of harvested materials for REX (real currency sold by players).
technically you can say this game is "free" however free in this case would be sadly comparable to slavery as you must act as a slave in order to obtain that amount of currency. this could take you weeks of gameplay which will not be enjoyable.
5. the dungeons are fantastic. they are generic at first but eventually you will have a reasonably challenging time. it's an enjoyable way to level up if you are playing as a tank/healer.
6. the questing SUCKS. It's the most grinding in an MMO i've ever seen. we're talking 50+ quests to get up 1 level at level 40+ (level cap is 60 holy hell)
in conclusion, do i reccomend this game? sort of. i play with my brother in dungeons etc but that's about it. the novely died off fast. for new mmo players this game may be completely overwhelming and without a friend who knows his way around you won't get far fast.

A very cute little, casual game with nice graphics.
Sometimes i still get surprised by games, Lili: Child of Goes was one of these rare occasions.
Didn't knew much about the game, but upon starting it, i was dragged into it's nice, colourful and delightful atmosphere.
You're going to play Lili (much surprise ^^), a girl, stranded on an island with strange creatures. You're going to explore the different locations of the island and try to free the creatures from the bad mayor.
The locations are divided into semi-large hubs, which you can explore, find collectibles, hidden chests and solve smaller quests. The locations have a broad variety and do look very different and have their own charme.
The graphics and artstyle are very beautiful in my opinion, which is a great strength of the game.
The overall gameplay is rather simple and casual though. There is not much "puzzle solving" involved, you rather run around the island, explore the locations and stumble upon secrets without a bigger challenge.
But even if the gameplay is quite simple, i had my fun with it and enjoyed playing it.
The main storyline is rather short, i guess, though you do have some collectibles and achievements which might keep you busy for a while.
I'd also recommend this game for a younger audience, as it's rather easy and casual and violent-free.

I've got a lot of feelings for OneShot, but I can't delve too deeply otherwise that would go into spoiler territory. It's
kind of game. Like the other reviews state, going in absolutely blind is the best way.
However, I can tell you that:
- The OST is fantastic. Sets the tone and mood perfectly for each setting.
- If you like/liked Undertale, this game is pretty similar in regards to atmosphere, though OneShot was actually made earlier and has less focus on humor (but there are funny moments). I will say though, Undertale's famous fourth-wall-breaking Flowey has got N O T H I N G on this.
- It has one of the most adorable protagonists I've ever seen in a game, among an already cute host of characters.
- Pixel graphics that are colorful and expressive without being a sore on the eyes.
- The puzzles are not frustrating.
- A beautiful, emotional narrative that feels less like a story and more like an experience.
- I legitmately can't think of any cons, other than I wish there was more. Just play it.
