I've had a chance to complete this game on normal only without the DLC. As a big lore nerd I find that story is an integral part of video games to keep me entertained throughout the gameplay experience. As far as I'm aware the story follows on from that of it's predecessors which is a little offputting because it's the same basic storyline throughout.
The cutscenes are a little annoying and look like something thats been slapped together without any proper rigging to the models so the sequences look a little "blocky" for want of a better term.
However, the upside of this game is that it's a pure nuke fest. The weapons look awesome throughout and if you've got some pent up anger, it's a good way to just release that rather than slamming your fist into the wall.
The monster models are a significant improvement from the previous games in terms of design and even on normal there are times it can be a little daunting with the waves that are unleashed upon you.
SPOILER ALERT:-
The bosses in the game are a little ridiculous, with little or no mechanics to them at all. The last boss for example I spent less time killing that the butcher in the orphanage stage, which is also by far the scariest level in the game. While nothing in the game will make you "jump out of your skin" the atmosphere in that level will get you sitting on the edge of your seat.
Overal the game is more of a time waster than an actual story based experience. By that I mean it could be just simply a game which you can play in any extra spare time you have or if your angry about something and feel like going on a killing spree. Don't buy it for the story.

One of the best puzzle-adventure games out there, with a bizarre story, great voiceacting and dark humor., Made by Ron Gilbert (Money Island series) and Tim Schafer, so you know what to expect. Puzzles are not too easy, but also not too hard and mostly logical. Game can be played three times with multiple outcomes and different characters with different abilities. "The Cave" is primarily made for controllers but can also be played with keyboard/mouse. I'd recommend a controller although sometimes character movement turns out to be a little imprecise, but not game breaking. Overall great game for adventure/puzzle fans.

Pros:
+ Nice enviroment, music, atmosphere and characters.
+ Interesting underlying idea (the cave is a symbol for the most deepest and darkest descent into one's true self).
+ 7 different gruesome stories each with its specific level and a moral lesson.
+ 60% of the puzzles are cleverly crafted.
Cons:
- The narrator's attempted jokes and story spoilers deflate the atmosphere, and only 30% of them made me go silently "mhe".
- The abundant backtracking and ladder climbing is tiring.
- In particular, the monk's level actually tests your patience and stillness and other zen-oriented traits, which I don't really think it's a very good design decision when it comes to video games. Life itself tests me enough, I play video games to escape life.
- The same replay of the previous visited levels after finishing the game once and picking other 3 characters. A cause-effect-slightly-different-levels idea for the common ones would have been nice instead.
7/10, passed my test, so I'd recommend it.

I think anyone who plays The Turing Test without having some major criticisms of the story has failed The Turing Test - in that, you've failed to think for yourself and have just gone through the motions of solving the puzzles laid out in front of you.
Ok, so it's playable, interesting puzzles, brings some new ideas to FPS puzzle games. It's good in that respect. I enjoyed the twist too. (spoiler: there's a twist) Play if you like puzzle games, it's worth it for that. (not a lot, like $15 tops)
But like so many puzzle games that try to be smart and have some sort of philosophy (notably: The Talos Principle) it utterly fails to think the philosophy through and so for anyone paying attention it just becomes annoying and dumb.
(spoiler heavy here)
In short: Why did no-one think "Well yes, exposing the entire Earth to an untested virus *is* dangerous, but we don't want to exterminate it either, so how about we just quarantine it until it can be tested properly rather than committing murder?", but no the "scientist" characters just whine on and on about the value of life and feelings as if that warrants endangering the species.
I mean, if they'd at least attempted some sort of reasonable argument about a third option with the AI I'd have felt conflicted about shooting them (remeber, it's an AI not an AGI, it doesn't know how to be creative! it can't come up with ideas without help from people!), but since they made no serious attempt to better inform the AI and just stood there like idiots in front of a minigun, the only reasonable in-character option was to gun them down. I only replayed it without killing them out of curiosity.

If Portal was set in space and Chell (Ana) was trying to find missing crew members and not fighting for her life to escape.
[SPOILERS!]
I liked it. Is there much more to say? The puzzles were fun, the game mechanics were taught pretty well (though I didn't know I could actually jump until, like, chapter 5, which made things so much easier). The mystery was a little obvious, maybe, in that there's an oversaturation in the scifi genre of AI super computers thinking they know what's best for humanity and taking over.
That being said, this story seemed like an awesome fresh twist. The secret rooms are well worth the effort of getting through them; we're led to believe that this plant might have made people go crazy and get paranoid. But actually, no, the crew isn't paranoid, TOM /is/ actually spying on/controlling them. But, wait, hang on, TOM's aggression isn't unfounded, because the plant /can/ actually destroy all of Earth, and the crew members /are/ letting their own personal judgement get in the way of logic and /millions/ of lives. But wait, there's the Turing test and the chinese room test, both of which prove that TOM physically can't be actually concerned for humanity's wellbeing, he's just acting in the interest of the company. Wait! But, /actually/, the Turning test /isn't/ cut and dry because there are dozens of problems and ways around the chinese room test, meaning that TOM /can/ have a sense of self and care about others.
I don't know. The voice acting was fun, the game was beautiful to look at, and I'm just a sucker for a story about self-awareness in which the AI is actually the one to make the most morally convincing argument.

It's quite a shame not to be able to recommend this game, as innovative and unique titles like There Came An Echo are exactly the tyoe of game I want to be promoting. However, the end product is not there at all.
There Came An Echo is a voice controlled Sci-Fi RTS with a big emphasis on story. Sadly a lot of that statement pinpoints the game's downfall. The voice controls seem so sick in theory but in execution just barely miss the bar, even the slightest of unresponsiveness leads to total frustration. The RTS elements are rather sparce with the only real tactical  choices being when to use or when to dodge the AoE gun. And finally, the story is hot garbage.
There are some very redeemable qualities to TCAE, the voice cast is above average with some serious powerhouse preformances by Ashly Burch and Laura Bailey. The music (although a little overshadowed in the production) is to die for and one of the best parts of the game. I cannot recommend this game's OST enough, it is worth every penny. While the voice controls are problematic, when they do work it does feel very awesome. Sadly an inconsistant control scheme can only be praised so much.
The true meat of the issue and the big reason to avoid the game is the story. Whoever else on this site tells you that the story is good is either confused or lying, the story is one of the biggest messes I've seen in recent memory. The script tries way to hard to be quick and witty and ends up bowling over key plot points and details, characters are often not introduced correctly and sometimes not given motivations until it's too late. The amount of plotholes and unanswered questions are staggering, I detail in my video review the multiple questions I had with the game's plot thoughout playing it AND this was after watching my footage multiple times to prepare for the review. By the end of the game the most sour taste will be left in your mouth after the storyline just dies and you realize the game was only 4 hours long.
I applaud the innovative game and the fantastic soundtrack but it is very, very hard to recommend playing There Came An Echo. Here's hoping their next game fares better
Pros:

Cons:

- Did I mention how bad the story is?

Voice control - it's not the newest kid on the block when it comes to gimmicks. We've seen it peppered around other mobile devices, consoles and old video games, but never in such a bold implementation as 'There Came an Echo'.
I was understandably sceptical about what my experience would be when I purchased this game. As a programmer, the idea intrigued me, but like everyone, when I hear "voice controls" I'm reminded of all the time in life I've spent yelling violently at inanimate objects.
"Go left", "Go left", "GO LEFT!", "ARGH F***! HOW MANY F***ING THINGS COULD I BE TELLING YOU!?"
It's an overstatement to say that my introduction to the voice commands in this game was smooth. In the opening sequence, there were definitely commands that appeared to be more effectively calibrated than others, and for a person with both an accent (Australian) and less-than-clear speaking voice, I honestly had a very frustrating first ten minutes.
Thankfully, once I was over the hump with the introduction, I found that almost every command in the core game, regardless of how I phrased it, was responded to quite-intelligently. While I didn't feel inclined to churn through this entire game in one sitting, the relatively pleasant experience that I'd had with the voice commands and the strategic combat kept me coming back for more.
The plot is written quite aptly (and is obviously influenced people with reasonable technical knowledge). It has a relatively light, but competent science fiction undertone, but probably won't rock any worlds when it comes to dialogue or character arc. I enjoyed the story thoroughly, it's no Hollywood block buster, but I'd never approach an Indie game with that level of expectation anyway, so I was quite pleased and it honestly far-exceeded my expectations.
I completed the story at 7.0 hours of play, with some screwing around in menus and the odd wave-defence mode. Generally speaking, if a game at this price point keeps me interested for more than 2 hours I consider it the same value as seeing a film; particularly because I'm becoming increasingly time-poor and don't have the attention span to dedicate 200 hours to the monotony that the triple-A scene is churning out these days.
Should you buy it? If your interest in isometric strategy, voice controls, or Lite-Sci-Fi brought you to this page, don't wait. You could do a lot worse.

There Came an Echo is an extremely unique experience that I would recommend to anyone and everyone. At its core, it is a single-player real-time strategy game that delivers excellent gameplay, fantastic voice acting, great music, some replayability, and a 3-4 hour long campaign. Whilst I did find that this was too short for the price at first, I realised that it didn't matter once I finished the game.
Just as with every RTS on the face of the planet, you can control the game with mouse and keyboard. But seriously, don't. The thing that makes this game special is not that Wil Wheaton voices the main character... well maybe a little... but the excellent game design that is the main focus of the game. Voice commands. I played the game entirely with voice commands and the occassional nudge of the camera positioning with my mouse, and I didn't have any problems with it! The voice recognition is spot on, and if you have trouble pronouncing some words or just want to mix things up a bit, you can reassign certain words or phrases with whatever suits you better.
As I said above, the story is only about 3-4 hours long - worth every second, I might add - but there is also a wave-based mode in the form of the "War Room" which might add some extra fun to the game for afterwards (or just to practice before tackling the rest of the game). The art and music are also fantastic, and so overall this game is just an absolute blast! Make sure that you use a headset or a quality microphone if you want to experience this properly as it will make the voice recognition work a lot better.
Enjoy! :)

This game inspires such mixed feelings in me.
It's rather attractive and at times really humorous. There's a conscious, snarky kind of wit to it at times that I think is one of the major strengths in this game. It's very much aware of the type of game it is trying to be and I've always had a fondness for games that break the fourth wall so there's definitely no complaints from me about that. I love it. Lili? I actually really liked her as a main character. One of the main reasons I kept playing was to see what kind of sarcastic, funny little thing would come out of her mouth. The rest of the characters as well (and there are a lot of them that you can talk to) were great fun and I loved going around and talking to all of them. This is definitely a game that made me want to explore.
That being said...the actual premise of the game was pretty grating and got boring way too fast. Almost the entirety of the plot is made up of what is best described as a mini-game where you pick flowers off of villain characters. It's something that I can see working well on an iPhone game but as a computer game it is a little obnoxious. Even the side quests really amount to nothing more than open up a chest that is easily found and return the item in it to the person who mentioned it offhand.
The in-game menu can use some work too. Your quests/side-quests are listed in the most basic manner without really giving you information about it. And honestly, it's just...clunky and awkward looking.
You can tell a lot of love went into this game and I can see it easily becoming something wonderful but at the moment it's just in an awkward place between iPhone game and computer game and it suffers greatly for it. I got it on sale and I'm glad I did. I wasn't really spend near $20 on it in the state it is now.

I was very pleasantly surprised by this game. Rarely have I ever enjoyed a game as much as Lili: Child of Geos. I actually found myself laughing out loud. It has a great sense of humor and includes some surprising game references, a little bit of dark humor, and even some social commentary. It is also self aware and of course makes fun of itself. However it does have character development, albeit a little thin but no less profound, as Lili discovers what she truly wants from life. Better yet, it features some amazing hats and customization. Another surprise came after the game was over when I was waiting for the credits and only five names were listed. The small team makes one appreciate the game even more, and it is clear that it contributed to the intimate feel of the game and the coding humor *tips fedora*. Five out of five; would definitely recommend.

Lili: Child of Geos is a beautiful yet very simple game that won't appeal to everybody.
As someone who was looking for a change of pace from the average brown, explosion based gritty shooter, Lili: Child of Geos was an amazing pallet cleanser. A nice simple story set on a beautiful island with some really nice stand out characters and an easy yet enjoyable mechanic made for an enjoyable yet short experience that I would recommend to people looking for something a little different.
As mentioned above, the graphics in this game are superb, every area is crawling with life and every nook and cranny seems to have been paid a lot of attention. The character models as well are all unique and portray an enjoyable visual style that makes them feel much more alive as characters, even despite not being voiced.
The dialogue of the game is light hearted and fun, even going so far as to almost break the fourth wall at times when mentioning some of the games obvious limitations.
Sadly, the game isn't voice acted which feels like a slight let down. I feel it could of been the icing on the cake here but as mentioned the dialogue is interesting enough to read through.
The actual second to second gameplay involves a lot of fetch quest like objectives and the whole game is very easy, you can complete it to 100% in about 4-6 hours but the gameplay isn't the draw here and sometimes the IOS roots of the game can be seen.
Lili: Child of Geos is an experience more than a challenge, a nice vacation from the stressful and grim games that most of us play a lot and I loved it, here is hoping for a sequel!

I actually really love this game, which is surprising because I'm not a big fan of zombie themed games or movies. I find them really repetitive and they're just the same thing over and over. However, with Typing of the Dead, there are different mechanics that I'm not used to using, like the whole keyboard for example. I like that it challenges me to type as fast as I can, and there are so many different dictionaries to download, which makes the phrases vary even more than they already do. My only real complaint about this game is that a lot of the achievements are really grindy. You have to play the same levels over and over again, which can get tedious when you marathon games like I do. I've played this game for 8 hours over the past 3 days, so I'm kind of sick of playin the same levels over and over. Even the thrill of getting another achievement has started wearing off. I'll just have to come back to it later to finish it off.
Basically, it's an awesome, fun game, and it'll challenge your skills when it comes to touch-typing. It gets repetitive, but as long as you don't marathon it like I did, it should be okay. It's definitely worth buying if you want to improve your typing skills and/or if you like zombie games.

In keeping with classic first person tradition, the plot of Hell and Damnation is skeletal—nearly nonexistent really, and uses the events of prior games to begin it's narrative while re imagining some of the levels from the original Painkiller and it's first expansion. You take the role of Daniel Garner who is trapped in Purgatory after a fatal car crash and wants only to be reunited with his wife who ascended to heaven after the crash. Death makes Daniel a deal, if he can capture 7,000 souls and return them to him, Daniel can be reunited with his wife. It's extraordinarily strait forward and plot development only comes after every three or four levels. Cutscenes usually punctuate the end of each boss encounter treating you to absurdly poor voice work and awkward character models moving the events forward.

Gameplay is also cut and dry. The levels themselves are not really relevant to the story, they are merely a change of scenery as you mow down countless enemies. The gunplay in Hell and Damnation is frenetic and twitchy and Daniel comes with an excellent demon dismemberment kit. How does dispatching your foes with a chaingun with an underslung rocket launcher sound? What about a gun that spits out shirkens at mach speed and launches bots of lighting? The absurd artillery of Painkiller is a welcome deviation from the assault riffles and sub machine guns that are staples of the modern shooter. Daniel moves like Usain Bolt as your weapons dismember the beasts of hell that oppose you, throwing their carcasses back the length of a football field. This joyous sensation lasts for about twenty minutes however before the you realize this charade is a shallow as the puddles of blood you leave in your wake. Most enemies wield melee weaponry and charge in without concern for props or any other impediments in the environment, allowing them to get caught up.  There are a few demons that have shields for defense and hulking strongmen that take a bit longer to dispatch but they fail to offer much of a challenge and make traversing Painkiller's levels an exercise in tedium. The design of the levels themselves is also rather abysmal. It's much like Ninja Gaiden or Devil May Cry where upon entering a room the doors slam shut and dozens of enemies spawn. At this time it is advised that you bunny hop in a circle until all of your foes have been rounded into the center and use explosives to dispatch them en mass. By reskinning the demons into sheep and Daniel into a border collie, Hell and Damnation could have been an excellent herding simulator.
Visually, this is the best looking Painkiller yet. That doesn't say much since the original game is almost a decade old and the expansions have been modifying the original game's engine. Now on the Unreal 3 engine, Hell and Damnation continues to remind us of the roots of the FPS genre. Corridors are generally pretty wide and empty into arena like areas with few props. This is done for two reasons, first to minimize impediments to your movement and to ensure that your frame rate stays high because nothing ruins a twitch shooter like a dodgy frame rate. While is does accomplish those two things it does look hopelessly antiquated. Most levels take place indoors to keep draw distances short, those that do take place outdoors employ walls and barriers that kill any illusion of openness. Many details like door handles are textured onto flat geometry and further reinforce the idea that you are not in a real place but a staged arena. The demonic aesthetic can also start to ware thin at points and evokes cheesy 1980's metal album art. There are some flashes of inspiration however. The hellish Loony Park is a delightfully twisted area that concludes with an on rails roller coaster shoot out sequence that injects some much needed variety into the proceedings.

Some people refer to Painkiller as the unofficial Doom 3, since the actual Doom 3 tripped over something in the dark, banged its head, and forgot that it wasn't System Shock 2. Sometimes all we want is relentless old-school action gaming, blended with the immersive greyish-brown of current-generation technology. That's a niche Painkiller fills beautifully. It hangs out in the classic side of FPS Town, where keycards and puzzles don't venture for fear of getting shanked. That's not to say Painkiller is nothing but murdering everyone; there's a series of unlockable bonus magic cards that make it easier to murder everyone, there's a soul-collecting gameplay element that results in a new and interesting way to murder everyone. . .OK, so maybe it is nothing but murdering everyone, but it does it so well what more could you want? You could explore the levels and hunt for secret rooms and treasures if you really must, but if more than a minute passes without a everyone and a murder, you're not playing it right. All you really need to know is that there's a gun that shoots harpoons and gernades. If you're looking for a great pick up and play FPS, you've found it.

The game itself, if you take a deeper look into it, is pretty story rich. In basic words, you're playing as teenager called Simon who gets hit by an unknown driver, later being unconscious wakes up, sees monsters all around and tries to get home safely.
While you play the game, the environment & the memories (the cutscenes) will actually try to tell the player what is actually up with Simon's surroundings. Not only it does it with the cutscenes, but also with the visuals of the main character, monsters, in areas where you go and so on.
What is the most important about the game is that it's not linear. The choices in this game really matter.
In total, there're 4 different endings. 3 bad ones. 1 the good one. So if you play it, think wisely!

A Scientist, Hillbilly, Timetraveler, Knight, Monk, Adventurer, and Twins walk in to a cave.....  No this is not a joke set up seriously these 8 people walk in to a cave in groups of 3 to launch a nuclear weapon, travel back in time to kill the caveman ancestor of their co-worker, burn a carnival down and have other adventures.
A fun puzzle-platformer that requires at least 6 play throughs to get the entire story so you get your money's worth. Each character has their own level and powers that you can play in any order. They do drag after serveral replays considering no matter what set of characters you choose you need to play the same 4 levels but the puzzles are challenging and real thinkers if you are in to platformers and headscratchers this is a game for you. Puzzle solutions are very creative such as using a parrot to record a dog barking, making yourself stink like a dinosaur to attract a live dinosaur to crush with an ancient wheel to make oil to run an ancient engine and other crazy puzzles. Ther are 2 endings for each character fun visuals, sorta silly jokes and a quirky narration by The Cave itself. Pretty much The Cave is the American cousin of the the Narrator from The Stanely Parable who is not as funny but would get a one shot Comedy Central 30 min special that is mildly amusing and watchable 2 more times before  becoming less humorous each and everytime afterwards and you end up flipping the channel to some reruns of Bob Ross to get his voice out of your head.
TL;DR
Fun, challenging puzzles, cool cartoony visuals, amusing narration, lots of replay to see entire game, kinda boring and repitive after several replays but still fun. 8/10 would play again. Also some hoopty-dooptey stuff about morals and true desires are corrupted by simple wants yada yada yada... something about being above your wants so you can attain true happiness.

I was very frustrated with this game once, when after a lot of progress it crashed and took the save file with it, so I had to start over. At that point, I put it a side for a year or two. But now, when I returned to it, there is basically nothing to complaing about. I still experienced a minor glitch, where gamepad stopped working in the final scene of the game where our heroues receive their trophies, that is the start/menu button on game pad still work, and the stick works while in the menu, but when you exit the menu I could not control the characters with the stick, they simply would not react. This was minor for me though, because it was in the very end and I finished the game with the keyboard.
Overall the game appears very well thought through. You cannot paint yourself in the corner no matter what silly things you do, the game reduces tedium by automatically bringing the two other character with you when the first one reaches an invisible "checkpoint" so you do not need to cover big distances with all three, and the difficulty level of the game was just right for me (some people may find it too easy). I finished the game with all seven characters and there were only two places where I had to google the answer (timetraveller well and monks lotus). On the other hand the game is not ovious, that is you still have to think how to reach the objective.
Graphics looks very good even today in 2016, and I also appreciate that games feels like it gives more "freedom" than your usual adventure. By that I do not mean freedom of choice of course, in this respect the game adheres to the genre standards, I mean freedom of movement. In that respect it feels more like a platfoformer than an adventure which is good. But unlike a platformer, it's much easier to succeed in jumps and climbings up a ledge, which is also good.
So providing that you do not lose your save file as I did, I think this game is a very good choice, so I'd recommend it strongly if you like adventures. This one is very, very good.

I think this is a great proof of concept, and there are enough good things about the game that I don't regret purchasing it. But as a whole I just can't recommend it to most other people.
Pros:
+ There's a handful of incredibly cool moments, when everything comes together.
+ The voice controls worked perfectly for me (though many people had different experiences).
+ Playing a strategy game with voice controls is not just a gimmick--it is a cool concept and it's fun to do.
+ The voice cast did an excellent job considering what they were given. Especially Ashly Burch!
+ The game is a good length, for what it is. It's short (4 hours or so), and doesn't overstay its welcome.
Cons:
- The stealth sections were painful, and clashed sharply with the innate imprecision of voice controls.
- There are bugs. Restarting at checkpoints (on death) was unreliable, and missions got stuck and needed restarts.
- UI clarity could have been a lot better: at some points (especially early on) it can be difficult to tell what to do.
- Map design could have been much better: the fixed waypoints are needed, but offer too few options.
- The dialogue is very cringe-worthy. Not even this very talented voice cast could save it.
- The plot of this "story-driven" game is just completely all-over-the-place bananas, and not in a good way.
A little more about the writing (as much as I can, without spoilers):
Basically this game's main interest, story-wise, is in taking on high-minded philosophical concepts. Most full-length stories can only swallow one of these brain-devouring ideas before they get full; this game tries to take on like three or four of them at once, and the result is that it's basically incomprehensible.
I don't mean that it's confusing, or too smart for the average gamer, or anything like that. The individual concepts are actually easy to understand. I mean that the story is composed of so many disparate, out-there elements that it does not form a whole that makes any sort of sense.
I normally love deep philosophical stuff in stories, so when other reviewers complained about the story, I figured it wouldn't bother me. I was wrong. The story in this game is not intellectually challenging--it is a hodgepodge of pseudointellectualism that tries very hard to be clever, and mostly falls flat on its face. And while the game itself is pretty well-paced, the story writing is so rushed and so pointlessly convoluted that by the end I genuinely did not understand what my player-character was trying to accomplish anymore.
I feel bad being so harsh. The writer also directed, edited, voice acted (pretty well!), and on the whole birthed the idea for this game from scratch. That's great, and I respect it a lot! But in the future I hope he will hire a dedicated writer who can help him to realize his vision in the way it deserves to be realized.
TL;DR: Buy this game on sale if you are a native English speaker, curious about the voice-control concept, patient about bugs and sometimes-wonky design, forgiving of totally-bonkers story writing, and want to support a unique indie developer. Otherwise, steer clear.

I really wanted to like this game, because I loved Sequence (which is now renamed Before the Echo) and I learned that this game is a continuation of it. I had heard that you could play the game with a mouse if you didn't want to use the game's voice commands, and so I decided to try it out, but I wanted to give the voice commands a fair chance anyways. On a technical level, they work fine, and the game never had any trouble recognizing my voice, but they just don't add anything to the gameplay. There are a limited number of phrases that you use and most of the gameplay is just directing your squad members to the right designated points on the map and letting them do their thing, and even with the option of being able to swap out the game's default phrases and words with custom ones I never felt like I was actually talking to a squad because the technology just isn't there for it to be able to recognize anything more than the handful of preset phrases that you'll recite over and over throughout the game. The natural assumption would be to just switch to mouse controls, as I did, but you don't have to play for more than a few seconds to see just how awful it is. Instead of having a traditional point-and-click interface, you play the game by holding the right mouse button to bring up a contextual wheel with various orders on it to emulate the lines you give to your squad when using the voice commands, and it's a massive pain to use in the middle of gameplay. If you have to shoot a particular person for a mission, for example, in order to shoot them with the mouse controls you have to hover over them, hold the right mouse button, and search for the "target unit x" option, instead of just clicking on them like most games. In a turn-based game this would be fine, but in a real-time game it's counter-intuitive and makes the game a chore to play.
The story is still there, so if you really liked Sequence/Beyond the Echo like I did and this game goes down on sale enough it might be worth checking out just to see the story (though the game is pretty short, so you may want to wait for a particularly deep sale), but overall this game is just another example of "if it isn't broke, don't fix it".

+It's beautiful, no doubt about that.

-My number one in this list has to be the motion sickness.
There's currently 2 choices of camera movement ...
fps style is bad if you suffer from motion sickness.
mmo style is better but the camera still swings enough and there's a motion blur to the sides when you turn that may make you feel ill if you have this problem. Sometimes Lili runs into things you weren't expecting and the camera can stop in a nausea and dizziness inducing way, so if you're one of those people affected by this I'd keep in mind that this

Lili: Child of Geos is a love letter to classic 3D adventure games but overall runs a bit long. You could easily burn through its content in a day but the majority of it sadly gets very repetitive very fast. At $20.00, it's a hard sell I'd argue.
You're dropped onto the island of Geos as Lili, a college student persuing a Vege-Magical degree, and become embroiled in a conflict between the island's ruling Spirits and their servant Constructs. Lili's pursuit is not entirely selfless (at first). She's here to study the flowers that dot the island, which most conveniently grow from the backs of the Spirits, forcing her to spend a majority of the game delicately plucking them from her enemies.
As a central mechanic, the spirit combat is great and well realized. The chase to catch a spirit followed by the aforementioned flower picking is great fun, hampered only by the finicky controls thinking you want to stop and either pick flowers or smash jars when you're in hot pursuit. Lili's origins as a tablet game really show up here, as the plucking mechanic has you selecting a flower and dragging it away from a spirit to collect it.  It is fun perhaps the first handful of times, but given that there are over fifty spirits in the game to fight with little variety aside from the number of obstacles that crop up on a spirit, it does make the game's pacing drag if you are going for 100%.
Geos has a lot of bright and colorful details to its world, and it is fun to just wander around the island and see what's in it as the Constructs go about their business. While not a fully realized world like in Deadly Premonition or Majora's Mask, where the characters all follow a set schedule, Geos nonetheless is a delight to get lost in for a few hours and take in the scenery.
It's also good to see Lili realized as a character; she has no love interest and she has no need of someone to come save her. As a plucky protagonist with ideas for what she wants to do with her life, Lili stands up for herself in a game that, while it has action, is at its core a non-violent experience, barring how you feel about picking flowers off the backs of monsters.
It's not a perfect game and suffers from having too many spirits to fight through, but for a quick delightful romp Lili's journey to Geos is one worth undertaking.

Lili: Child of Geos is one of the bizarrest games I ever played: an open-world flower picking simulator with a stroke of the RPG-brush.
You play Lili, who visits an inhabited island to collect flowers for a school project. But she does not pick these flowers from the fields or gardens, she only picks the ones that grow along the streets and on the monsters.
Yes, this game features flower-picking based fighting. You chase a monster and then, during the actual fight, you pluck flowers off the monster. Maybe using the mouse makes it too easy, but I never lost one of these fights.
To be fair, this fighting model makes more sense on a touchscreen device. This is not as surprising since earlier editions of Lili: Child of Geos were published for mobile devices. And after all, it seems new and creative to me.
But the open world of Lili: Child of Geos offers a bit more than flower picking. You can explore, collect stuff, talk to people and solve sidequests which consist of exploring, collecting stuff and talking to people.
Lili: Child of Geos is rather short and small. It took me about three or four hours to do the main quests, all the side quests and get all the nonrespawning collectibles.
On a more negative side, this game features no voice acting, only textboxes.
So, was Lili: Child of Geos any fun for me? Yes, but not 20€ worth of fun, more like 10€.
Conclusion: If you need a tiny charming open-world game for inbetween with an uhmm innovative fighting mechanic and this game is on sale, then give it a try.

Painkiller: Hell and Damnation represents a bit of a mixed bag. On one hand this is easily the best entry in the series since the original, on the other it is mired in some bizarre choices. Notably HD is something of a retelling of the first game. Not that anyone should be playing Painkiller for the story, but somehow HD's narrative manages to be even more nonsensically bad than the threadbare excuse found in the first. Utterly listless voice acting doesn’t help the matter. The second, more glaring issue is the omission of some of the best classic levels such a The Town. While available as DLC, to hack the original apart and hide bits of it behind a pay wall is idiotic.
HD features the addition of the Soul Catcher weapon. Despite being shoehorned into the plot, the weapon simply isn’t very fun to use. The primary fire is decent, while the secondary’s soul drain function is tedious at best. The weapon’s big draw, the ability to possess enemies once enough souls have been absorbed, is redundant when you can wipe out entire swaths of demons with a single rocket.
Still, there is plenty of free DLC and the game retains the same classic Painkiller feel and is every bit as fun as it used to be. Co-op modes and multiplayer helps to stretch the experience out despite the truncated campaign's best attempts. This game is only worth the money if one happens to be a fan of the first game, wants to give the new content a go, and manages to catch it on sale.
Tellingly all the best parts featured in this update are the ones left more or less intact from the original version. The new additions, almost uniformly, simply fail to measure up to bar of quality set by the first game. Hopefully the heavily implied sequel this remake sets up does much better. Newcomers to the series would be far better off simply buying the Painkiller Black Edition and simply pretending all the other titles in the series didn't exist.

The Turing Test is a first person puzzle game, similar to games such as Portal, The Talos Principle, Qube and Qbeh.
The game is structured as a linear sequence of puzzle chambers, where your objective is to figure out how to reach the exit and progress to the next chamber. The main puzzle mechanic focuses on power management. Each puzzle chamber contains several objects which require power to function, including doors, lifts, moving platforms and magnets. You have a gun which can absorb balls of energy from sockets placed on the wall, and then fire it into different sockets to power the connected objects. The challenge comes from the fact that you never have enough power to turn everything on at the same time.
The complexity starts to increase as you discover that there are different types of power, represented by different colours. Blue is always on, green turns on and off at regular intervals, and red only works for a limited time. For example, if you use blue power with a moving platform, it will move to its second position and stay there. Red will send the moving platform on a return journey one time, while green will make the platform constantly move back and forth.
Other puzzle mechanics include the obligatory inclusion of pressure plates that can be weighed down by objects/yourself, and towards the end of the game you’ll be able to remotely control a robot to perform actions in areas of the chamber that you can’t reach yourself.
There’s a decent story about a research facility on one of Jupiter’s moons, some missing scientists and the AI who controls the facility. The main theme is about the difference between Artificial Intelligence and Human Intelligence, which is a topic I usually find quite interesting. Voice acting is pretty good.
I didn’t encounter any bugs, and I completed the game in 6 hours. Controls are fully rebindable, although you can’t use arrows for movement because left/right arrows will turn you instead of strafing (a potential solution on the forums didn’t work for me).

If you like puzzle games, you should enjoy playing The Turing Test, however due to the length I’d recommend picking it up on a sale. I bought it for 50% off, which feels like a fair price.

So Lili: Child of Geos is a quirky, lite RPG, and action-adventure game. The mechanics are simple and easy to understand for gamers of most ages (granted those gamers can read), and the rest of the game is made to be a family friendly adventure. Combat and violence is replaced with a fun little mini-game (which feels awkward on the mouse at first, but you'll get used to it) where you chase enemy spirits across the island, hop onto their backs, and pluck Spirit Flowers off to weaken them while avoiding the thorns and bomb plants that grow there as well. After defeating a spirit you can earn a score and a rating measured in stars, if you earn 3 stars you'll also get a colored version of that spirits mask (there are also fifty unique spirits to encounter, so that means 50 unique masks to unlock). Outside of that minigame, the rest of the game sees you running or walking around the island of Geos, slowly unlocking new zones to explore freely and to find new spirits to defeat inside. The exploration of these zones remind me a little of The Wind Waker, as the island is bright, colorful, and actually very pretty (especially on the highest settings). Unlike Wind Waker though, there are no dungeons to explore (unfortunately) but there are a lot of fun little puzzles to undertake, quests to do for the wood-construct citizens of Geos, and every time you enter a zone, a whole batch of Spirit Flowers (the same kind that grow on the heads of Spirits) spawns in random places for you to collect. Unfortunately a few bugs appear where flowers will grow inside walls or under bridges or just places you can't reach, and there are the occasional clipping issues that block Lili off from small areas she should be able to access, or temporarily stick her into the environment (only happened once for me, but it took me five minutes of running in a circle to get her free), and the zones themselves really aren't too large. However you will find yourself scouring these zones over and over while hunting for spirits, treasure chests, and flowers and the zones are well designed and so different from each other they surprisingly don't get old after a few hours of playing, and with the flowers you find you can sell them for gold coins (used to buy outfits, upgrades, and powerups for taking on spirits), trade them for keys (one key will open any lock on the island, but is destroyed after each use) so you can loot or explore the various houses and shops on the island, or you can use the flowers to gamble with in a minigame I found quite easy (probably just because I have good eyes and reflexes) to try and earn even more gold coins.
I bought the game on a whim because it was on sale and looked cute, and surprisingly it is now my favorite game of all time, simply because it is so fun, cute, and happy it always makes me feel good when I play, no matter how poopy I feel before loading it up. I've already finished the game (it is rather short unfortunately, but I've heard you can play it for about 40 hours before collecting every single hat, outfit, lore item, mask, pet, and completing every quest) but I want to keep playing it and try getting the game's other ending and explore the bird poop mechanic a little bit more. Yes, there is a bird poop mechanic where if you run too fast while scaring birds, the poor things will fly away and poop all over Lili, leaving rainbow colored droppings all over the girls face and clothes (this always makes me laugh because she always has a calm smile on her face throughout the game).
So would I recommend this game? Yes, however the majority of Hardcore gamers probably wouldn't like the game for much more than the billions of references to Dark Souls, Oregon Trail, Mario, Zelda, Minecraft, Prometheus (yes, the movie), and much more. Children would probably love the colors and characters, but a lot of jokes and dialogue would probably be wasted on them. But if you're a total nerd who wants to play a peaceful game that'll just make you laugh and give you at least 3 to 5 hours of sheer happiness (that's the minimum time to beat the storyline), you'll probably love it as much as I do.

This game is a lot of fun but is very obviously in development. It is one of the smoother and better early access games I've ever paid for, though. I really like this game, it just needs time. As long as the devs continue to care as much as they have since their game came out, this game could turn out to be amazing.
The game has run really smoothly for me. The FPS has been good and consistent. The movement needs a little work (mainly the jetpack physics with momentum and gravity) but it never feels clunky or sluggish. I am also a big fan of a "hand made" world rather than a randomly generated one.
Aside from the bugs we all know are present in early access games or Ubisoft titles, the main issue with the game is lack of content. Although it's a hand made world, there really isn't anything to find other than a plethora of dong-shaped rocks and the same ~8 resources over and over. What I look for in a hand made world are interesting things to find -- a cool laser rifle behind a rock or an abandoned colony I can loot for scrap and resources. Right now there isn't any of that. There's an empty cave and some solar panels you can't interact with and that's about it.
I'd buy it if $25 isn't a big deal to you. If it is, wait for this to get more content and spend it on something else.

is a game where you crash land - though it is unspecified how you crash - on a planet, explore it, and make an attempt to survive.  The game is not geared towards a harsh survival experience, but it is more focused on adaption and progression of technology as you advance throughout the game.
Rating: 9/10
The graphics in this game are amazing, considering that it hasn't be around all that long.  I was not using any dedicated graphics card by any means, but I was able to push them at max settings and they were great.  I would not consider them extremely realistic, but they were great enough to make my experience a lot more satisfying, being a game based around exploration.
Rating: 8/10
The mechanics of this game were certainly not lacking, everything functions as should.  Nothing bad to say here, though they didn't stun me in any way.  There could be some minor improvements here and there, to make the game even more fluent.  I think the gun mechanics are simple enough.  You see what you need to see, and considering that the game is not about fighting and killing monsters all over the place, they do the job.
7/10
The interface is a little bit confusing.  It is left unexplained and it's up to you to figure out what everything means.  It's clean nonetheless and functions fine.  The user interface can be the same sometimes.  It can be a lot more simple and compact in some ways.  Instead, there is a lot to look at.  I do like the way you look at some sort of wrist watch when you open the menu screen with Esc, kind of transitions the game world and the real world.
8/10
The experience was really fun and exciting.  There is a lot of walking and traveling involved, but if you enjoy periods of silence and thought, then you shouldn't have any problems at all.  I do feel like the alien settings by default should be set to a lower setting.  Unless you've worked your way up and have a considerable arsenal that allows you to take on creatures easily, you spend a lot of time weaving around alien creatures during traveling because they are just about everywhere.  The progression of technology is based mainly on how much you travel, and what you find during your exploration, and not so much about hard work.  As of now, with no interplanetory exploration (soon to come I hear *wink*), there isn't too much of a point to continue surviving once you build everything.  Keeping yourself alive isn't all that hard, and in fact, a survival aspect is hardly present in the game.  I feel like this should be a bit more of a thing, but not so much that it overrides the exploration factor.
Osiris: New Dawn is extremely impressive for it's time on the market.  The developers are kind and responsive, and they seem to be off to a great start.  If you're interested in getting into what could potentially be a massive survival exploration game based in space, this game is for you.  At this current point in time, it could use some small improvements to the system, and a lot more features to keep people playing.

A short but very enjoyable game that has the basic room-puzzle structure of Portal with a genuinely compelling and original sci-fi plot.
The only complaint is that some of the tools for puzzle solving do not get much of an introduction and you are expected to stumble across them eventually. Also some of the secret rooms have puzzles that have no clues and require brute force attempts to solve them. (I am looking at you Secret room 1)

I love this game. Please note: my total playtime recorded on Steam not only involves the completionist playthrough, but also a lot of time where the game was paused when I needed to leave partway through a puzzle, playing the alpha build, etc. So, it was actually about 8-9 hours of actual playing time, for me, which will vary widely depending on how you pick up on the puzzles.
The gameplay mechanics and set-up are impossible not to immediately compare to Portal, with The Talos Principle mixed in. Essentially, you are guided and caught up on the story via an AI companion, needing to work your way through an extensive series of puzzles, learning more of the story as you proceed, These puzzles involve using a series of energy cubes and energy bolts (fired into place with one mouse button, and retrieved for use with the other), along with switches and other mechanics to find your way through the locked doorway and into the next room to the next puzzle.
Each of the seven "chapters" of the game includes ten puzzles, as well as one "hidden" (not really - if you learn where one is, they're obvious after that) optional puzzle. The optional puzzles, as well as the concluding room of each chapter, are used to most greatly advance the plot of the game via audio recordings and written files and other items, though there will also be dialogue between you and TOM, the AI interface, as you enter every room. In the interest of a spoiler-free review, I won't go into any real detail here, but the story is engaging and develops at a good pace that keeps you interested, with a really nice twist (which also adds a great new gameplay element partway through). That said, there are also some very noticeable plot holes in the end, and while it is nice to have two options of an ending, it is disappointing that which choice you make makes no real difference to the game. So, it's good, but flubs a bit at the end.
There are a lot of puzzles in this game, and in a fairly wide variety. They often feel like they lean on the easy side, but as the game developed and more elements came into the picture, many did become truly challenging. This is especially true where new rules and gameplay dynamics were formed in the process - you wouldn't know something could be done until it finally occured to you to try. Things can feel a little repetitive at times, as you are, essentially, repeatedly finding a way to get through the locked door by manipulating the energy in the right way. But, as a fan of the Portal games and such, I really enjoyed having a new incarnation along those lines, as there are far too few such games available.

The game also has a strange way of pacing the game (which I won't tell as it relates to the "story") as well.
Though the story has its flaws, it makes up for it through raw gameplay, the aethstetics fit into the setting of the game and does not bloat the game like in Battlefield or CoD or Crysis (All are good games but...) where graphics need to be an ever present concern that it cripples the game's framerate to an all time low.
In conclusion, I feel that Red Trigger is a game that demonstrates gameplay, good level design, and a smooth framerate can be all that is neccessary to make a game great as games start to look for shiny graphics, unneeded features, and movie-like seriousness in plots (Seriously... If I want to have that, then I'll just go to the movie theatre! I want fun gameplay!) to grow their audience.

Evolve Stage 2 is an extremely flawed game. People whine it's hunter-sided, others that the monster is op, or that a specific monster is op. This is because the game has NO balance.
When you start playing the game, you will find out that the monster loses almost constantly. This is because the newbies have no clue how to play it, they panic, and end up fighting too much and losing. However, after some 20 or so hours, you will start to notice the MONSTER winning all the time. This is because it's much easier to learn to play one character than it is to successfully coordinate with a team of four (even if you're all on teamspeak). And lastly, once a good monster starts to run into good hunter teams, then the monster has no chance. He simply can't out-dps a well-organized hunter team, nor catch them off-guard. To top it off, playing against good hunters as the monster is one of the most frustrating and awful feelings I've had in online gaming. You're the helpless kid on the schoolyard who is surrounded by bullies and there's NOTHING you can do about it.
The game is deeply flawed. Have I had fun in the 50 or so hours I've played it? Sure, but most of that was because I was on teamspeak with my mates as the hunters, or absolutely stomping pubbies as the monster (as evidenced by a 96% win-rate as the goliath). The only games I lost as the monster were frustrating, and I can recall TWO whole games where it was a back-and-forth, balanced fight. One where I was the monster, the other where I was the hunter. That's not a good percentage out of some two-hundred games.
Despite giving the game a negative rating, I would still say give it a shot. But don't expect it to become a long-term time investment for yourself and if they actually implement the cash-shop at some point, I would advise against spending money on it. It's quite easy to obtain silver keys just by playing and chances are you won't be playing for long.

(Full review follows below)
is a downright riot.  I loved the hilarious, cheesy B-movie dialogue and the nonsensical story.  And the gameplay itself was various, different, and entertaining.
The story isn’t written that seriously and the dialogue fits perfectly with intentional cheesy lines and some just plain hilarious writing.  I played through the game a total of 4 times (for achievements) and I found myself watching the cutscenes -almost- every time because they just entertained me that much.  The voice acting was pretty good overall; even when it faltered, it still fit the overall ambiance of the game anyway.
The typing mode is the selling point of the game.  It definitely provided me with a novel experience; I don’t think I have played a game with a mechanic like there is in this before. The original
came out in 1999, but I had never played anything like it until now.  I enjoyed it a lot.  Playing on hard, with DLC and/or workshop content can make it a lot of fun with various hilarious things to type out as fast as you can without making a mistake.
The classic mode was also enjoyable to me.  It is an on-rails shooter, staying true to the original, light-gun arcade style.  It definitely brought on some nostalgia playing it.
Staying true to the hilarious, light-hearted nature of the game it is not difficult at all.  You have unlimited continues, so even if you mess up you just keep going (and don’t even have to drop in another quarter).  There is no backtracking required too.
The graphics were not the best, but it’s mostly intentional:  there is supposed to be an old-school, drive-in, grindhouse feel to the game.  However one thing that isn't intentional and occurs on a lot of user’s systems is that random parts of the models (an arm, both arms, the head, all of the above) of the mutant-zombies will pop in and out… and this did occur in my game too.  It didn’t really bother me that much in the typing mode because I was focused on the sentences, but in the classic mode it was a little disappointing shooting at invisible, un-rendered mutant-zombie heads.  There may even be ways to fix it depending on your system, but you will have to look into that yourself.
If you are a gamer who is looking for a taste of something different and novel, or a taste of something from ghosts of arcades past, this game has an offering of both.  With the available workshop content the typing mode has limitless possibilities.  Mix all that with some hilarious scenes, and homage to cheesy, horror B-movies and you get a just simply entertaining experience.

A action-stealth game of epic proportions, Dishonored is a game about choice, stealth, and that little panic that happens whenever someone looks your way at the wrong time.
In Dishonored you can make your way through the streets and sewers of the city of Dunwall as you sneak or slaughter your way through patroling foes and plagued citizens to accomplish your missions and explore a city on the verge of ruin. To help you on your way you have a number of otherworldly powers allowing you to teleport, manipulate time, summon rats, and other useful abilities.
You also have an arsenal of equipment to assist in your endevors, state of the art weapons, high tech gadgets, and a telescopic mask that will allow you to choose weather to fight your way through your enemies, or take a more subtle appoach and mearly knock them out.
Choice takes a major part of this game as you must not only choose your appoach through the missions and their multiple paths, but you must also choose how to deal with those who wronged you and caused your dishonor.
All in all Dishonored is a great game that will captivate stealth fans as well as offer something even for those who prefer a more direct route, as you explore a wonderful world on the brink of collapse.

A true masterpiece of a game, and a revolutionary take on gaming experience that'll never truly be improved on. Very few games are as approachable as Dishonored, in that a very average player can play this game and enjoy it to their fullest, while a veteran gamer can do the same in their own manner, at completely different paces. Choices matter in an impactful way, something many other games fail to achieve as fluidly as Dishonored.
If you decide to be an aggressive, revenge driven killer, you truly feel like it and you see the consequences first-hand, while still satisfied with yourself for doing it. If you decide to be a stealthy assassin, picking off those you deem corrupt from the shadows unseen, you truly feel the rush of trying to escape unseen while flying from rooftop to rooftop. If killing isn't for you and you would much rather solve your issues in a "diplomatic" way, by all means, you can, and you will feel like you actually did some good whilst doing it. There are so many ways you can go about this game, so many routes, even though they all ultimately bring you to the same place.
Your pathing, your tactics, your timing. All important depending on your play-style. The combat system is fluid, fast and satisfying. The stealth is incredibly dynamic on higher difficulties. The abilities are all useful in their own ways, allowing you to take many approaches to the same obstacles. Everything about this game makes you feel challenged, but not hopeless, powerful, but not overpowered, tactical, but not unbearably bored. If you're looking for a game that lets you play it the way you want to play it, with plenty of replay value, engaging story and intuitive mechanics, this is the game for you. I only wish the second installment of the series was as polished.

Long story short, this game is really damn amazing. Between the voice controls and art style to the story and music/voice-over, this game is a prime example of what games could become. Combined with the ability to create your own voice commands, this game can be either Highly customizable to the point where you just want to say "SHUT UP, WESLEY!" for every action in-game

We all know Deadpool is the frikkin notorious fourth wall breaker. We love it. But how do you maintain that wall and, at the same time, maximise immersion?
You put the player on the other side. That's what this game does. You're no longer in control of the hero, you ARE the hero (providing tactical support for your squad, but nonetheless). You are the voice of your hero. Sure, they may not call you by your real name (the chances are pretty slim), but it works as a miracle. I don't think I've ever been so deep in a game, not even FPSs, with you taking the perspective of your character, provide that much feel, that much immersion, and all that.
The voice recognition system works almost flawlessly, allowing me to release my inner Brit without the fear of slowly going crazy from talking to myself. Seeing that there are four varieties of English included, as well as some other languages, my inner linguist is also rather satisfied. The Realsense keeps me curious, but unfortunately, I do not have the hardware supporting it. Bummer. I'd be waving my hands like a mad man, like talking to the computer wasn't enough. :)
The plot and the characters are well written, as far as I can tell. Placed in the gameplay as they are, they keep you interested and immersed, something you'd expect from an RPG rather than a strategy.
I haven't finished the game yet, I've probably just scratched the surface.
It's been more than enough for a good impression.
Also, there's Wil Wheaton, Ashly Burch, and Yuri Lowenthal, what more would you wish for? :D
Edit: OK, so I've finished the game. It's rather short-ish, but still worth every penny. The plot bears some resemblance to AC series (don't want to spoil, so I'll leave it like that), but it might just as well be my impression only. And also, it's not a bad thing, it's still well-written nonetheless.
Only about 3 hours long, but well worth the price of admission.

“Wow, it actually works!”
My first experience with There Came An Echo was filled with careful hesitation followed by eager disbelief and curiosity. It might not be the first game to attempt voice commands, but it’s definitely the most successful at making it feel seamless and authentic. It’s such a brilliant hook that it almost feels like enough to carry the game, until you step back and look at how hollow the experience actually is.
The idea behind There Came An Echo is that it’s a game played almost entirely with your voice (there are mouse controls but I can’t imagine wanting to use them). Viewed from a tactical, isometric perspective you issue orders to characters, telling them where to go, who to shoot, when to reload; the sort of commands that have become instinctual to me over so many years of playing games, but here required I relearn how I interact with this sort of game down to the most basic function. By requiring I put previously silent button presses into words, There Came An Echo felt intensely engaging. I couldn’t rely on muscle memory and doze off, I had to constantly be aware of what was happening and find the words to convey that to my troops if I wanted to make it through a mission.
Where There Came An Echo rises above other voice activated games is in how much freedom you have in creating these commands, and how well the game interprets them. Rather than a strict list of possible orders I could give, I’d often find myself just naturally forming sentences and being shocked at how often they came out the way I wanted to. There were some instances where I attempted more complex commands than the game could comprehend and needed to break them down, but when There Came An Echo is working as intended it feels like something revolutionary, which thankfully is far more often than not.
But what are you actually doing with all these commands? That’s sort of the problem. While There Came An Echo incorporates some impressive tech, its other systems are comparatively very shallow. My first thought when realizing that the voice commands worked as intended was to wonder how far I could take them, but most scenarios I was placed in gave me little room for dynamic play. Maps are narrow and linear, and different weapon loadouts offer only very slight alterations to how you play. In a sense it feels like the game is directing you as much as you are your units, putting restrictions on what you can and can’t do while pretending to be more strategically deep than it ever becomes.
I’d have likely accepted this though if what There Came An Echo cares about most, its narrative, was worth the immense amount of time spent on it. Far from being merely drawn out and overbearing though, the writing here is positively painful. It’s also very, very weird, in its plot, its tone, its character motives; everything, really. Each line is full of earnest attempts at self-awareness, baffling plot twists, and unending amounts of technical mumbo jumbo.
It isn’t even that There Came An Echo is written so poorly, but that it gives off such a strong impression that it thinks otherwise. It tries so hard that I sort of just feel sorry for it, wondering if there was some way it could be salvaged but always coming up empty. But when it takes up more of the game than anything else, it’s difficult to write it off as just regrettable. The narrative is always there, pushing its one-dimensional characters, overreaching plot, and shallow questions as to what it means to be alive in your face and forcing you to humor them. And then it fridges one of its female characters and reminds you yet again that “♥♥♥♥♥” is its favorite word and any sympathy quickly disperses.
I’m not exaggerating when I say There Came An Echo’s use of voice commands is one of the coolest ways I’ve played a game in years. It never stops being cool either and I hope other developers will look at this and start experimenting with their own games. There Came An Echo succeeds at proving an idea works and can add a lot to a game, but when that’s all it does while bringing along with so much fluff it’s difficult for me to recommend playing it on that basis alone. I don’t consider voice commands a gimmick, but them being the sole draw here has effectively reduced them to one.

Full disclosure: This game was given to me to play for my YouTube channel.
Regardless, here are my true thoughts:
It was short, yet sweet. Based on Lovecraftian themes, this game ran for approximately 3 hours with 2 sets of difficulty. I played under normal difficulty and found myself enjoying the game, which emphasized less on puzzle and more on story building. It was easy to follow and unneeded of a walkthrough. The only thing I could not manage, was finding the secret ending. Don’t take my word for it, but this made me believe that it could only be found playing the hardest difficulty: Nightmare mode.
This game had a few short comings, but no game-breaking bugs, such as rare spelling errors. A personal argument of mine was that the game could have enhanced its visuals by changing the typeface during certain cutscenes to match the moment more as oppose to using the same typeface but only changing the font to red (such as when the monster talks). Overall, it’s a wonderful little game to play. You'll certainly find yourself immersed in the world that the creator has made. I would recommend this game for all Lovecraft enthusiasts or sci-fi horror fans. Feel free to check out my playthrough of the series in the link below.

Ayumi: Enhanced Edition is a great little game.  I purchased this in January shortly after the 2.55 update, and was pleasantly surprised at how well this title is put together.  The game makes heavy use of pre-made assets, but it does so in a way that builds an atmosphere of horror and suspence.  The scares are spaced out in such a way that the game builds up a sense of dread, and then does something shocking, which made me jump more than a couple of times.  As far as content, there's a lot of game here.  You can finish this title in about an hour or so, but there's so many little things to find, as well as alternate endings.  The game's story is interesting, and is sprinkled with bits of Lovecraftian mythos, which really helps to set the stage.  This product is well worth the asking price, and the creator Lord Rutsah has put a lot of love into this title, and it shows.
TL;DR: Crazy space Cthulhu horror game with Yellow Mythos, and lots of scares!  Buy it!
Worth buying~

This review is based on the 'normal' difficulty. I'll edit it in future if I ever feel like trying out 'nightmare' for the different ending.
I really wish Steam allowed us to rate more flexibly than simple positive/negative. For the moment I'm going to go with my gut instinct and say that no, I wouldn't suggest the full price for this game. I give it roughly a 4/10 for now.
'Ayumi' isn't a
game. In fact, there's a lot of potential which I am hoping is tapped in the 'nightmare' difficulty. However, I don't particularly feel drawn to dive right back in to find out.
While it is certainly creepy wandering around the blood-splattered spaceship, catching twisted hints to Lovecraftian themes, I can't say that a 'normal' playthrough provides you with enough meat as I would have hoped. I've read/viewed some Lovecraft but not much of Hastur. This perhaps stifled my enjoyment.
Unless you are completely dense, you'll almost immediately work out that
. You do have a sense of pity for the little scamp.
The story did appear to be going somewhere dark and intriguing. You simply wind up walking into a
ending far too easily in the 'normal' mode. I even went back the first time to try to make sure I cleared an area. Still not much more to add to the story.
It's possible I missed something because although I tried to be thorough, there are portions of the spaceship which are frustratingly labyrinthine. If I could have bought a map from the small stores you find throughout, I feel this would have gone a long way to easing my frustration.

I think that if you buy this, perhaps skip to 'nightmare' mode? I'm not sure you'd actually miss much from the 'normal' setting and you'd probably find a satisfying conclusion. There are plenty of free RPGMaker games out there with quite a bit of content (go look up the sites) so it's hard for me to justify one with what feels like a demo as it's 'normal' playthrough.
This has promise. Maybe I'd find it in the other mode. We'll see when I muster the will to run through this game again.

Wow, the graphics for this game are just adorable. Colorful, cute, plenty of detail in the environments and (mostly) sharp textures.
But gameplay wise you can tell it was designed with mobiles in mind, because there's a mini-game where you have to use the mouse to pluck flowers and the gameplay and story are rather shallow.
The player has to find red flowers by chasing spirits and solve mini-quests ('quests' would be too big of a word, since they usually take a couple of minutes to complete), among other things (like plucking white flowers and opening treasure chests). That's all there is to it really. There isn't much to do, except for a couple of small sidequests.
You can also level up the character in several ways, but these character upgrades are mostly useless because I didn't seem to experience much of an improvement. Experienced gamers in general won't find the gameplay difficult anyway. There's no health bar, you can't die. The only thing that can happen is that you get thrown off the back of a spirit and even then you can try again without any problems. And there are also potions that you can use to speed up your character, make her invisible or that allow you to throw a bomb in order to stun enemies.
Lili Child Of Geos also isn't a long game. I was able to complete it in 2-3 hours. Which was more than enough because the gameplay becomes very repetitive after these couple of hours.
I still think the game is worth the money, if only for the beautiful graphics and for the first few areas. And who knows, maybe they can flesh things out for a possible sequel, make things a bit more interesting ? I'd like to see one, in any case.

Back in years long past, when I was a wee lad, schools sought fit to have an entire class devoted to developing proper typing skills and technique. Maybe they still do? Why would I know? I don't hang around schools, that would be weird.
Anyway, we would naturally rush through our assignments to play games like Chip's Challenge on those silly lab computers. This game reminded me of that time and what could have been. Perhaps you remove the grindhouse context from the game and put something nice and PG there, and man that would've been an entire class.

Here it's particularly well done, being simultaneously cheesy but delightful in a semblance of originality that permeates the game from the gameplay itself to the presentation. If you liked Portal, you are sure to like The Turing Test. The overall feel of the game are very much alike, but the puzzle mechanics are very different.
Pretty great basic idea for the story, certainly enough to keep you wanting more, and learning about the crew and their mission to Europa.
Even though the nature of the puzzle mechanics make solving the puzzles easier than in Portal (interaction and outcome of the puzzles are much more limited), this game is well worth the admission price.

Nice puzzles, not too difficult, yet challenging. There's also a bit of a story line, although it's not necessary to follow the story line to solve the puzzles. The optional puzzles are a bit more challenging, which makes them even nicer (even though they really are optional). All puzzles are relatively small (a bit like the Portal puzzles).

Overall, The Turing Test was an interesting puzzle game, in a similar theme to Portal, or, less so, to The Stanley Parable, as others have mentioned as well.
It is a singleplayer based 'room puzzle' game, with the story being given in the form of dialogue between yourself, crew members, and the base AI, along with audio recordings you can find, and some notes scattered about.
Some of the puzzles will really make you think outside the box for solutions, and I thought this gave it a leg up when compared to, say, Portal, where once you learn how a game mechanic works, that's pretty much it, whereas with The Turing Test, you'll often have to do things in new and unpredictable ways.
It would also be really interesting if they added a development kit for making our own modular puzzles, and hosting them on the Steam workshop. I think the community could really make some interesting things.

I thought the Epilogue [ending] seemed a bit... rushed? perhaps? I was expecting more a battle between T.O.M. - either fighting it out as TOM tries to lock you out, or more of a mental fighting - Eva slowly trying to reverse the control - exerting influence over T.O.M., instead of T.O.M. over her (as Sarah continually mentioned 'You have to try and control him!').
Beyond that, to the end, I had harbored a suspicion that Eva was actually an AI herself, and that the 'Turing tests' we went through in the game, as well as ''the game'' itself had two objectives - the first, a basic test - can this 'AI' think laterally, while also thinking 'effectively' (as opposed to T.O.M. at one point, when Eva asks for help, he suggests she cut off her arm to weigh down the pressure pad - not a very good solution, eh?).
But additionally, with the dialogue of the crew, T.O.M.s attempts at control, ect, I theorized that this was the second objective of this Matrix-like environment (assuming the entire 'world' we see is a simulation of some kind) - to see how this lateral-thinking AI responds to the ideas of free will, of human independence - would this AI go with the 'logical' thought that, obviously, total enslavement to a machine would make for a much more ''productive'' and ''efficient'' society - it's just ''logical'' - or would this new AI see value in the exercising of free will, of chaotic choice, that humans have?
To be honest, I could entirely see a addendum to the story that had 'Eva' actually waking up to find that we are actually an AI being tested to see if we would support human free will, or always make the ''logical'' choice, even if it is morally and ethically shaky.

Here's a list of some key features:
- Resource Management & Trading
- Tech Research
- Creating Division Templates
- Diplomacy
- Auto-Calculated Land, Naval & Air Battles (with naval & air influencing land & air influencing naval)
- Production of Equipment & Vehicles
- Construction of Factories, AA Defenses, Forts & Radars
- Front/Army Management (you can give orders to a general, like attacking on a line you've drawn)
If you get the game, check up a guide on how to do naval & air invasions. They require very specific circumstances in order to be executed.
