A action-stealth game of epic proportions, Dishonored is a game about choice, stealth, and that little panic that happens whenever someone looks your way at the wrong time.
In Dishonored you can make your way through the streets and sewers of the city of Dunwall as you sneak or slaughter your way through patroling foes and plagued citizens to accomplish your missions and explore a city on the verge of ruin. To help you on your way you have a number of otherworldly powers allowing you to teleport, manipulate time, summon rats, and other useful abilities.
You also have an arsenal of equipment to assist in your endevors, state of the art weapons, high tech gadgets, and a telescopic mask that will allow you to choose weather to fight your way through your enemies, or take a more subtle appoach and mearly knock them out.
Choice takes a major part of this game as you must not only choose your appoach through the missions and their multiple paths, but you must also choose how to deal with those who wronged you and caused your dishonor.
All in all Dishonored is a great game that will captivate stealth fans as well as offer something even for those who prefer a more direct route, as you explore a wonderful world on the brink of collapse.

A true masterpiece of a game, and a revolutionary take on gaming experience that'll never truly be improved on. Very few games are as approachable as Dishonored, in that a very average player can play this game and enjoy it to their fullest, while a veteran gamer can do the same in their own manner, at completely different paces. Choices matter in an impactful way, something many other games fail to achieve as fluidly as Dishonored.
If you decide to be an aggressive, revenge driven killer, you truly feel like it and you see the consequences first-hand, while still satisfied with yourself for doing it. If you decide to be a stealthy assassin, picking off those you deem corrupt from the shadows unseen, you truly feel the rush of trying to escape unseen while flying from rooftop to rooftop. If killing isn't for you and you would much rather solve your issues in a "diplomatic" way, by all means, you can, and you will feel like you actually did some good whilst doing it. There are so many ways you can go about this game, so many routes, even though they all ultimately bring you to the same place.
Your pathing, your tactics, your timing. All important depending on your play-style. The combat system is fluid, fast and satisfying. The stealth is incredibly dynamic on higher difficulties. The abilities are all useful in their own ways, allowing you to take many approaches to the same obstacles. Everything about this game makes you feel challenged, but not hopeless, powerful, but not overpowered, tactical, but not unbearably bored. If you're looking for a game that lets you play it the way you want to play it, with plenty of replay value, engaging story and intuitive mechanics, this is the game for you. I only wish the second installment of the series was as polished.

TL:DR A pretty decent puzzle/platforming game from Double Fine. Only major downside is having to complete multiple playthroughs to get all the different characters endings as the game gets a bit repetitive after playing through a couple of times.Probably not worth it at full price but a good buy if its on sale.
Full Version:
The Cave is a platforming puzzle game that has you controlling 3 different characters, who you pick from a group of 7, that you can switch between and control to complete the various puzzles and sections you encounter. The characters are all different (Monk, Knight, Scientist for example) and each one has a unique ability. They also each have their own backstory which is told via slides you collect as you go through the cave with the resolution(good or bad) being obtained when you complete a playthrough.
The Cave itself is the setting (as well as the narrator) with your route through it depending on the 3 characters you pick at the start. There are two types of sections you'll go through. Generic ones which you'll have to go through on each playthrough, and the unique ones with each character having a unique section each and are dependant on which ones you choose.
The gameplay itself is pretty simple with most of the puzzles not being too difficult to solve as well as the fact that you cant die because as The Cave puts it "Nobody dies in The Cave".
Good points:
-the dark humour in this game is quite enjoyable and it has its funny moments
- the cartoon style of graphics fits the game quite well and the way the level design all ties in togther is quite clever
Bad points:
-to playthrough with every character will take 3 playthroughs with another 2 if you want the good and bad ending for each character. While this isnt too bad because of the unique sections for each character, the sections that you have to playthrough every time do get boring.

The graphics and sound of the game is in a bit goofy, cartoonish style. But it all comes together really well. I enjoy the idea as well as how they set things up to remind you visually that you're still in that cave even though the setting may change.
The gameplay is more tricky than I expected. The hints are subtle and smooth, easy to miss if you're distracted outside of the game and not paying attention. Could be one of the reasons why it become so satisfying. Most things can be solved with some common logic though, the rest may need some goofy logic which makes it pretty amusing.
The humor is definitely a big reason to why I enjoyed this game. Always able to smile every now and then at silly or stupid comments makes this game great.
The only downside I can see is the constant running distances, both back and forth, which feels like I'm just wasting time. The design of the area makes it enjoyable in a way, but not sure if it's enough for me to make it feel worth it to pass through there several times while just running... not sure if it need to be that spacious.
Great game overall though which kinda makes up for it.
I definitely recommend it for people that enjoy puzzle games with humor.

Lili is a short, casual, visually exceptional 3D adventure game that's heavy on atmosphere and charm but light on story and variety.
Pros:
- Visuals are gorgeous. It does not look at all like a mobile port and has some of the best visuals I've come across in an indie game.
- Fully 3D world that you can wander around in at your own pace.
- Nice atmosphere. The island is populated with lots of whimsical characters and the game oozes charm.
- Non-violent, suitable for children old enough to have a fair degree of reading comprehension but also accessible for adults. (I realize this may be a con for some who are looking for a more meaty sort of game)
- Unique. It's a bit different than pretty much everything else out there.
Cons:
- Not the greatest value considering the price to length ratio. I like short games but $20 for a few hours play feels a bit steep to me.
- Game play is rather repetitive. You do the same few things for the entire game, namely collect items and play the same sort of quicktime mini game in lieu of actual battles. This is somewhat forgivable given the very short length of the game however.
- The 4 zones are small and there's not much interaction with the environment.
- Story is rather thin and there is no intro; you just get plopped in.
-
- Full controller support has now been added. Sort of. They basically did a virtual mouse pointer that the left analog stick controls but it feels very shoehorned in as an afterthought rather than controls designed around a controller. Control directions in the UI still don't reference the controller when you are using it either.
Neutral:
- RPG elements are quite lite. That's not a con. The game is what it is, but calling the game an "RPG hybrid" while not technically incorrect, may give an inaccurate impression. There's some very minor leveling and skill progression but don't expect hitpoints, skill trees and such.
- No voice acting. The game is fine without it but I feel it would have added that extra bit to draw you in even more. Also it would allow for younger children to play. As non-violent games are somewhat rare, it seems especially suited for young children but the amount of reading creates a bit of an age barrier.
- Feels like a missed opportunity in some ways. The visuals and atmosphere are excellent and the game well done as is, but part of me feels like it could have been so much more with more variety and length.
- A couple of aspects still feel like a game created around touch input, namely the mini game where you pull flowers which is a major part of the game. Also the level up menus with the big wide buttons to hit and just the general sort of largeness of the UI. These do work just fine with a mouse though.
- The battle / mini games on the keyboard and mouse have a totally different feel than on the controller. The former has a more tactile almost Angry Birds type of feel with pulling while the latter feels more like DDR. I'm not sure which I like better. They're very different.
I enjoyed Lili for what it was, a unique, short, charming and visually stunning adventure game but part of me wished it to be more than it was, that it were much longer, the quests more complex, that Lili had companions, there were more choices etc. The game does end leaving future adventures for Lili a possibility so perhaps a sequel could be based around the PC platform from the beginning this time and more complex. It's a fun possibility to contemplate.
This isn't to say that Lili is incomplete. It's not, it's just a short and casual game. Sometimes it's nice to have those as a break or when you don't want to get into huge commitment with a new game.
The $20 price point I feel is a bit high for the short length of the game but if this sort of game appeals to you I'd recommend it when it goes on a sale.

First of all i have to say: If you buy the game, you probably won't get what you've expected. The game itself is a charming little piece of entertainement, but after reading the steam-description i just expected something completly different. I would not say that it's an RPG ( but some might call it one); To me, it just doesnt look like an RPG, more like a game that's made to have some points an RPG needs while beeing a mix of puzzle, minigames and collecting stuff. For example: You get something like a "Skilltree" but it doesn't really matter where you put your points, since you won't get any new abilities. As I said, the game is okay, its colorful, it cheers you up when playing it, but it is not what steam promises you.
The game itself is, as i said, a mix between puzzling, running around, minigames and collecting stuff (a lot of stuff). If you're into that, you'll be just fine, but if you hate spending too much time running back and forth while collecting items that add absolutely nothing to the game, then you'd might regret buying this.
The Graphics are pretty good, but I was told to have low standarts. The Characters are lovely designed and you can feel that the developers really cared about every single friend or foe you face throughout the game. However, the story is rather basic. I don't want to spoil anything, so just let me say this: The story feels like a weak version of another game (if you know what i mean.. you probably don't.) There's just not much depth in the story, you spend way too less time with the characters to really get into it. When I first saw the game i kind of expected a heavy story, so i was a little disappointed. But again, not every story has to be deep.
The gameplay is very repetitive, but this does not matter that much because the game is rather short. Just let me tell you, the "quests" you get sound all the same, you have 3 items you can use and every "battle" is exactly like the one you fought before.
Overall Lili; Child of Geos is a game to play when you don't want to start a biiiig, looong game with a deep story. Its a game you choose to play when you have little time but still want to enjoy a good game. I personally give it a thumbs down because it is a fine little game, but nothing like you'd expect after reading the description.

Short but sweet, if I had to summarize in one sentence. A game I think people of all ages could enjoy depending on what they're looking for. For younger kids you have a virtually non-violent, beautiful and funny place to explore. Older audiences might find entertainment in the occasionally dark humor and the game's weird inhabitants.
Gameplay-wise
is a very short game. I'd estimate around three hours of casual play. If you're going for collectibles and a perfect ranking against all enemies you may add two or three extra hours of game time. It's not a very challenging game either if you play on easy or medium. During the game you will attempt to "de-flower" spirits walking about the game world. You do this by playing a sort of minigame where you drag and drop flowers and other items off a spirit's head. You can tell this game mechanic was designed for the use of a touchscreen, which isn't too strange as this is a PC remake of a mobile game, but the developers made it work fairly well with a mouse. Depending on your skill, you'll master this part of the game quickly. It does get progressively harder as the game goes on, but it never reaches a level that will really challenge you and have you retry beating a spirit more than a couple of times. I have yet to play the hardest difficulty setting though. There are three settings, of which I played the middle one.
Controls are a bit wonky. Camera control takes a bit getting used to. Mouse sensitivity have only four presets which is the part I found the most annoying about the game. Some weird collisions here and there. Otherwise well made.
Would I recommend it? Yes, but try to find a bit of gameplay to watch before you decide whether or not to purchase
. It's a game best enjoyed if you go at it with a relaxed attitude. If you're up for exploration and fun in short bursts. It would be easier to recommend this game if it had been cheaper. I don't really think the price suits the length or content of the game. But all in all I'm having fun with it.

Having sailed to the island of Geos for a school project, you are tasked with gathering up rare flowers to report back to your professor.
However something is not quite right on the island and you soon discover that the constructs (creatures created from wood) are slaves to their masters; the spirits and their Mayor.
You decide to unshackle the local natives from their forced labour by doing them favours in exchange for flowers and other rare items. The island is full of life, its characters witty and charming where I couldn't help but laugh at some of the dialogue that was exchanged.
Where its similarities between Zelda lie are based around the Islands and town hubs which you would find in a Zelda game.
Imagine taking those areas from Wind Waker and putting them on this island. The exchange of dialogue is something you would find straight out of a Zelda game. Don't expect voiced characters but instead small sound bites like "Hi", "Bye" and other gasps throughout the dialogue.
Don't expect to be crawling dungeons and having a boss fight. This is not where its comparison with Zelda lies.
There are lots of Easter eggs to discover throughout the Island in treasure chests that reference some classic Nintendo games. Another character will throw some Video game trivia at you, asking you to guess what game it is referencing. "Praise the Sun".
Hats can be found in treasure chests and by doing services for the locals. Masks can be unlocked by beating Spirits.
As a collectathon it has similarities to Banjo-Kazooie. Achievements are awarded for smashing pots, finding treasure and picking flowers.
Fighting in the game is composed of hopping on the back of a Spirit and attempting to pluck flowers from its back while they put obstacles in your way such as thorns and bombs.
There is currently only partial controller support, with the mouse really only needed for the Spirit fights and closing menus. I'm sure adding a button binding for B to close menus will soon come in an update. I am unsure how Battling the spirits with a controller will work though. Its interaction seems more suited to a mouse or tablet, although the developers have said in the forum they are working on full controller support.
Overall I would highly recommend the game if you grew up playing Nintendo games like Zelda, Banjo or Mario.
While there is no platforming involved, a mixture of all these games can be found in Lili: Child of Geos.
The graphics are just downright gorgeous and full of colour. The music sounds like something that belongs in a Zelda game. It's a casual adventure game with some very basic RPG elements that involve levelling up your Speed, Grip and Stealth.
I haven't played a game like this since the N64.

Lili: Child of Geos is a collect-a-thon that just exudes charm. I've never had such a fun time collecting flowers and strange garbage from chests in a long time. Just don't go into this expecting Zelda-like combat or something similar to Banjo-Kazooie. You're simply plopped onto a charming little island that can simply be described as something out of a dream.
Here's a Quick Look video to see what the game is like, since it's hard to describe with words. But if that's not your thing, then just read my quick and concise review below.
I'll begin by describing the basic mechanics of this game. You play as girl named Lili who is an explorer, and she comes to the island to collect flowers for a report she's doing. You get these special flowers by finding spirits--basically human logs with masks--straddling onto their backs, and plucking white flowers that pop up on their backs until you reach the red one that you need. A fun little mini-game that's somewhat challenging if you're going for the best rank. The other things you'll be doing to progress the story are exploring the village, talking to the inhabitants, and generally exploring for neat things to collect.
But what makes this game so charming? The game's art style is truly breathtaking. It makes the game's main feature of exploring even more enjoyable when there's so many interesting things to see. I even enjoy scaring away birds and laughing at the rainbow turds they leave behind occasionally. Even talking to the local inhabitants is a joy. They have no qualms making fun of themselves and enjoy pointing it out to you. I found it very refreshing to actually WANT to talk to every NPC and find out what their story was. Not many games can pull something like that off.
Other neat features the game has is the ability to chose how you want to upgrade yourself. You can choose to upgrade your speed, grip, or stealth however you wish to suit the playstyle you enjoy. You can also purchase upgrades in a wide range without much restriction. Personally I chose to get a map and key early rather than items to help me fight spirits since I just like exploring more. But if none of that is your thing, you can also just unlock different color swaps for Lili to make her look even more adorable. The choice is yours.
However, this game does come with a few negative.
*I found a game-breaking bug early on. I had collected all of the flowers on the map before hitting up the trainer, who wanted me to collect 5 FRESH flowers. And since none were left, I couldn't progress the game. (I've found out another work-around for this is just quiting and loading your save again. However, I still think it's an issue if you have to do such a strange thing just to continue the game, so I'll leave this as a negative.)
*
*There isn't an voice acting besides the occasional "Hi" and what not. While it's not really a big deal for me, I'm sure some people might not like the fact a game with such interesting characters in it aren't voiced. It could've added a lot more to the experience if they found voice actors to bring more life into this already vivid and imaginative game.
*
*Some people may take issue with the price of the game since it's cheaper on the iOS. However, you're not getting the same experience as you will here, and you can always wait for a sale. But still, I'll list this as a negative just so people know.
But even with those few minor negatives--and I say minor because it was only the beginning of the game where I had to start over--I highly recommend anyone to pick up this game if they want a laid-back adventure with good humor. This game makes me feel like a little boy again. I was just curious about everything, and it's been a long time since any game has done this for me.

Great Puzzle Game, but VERY short.
This game is only going to you 2-5 hours total, depending on how good you solve puzzles as well as how much you look around in the optional sections/between chapters.
With that said, I got this game on sale for $10 and got about 3 hours out of it personally. For me that's a bit on the pricy side for $/hour, but if this metric doesn't bother you, I will say that this game is great.
So overall, I really enjoyed my time playing The Turing Test. The learning curve is very gradual, and the game doesn't spoon-feed you on game mechanics, but rather teaches you through level design (which is great). I think that this is a first person puzzle/platforming game executed amazingly.
The puzzles are very fun, albeit on the easy side, the narrative is great, and there are even easter eggs thrown in here and there. There are 70 different "puzzles", which at first sounds like a lot, but many of them go by very quickly (especially in the first few chapters where the game is simply teaching you game mechanics rather than giving you real puzzles).
If you're a fan of first person (and to a much lesser extent platforming) puzzle games, then you'll enjoy this game. You need to decide for yourself if the price tag is worth it however, as I mentioned earlier, I bet 90% of people will spend 2-5 hours for the whole game regardless of how you go through it.

As much as I want to give The Turing Test a hearty thumbs-up, all I can honestly give it is a halfhearted shrug.
THE PUZZLES:
Though the creators give themselves lots of interesting options -- especially once the remote-controlled robot enters the picture -- they never fully commit to testing your mastery of each mechanic. I frequently ended rooms with leftover pieces, and in two cases I didn't even need to explore the entire chamber. The optional puzzle chambers are a much-needed challenge but there are far too few of them.
(I would love to see what sort of devilishly tricky chambers players could make if The Turing Test had a level designer like Portal's)
THE STORY:
The Turing Test touches on a couple thought-provoking concepts regarding consciousness and morality, but again it doesn't delve deeply enough to be satisfying. Observant players will figure out what's going on long before the protagonist Ava does.
IN CLOSING:
While not a bad game per se, I spent most of my time in The Turing Test being reminded of other, better games.
If you want some truly mind-bending puzzles, I recommend trying The Talos Principle or The Witness.
If you want you mind blown with a sci-fi story, I recommend SOMA.

It's hard not to compare this game to Portal, so I will. If you've been yearning after another puzzle game in the vein of Portal, this one has you covered in spades. It kind of fits between Portal 1 and 2, having the head scratchers of Portal 1 with the plot and exposition of 2. The puzzles are not the mind-binders Portal's were, and there's a few whose solutions felt more like tricks than actually reasoned results, but there's also a few good stumpers, too. It replaces Portal's humour with some enjoyable pop philosophy, and includes one of the best plot twists I've encountered in a video game.
Overall, I highly recommend it. Good entertainment for an afternoon or two.

-

The good news is that Osiris: New Dawn has good bones.  The bad news is that good bones is pretty much all it has going for it. Beneath a thin veil of basic gameplay and decent visuals lies an even thinner survival experience, lacking both breadth and depth.
It's heartening to know that O: ND is being published by Reverb Triple XP, a reputable publisher with a track record of hits like Rocket League and ARK: Survival Evolved. The game is being developed by Fenix Fire Entertainment, with whom I'm not immediately familiar, but their bio is solid. Even better, it's been released into early-access right after the intergalactic♥♥♥♥♥♥storm that is NMS, which means lots of folks are likely to get on board which in turn could mean that Osiris: New Dawn gets some much-needed love from its developers.
Trudging through the sandy soil on the first (and only) planet (moon, technically) gives you a sense of awe and possibility that I haven't felt since the first time that I booted up Subnautica (which, spoiler alert, is a WAYYYY better game at the moment). Floating boulders, gargantuan skeletal remains, a surprisingly well written score, and competent visuals give the sense that anything is possible. The sad truth is that O:ND is that practically nothing is possible.
At first, I chalked the aforementioned trudging up to the fact that hey - it's the beginning of a survival game, it's meant to be a bit painful, right? Trudge over here, wack this boulder, trudge over there, wack that boulder. It's all meant to build a sense of accomplishment once you manage to cobble together your first shelter, weapon, vehicle, etc. The problem is that the primary gameplay mechanic of O:ND is, in fact, trudging.
Resources are so thinly sprinkled on the vast landscape that if you choose not to use a wiki like me, you could be wandering around in circles for significant stretches of time without doing much of note. Before long I found myself wishing this game had an auto-run button so that could finish reading more of my book while I haphazardly jetpacked from one resource node to another.
All of this plodding is exacerbated by the fact that Fenix Fire provides the player with almost no tools to help navigate the considerably sized landscape. There's a pretty basic map tool (which "maps" nothing but basic topography and X,Y coordinates - you can forget about any resource bookmarking or pathfinding here), a beacon that doesn't appear on your HUD or the map, and a FLAG. That's right. An actual FLAG. As in, useful for finding where you're supposed hit that tiny white dimpled ball, but not terribly useful for marking resources hidden behind a giant space worm skeleton. Top that off with the fact that even with all that dust and sand around you don't leave any footprints, and it's easy to forget exactly which nearly-identical crater you left that oh-so-important unobtanium in.
If the lack of navigational aids wasn't bad enough, until you build you first hoverbike (which took me about 5 hours) there is absolutely ZERO upgrade to traversal speed. No ultralight boots, no upgraded jetpack, no super fuel, NADA. I would have given an arm and a leg for a space-unicorn to flog to death if it meant a 10% speed increase.
All that wandering about might be forgivable if the crafting tree weren't so poorly designed. Unclear and occasionally misleading descriptions, missing features, and poorly balanced resource requirements make crafting more of a chore than a reward, and even when you do manage to cobble together some basic structures, you're then tasked with INDIVIDUALLY FILLING IN EACH BLINDINGLY GENERIC WALL. So out you go, back into the not so dangerous desert-y landscape to do a bit more alien grocery shopping.
I use the term "grocery shopping" because there is hardly any drama while you're out collecting resources. Most of the limited alien species that inhabit our extraterrestrial Food Lion are only "hostile" if you get close enough, and even then they just poke at you with whatever gangly appendage they happen to possess. In spite of their visual diversity, each alien is essentially the same unit with a different skin and more or less hit points. Combat feels more like trying to end a conversation with your overly-chatty neighbor than fighting for your survival on an alien planet.
That is, of course, aside from the baddies who come out at night. The first night cycle in this game was one of the only truly outstanding moments for me. I was wandering through the abandoned ruins of another settlement (nothing to be found there but sand-blasted, half built structures, and empty hopes I'm sad to say) when I was attacked by some vaguely Ridley Scott esque alien dudes, and was left scrambling after I ran out of auto-rifle clips. It was pretty terrifying right up until I discovered that in spite of their considerable agility, they couldn't figure out how to get up onto the roof of the structure I was on. So I left the game running, read some Kotaku articles and drank a beer, while half-heartedly pew-pewing them to death with my pistol until the sun rose. Ho hum.
Fast forward a couple repetitive hours spent hacking together a few different crafting tables and structures, and you're ready to build your first hoverbike; which is both great (because you can skim along the surface of the planet quite effortlessly, shoving masses of resources into your luggage) and terrible (because you realize just how thin the developers have spread the content by limiting storage and flinging resources across the landscape). Shortly thereafter, you can put together a similarly awesome spaceship, and fly into similarly empty space.
Hope - as they say - is a fickle ♥♥♥♥♥.
Add to all of this the fact that multiplayer doesn't have a great reputation on the review boards (I didn't bother with it), and what you've got is a strong promise (premise?) but little follow-through.
My advice? Keep your hard earned cash, or go check out Subnautica. This rock ain't worth your time....yet.

I also fixed the spelling on Ridley Scott's name - sorry about that, buddy.
Additionally, since this title looks like it might get updates fairly regularly, I'll try to check in every few weeks to make sure this stays current, and honest to the current state of the game.]

This is both a fun and frustrating game, with lots of potential. I'll let you read the other positive reviews as to why this is a fun game and get down to the frustration and why I am ultimately posting a negative review:
Major game mechanics are broken. And I'm writing this review nearly a year after the game has been released, and gone through multiple paid dlc cycles. And many of the mechanics I mention below have been broken since release:
-Land-based aircraft only attack once in naval battles regardless of how many days the battle goes on for; they're supposed to attack 2-2.5 times per 24 hours. This warps all naval gameplay, and this has been bugged since the last 6 months, perhaps since release.
-Huge naval Invasions are ahistorically easy to pull off, as you don't need to build landingcraft, nor do you need naval or air presence except for 1 hour at the beginning (even for an invasion that takes weeks to complete), and the invading transports are very difficult to stop via planes or navy at sea, and are similarly difficult to destroy even when intercepted. This completely warps gameplay for majors, especially Italy, Japan, and Britain. This results in fun stuff like Germany getting navally invaded by England during the invasion of Poland despite complete Germany air superiority. Broken since release.
-AI Front battleplanning has been hit or miss since release, as well as AI war declarations. But at least in this area, there's evidence they're trying.
-AI building prioritization, given the recent changes to make building units very resource shortage sensitivity, German AI basically almost always loses by 1941.
There are others, but these are the ones off the top of my head. There's really no excuse for this sort of stuff 1 year after release. Thumbs down.

Paradox is of course infamous for putting out ludicrous amounts of DLC for every single one of their games, but I've always felt that most of their games, in particular EU4 and Stellaris, are all complete games of their own and can be enjoyed without requiring the DLCs. However, HoI4 is the first time I've played one of their games and felt that it was lacking something to make it 'complete'.
As it is, the game boils down to simply drawing lines on the map and push a button to tell your generals to advance, the AI of which feel both unbearably dumb yet completely necessary if only for the sheer number of forces and fronts you have to wage war on. Perhaps people who really enjoy micromanagement can get more enjoyment out of this game, but for me it just felt kinda dull.
I've heard that the multiplayer is way more interesting than single player games, and I can certainly see how that can be. While the game covers land, sea, and air, and in single players it's hard to get keep up with research on all 3 and even harder to have an industry to keep all 3 up to date. Perhaps in multiplayer, where each player is free to specialize in their own areas, it might get more interesting, but sadly I've only gotten to experience this game in single player mode for now.
tl:dr, this game is decnet, but definitely not worth the full price in my personal opinion.

Great game, highly recommended for Portal fans.

TL;DR: If you liked the puzzles in Portal and/or Talos Principle, you'll probably like the puzzles here.
--
I'll be saying nothing new to note that this game is essentially Portal and Talos rolled together. It takes the "gun" mechanic and indoor environments from portal and the philosophy and energy mechanics from Talos. However, it didn't have any of the personality of Portal or quite live up to the rigor or Talos.
In fact, it took something I didn't like from Talos: weak philosophical writing. Without getting into spoilers, the game takes place on one of Jupiter's moons where a small team of highly select scientists are sent to look for life. Unfortunately, the space agency didn't perform any psychological screening or training and, despite at least two of the scientists being labeled "exobiologists", didn't ask if the crew had a really narrow, closed-minded view of what life is. This is the same problem I had with the remake of Battlestar Galactica. The writers manufactured drama by making the characters extremely intractable about how robots can't think. At least the BSG characters had the excuse of imminent extinction. The characters in Turing Test are just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
What the game does right, though, it does very right. The art team is clearly very talented. Models and animations are all great and the engine is put to good use. The sound design and music is also great. The voice actor for TOM (the AI) is superb (if not directed a bit too on-the-nose in some lines). As well, Sarah's VA does a great job conveying genuine emotion throughout.
But again, the game falls prey to problems that stop it from being as good as the games it emulates. The acting is inconsistent between actors, with some being overly quiet or lacking emotional range. Some of the voice logs are mixed such that it becomes very difficult to hear what's said (and not just because that's what the developers intended).
As far as the puzzles themselves, they range from very entertaining to downright lazy. Especially in the last chapter, some of the puzzles become meaninglessly easy, leading me to believe they just needed a few extra to make their progress indicator a perfect square. There are also a few times where I'm pretty sure I beat the puzzle via an exploit in the level's geometry or some other method that the developers didn't anticipate.
Conversely, some of the puzzles are quite clever. I even physically laughed at one of the extra puzzles when I figured out the solution because of how silly and ingenious it was. However, none of the puzzles stumped me. I certainly never felt the kind of pressure or reward as I did playing Talos. I'm certain some people sat down and walked through the game in the span of a couple of hours.
I imagine some of the controls will be either loved or hated by players. For instance, the control panels where you have to hold E and then move the mouse to move an object. It seems like it would have been far better to just have E be a toggle and then use WASD to move the object. I'm not sure how much of that may have been because of controls designed for a controller and backported to KB&M.
--
In the end, it was a worthwhile purchase for $10. For anyone that likes puzzle games, I'd certainly recommend it.
If I had any advice for the developers, it'd be to reevaluate their writing. Games like this either need to not take themselves too seriously (since the mechanics of the game simply can't be justified as realistic), in the same way that Portal and Stanley Parable approached it, or they need to have something meaningful to add to the philosophical debate. Clumsy interactions between unlikable characters and a too-transparent AI founded on artificial tension between basic Humanist and Transhumanist ideas harms an otherwise enjoyable game.

I will break it down into categories with grades:
Graphics: Unreal Engine - 5/10 - Nothing special but in no way bad either.
Gameplay: Puzzle solving - 7/10 - Can be a little repetetive but with amazing side challenges. 6-7 hours depending on skill.
Plot: Man Or Machine? - 8/10 - Very predictable but with great depth in the concept which increases rating.
Soundtrack: Incredible - 10/10 - Think low-key interstallar. Makes the game more than just "other Portal game".
Overall: 7.5 - Strongly recommended.

A Unique, Mediocre MMO.
- Many hours of content (with sufficient replay value)
* Questing is unrewarding and outdated. For the most part, the quests are fairly predictable and typically are shallow in regards to how involved it makes the player feel. (I do admit that some quests are quite the exception to this, and I do wish that the developers would be attentive to the quality of all of their content. I often see that many developers focus on the newest content instead of revisiting the older content to keep it on the same quality level.)
* This game breaks down the level barrier. I personally find that the mentor system is one of the best features of the game. However, the execution could be made more rewarding by implementing item/currency rewards (that scale to your actual level) for those seeking to revisit older content as they level past it. Currently, rewards corresponding to your level is only awarded by Instant Adventures. I would like to see it applied to the other content, such as dungeons and questing.
* Instance Maps are ineffectual at aiding players that are unfamiliar with the instance. It detracts from the experience of group content when even the group leader has to stop and figure out where to go next. It is true that player experience solves this problem, but it is likely to happen to the majority of players atleast once.
- Great concept of character customization, albeit poorly executed.
* Much of the effectiveness of the class is locked within certain builds (likely for balance reasons), and it would be far more useful to the player to have effective hybrid builds instead of hybrid builds that serve only for utility because they cannot perform the role of a tank, healer, dps, or support.
* Wardrobe Update changed customization for the better by ease of use and made collection far easier by removing the storage requirement.
* Character models are beginning to show their age as far superior character models are entering the gaming industry. It also is unhelpful that some of the new designs are money/REX locked.
- Expect slow progress with regards to obtaining more content
* I do not disagree with their shop system as I understand that its a business; however, it seems far to make it a point that if you want to play free then you will have to be very savy with your platinum to get far in the game. (Also I should point out that the newest content is currently obtainable only by gifting [having paid platinum to someone who bought it with cash] if you are set on playing for free.)
After all of this, I still find the game enjoyable. I admit to getting burnt out on it several times (even at 8-12 hrs. a week). The mixture of deficiencies and great concepts make it mediocre as well as unique.

In There Came an Echo, you play the mysterious voice-in-the-ear commander of a growing squad of people caught up in a digital-based conspiracy that affects all their lives (though as far as I can tell, doesn’t really have dire consequences for the rest of the world). You are essentially Morpheus in the first 20 minutes of the Matrix.
So the big question: how is the voice control? The answer: not bad. I only encountered two real problems with it and they were both easily solvable. The first was that I was speaking too fast for the recognition software to pick up anything. I solved this by slowing down my speech and being more clear (no s**t). The reason I was even speaking fast in the first place was because There Came an Echo really puts you under the pump. There’s no pausing to give commands or survey the battlefield. It’s all in real-time. Which means you need to give concise and correct commands there and then, otherwise your squad members die. That being said, there’s still a bit of wriggle room as there’s no one-hit kills or anything like that. There Came an Echo has done really well to balance out combat pacing and excitement alongside a forgivable command system which still has consequences for bad, slow or incomprehensible commands.
That being said, the voice control isn’t perfect. I still have to repeat my orders every now and then and as the game constantly reminds me, shouting into the microphone is not the way to get your orders across. Still doesn’t stop from me from cursing Wheaton’s name when he asks me to repeat myself.
Do I recommend There Came an Echo? Yes, the game is fun, intense and exciting. And by using voice recognition, you feel slightly more immersed in the world and universe. You’re not longer a dude or dudette sitting a computer playing a game. You are a commander of a slightly disfunctional squad and you are in a position of power.

The game is just something... new. Its not the hardest game ever, although it isn't a walkover. And the tactical combat - the game's core - isn't as deep as other games, but if that is the only thing you are looking for then this is not the game for you.
The game is focused on 2 things - the story, and the controls. The easy one first - the story. It is an interesting story with lots of twists and turns, delivered through cutscenes (:/) and what the characters talk about during missions (:D). If you like story, I'd say this game delivers a concise, intersting one.
The main thing about this game? The voice control. For one thing, its much easier than using a keyboard/mouse, although I feel that is deliberate. The voice recognition is generally good, althouh didn't always pick me up. The commands are logical and clear and you can write your own, which is good, although I feel probably works best if you speak US English (my custom ones didn't really work with my UK english).
The voice control feels really cool though. Its combined with a logical, intuitive design - waypoints in good places, easily marked, distinct character names, distinct weapon names, and a good system for understanding you shorthand - for example, you can just say 'Corrin Alpha 4' to tell him to move there, and if you then said 'alpha 5' it would know you are still talking to the selected character.
Queing up orders is also satisfying, allowing you to play out a planned manouver. You can que up multiple strings of orders, so you could give the first order to move people into positing, a second order to assign targets, and a third order you activate when their first targets are down etc.
Overall, the control system does seem to work and do a good job, and realy makes the game special far more than anything else. The combat is solid but not extrodanary, the story is good, but the control system and gameplay it brings is great!

I wasn't sure what to expect with this game.  I didn't put much thought in to it's purchase.  I glanced through the information, saw the name "Wil Wheaton" and my eyesight went a tad blurry.  Don't worry, I'm ok.  Tears of joy.  I had to buy this game.
If you're reading this Mr Wheaton, you are awesome.  If I saw a movie poster "Twilight: Now with Wil Wheaton" I would watch that movie.  If I saw a CD display "Justin Beiber: Wil Wheaton duets" I would buy that CD.  I eagerly await the day I can put a "Wil Wheaton 2024, Lightyears ahead in the Presidential race!" sign in my front yard.  So, yes, I bought this game.
It's a good game too.  Anyone remember the Full Spectrum Warrior games?  The combat reminds me of that.  You move your people around, give them simple commands, watch them shoot the bad guys, etc.  You don't have to tell them to shoot every time you want them to shoot.  You're more in to the big picture.  Setting up flanking, luring them in to ambushes, things like that.
Graphics are decent.  Music is pretty good.  The voice actors are all good as well, real professional.  Gameplay is smooth.  UI (I'm using my mouse) works great. Charming. From art, to voice work, to story; There Came an Echo exudes charm. Without spoiling anything, the story does seem a little odd, starting in the near future before graduating to some deep questions about identity, and self which I wouldn't have expected to find in a game.
Technically speaking, I think there were some things that could've been done better (for instance, a load check point option would've been nice as I found myself throwing my soldiers into walls of soldiers just to rewind quicker). The voice recognition kit's pretty solid, and the decision to limit movement to a preset check point system makes sense in this context, even if it is a little frustrating at times.
Trying to run a tactics game in real time by voice is a challenge, and I found myself having to force a calm state if only to keep my commands clear. It's a great sensation and one that isn't usually found in most games where victory tends to go to those with the quickest reflexes and the most energy to detonate at the right moment.
I think I would've liked this game more if it kept a step away from the metaphysical storyline, but that's not to say this was unwelcome. The pacing of the story is good, and ends early enough to not feel repetitive or dry. In short, recommend it highly, if only for the different experience of tactical squad command with your voice.

Disclosure: I backed this game on Kickstarter.
This review is about the 1.06 version of the game.
There Came an Echo is a game made from independent game developer Iridium Studios.
It is based in a not too distant sci-fi setting and has teambased RTS elements.

The innovation of the game is that the issuing of orders to your team is done with voice control,
meaning you issue the commands using a microphone, the game registers them and the respective units execute  the orders.
It is possible to play the game without using a microphone though i do not suggest it since the voice control is fairly responsive.
Before some patches where issued i had some trouble with the voice control as some commands wouldn't register.
It also wasn't helping that i was mispronouncing some words like recharge, which is pronounced rechárge and not récharge.
However at 1.06 version i had barely any problem since the vast majority of the commands  was registered correctly. One time where i had a consistent problem was selecting the 4th  unit. Thankfully, it is possible to put in the command alias alternate names for the units and commands, so i nicknamed the unit Jack and everything flowed great after that.
Something else to take in mind is that it will be nigh impossible to play the game in a noisy environment since the voice commands will be riddled with noise. Also a standard quality microphone (not the 3 euro ones) will suffice.
Storywise the game has a nice, kind of geeky but not too difficult to understand, compelling story with some interesting ties to the other game Iridium Studios has made, Sequence (renamed to Before the Echo, for legal reasons). It isn't necessary to have played it, since everything is explained, but if you have it's nice.
The voice acting is great, believable characters and dialogue. The music is also great too, made by Ronald Jenkees, someone i had never heard before but got in my radar with his exceptional music, also featured in Sequence (renamed to Before the Echo, for legal reasons).
Voice command for English (US) for a non native speaker with almost no accent (me) is very responsive, provided that you speak in a calm way and with small pauses between commands.
The game features 4 weapons. The primary and always equipped one is the Pistol. The other 3 are unlocked as you play and have different unique abilities. A strategic  element is introduced in combat by the fact that apart form the pistol the other weapons drain your energy to use so you can't just equip the heavy hitter and blitz the game.
The story features 10 missions with a total duration of 4-6 hours.
Unfortunately the main story doesn't have replayability since you have already seen it once.
There is however the War Room, a challenge of 12 waves of enemies to defeat with no healing between waves.
Also unfortunately, there isn't workshop integration with steam so no User Generated Content.
The achievements can be completed 100% though 1 or 2 are tricky to do.
The good thing is that the game has a good price tag at 15 euros.
I recommend buying the game for both the story and the voice control mechanic, which is something very uncommon in video games.
If you have a comfortable living, 15 euros is a great price.
If your economics aren't very good and you are concerned over the short duration of the game then i suggest getting it at a sale further down the line, at 33%, maximum 50%. More than 50% price cut and you would be robbing the developer.
Final verdict: Very good game, worth the money.

In short: a solid game with a novel, well-realized mechanic. On the short side, but worth playing.
The basic appeal is undoubtedly the voice controls - I'd say not to bother if you're going to use more traditional control schemes. In my experience they were 100% responsive and intuitive once you understand how they work. They do a great job of making you a part of the universe; you play as a character sitting behind a screen shouting orders at the characters. If you have any interest at all in alternative control schemes and new approaches to interactivity, There Came an Echo is a must have.
The story is a bit on the convoluted side, but it's engaging with some well-defined and likable characters, who are definitely the best part of the narrative. Great designs, too - in fact, the artstyle in general is really appealing while remaining functional. The length of cutscenes is probably my biggest criticism, but considering the gameplay, there's no real alternative. Mixed feelings, but the game itself is paced well enough that I don't mind the story's issues.
Overall, it feels fresh, and the new technology being utilized more than makes up for its non-gameplay issues. Again, it's short (about 4 hours of story with a bit more in additional missions), but there's no filler at all. Quality over quantity - but you might want to pick it up on sale.

Personally I absolutely love this game, I can play it with a friend or two for hours on end. This game has provided me with over 600 hours of fun. I have a couple of issues with this game, but I'll go through those later in this review.
Hearts of Iron 4 is a grand strategy game that takes place before and during the second world war and it lets you play as any country in that time period. The game in my opinion has a rather steep learning curve where players new to hearts of iron or paradox games as a whole are completely clueless and are provided with a massive amount things they need to and can do. I know there is a tutorial, but it is indeed a bit lacking. The tutorial covers only the very basics of the game and needs to cover more such as how to stage naval invasions along with the rest of the options in teh battle plans, justifying and declaring and the other country options, a little more on the advisors and government screen, more on naval warfare and overall just more regarding warfare. I've played with many friend from when they bought the game to when they have become experienced players and I've seen the steep learning curve first hand. All though once you get past that part of learning hearts of iron you'll excell in the game and liked it a lot more. So I advise any new players to watch a couple of youtube videos on hearts of iron or ask a experienced friend to teach you a little. There are a couple of problems with this game that aren't related to learning the game such as the AI, which has become a meme in the hearts of iron community for being so bad. The AI is diplomatically ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, if you're not playing on historical mode in the base game without any mods this won't happen because everything is pre-planned. Now if you're not playing the historical mode where every action taken by the AI has been pre-planned the AI will join factions for no reason (the faction can be in a war that it is losing and will provide the country joining with nothing of use and the AI will still choose to join.) AIs will also sometimes contradict their choices such as Germany doing the support China focus and then giving Japan volunteers. The AI can also not reason in simple situations such as what divisions to send as volunteers, if the Soviet Union who isn't in a war (ofcourse since you can't send volunteers if you're at war) and has tank divisions that are far better than it's infantry and are fully equipped and ready for deployment they'll send a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ infantry division to do almost nothing in a foreign war. There are many situations like this where the AI will be completely mentally disabled (a lot of the time regarding how they handle their troops and battle plans. The AI is mostly biggest issue I have with this game to be honest, but with that in mind this game is still a very fun, complex, well made and interesting game.

In a year of fantastic releases and multiple Game of the Year candidates, it's a shame to see OneShot get buried in the mix.  Whether it's due to a late December release putting it at the fringes of the years,
or due to it being overshadowed by other gaming experiences, this game provides that ~10 hour experience that sticks with you.
A puzzle adventure game in the style mirroring an RPG-Maker game, you control a "cat" named Niko on a quest to save a world unknown.  As you travel, you learn things about Niko, the world,
.  To write a review on a game like this is hard because, in the veins of other games like Undertale or Pony Island, a blind experience is so much better, but to say this game gripped me within the first 5 minutes is no exaggeration.  The story itself seems simplistic, but the characters are a joy to interact with and the atmosphere and music bring forth a sense of worry and wonder.  I found myself more attached to Niko than I did with Frisk from Undertale, which makes certain decisions that may seem easy that much harder.  Some of the mechanics are also incredible, but that's also heading into a sticky spoiler territory.
As stated earlier, OneShot is a short game, and you can see most everything in about 10 hours
.  This shouldn't deter you from trying it out as it makes the most of its short playtime.  The puzzles range from point-and-click style tasks to find and combine items to interacting with elements of the environment and aren't too difficult. It's hard to go on on a game while keeping the surprises hidden, but this is truly a fantastic buried gem of a game and one of my favorites of the year, whichever one you prefer.

This game brings atmosphere, feelings and a good sense of exploration, all the while it also manages to bring unique puzzle solving elements to the table. It's absolutely fantastic, and I believe it's best enjoyed by going into it knowing as little as possible about it.

Some of the puzzles are not intuitive so this game will be frustrating if you're not comfortable with hours of guess-and-check.  The humor isn't bad but nothing great.  Also, I highly recommend a controlled as I was experiencing over a second of input lag with keyboard.

At first glance, this is a cute game with quirky characters and fun puzzles. They're varying in challenge, but usually intuitive, even if the tutorial is easy to click through (which leaves you not realizing you're supposed to use the character's powers if you're me). The light humor isn't gut wrenchingly hilarious or anything, but it's suited to the mood. The character design is cliche but on purpose, which makes the game better in my opinion. Each of them was fascinating, and in many cases lovable, even as you learn what they have done.
When examined more closely, you discover how deeply flawed the characters are. Viewed through this lens, the game us an excellent lens into the concepts of redemption or condemnation. The number of characters lends this game a ton of replay value, as well, though the parts that remain the same regardless of party choice get to be a little old after a while.
It would have been interesting if the "good" ends had required a bit more to be different from the "bad" ends, but as it was this is a fun game with a solid story and very shiny art! (The voice of the cave is also wonderful)

A puzzle platformer where you chose 3 characters from a roster of 7 and go on an adventure in a talking cave, finding out that each character is not so secretly evil (or maybe not).
For a puzzle platformer, the puzzles are insanely easy. This comes from self-contained level based gameplay combined with the "feature" where each character may only hold one item at a time. As a result, no puzzle requires multiple inventory actions.
The puzzles are also fairly obvious:
1. You need to cheat a "guess your weight" game. You have a barbell and a magician that can turn items invisible to help you.
2. You need to use an elevator, but the fuse is missing, luckily there's a fusebox with a fuse on the other side of the map that doesn't do anything.
Insultingly, puzzles are padded to increase game length. One section requires two characters to stand on different colored pressure plates while the third navigates a maze. Rather than just doing it once or twice to demonstrate that you understand the mechanics, you have to do it half a dozen times. The worst is a four story mansion themed level where you must constantly run up and down the stairs, padding the game further.
Even worse, puzzles have similar solutions. This one is especially heinous. There are 13 levels in the game. 7 of the 13 are character specific while the others are generalized. Of those 6 general levels 2 of them have no puzzles. On top of that, the last 2 generalized levels have the exact same solution which involves tricking an NPC with a tape recorder. This is inexcusable and really shows they were running out of ideas.
Speaking of levels design, when you enter character specific levels, your other two members become dead weight except for occassionally weighing down platforms. In the mansion themed level, your other two party members can't be used at all. To make matters worse, there's a mine themed level where you need to slowly navigate 3 levels of a labyrinth-like mazes. The catch is that every time you complete the puzzle on one of these levels, you need to individually walk each of the 3 members up to the next level and insert them in the puzzle. Its frustrating, time consuming, and only serves to pad the game to a barely acceptable run time.
Luckily, the environment and style are pretty good and 2 of the NPCs are even charming.
Finally, the game has no replay value, despite requiring a minimum of 5 replays to get all 14 endings. The insultingly easy puzzles are a cake-walk once you know the solution. The only reason to play the game more than once is for achievements. Nobody cares about character endings. They're all incredibly obvious and the characters have no personality. The Cave has no replay value, but demands many replays. To make matters worse, because there are 7 characters, but your roster only has 3 characters at a time, your third playthrough will only have a single new level.
For all of these reasons, I cannot recommend The Cave, even though there were parts that I liked.

Painkiller franchise is a great shooter to experience.

While looking prettier than the original and keeping that which it remade (mostly) intact, this "HD reimagining" or whatever it may be called feels quite lacklustre.
All the weapons are there, but they just dont quite have that kick or oomph that the original managed. Youll occasionally be able to fling an axe monk across the map with a shotgun blast or turn a clown to mincemeat with the painkiller, but it almost feels scripted rather than being an innate part of the physics of the game.
In addition, the difficulty feels like it just gave up.  Past the initial rushing enslaught of enemies, their actual threat has been quite drastically toned down. Bosses in particular are guilty of this, though perhaps for the better in certain cases, they feel very little of a threat - more a chore that must be rushed through or painfully waited out when forced to.
The levels themselves are also different: a number directly torn out and (only some) replaced by what only play like bad knockoffs. No more bomb and bullet infested Alcatraz and no more cramped, ghost-riddled mansion to fight through.
Is this all a testament to the original or something of incompetence from this new developer? Probably both: the best things are that which remained untouched. Bit of a shame, really. If you havent already, just get Painkiller Black Edition and stick with it. A few prettier pixels (with shoddy performance, mind you) and some unecessarily shoe-horned cutscenes should not sway you any.

Ah, yes. The 'sci-fi 3D puzzler with a narrator' genre.
If you've not played Portal or The Talos Principle (how did you get here?), I'd suggest you pick up one of those instead.
If you have, well, you won't find all that much originality here, but everything is competent enough.
The story is your usual philosophical sci-fi fare, with an interesting enough premise and some cool moments but a few flaws in execution (writing that sometimes feels weak, some questionable voice acting, etc).
The puzzles are fun enough. New mechanics are constantly introduced, which keeps things fresh. I liked that the puzzle rooms mostly never get too big and complicated. This does mean the difficulty never gets all that high, so if you're after that feeling of inadequacy you get when you start having to tab out and scour youtube for poorly edited video solutions you might be disappointed.
I completed the storyline in - apparently - 5.4 hours. That might have been a little disappointing if I hadn't picked it up on sale.
All in all, a cautious recommendation.

From start to finish, the atmosphere is strong, thanks to a very fitting marriage of art style and music. The novel voice-controlled gameplay is surprising—not only in how well it works, but in how the act of speaking directly to characters helps bring them alive just a little bit more, in your mind.
It was a shame for me, though, that those characters didn't come across very well. The disembodied voice of Val was the most likeable by far, Farrick was interesting, and Miranda was a memorable hothead, yet I found the rest (through, I think, no fault of their performance) to be either basically unlikeable (see Grace and Corrin) or simply leaving not much impression at all (see Syll and Adam). I don't really know what to blame for this, though. Maybe it's too large a cast for such a short story, spreading each character's "screen time" too thin? I find it hard to say.
I see a fair amount of reviews mentioning the voice recognition not working out for them, but I can say that it seemed flawless for me, and seemed wonderfully flexible when it comes to dealing with natural changes in speech patterns, stutters and last minute corrections and all those sorts of things that I'm used to seeing other speech recognition platforms get tangled up in. I thought it was impressive.
While quite a short game with a story that's anything but novel, I think it's reasonable for its price, and most of all, an inspiring demonstration of one kind of control scheme that I think will be a prominent part of the near future in video games. One that would seem to pair quite well with the imminent eruption of VR.

There Came an Echo has a lot of things going for it.  Great voice acting, interesting tactical combat and an enervative voice based control scheme.  It’s the last part that has issues, at least for me.
You control your characters using your voice but like dictation software it works 90% of the time. It’s that 10% of the time where the frustration comes in.  To make matters worse there are times when your timing has to be perfect and at those critical points I find myself repeating commands only to fail the objective when the system does not understand what I’m saying.  Now it might be my accent or cadence but I use other voice control software (Voice Attack) with other games and I have had less issues.
I kept thinking though the whole thing that I wanted a controller to move and have the voice for all the secondary functions.  Instead of feeling like an empowered squad leader I felt like Scotty in Star Trek IV talking into the mouse. Computer! Computer? Computer! Just use the keyboard…
I really liked the concept of the game that so I kick stared when I first read about. That said the final implementation has left me cold. All it did for me was make me want to load up Xcom and get it working with Voice Attack.

There are a few glaring issues with "There Came An Echo".
First and foremost the voice recognition is *very* hit or miss; I couldn't even control Syll until I made him "Sam" because apparently saying "sill" in a non-regional American accent is unintelligible. There were times I would tell Syll to do something and Miranda (or "My" as I named her) would swap weapons or run to hard points.
Secondly, the in-game cutscenes aren't just unskippable, they take the camera hostage and throw you into the action without notice. This would be fine if it were simply added for dramatic effect, but your team is taking damage and it doesn't zoom back out or tell you that you're *actually* in a battle. Even ignoring the game's bland art assets and scene settings this was poor design.
Thirdly, the story and voices are duller than a Playdoh spoon. I'm not saying the script writers and voice actors *literally* phoned it in, but they sure as♥♥♥♥♥♥did metaphorically speaking. The only characters that have any actual "character" are Val and Miranda, but even then it's glaringly obvious there was direction or inspiration given to their respective voice actors.
Lastly, while I was playing the game in English I came to a point where a countdown might compromise the mission unless I said "Anular". After saying a combination of "anular/Grace go to anular/team anular" etc. a few dozen times I figured I must be pronouncing it incorrectly. No, it turns out "anular" is the game's Spanish equivalent of "Activate Override". Is it a nitpicky point? Yup. Was it also an incredibly irritating and stupid oversight? You betcha.
I'd love to see more voice-controlled games in the future, but this simply falls short in every regard apart from the novelty are attempting it.

I enjoyed the game but rated NOT RECOMMENDED. Why?
================================================
It's actually NOT RECOMMENDED
================================================
And - I do know it's an early access.
This game might be a killer when finished. Now, it's like 10% of what I've expected really.
You start off as a survivor from a crash landing. You have to make your way through a desert planet to mine minerals, build base and everything needed for survival killing hordes of alien animals and huge bugs on the way. Beginning is well done, tutorials are not bad. And, you can do that alone, with friends or on a public server.
Why it is only 10%?
Cause most of the things you build doesn't work. It feels like a presentation how this game could look like when finished. You can build a bio dome, plant green there but it's just a placeholder really, you don't have to have anything to plant there and it gives you nothing back.
You can build a spaceship to fly off planet but there's nothing there, just a bunch of asteroids (broken) and a placeholder for a space station.
You can build a computer for blueprints but... It's just a decoration for now on.
You can build sniper rifle ammo but... Not a sniper rifle. Or, I wasn't able at least.
So, my guess, wait. Wait for the content, because the gameplay is enjoyable, the graphics and sound is amazing, the feel is really nicely done.
Now, onto the multiplayer. There are like 16 players per map if I remember right. But, so it happens that the public server run out of structural limit
fast.
What does this mean, it means, that when you build a dome it does -1 to the structural limit on the server. And it's like a 50? 100? I don't know. So, I've built a habitat, an airlock and... I'm done. Can't build more.
But, there's a solution. You can start your own private server and invite friends from steam. And this little feature is a GOLD. Very good system to get 5 friends to play with you. You go on publick, you gather 5 people who listen and are not raging kids and you start a private server. You can enjoy the game there, but...
Um...
There's not much to enjoy really. I've hit the end game in like 6 hours on my private server with a friend. We got everything we could, all the vechicles. And, well, we flew to the space, looked around...
Landed and...
Meh...
What now?
Won't play the game till some major update comes round.
Pros:
- great graphics and sound,
- nice gameplay,
- got just the right atmosphere,
- the feel of danger, survival, it's all there, incredibly well done,
- private server for mutliplayer
- friendlist invites,
- it's fun.
Cons:
- not enough even for an early acces,
- some stuff is just too easy to achieve, it's not balanced,
- well, there's not much of a game in the game yet. I know, I'm repeating myself but, really, there's just so little of it.
- lotta bugs, but that's an early acces,
- after some time it feels more like a demo, a presentation, not actual game.

Cry of Fear was probably one of the most devilish experience I came across. A devasted town, a suicidal lone hero trying his best to escape the place and reach his mom home, and gruesome enemies reflecting aspects of depression.
The story by itself is not particulary deep for most of the gameplay (once again, this is a game that hold it's explication till the very end) , but every aspects show how messed up things turned out and many elements could really affect your mood while playing.
The shooting gameplay was well made. In term of pure gameplay, this is a little bit like playing L4D2 with CS 1.6 motor engine,  and with bullet restrictions. And it works.
I really wish the multiplayer was being played at by more people though, because I unfortunately never got the chance to play with anyone yet, and this seems pretty hard to play alone. On that aspect, it's a pity the game don't include support AI like in L4D2.

In a year of fantastic releases and multiple Game of the Year candidates, it's a shame to see OneShot get buried in the mix.  Whether it's due to a late December release putting it at the fringes of the years,
or due to it being overshadowed by other gaming experiences, this game provides that ~10 hour experience that sticks with you.
A puzzle adventure game in the style mirroring an RPG-Maker game, you control a "cat" named Niko on a quest to save a world unknown.  As you travel, you learn things about Niko, the world,
.  To write a review on a game like this is hard because, in the veins of other games like Undertale or Pony Island, a blind experience is so much better, but to say this game gripped me within the first 5 minutes is no exaggeration.  The story itself seems simplistic, but the characters are a joy to interact with and the atmosphere and music bring forth a sense of worry and wonder.  I found myself more attached to Niko than I did with Frisk from Undertale, which makes certain decisions that may seem easy that much harder.  Some of the mechanics are also incredible, but that's also heading into a sticky spoiler territory.
As stated earlier, OneShot is a short game, and you can see most everything in about 10 hours
.  This shouldn't deter you from trying it out as it makes the most of its short playtime.  The puzzles range from point-and-click style tasks to find and combine items to interacting with elements of the environment and aren't too difficult. It's hard to go on on a game while keeping the surprises hidden, but this is truly a fantastic buried gem of a game and one of my favorites of the year, whichever one you prefer.

Remember Doom? Quake? Wolfenstein 3D?
Remember when FPSes were about shooting stuff and collecting all the goodies you could grab from the stuff you shot?
Remember when you died 27 times trying to beat a level on Doom in the hardest difficulty, and all you were rewarded with when you finally made it through was a notice that you took way longer than the developers did? If you don't, then please stop reading here. Painkiller Hell & Damnation is about restoring the glorious golden days of FPS and it does it with finesse.
In Painkiller Hell & Damnation, you play as the illegitimate child of Bruce Campbell and The Doom Guy, and you really hate Evil, Undead (hah) creatures. And if you're waiting to hear about the story, forget it, because we're not going to bother with that.
Basically, you run around semi-linear levels which take place in creepy, gothic locales such as cemetaries and demonic cathedrals, blowing the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of witches, ghouls, and skeletons wearing medieval plate armour because oldschool. Do not try and reconcile this game's concept with any sort of logic or rationality. If you have ever thought, at some point in the past several years, that FPS has totally abandoned its roots and now takes itself way too seriously as a genre, you are going to play this game thoroughly and with as much love and respect as I am now. If you haven't ever thought that, then please return to Call of Duty and don't ever ever play this game because it was not meant for you.

Несмотря на заявленный римейк, игра является сюжетным продолжением, но с похождением по всем уровням оригинала (Black box), где ГГ - Дэниелу предстоит победить на сей раз Смерть и официально встретиться, блждь, с самим Белиалом. Игра начинается сразу после "освобождения" Евы, при этом разработчики учитывают каноничными только Black box и мой любимый Overdose, отбрасывая весь сор, который был выпущен фанатами и выдан даже в продажу, впрочем уровень в Искуплении со сражением с обезображенной и демонической Евой в Соборе с ордами демонами можно только взять за канон т.к. в "Аде и Проклятии" разъяснений не будет и мы возвращаемся в самое начаоло - на кладбище.
К сожалению отличную франшизу на удивление никто на данный момент не развивает, планировался Пейнкиллер 2, но судьба его на данный момент такова:
Чешская студия Mindware должна были делать полноценный сиквел к игре: после Cold War и Overdose майндваровцы были на хорошем счету у правообладателей франшизы (тогда еще Dreamcatcher) и им уже в 2007-м хотели поручить разработку сиквела. Под всё это дело хотели выделить весьма большие деньги, и в Майндваре сильно воспряли духом и надеялись, что в Чехии наконец-то появится свой настоящий ААА-блокбастер, и локальная индустрия вылезет из задницы.
Painkiller 2 вступил в стадию препродакшена. Сюжет должен был основываться на "Божественной Комедии" Данте Алигьери — протагонисты двух предыдущих частей, Дэниель и Белиал, спускаются по девяти кругам Ада, где в конце концов должны сразиться с Сатаной. К слову, местную "Беатриче" должен был заменить никто иной, как Иуда (продавший Христа за 30 сребреников, если кто не знает). Ну или по крайней мере так планировалось.
НО разработчиков ждал полный облом... Dreamcatcher, переживавшая и без того неважные времена, была с потрохами куплена JoWood. Финансирование проекта остановили. Начались кадровые перестановки в издательстве и в самой студии разработки. Проще говоря, Майндваров кинули на бабки; Джовуд решили, что нет смысла тратить деньги и легче повторить схему Овердоза — то бишь заказать "сиквел" группе фанатов, которые с радостью будут работать за 15 монгольских тугриков и еду. Что было дальше — история уже известная: появился Резурекшон, а Майндвары, несолоно хлебавши, решили собрать хоть что-то из уже имевшихся на тот момент ресурсов и сделать малобюджетный Dreamkiller, который вообще ни о чём и не связан с ПК... Так и завершилась судьба Painkiller 2.
