First of all I WOULD NOT RECOMMEND THIS GAME TO MOST NON-NATIVE SPEAKERS. I`ve spoken english since I was little and even lived in the US for a while but I often had to restart a mission because my commands weren`t being recognised.
Now for the review:
There Came an Echo`s excellent voice commands are a dream come true to a lot of gamers! For them alone the game is worth buying. Fortunately, however, even if you`re not all that interested in voice commands, the game still doesn`t disappoint. Here`s a general idea of what I thought about the different parts of the game.
Lenght: this is the first topic, since I think it will be the deciding factor for a lot of people when considering whether to pick it up right now or wait for it to go on sale. The game is short. The 4ish hours it takes to complete the campaign are very good, and the game does have a proper ending and a good pacing, but the lack of a "horde" mode, or a mission editor hurts the replayability and therefore the value of the game. And that`s sad, because I would probably spend hours playing those modes if they were there, I just really liked the gameplay.
Mission design: Over the course of the campaign the game throws various scenarios at you and each one approaches the mechanics in a different way. The developers got really creative with the ways they could explore the game`s systems and mechanics. The game never gets repetitive. And I think this is one of the things that sets this game apart from other tactical shooters in a good way.
Story: The story is good and unique. Nice refresher from the usual generic plotlines. However it feels very rushed, most plot points go by extremely fast with barely any time for them to sink in. And it hurts the game because it has some pretty intense plot twists. You`ll often find yourself wondering how in the world did you get to where you are right now. Character development is also pretty weak sometimes. Most characters are gone so fast after you`ve met them that you can`t find yourself caring for them. The characters themselves are good though, and if they had more time to be fleshed out they might`ve turned out to be some people`s favorite video game characters. What I`m trying to say is you can see a glimpse of their potential every now and then.
Voice acting: I don`t usually have a problem with voice acting, this game is no exception.
Music and Sound design: The music is awesome, one of the best soundtracks I`ve heard in a game recently. The sounds are great too, very immersive.
Art and graphics: Although the graphics aren`t ultra realistic or anything they`re fine, models look better than in Wasteland 2, for example. The art though is really nice, I loved almost every level, and the UI is very nice to look at too. Definitely a pro!!!!
Combat: the voice commands make the game`s combat stand out. Otherwise it would be a passable tactical shooter. There are enough weapon options, but the fact that better weapons drain the same resource as your hp, and the way enemy waves approach you left me using no more than 3 weapon types for the duration of the campaign.
Level Design: the level design usually changes with the mission design, but cover and enemy placement does manage to get repetitive by the end. Also, one of my biggest gripes with the games is that, specially at the later levels, there are cover points that can`t be used by more than one or 2 party member, and I found myself more than once in a situaltion where I was left with only or two character who were able to take cover and other times, I had the problem where characters couldnt shoot from cover. For a game where your movement is limited to what cover points you`re allowed to send your party members this is a big issue.
Bugs: Overall I didn`t find many bugs, I recall having to reset a checkpoint a couple of times because a character didn`t transition into the next area, and that`s about it. Never a crash to desktop or anything. And the devs have been really fast and good at delivering patches!!!!
In the end, There Came an Echo is a very nice game that delivers 100% on its promise. However, the minor technical issues and the short story might mean an on sale purchase for some people. To me, however, the small team of devs have done, and keep doing, such a good job that I feel compelled to buy it at full price just to support their studio!
I`m really looking forward to a sequel, expansion, new game mode and/or map editor open to the community, like in Shadowrun. Hopefully the devs fell the same.

Personally I absolutely love this game, I can play it with a friend or two for hours on end. This game has provided me with over 600 hours of fun. I have a couple of issues with this game, but I'll go through those later in this review.
Hearts of Iron 4 is a grand strategy game that takes place before and during the second world war and it lets you play as any country in that time period. The game in my opinion has a rather steep learning curve where players new to hearts of iron or paradox games as a whole are completely clueless and are provided with a massive amount things they need to and can do. I know there is a tutorial, but it is indeed a bit lacking. The tutorial covers only the very basics of the game and needs to cover more such as how to stage naval invasions along with the rest of the options in teh battle plans, justifying and declaring and the other country options, a little more on the advisors and government screen, more on naval warfare and overall just more regarding warfare. I've played with many friend from when they bought the game to when they have become experienced players and I've seen the steep learning curve first hand. All though once you get past that part of learning hearts of iron you'll excell in the game and liked it a lot more. So I advise any new players to watch a couple of youtube videos on hearts of iron or ask a experienced friend to teach you a little. There are a couple of problems with this game that aren't related to learning the game such as the AI, which has become a meme in the hearts of iron community for being so bad. The AI is diplomatically ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, if you're not playing on historical mode in the base game without any mods this won't happen because everything is pre-planned. Now if you're not playing the historical mode where every action taken by the AI has been pre-planned the AI will join factions for no reason (the faction can be in a war that it is losing and will provide the country joining with nothing of use and the AI will still choose to join.) AIs will also sometimes contradict their choices such as Germany doing the support China focus and then giving Japan volunteers. The AI can also not reason in simple situations such as what divisions to send as volunteers, if the Soviet Union who isn't in a war (ofcourse since you can't send volunteers if you're at war) and has tank divisions that are far better than it's infantry and are fully equipped and ready for deployment they'll send a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ infantry division to do almost nothing in a foreign war. There are many situations like this where the AI will be completely mentally disabled (a lot of the time regarding how they handle their troops and battle plans. The AI is mostly biggest issue I have with this game to be honest, but with that in mind this game is still a very fun, complex, well made and interesting game.

It's basically "Ark: Survival Evolved" in space, but even in the state its in it's leagues better than Ark.
It has it's issues, but nothing that's unexpected from a game that's EA. My biggest issue is getting timed out in the middle of my game which can be a setback if I'm half-way across the planet gathering resources, or worse 300km away from the starter planet trying to reach a new planet.
Other than that you have your standard glitchy enimies, falling through the enviroment, occasional movement bugs.
The pro's far outweigh the con's if you ask me.
You have an actual intro that helps you establish your little base, weapons to help even the odds from hostile npcs or bandit players, and you don't lose 100% of your gear when you die unlike other survival games I've played.
So far the Dev's have been my favourite aspect of the game; they're constantly scrolling the forums and bug reports looking for ways to fix the game and improve it, you know, actually DEVELOPING the game.
I'm super stoked to follow this game through to full release, I'm hoping the dev's keep up the constant updates and listening to the community! Recommend this game 100% to every survival/base builder fan

The Cave is a light-hearted platformer with a lot of dark humor and isn’t nearly as deep as my title suggests. You start off with a choice of seven characters and you have to choose 3 to go spelunking the depths of The Cave. By the way it’s a talking cave. The only other voice being the salesman of The Cave’s gift shop.
You start off mildly enough, just a small quest for the gift shop. Grab three trinkets and return. Here you get a small taste of the quests The Cave has to offer. There aren’t any enemies in the cave but everything can kill you. Fall from too high you die, stay underwater too long you die, get blown up, etc. However, the game is very forgiving in that it automatically respawns your character close to where you were before you died.
When you finally descend the depths the experience is tailored to the characters you chose upon starting. The Cave says that it explores the depths of each of the character’s hearts to find out what they desire most. What that entails is minor explorations of a major event of each chosen character’s lives. There are also paintings highlighting all the character stories you will encounter during your playthrough.
It will take a number of plays to get through every character’s story and since each character has a different ability how you approach a puzzle will differ slightly according to your party. For example, the Time Traveler’s ability to phase through walls is incredibly helpful in skipping a couple of puzzles but if you don’t have her in your party you might have to think of another way to get the item you need. Each ability will have some use during your journey so you’ll never feel like you’re relying on one character or the others aren’t pulling their weight.
As for graphics and settings the Cave’s environments are quite diverse. One section you can be on a deserted island or a carnival to a top secret Bond like nuclear missile facility. Every time you reach a new depth you get a different setting. The puzzles are terribly difficult and the narrator and other inhabitants provide small hints in speeches.  The game took me about 4 hours to get through the first time. And since there are 3 standard quests that occur regardless of your party you can use the same approach for the non-character specific parts. You can even carry certain objects into other areas allowing for you to completely skip one section.
There are 2 endings per character so it will take about 5 plays to get the complete story but it was fun each time although changing up the characters didn’t affect how I approached the puzzles drastically different. Overall it was a cool, quirky enjoyable experience. It wasn’t as deep as I thought it’d be but also not so shallow that I felt unfulfilled.

Unfortunately, this game has very little replay value.  Each character gets their own unique level, however all of the transitions are identical to one another.  After your first play through, the mandatory tutorial becomes tedious.  Until you reach a new character's dedicated level, the transitions become a grind.
I very much hoped for a Spelunky-like procedural level generation at least in the transitions between each character's static rooms, but I was let down.  Much of this game is static and repetitive, though it is certainly very good looking.  I wish the developers would have put more resources into making the game playable more than once rather than making it shiny.
Wait for a sale, I wouldn't recommend paying more than $5 for this game.

What I though I was buying: An easy shooter game with a 1930's style
What I actually bought: An AMAZING and difficult adventure, involving patience, skill, and quick thinking...
Overall opinion...
Cuphead is by far, one of the best games I have seen, with an amazing soundtrack and animation! And the fact that it took 3/4 years to make is just MIND BLOWING. Take note that that Cuphead was COMPLETELY hand-drawn, and the soundtrack was made completely by the them!
Now, on to the "Gamplay" Review... (and a few tips)
Cuphead is a difficult game, requiring much patience, and skill, don't get distracted by the boss's awesome design, or the cool animation! One wrong slip can cost you a life. Consentrate your best, and you will be fine. This goes especially for bosses send out several projectiles at you, like Cagney Carnation, and Captain Brinybeard. Never leave a minion of the boss be left untouched, and whatever you do, don't stop shooting! On the Run n' Gun levels, make sure that you shoot every enemy coming at you, for the Mini Bosses, their attacks should be in a simple pattern, just follow it.

This is a great game.
A visual novel telling the story of Daphne Delatour, who finds herself embroiled in the middle of a supernaturally fuelled age old family feud, after inheriting her estranged grandmother's castle.
It's a good length to tell a decent and compelling story, without ever feeling like it's dragging on too much. No filler material.
The story has several twists and branches, with the choices that you make being rather important for the outcomes that occur. I've played it through enough to get almost all that could be seen (just missing two achievements).
I think they do it well in making the choices less about you the playing picking what happens, and more so you making choices that reveal the type of personality that Daphne has, and letting the plot progress from there. You're not choosing what she does, you're choosing who she is. I really like that from a VN.
The art direction does a wonderful job of setting the tone of the game, truly making you feel immersed in a surreal experience. The soundtrack is simple, but likewise helps set the mood.
This is a game that makes no effort whatsoever to adhere to the typical anime tropes that always seem to drag down most visual novels out there, and for that I absolutely applaud it. We need to see more of this.

Interesting visual novel. I really liked the artwork. It was neat that you could be several paths for the character based on text choices and how the character's clothing changes by the choices you make. Either you embrace your light side on the 'magic' portion. As indicated by a sun for light, moon for magic related issues. Or your dark side as listed by a moon icon. The world icon at the top seems to represent rationality and a scientific mind (meaning you don't draw conclusions about magic). On my run through I got light magic. It might be interesting to go for a purely scientific ending (but perhaps a little more boring, or to try for a more 'gothic' approach. I did think the price was a little steep for something not reviewed much, but the story line was still worth it just for the amount of effort put into the story. I like that there is a real depth to these characters, and how things fill in as you go along, keeping the story fresh (this idea would translate well into a real gaming experience, if you ask me, but I'm sure you don't have plans for that at this time. Or maybe don't have the ability to make that happen, but I know a good story when I read/experience one). All the dream sequences were pretty neat too, many artistic shots for screensavers. I do find it highly amusing that you can do a play through where you marry 'blondie' but it seems like a sad option really. Frank makes the most sense, but it's nice that there's different options. Worth a 2nd playthrough at least. This is a visual novel, but do I recommend it, yes it has more story than some others out there, but it's not overly complicated either. It makes you think about life in general and relationships.

Last night I finished There Came an Echo. A short game, but a good one. about 3-4 hours in total for a tenner. All in all not bad value, but not great either. Most of the entertainment comes from the voice command system, so it's a gimmick game. That said I can forgive gimmick games if the gimmick is done well.
In this case it mostly is. Commands work and are mostly logical, alternative words can be used for commands and selection too, giving you options for customization if there are words you have difficulty with. Does drop words every so often, but by far one of the better voice command systems I've used.
The setting and plot are both very tongue in cheek, kitschy cyberpunk. The plot is perfectly functional, but nothing special. The ending comes a little bit out of left field but hey, it's kitsch. At the end of the day I enjoyed it, it was nice to see a game that didn't seem to feel the need to take the plot too seriously, while still trying to deliver the best experience a decent-ish writing could. Would like more, it's mooreish in a popcorn sort of way.
The gameplay is a squad based RTS. Imagine a real time XCOM:EU battle and you've pretty much got the basic formula. You have up to four squad members and you can issue commands to, such as changing weapons moving to defined points on the map, targeting priority and so on.
The voice commands generate interesting tension as you can only give orders as fast as you can speak. As such the game rewards forward planning rather than just barrelling into hostile territory and making it up as you go. Crucially you can also stack commands to trigger when you say 'Mark'.
Either way, the game gives you plenty of tools to get the job done and provides an interesting variety of levels to play them across.
At £10.99 I think it's a little steep for the short length but it's certainly one to consider when on sale. I'd say I got my money's worth but I'd also say I'd be lying if I didn't feel a little short changed at the same time.
The game can be controlled normally, but really if you do that you're paying for a sub par, very short XCOM clone. Which is telling of how well done I think the voice commands gimmick is.
All in all, pretty solid game, but a tad overpriced I feel.

At one point a character is having a dramatic moment with an antagonist in the story and I realized... I really don't care about any of these characters.  They were all introduced very briefly and not expounded upon in any meaningful way.  And when I don't even care about the main characters, how am I supposed to care about the over all story?  It just doesn't work out.  And the premise of the game itself just tries way too hard and falls well short of its intent.
The voice acting is just bleh.  It is very uninspired.  It comes off more like people just reading a script than actually acting, which is weird because it actually was at least 1 legit actor.  But at least the music is good.
As for gameplay.  It was fun to control characters with voice and the game does seem adept at it.  But I think in the end it just ends up being a gimmick that gets boring a couple missions in.  You can't move anyone around freely.  You can't give them interesting commands.  Nothing works other than preset commands.  It just lacks that extra polish.  In most of the fights I don't even feel like I have to even try, and that is a good thing because they've made it very difficult to actually try hard.  Gun fights are over pretty quickly and the gap between being able to give commands and commands registering is just unfortuneately too long.
Most of the input I have is just telling them when to heal and sometimes to switch to a weapon, which by the time it happens, I no longer need them using that weapon and the longer they use it they just end up killing their own shields anyway.
Just the bullet points of this short review:
- game play is gimmicky and doesn't stay interesting long
- voice acting and story is below mediocre
- voice input, while interesting and somewhat accurate, just ends up taking a long time and feels unrewarding for the effort
- However, the music is good.

Liberation from the control of an ompotent AI falls a bit flat with mediocre puzzle game
As a fan of Valve's Portal and Alexander Bruce's Antichamber, I had high hopes of having a chance of playing a similarly designed lateral-thinking puzzle game with this title. The visual style and the potential of the nearly brand-new Unreal 4 Engine as well as the setting of being stranded on the Jupiter's moon Europa against an evil AI drew my immediate attention, as I was browsing through the Steam's midweek sales. Sadly, this game fell a bit too short in order to achieve satisfactory level gameplay for one, who previously has played through a couple of puzzle games, and there were a few reasons for this.
The first, and frankly the most important thing in a puzzle game, is of course, the level design, which was a slight disappointment. It was obvious, what the developers were thinking about with the puzzles of this game: they encourage the player to think outside the box and utilize whatever items there were in the Turing Test Chambers. The levels were creative and versatile with enough variety to keep the player going. Unfortunately, after playing both Portals this game could not offer enough challenge with its puzzles, because these were quite similar to Valve's titles and easy enough to sprint through in a matter of hours.
The second thing was the plot, which for a sci-fi fanatic, seemed rather interesting at a first glance. However, the way it was implemented to the world of the game, felt like it had been seen already. Without spoiling anything, I would just say that I wished more. The lore was there, and the characters were extremely fascinating, especially the relationship between the protagonist and the antagonist, but there was not enough gameplay time to affect the outcome of the game, and most of the big events felt like you were going on rails.
Both of the previously mentioned aspects let me play the game in a total amount of five-odd hours, including nearly all of the secrets and every single achievement in the entire game. If you are someone, who is fascinated by the AI-controlled future in the style of the 2001: A Space Odyssey, I would suggest that you would wait for a bargain. Despite of the great amount of faults, I feel that this game is worth to have a look at.
Final verdict: 6/10

There’s a noticeable systematic use of padding to artificially increase playtime, a very obnoxious practice.
The stories for the individual characters are serviceable but kind of shallow so it’s not really a strong story-telling game. In particular the "good" endings for the characters make little sense and feel like an afterthought, as if they were too skittish to make a game full of nothing but lurid black comedy.
The reason I still recommend it is that the atmosphere and humor are quite good, so I enjoyed the game despite how sloppy it is in a few places. I wouldn’t advise paying full price for it, though.

It's a bit difficult to know how to review this game, because it's one of those games where almost anything you know going into it will detract from the experience.  OneShot is unlike almost every other game I've ever played.  The extent of its fourth-wall breaking is ludicrous, but unlike the way most games do it, it feels... real, and meaningful, in a way that's difficult to properly convey.
Perhaps the best thing to say is simply this: in OneShot, *you*, as in the person at your computer, are very much a part of the game, and your connection to the characters in the story is both profoundly meaningful and at times heart-wrenching.  It's a short game, one that can be easily completed in a day or two, but I know for certain that I'm going to be thinking about it long, long after having actually finished it.  It's a fun puzzle game that anyone can play, and its narrative is going to be with me for a long time.  If you're at all interested, please do yourself a huge favor and pick it up.  You won't be disappointed.  For only $10, it's a steal for its value.

I've played this game for several days. It started slow (try and give it a chance first) and I gave up once before. But then my brother started to play it and I decided to give it one more shot. And I didn't regret it. There's so much to do in RIFT. World events, invasions, rifts, and random quest that you can get underwater, on the ground, and even from a troll you just killed! In my opinion, RIFT excels in random events like these ones. The class system is intriguing. Remind me a bit like Path of Exile but not as complicated, but still interesting and fun to tinker with. The game is huge. Not just in term of contents and stuffs to do, but in term of how massive the world is. You can keep exploring for hours and hours and not get bored. While exploring, you will find Artifacts to collect and when you've complete a certain set of Artifacts, you'll be rewarded. The rewards are awesome/useful most of the times. When you're not off fighting monsters and planes creatures, there's a lot to do. For example, Professions (crafting and gathering). Crafting is deep and quite intricate. The gathering professions (mining, foraging, butchering) is fun too. It gives us a reason to explore (if there's not one already). The developers are constantly creating something for the players. There's never short of contents and updates. And they always keep in touch and interact with the players. A quality that is hard to find in this era of MMORPGs. But be warned, this game is GPU intensive. Its not gonna look good in a low-end PC and that might take away a significant amount of the joy. Some of effects are dull (even in ultra settings), like spells etc. But the rift's effects are top notch. Overall, I highly recommend this game. I hate generic point and click MMORPGs like WoW. Too boring for me. But somehow, this game managed to draw me in. I tip my hat to you, TRION.

+I LOVE the on-rails shooter style this game provides. It brings back the arcade nostalgia for me.
+The core concept of the game is incredibly fresh and fun. It's a great way to brush up on your typing speed.
+The words and phrases you will be typing are at times, hilarious. Examples include: Blue♥♥♥♥♥♥ Cumquat Smuggler, Goat Curry, and Leper Handshake
-The characters are annoying as hell, and so is their back and forth banter. The characters themselves are cheesy and over-the-top (which I know is the point), but it gets really annoying.
-Bad humor EVERYWHERE. I curse like a sailor in my daily life, but Jesus Christ the language and humor was just over the top ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It eventually got to the point where I just turned the game's master volume down and pulled up youtube in another window...thats how boring the "story" is. And YES, there are a few times I found myself chuckling, but overall, the jokes were just plain dumb and cheesy as hell.
-The voice acting from some of the characters in the game was terrible. Especially from one of the female characters, she just sounded unnatural when she cursed (like she was trying too hard).
+There are boss battles at the end of each level, which is a nice touch. Unfortunately some bosses are just TOO easy, but overall the bosses were unique enough to keep me interested.
-The campaign is short. It took me 3.2 hours to beat the story mode on normal mode.
+Varying levels of difficulty can make the game challenging as hell.

Introduced to 3 lead characters the task is to help other students pass exams by cheating (surprise!). Game does include a background story that is well presented in a comic book style between chapters which involved the janitor and his past history with the school but I won't elaborate and spoil the plot.  Store page mentions 'episodes' which refers to each chapter, all 5 are included.
Characters have their own personality traits and special abilities which increase your chances of success while classes (missions) had different teachers who carry their own unique skills that did the opposite. Levels start on the easier side and gradually introduced new obstacles, coming in the form of awkward chair placements, classmates who spot trouble and inform the teacher and general improvements to enemy skills.
Game really opened up after the first chapter. Given access to the Cheaters Clubhouse where you can upgrade skills, craft a wide range of new gear including 1 use items and take on side missions along with repeating completed ones. Item choice does end up being critical since characters have limited slots, thankfully they can be swapped in level. Characters also had stats that raise passively through skill usage which added some extra rpg elements.
Gamepad was not supported given the multi-tasking nature but mouse controls were intuitive helped by the clean UI. Only a few minor issues with character selection in later levels but probably more a pebkac error. Graphics are simple but effective, biggest flaws would be the lack of steam achievement integration and extremely repetitive soundtrack, which was good for about 5minutes before I had to disable it.
Overall I've enjoyed my time with the game. For the fair price point and surprising amount of depth it's recommended and worth taking a look at. More so if you like time management and lighthearted strategy games. Cheers folks. :)

All together it's still a cute, fine game, worth playing for fans of indie games in that genre. But it certainly not some Must-Play like for example To The Moon was.

TL;DR: A decent puzzle game with some cliched philosophical AI discussion. At the end you have to make a choice between two dramatic but not totally rational options, which just frustrated me to death. Puzzles weren't anything exceptionally clever or challenging, but not bad either. I completed the game in about 5 hours, which seemed short for the cost.
***Minor spoilers below***
The game isn't too bad, if you just come at it from the puzzle perspective. The puzzles really don't have any fresh elements to them. The main mechanic is power switches that allow you to energize circuits by moving power cores with your power-gun. There's some weight switches and blocks that can be used to energize circuits, which we occasionally use to break LOS for some out-of-the-box thinking puzzles. Locked doors, lightbridges, a few pieces of movable equipment (controlled from stationary control panels) all make appearances too. About halfway through they introduce an element where you can toss your consciousness into cameras or robot drones, allowing for some two-person puzzles with LOS limitations. There are also power-cells that don't provide constant power, thus introducing a time element -- there were a few interesting puzzle mechanics with those.
There are 70 isolated puzzle rooms, which are somewhat reminiscent of Portal's test-chambers. There's 7 optional puzzles too, including a combination-lock puzzle where you find the solution later in the game. (There are a few puzzles where you find passcodes later in the game for locks only accessible earlier... necessitating multiple playthroughs to get the last achievement and see all the flavor-text.) I found most of them incredibly easy. Towards the middle, about half the puzzles I'd just be fiddling with elements to see the entire chamber, and I'd solve the puzzle unintentionally. The last 3 chambers took some thinking, and the 70th had me stumped for a bit.
From the philosophy perspective... They wanted to be like the Talos Principle, although with metaphysical discussion of AI and consciousness rather than Talos' ethical discussion of obedience vs independence. They ultimately failed because: first, the discussion had no bearing on the story, even with the big decision at the end; and second, the "discussion" was really more of assertions of opposing viewpoints than discussion. There is some flavor text that includes classic arguments on the topic, which were far more interesting than the character's voice-overs (there's mention of a "mathematical objection" to the possibility of thinking machines, citing Godel's work, which I haven't heard before and need to investigate.)
***Major spoilers below***
At the end there's the big decision between two irrational parties about issues that really don't relate to the discussion of AI minds. The colonists want to return to earth, bringing with them a pathogen that brings "immortality" (although in their discussions, it sounds like it's really more of an end to aging) but also may make diseases "immortal" (incurable) and also mess up the human growth cycle, doing who-knows-what to children. It's unclear if these concerns are conjectures or known facts. The AI, on the other hand, says it's too dangerous to return the pathogen to earth, and since the colonists broke free of his mind control and don't respect his authoritarian stance as the government's representation, his only solution is to kill them. Of course the colonists need to shut the AI down for their plan. Kind of sets up for the "does a machine have a right to live" question, but it's not discussed at all... and besides, it's overshadowed by the whole "fate of the world" thing, and the fact that the AI has been mind-controlling and then trying to kill the colonists.
I think it's intended to be the old "logic vs emotion driven thinking," but the computer didn't seem nearly rational enough to really make me buy in. I mean the AI has control of the ship, and there's no reason it couldn't scuttle the ship and live in the planetside computer alongside the colonists. Or maybe, it could just warn Earth the colonists are coming, allowing them to set up a quarantine for the colonists until all the social implications can be worked out... or at least until the xenobiologists find a way to control the immortality pathogen. But no. Either the colonists die or earth is destroyed.
***End of spoilers***
Still... it's a decent puzzle game if you're looking for that. I had doc's orders not to sleep a particular night, and for $10  this kept me occupied (both in the game itself and the time writing an extensive review). I don't feel regret the purchase. I'm not sure I'd recommend it though, unless someone really wants a puzzle game and this is the best they can find.

"Everything is a remix", according to an interesting video series of that name. This is true even of a game like Portal, and those that came before it. It's not surprising that Portal has influenced so much of modern gaming, and the influences here are obvious -- a first-person puzzler with AI themes and bare rooms. It's also a formidable task to fill Portal's shoes. So at first, I was surprised to see some clever uses of familiar mechanics and I was getting drawn into the story and gameplay. Near the end though, it sort of fell apart.
Story:
It's refreshing to see a serious and thoughtful take on the Turing Test as a thought-experiment along with all the related thought-experiments presented. The medium of a video game gives the player have ample time to process it all and see it play out in a narrative. The twist is also nice. However, every plot point gets repeated and rehashed about five or six times each.

This is an RTS in which you command a squad of 4 soldiers through a few missions using voice commands, yeah that´s right, you can play the entire game using only your voice (and mouse to move the camera) and it's just as awesome as it sounds, at least if the game responds to your commands and that's why I cannot recommend it to everyone, the game has a difficult time responding to accents, and although you can choose from different accents (Brittish, American, Canedian, Australian and Indian) in the menu to help the game reconising those commands better it does a poor job reconising commands I yel through the mic with my Dutch accent. From what I've read the devellopers will add support for other languages but in most cases Dutch isn't going to be one of them but they will probably add spanish, german and french and maybe a few other european languages. And even if they add Dutch the game probably still won't reconise English with a Dutch accent (Dutch sounds pretty cheesy in those kinds of games so I rather stick to english) after quite a long moment of calibrating the voice reconition system (or whatever it's called) i set the language to "English-Indian" because that one seems to work for the most part and after a bit of practice I did get the game to respond to most of my commands untill Syll becomes part of my team. I cannot command him to do anything AT ALL, unless i change the language to "English-United States" but when i do that the game doesn't respond when i use the word Alpha or the number 3 making it practicly impossible for me to go on. You can add custom commands and names so I tried giving Syll a custom name but so far no name I've tried seems to do the trick. furthermore I've had a lot of trouble commanding Corrin as he doesn't always respond to my commands and the game has difficulties reconising the word "mark" even though the command "Miranda, move to Alpha 2 on my mark" works perfectly fine. One of my favorite games I've played was Tom Clancy's EndWar. Not for it's strategic depth or crazy multiplayer, but because of the voice commands that allowed you to control troops around the field. After learning that There Came an Echo shared a similar control scheme, I was interested immediately. Having now completed the game, I'm more than happy to say I enjoyed my entire ride through. While the game is incredibly short, it holds a fantastically told story and a clever use of a health/stamina system.
You play Sam, a faceless character that plays a squad leader role to various teammates, the main named Corrin (voiced excellently by Wil Wheaton). Input is offered via voice commands, keyboard/mouse, controller, or a Intel RealSense device; the main selling point and my preferred method being through dictation.
Pros:
+ Fantastic story. Extremely well told from beginning to end, with no true “meh” interludes.
+ ♥♥♥♥ing incredible music. Just beautifully done throughout. The standout of the package without a doubt.
+ Voice controls that work! I know some people have had trouble, but my accent was picked up without issues a large amount of the time. When I had trouble pronouncing names, or said key words the game didn't recognize, the game allowed typed-in custom words to be added.
+ The health/stamina system was a fantastic balance. Power weapons will drain the shield that protects you from the damage you're receiving – do you continue to fire your average shots to keep health high, or switch to a power weapon at the risk of a fast death? Awesome design choice.
+ A lot of awesome themes based on future technology and religion. A theme that is very easily understood and grasped while these complex ideas are being told.
Cons:
- Grace's lines are really, really hard to enjoy. Her character was consistently infuriating and some lines were just so out of place and generally horrid. She has a major turn around towards the end of the game, but you'll never forget how bad it was before.
- It ends. This is an incredibly short game, and once it's done, there isn't much to go back for. There is a training room to access, but it's one level of predictable waves of enemies. With the full realization this game was Kickstarted, it still really upsets me that there's no type of multiplayer/horde/level designer/Workshop to come with this game. I still want to continue playing, but I don't have anything to do.
- Different missions have different (read: inconsistent and frustrating) levels of zoom. I really wanted to pull back the camera to get a more tactical view in some levels, but the game never budged. This made it very hard to get an idea of the battlefield at crucial points.
I love this game. The short stay is a welcome one, and I can only hope the developers can squeeze in some extra levels or modding tools to help this game continue to thrive. Absolutely worth the asking price.

There's nothing like There Came An Echo. At least not in my experience. I play games for a lot of reasons--satisfying gameplay, a good story, a comforting set of upgrades and achievements to collect--but one of my favorite things is a game that provides an utterly unique experience, one that is not otherwise possible in other games or in real life. I've never been a military commander, far from it. But There Came An Echo makes me feel like I'm part of the team, barking orders and trying to stay calm even as my troops wither under heavy fire. There's a lot to like about this game, from the gorgeous art to the thrilling soundtrack to the head-spinning depth of the story, but first and foremost for me is that
, that amazing, heart-pounding "Oh God how do I solve this" real-time tension. I'm not just a player pushing buttons on a controller, because there is no controller. There's just me and my voice, in the middle of the action and responsible on a gut level for what goes down in the next few minutes. That's great. That's very special.
Surrounding and supporting that feeling at all times is a beautifully executed roller coaster experience. TCAE may be short, but it offers a rich emotional journey, a blockbuster sci-fi experience that brings on entertaining characters, sets them against great odds, and then lays their secrets bare, culminating in a sequence asking why we continue to strive even when things are at their most hopeless, even when everything tells you there's no point to continuing. In the end, TCAE isn't about the lasers or the *spoiler deleted* saucy robots *spoiler deleted* sous-chef *spoiler deleted* jazz saving the world. It's about how meaning doesn't come from outside, it comes from you and the people you care about, and how that caring is the fulcrum by which a lever might move the world.
It's been a frustrating experience for me, reading professional reviews of the game. TCAE doesn't really fit into the schematic of product reviews--x out of 10 for sound, y out of 10 for replayability, etc. In writing this review, I can't grade the art or the music for you; I can only tell you that some of the soundtrack has been stuck in my head for days, that the art is both functional and evocative, that both work together to express a cool and thrilling futurism. I can't assign to a number to the performances; I can only say that there are scenes of unexpected humor and others that cut painfully deep. I can tell you I will replay it, not as one returns to a game for DLC or bonus modes but as one returns to a movie, excited to see the story again.
TCAE is an experience, a work of art as much as it is an entertainment, and it demands to be engaged with on an emotional and intellectual level as much as, or more, than the consumer perspective. Too often gamers are looking for the right number of pixels or a well-crafted Skinner box, so much so that they forget to just enjoy having fun. I know I'm as guilty of that as anyone. But those who find themselves in that situation would do well to spend an afternoon with Corrin and his friends, playing the way children do, ordering them to run here, do this, shoot that, win the day. If you're anything like me, the first time the characters talk back to you, you'll feel that spark of excitement that is, in the end, the reason we play games.

The artwork is really stunning and the music is lovely too, though not very varied (it does get a little repetitive after multiple playthroughs).
The only real problem with the game is that there are parts where the translation from French to English is . . . dubious, strange use of tenses and things that may have been translated too directly. I wouldn't normally mind so much but as it is such a heavily text based game I feel more care should have been taken; but for the most part it was clear what was being said and what was going on. Voice acting would also have been nice but I found I didnt mind so much after playing the game for a while.
It is a relatively short and slow game/story and is entirely made up of still images and text but it is definitely not boring and has heaps of replayability. Happy to recommend.

I was surprised by Along the Edge. I was made aware of the game by writer Geoffroy Vincens, who contacted me after seeing our coverage of Lucy Blundell’s One Night Stand and thinking the game might grab our interest. While I was initially a little skeptical about an “Adult Interactive Visual Novel with Occult Elements”, I am pleased to say my judging of this book by it’s cover was misplaced.
Along the Edge is certainly a mature story, dealing with adult themes, but it’s not over sexualized, or trying harder than it needs to to be taken seriously. Likewise, the occult elements of the story are not misplaced and don’t feel slapped on for ‘spice’. They are an integral and well constructed part of the plot.
More than anything, Along the Edge is a story about a woman, Daphne, dealing with past trauma and turning over a new leaf. This is not a story to put yourself into; it is Daphne’s story, and Along the Edge‘s dedication to this fact helps make it an engaging and thought provoking story where the choices you make really do matter, and have the potential to create entirely different narratives.
Along the Edge casts you as Daphne, a young woman who is in a pretty serious rut, unsatisfied with both her personal and professional life and having recently gone through a number of life changing traumas. One day, you find out your grandmother has made you the beneficiary of her estate, a large castle-esq villa in a french country village. You take this as a chance to get away from the negativity in your life and turn over a new leaf, taking a substitute teaching job in the villages school.
Suffice to say, there’s more going on than is let on at first glance. We won’t spoil anything, but by the end of things there are romantic relationships in play, generations old family feuds, ancient magic and prophetic dreams. All of this hinges on the choices you make as Daphne.
Note, I didn’t say ” The choices you make”. I said “the choices you make as Daphne”. Along the Edge is very much a story about a character who is already established, already has a history and motivations all her own. She is not a character you can easily mold to be your vision of yourself in this situations, and that isn’t the goal of the choices you make in Along the Edge. You’re guiding a character in one of a number of different ways, but these choices are firmly planted in the context of the world.
To me, this gave the story of Along the Edge, and the choices being made, a surprising weight. By restricting the reactions, choices, and ways things could play out based on the mindset and personality of an already established main character, the developers created and incredible sense of validity. True, there was less of a sense of self-reflection in this character, and you feel more like an outsider watching a story unfold as opposed to some other visual novels and narrative games that emphasis putting you into the shoes of their protagonist, but the choice is incredibly successful in engaging the player and getting them involved in the story.
Mechanically, the choices you make in Along the Edge are selected from the screen, and then the impact of those choices are relayed back to you in the form of a four-pointed compass at the top of the screen. Your choices each impact one of the four points of this compass: The Star, The Globe, The Sun or The Moon. Some choices will stagger between two of these symbols, but ultimately the choices you make will fall somewhere on this compass much like a four pointed alignment chart. Additionally, after particularly momentous decisions in the game, there will be very obvious visual changes to Daphne as she grows and learns about this world, and about herself.
By making these choices, character will change the way they react to you, enter or leave your life, or reveal new opportunities. One of the major axis that revolve around this compass is your acceptance or rejection of the magic imbued into this new environment. It’s clear there is something of a supernatural nature going on in your grandmother’s castle, and in the town, but you can steer Daphne towards either welcoming this magic with open arms, or pragmatically shutting the door in it’s face. This particular aspect of the game’s narrative over joyed me, as typically the acceptance of magic in stories involving it is a given fact. It was a wonderful change of pace to instead give the player a chance to accept or deny this fact, and see how this affected the characters in the story.
As noted above, this is spoiler free review, so we won’t reveal the major twists of the story, however you can rest assured that the choices made in Along the Edge are not only cosmetic. They have a real impact of the way this story unfolds, and the way Daphne fulfills her role in it. This fact alone gives Along the Edge an incredible amount of replayability, as there are numerous narratives to uncover and explore.
The art of Along the Edge is beautiful. The painterly scenes of castles and sleepy town shift between season and realities. The town is charming and beautiful, and Daphne’s grandmother’s castle oozes with mystery and history. However, the art chops of Along the edge really get to show their stuff in the dream sequences, which are trippy, fantastical and full of symbolism.
The music is just as fantastic, full of haunting piano melodies that are all at once haunting, morose and calming. The Art and music of Along the Edge combine beautifully and do a superb job of getting you in the exact brain space for this kind of slower paced narrative experience.
Along the Edge is a fantastic narrative experience that drops you into the life of a character in conflict. In conflict with herself, her environment, and even her reality. By guiding this character and making meaningful choices for her, you are made part of a story where those choices has demonstrable effects on the narrative and its conclusion. It’s a rewarding journey alongside a slice out of this character’s life, which I thoroughly enjoyed.

Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is cool. If you were disappointed with No Man's Sky, this could eventually be the game to fill that gap. Osiris: New Dawn offers a lot for an indie early access game. As of 10/8/16 the game is mostly focused on surviving on an alien planet. Space travel and exploration are pretty terrible at the moment, so if you're looking to explore a whole planet, that's not going to happen. As of now, the planets are not spherical. The way land and space works in O:ND is like this: the map is a giant circle/square of developer-created land that is the "play-area". Outside of this play-area is nothing but bland desert. Once you build a space ship, you can fly around the play area and pitch up to go to space. As you go to space the play-area is covered by a texture of the spherical planet to make it seem as if you traveled a far distance and are in orbit, but in reality "space" is just in the sky of the play-area. Space is boring too and has a few bugs. Hopefully the devs take the NMS apporach and make the planets spherical and space a little further out. As for everything else, it's very well developed. The soundtrack is great and flows well within the game. The graphics are amazing, everything looks very realistic, even the aliens. The combat system is executed near perfectly. The weather in this game is annoyingly great. Surviving in this game is not the hardest task but definitely takes some time to pass the challenges. Base building is fun, but needs more buildings and customization to be added. There is absolutely no story, and it's important that this game gets one, as there is not much to offer after you've built everything and have gone everywhere. Last but not least, there are many bugs in this game (as to be expected with Early Access). Another thing worth mentioning is that this game heavily revolves around resource gathering. Overall I give O:ND a 7/10 considering it's creativeness, problems, price tag, etc. I would reccomend this game to anyone who loves the space game genre, or those who like the indie survival game genre. Osiris: New Dawn is a pretty damn cool game, and I can't wait to see what the developers have planned for the future.

OK, this is my first review of a game.... but feel strongly about this one so thought what the hell...
I really like a good open world survival game. I have played subnautica, Solaris and ARK into the dirt and still play them pretty frequently. I have also played some bad survival games which after watching the steam trailer, I have spent money on... and have been a massive disapointment. I am happy to say that after spending 15ish hours on this game I am not regretting the perchase one little bit. However, you need to be aware that it is veeeeeeeeeeery early access and has a number of bugs but even only 4 days after release, at least a few of these bugs (the most important ones) have been sorted with bandaids and patches. The Devs seem to actually look through the forums and make a true effort to tackle complaints quickly.... which is what all indi Devs bringing out a paid game with potential should do. Sooooo.... Nice one Devs!
At the moment it seems a little limited from a crafting/construction point of view and crafting feels a little janky. The attacking aliens are a little clanky and will kill you quick if you are not prepared to deal with them. There are a few other problems, all expected for an early access, but are already slowly disapearing with updates.
The graphics of the terrain are pretty impressive, the texturing and light/shadows are top notch and run at a pretty stable 57-60 fps. (my rig being a 4 core i5, overclocked gtx980, 16gb RAM. Runs it no worries)
I still havn't played online but will be attemting this soon once I have a propper grasp of the game.
Anyway, on to brass tacks...

Adventure?
Puzzle?
Platform?
Point and click?
How about all of the above?
It is a combination of all of these so that certainly makes it "different" sort of game ---- but there is some fun to be had here, if you can tolerate the rather slow pace (due mostly to a ton of backtracking).
Kind of slow getting started, but you pick your three characters from the seven offered (each with a different story), and off you go to various parts of the cave itself. And the cave is beautiful, and fun to explore. Some of the puzzles are super easy, others not so much. But even though the pacing is slow, the game itself looks like it will be short. The replay value is good though ---- just choose different characters for each playthrough. And with all the slow walking and backtracking, that kind of pads out the game length. I guess I just expected more, because I kept waiting for the pace to pick up, but it didn't.
So I'm glad I got it on sale, and that's how I'll recommend the game with some reservation ---- 75% off only, I would think.

It's  a fun adventure game but not really to the same level that I expect from Double Fine for a few reasons.
First off, it may seem like a small thing but I think it's annoying that there's 7 main characters but you can only do 3 per playthrough. This means that you can have 2 completely unique playthroughs, but then if you want to see the 7th character's storyline you'll have to do a third playthrough with mostly repeated content.
Second, I feel like this game would have benefitted from more voice acting, although I understand this might have been due to budget restrictions, but if it was a stylistic choice then I just don't get it.
The characters you play as are supposed to have these big dark backstories that you uncover, but there's never any opportunities to show their personalities, even when I was playing as particular characters I felt like the story that was being revealed was for NPCs not the characters I was controlling. I think this could have been showed off more through voice acting.
However, the game is still very charming. You're led through the game by The Cave itself, an omniscient narrator who has a dry sense of humor as he details all of your experiences. It's actually pretty fun. In addition, there's quite a lot to like about many of the levels, especially the ones that are specific to certain characters. The hillbilly's carnival level in particular was  a lot of fun.
The games not very challenging. If you're paying attention most puzzles are pretty easy. However, there are certain parts that seem to drag on.
It's definitely not perfect, but overall I think it's a decent game, although the writing isn't quite up to what I expect from Double Fine.
Platformers sometimes make me nervous as a casual gamer, but this was great fun. I enjoyed the puzzles and dry humor.

I call this the Poor Man's World of Warcraft. The game is basically that. You've got a fairly large world to explore, the game is constantly updated with content and bug fixes, and if my computer were able to handle it, I'd probably say that this game looks stunning on high graphics settings. Really I can't think of anything else to compare it to other than WoW. The HUD is basically the same, skill bar on the bottom, bags and money on the right, yadda yadda.
The gameplay is rather repetative I must say, but I think that if you dumb it down to what you're basically doing, you're ruining the experience for yourself. You go around, find quests, mine ores if you want, collect plants or flowers, fish, kill some things, deliver items in some cases, make weapons and armor, and more. There's a bunch of skills to learn, but I believe you must pay money if you want to learn more than 3 skills such as mining, foraging, and fishing for example.
While I'm on the topic of paying with real money, the game has a store in which you can buy many different kinds of items, mainly cosmetic items or dimension items. Dimensions are basically player owned homes. These are bought with credits, which can be bought through the store, the cheapest being $5. As you buy with real money, your loyalty meter goes up. The more you have, the more in-game rewards you recieve. The main problem about this loyalty system is that use of the auction house requires you to have a certain amount of loyalty in order to sell items. So unless you have a couple of spare $$$s in your Steam Wallet, you don't have access to the AH.
The game also has PVP, which can be played in things called warfronts, which are closed arenas where players either play a domination-like gametype, or a gametype similar to Oddball from Halo, where a team needs to hold a shard that damages them over time, but also gives their team points. There are a few other gametypes in warfronts, and when completing a random one, you may recieve some sort of loot that contains either a pvp item or pvp currency called favor. Players can also duke it out throughout the entire world, as there are some servers that are PVP only, but you are also able to PVP in the servers that are PVE only. I do not mean that you can be minding your own business and then all of a sudden some guy comes up and kills you in 2 seconds. In order to PVP in PVE servers, you need to enable it.
In the time I've played RIFT, I've managed to get to around level 37 or so, the max being 60 I think. There are many classes and "souls" to choose from. These "Souls" are basically skill trees for whatever class you choose, such as support, tank, healer or damage. The game automatically chooses these souls for you, but you have the choice to choose your own set. As for the endgame, when you hit the max level, the only thing I can think of doing is either PVP or starting anew with a different race and class.
In short, it's free, it's like WoW, and if you're interested in something like that, why not try something that's free? The only thing you have to lose is your time, as this game is a 15GB download, on top of future updates.

Okay so the first thing people will compare Rift to will be WoW. This is mainly because WoW is the most popular MMORPG ever created. If you/re looking to have this put simply, think of Rift this way. "A lot of the familiar elements of WoW, done better with better looks, for free." Rift is very similar to WoW with raids and parties, questing and shops, bosses and guilds, and classes and combat.
Let's take a look at the big positives Ive noticed so far.
-You dont have to spend and arm and leg to get am decent mount in Rift.
-Combat system (to me) is more fair and allows players to use and play with abilites more.
-You can quest and level up solo or joiun into big parties to quest with others, i.e. teamwork is fun and easy to work with.

-Rift gives you TONS of different ways to play a character, making for unique characters that are your own.
-You gain multiple skills to play with at early levels so you/re always getting new things to try out.

-Lots of different armor and weapons int he game

Now here are some things I find un-attractive about the game
-Farming seems hard to do with low XP drops from enemies (quests giving abut 10X the amount of of one enemy, depending on the quest).

Altogether Rift is amazing. It is super fun to play and there is LOTS to do. With my only gripe being the poor focus on classes I still think this game deserves a solid 10

Cuphead, one of my most favorite games because of the difficulty, the amazing soundtrack, and how the game plays; it's seriously one of the most amazing games of 2017.
It has a different variety of bosses in each Isle, and can be either flying battles or on ground battles, which makes it very interesting. I've been raging quite a lot at these battles, but these bosses are REALLY hard, especially when it gets to Expert.  I have messed around with some expert battles, and the bosses change with how fast the projectiles move, and they have more hp and some different mechanics in some phases. Speaking of phases, as each phase goes, they usually use new attacks and different looks which makes it look really cool. There is also Run & Gun levels, where you have to get through the whole level by taking down enemies as you go through, but you can go at your own pace. You can get rewarded for doing them by coins.
Speaking of coins, you need them to buy upgrades like different weapon types,  and charms. There is a unique weaponry and each one works differently and does certain amount of damage and they can be helpful in your strategies. The types of charms that exist are really good include getting an extra hp, or a smoke dash. These can be helpful as well because of how you can use them to your advantage, and now to the specials; the specials are earned in a interesting way, and there is only three of them. These are unique powers when your special is maxed out. I did forget to mention that you can use your special as it's not maxed out, but it's not using the special but using a different move depending on the weapon you have equipped. Each weapon has a different special shot.
The story is really interesting and basically it's like doing the right thing in all of this. Of course you have to defeat all of the bosses for their Soul Contracts, which are required to have to proceed to the next isle. But they are also in the Devil's Debt like you are, and you were going to have to give your soul contract to him, but instead of doing that, the Devil wants YOU to get the debter's soul contracts.
Overall, I rate this game 10/10 for it's amazing soundtrack, game style, difficulty, story, weapon variety, battle types, etc. This would be definitely on my list of top games of 2017.

For this one, I'll just do the TL:DR up front. Very good game, but also very short. Wouldn't recommend to pick up at anywhere above $10-12 . Also, if you're into game soundtracks, this one is very good.
So, There Came an Echo is a game that could stand to advertise itself better. It spent more time talking about having Wil Wheatley, Laura Bailey and Ashly Burch as VAs and its voice command gimmick than actually talking about what the game was about. I can get that it's impressive for a Kickstarter game to have all that, but still.
It's a very linear narrative-driven game, with gameplay along the lines of XCOM. You can use mouse or keyboard to order the troops around, but it's much more efficient to use the command system. The combat itself can get pretty hectic, but is very fixed and doesn't offer too much in the way of variety. More on that at the end. I've read complaints about the command system, but I didn't experience problems. It could be because my natural voice is loud enough that it would occasionally tell me I was being too loud, but still...I can't really fault it if I didn't have problems with it, but I guess be aware that some people have complained about it if you're soft spoken or don't naturally speak clearly? I don't know. I also did have a couple bugs here and there with characters not moving to the place I told them to (going to alpha one instead of alpha three), but I was generally able to work around them, so they weren't gamebreaking.
The story is the real draw here.The story itself is something you'll have to pay attention to, but it doesn't get so complicated you can't follow. The characters were simple, but effectively got their personalities across.The climax at the end was very well done. The writing was generally solid, but could occasionally be a bit too on-the-nose.
Aesthetic wise, what's up there is a good representation of it. The soundtrack is extremely good, and I'd recommend picking it up if you're into soundtrack collecting. I'd compare it to Mass Effect's music, very electronic and futuristic-sounding, if that makes sense.
With all that praise, it's a short game with little to no replayability. The story's the main draw and is linear, so no reason to replay there. Unlike XCOM, which I name-dropped earlier, there's also no variety in the gameplay, so that's also no reason to go on. It took me four hours to complete, and while they were a good and satisfying four hours, how much you're willing to pay will really come into it. So buyer beware.

Parto subito con il dire che questo è un remake un po' strano ; come potete immaginare un remake dovrebbe essere una rimasterizzazione in HD di un videogame vecchio , migliorandolo tecnicamente e graficamente , senza modificare troppo il gioco in questione. In questo Painkiller , stranamente , prosegue la storia invece di riniziare. Scelta che io non capisco.
La trama racconta che la "Morte" propone a Daniel Garner , di raccogliere 7000 anime per rivedere sua moglie , cioè Catherine. Per fare ciò , il tristo mietitore gli da un'arma , Soul Catcher ( unica nuova arma in questo painkiller).
Quindo dovremo raccogliere queste anime in vari livelli ( già percorsi nel vecchio PK ). E' da qui parte un'altra cavolata ; il vecchio painkiller conteneva ben 24 livelli , ma questo qui ne ha solo 14 ( compreso i vari boss). Quindi su per giu' sono un 8 ore di gioco , che sono alquanto poche per un painkiller. La longevità aumenta solo se si gioca in difficoltà incubo e trauma ( aumenta per modo di dire , io in incubo l'ho finito ugualmente in 8 ore , ma comunque per qualcuno durerà un po' di più). Altri elementi che aumentano la longevità sono gli extra e la modalità copertiva , quest ultima un ottima aggiunta , per spappolare nemici in compagnia! La difficoltà è rimasta tale , sempre tanti nemici da eliminare , quindi un gioco abbastanza hardcore ; ma la nuova arma (Soul Catcher ) semplifica un po' il gioco.
Graficamente , niente da dire , si sono fatti grossi miglioramenti ed è un bene per un remake.
Invece il multiplayer è stile arena , gioco molto competitivo e difficile. ( Lo sconsiglio per chi gioca a giochi non competitivi). Ci sono tante modalità e tante mappe da giocare , quindi un bel po' di contenuti.
C'è da dire che painkiller contiene vari bug , sia multiplayer e sopratutto in single player. Bug dovuti anche IA del nemico che , per esempio , può capitare che si incastra in 2 oggetti...
Questo remake lo consiglio ai fan di PK e ai fan del genere di gioco , che rimarranno contenti grazie al divertimento che può offrire questo gioco e al multiplayer competitivo. ( che in giro se ne vede poco...)
Gli sviluppatori potevano impegnarsi un po' di più e ne usciva un prodotto completo e senza difetti vari.

OneShot is, to say the very least, interesting. The game seems lighthearted from first glance, but it's actually way deeper. The plot is amazing, and the game executes it in a very beautiful way. The game has an overall eerie soundtrack, with a few short outbursts of cheerful, little tones. As the story progresses, you get to actually feel the main character develop emotionally, and slowly you attach yourself to this world within.
The game creates a tense and somber atmosphere, as though breathing one sip of air could overwrite timelines. It keeps this theme throughout the game, excluding small parts of lighthearted humor. There is much hidden underneath the surface; the characters, which may initially seem flat and boring, actually may be round characters. OneShot manages to put some lore within the shadows of characters, making them much more interesting. OneShot also leaves many obscure hints for you to discover and find in order to progress the story (the game took me 9 hours only because I'm too dumb to find and/or comprehend them).
Basically, if you're into games with deep, intuitive topics, you should give OneShot a shot (I feel disgusted with myself). I am definitely not the best gamer, observer, or writer, but even so, I feel as though this game should be given more than just one chance, and should be enjoyed by many.

A Grimbright/Noblebright mix of 2001: A Space Odyssey, Virtuality, and Portal,
with the atmosphere of The Talos Principle and the witty intricacies of Asimov's robot series. Also, some transhumanism from the Human TV series.
Now, though, you have to buy this game for its adventure, not for its puzzles. The tests are meant to illustrate the story by providing an ironic and poetical minimalist immersion. (What with the almost seamless analogies between TOM's lines and the last test chambers of Chapter 5... The tests were key on pertinence, but the puzzle mechanics are not meant to challenge. Once that's clear, there should be much less disappointment.
The Turing Test is a jewel.
Its characters, narration and plot are superior to those of the Portal games. Its philosophy makes more sense than the philosophy in the Talos Principle.
Also, it's best played twice: once to discover and once to appreciate.
Now, Regarding Ava...most of her lines make more sense and are more open minded and likeable than that of most other past human protagonists who've been put against machines in media ... at least in the first half of the game. But I'm not going to spoil.
So, yeah, she's an engineer, she knows the music and she begins playing it fairy well.
However...just like in The Talos Principle, (though much less often) sometimes I felt like pushing the protagonist aside and explaining things to T.O.M. myself. I guess that means the game felt very realist. SPOILER: For example, when we find out that TOM used to mix up being sentient and being similar to humans, through the secret test room. Or when he was so sure that without his control, human nature would make humans choose their safety over that of others. And there are so many questions I wanted to ask it/him, that it's not even funny.
PS: I actually played about 5 hours so far.
Loved the game! Great puzzles, thought-provoking story.

For me, the story behind this game was so compelling, that at some point, the puzles stopped being important (even when it is suposed to be the goal of the whole game), its true, most of them feel easy, but nearing the end of the game, I saw myself in the need of taking a few steps away from my PC, in order to "replendish" my "out of the box thinking".
I know i'm not the first to say it, but the game really feels a lot like Portal, except T.O.M. feels more logicaly inclined than GLADOS. And it's actually here where I believe The Turing Test triumphs Portal. During the game, through the documents and audio logs, we find the land crew's side of the story. And through the conversations Ava and T.O.M. have, we are given his side of the story, and he tries to explain to us through logic, tht he did no wrong. In this, T.O.M. feels a lot like V.I.C.K.Y., from I Robot.
While in Portal (at least the first, I haven't played Portal 2), I feel we are never given a reason of why GLADOS behaves in the way she does, she's just a murdering lying robot (don't get me wrong, she's awesome, but seems to have no reasons to be like she is, other than something going awfully wrong with her programming).
Totally recomended for those who, like me, enjoy overthinking stuff.

Unveil's poor user Interface and lack of content make it hard to recommend for the price. Wayward seems to be the game Unveil was trying to be so I'm going to try it instead. If you still want to try Unveil wait for a sale.

This is almost a neutral for me, as there are definately aspects of the game that I like (such as a lack of combat and the absence of an apocolyptic world, the presence of either of which I detest in games). If Unveil was more evenly balanced or offered variable difficulty settings, my recommendation could change, but, in it's current form, it's really more of a death simulator than a survival simulator. If that appeals to you, then this might be the game for you.
Some mechanics, however, seem to be fatally unbalanced. For example: Fishing. Avoid it at ALL costs! Why? Because it costs 2 energy to dig for worms, you only get a worm about 25% of the time, the rods cost a LOT of energy to make, and the fish you catch, once cooked on a campfire that costs 5 energy to light (to say nothing of the pickup costs on the wood fuel), are generally worth only 5 energy each. So, you spend a good 50 energy, minimum, getting fishing stuff and end up with a handful of fish worth half that cooked, if you're lucky. Fishing is a good way to die quickly, and is basically an utterly useless skill because of this. It's just not worth the energy it costs.
That said, there are other game mechanics that, at least, will keep you alive in some scenarios, but you starve incredibly fast. Even in Subnautica (where you are swimming all the time), you don't starve this quickly. In my humble opinion, this game is just too difficult, and that makes it hard for players like me to enjoy. I gave it a fair try, but I can't bring myself to recommend it. In four hours of gameplay, I managed to clear the first two "Tutorials", after having to restart each at least a half-dozen times. Here's to hoping it improves one day (as it's an interesting game concept), but, for now, I'd advise others to pass on this one.

Personal Rating: 6 of 10
ToTD is a railed-shooter that provides both mouse and keyboard gameplay. Yes there is also House of The Dead bundled with this game without any DLCs. The game is decent if you are simply looking to improve your typing skills and aiming with mouse aiming and response skill. You will also need to be rather observant to notice unlockables and power up items during the game.
My beef with the game is that there is a really serious bug which causes mutants to have missing texture. Very often you see mutants with missing head and arms or torso. While this doesn't affect you in anyway in ToTD, it may get frustrating when you miss a shot in HoTD specially when you are gunning for achievement. It seemed to happen to both graphics card brand and there are no known fixes for it.
For a railed shooter, the game is pretty well made. Scene are skipped when you killed the mutants beforehand but it will still focus when there are collectibles. This is how detailed the developer went. However, the game comes with a real lousy plot and dialogue. I know the game is made this way, dark humour and very 80s feel but overdoing it really kills off the mood because it only gets annoying (specially the swearing part). I find that I am skipping cut-scene mainly because to this.
Gameplay is repetative with limited mutants type or behaviour that changes gameplay but there are unique bosses across each chapter. Mutants sometimes appear out of thin-air and bosses moving and dodging across the screen for you to find the right opportunity to shoot. In ToTD, all of these makes no different as you simply await the letters or words or sentences to appear and type them. HoTD offers a variety of guns and upgrades which all behaves differently and really impacts the gameplay which is a huge plus side to the game.
DLCs are optional as it only adds different sentences or word to the game. Do take note that you need to manually enable this feature in-game as I manage to complete the game without having experienced the DLC even once.
Graphics are rather outdated as the game was developed back in the 2000s and the textures are not updated as well. They do support 1080 resolution but I can't really see the difference because I was playing with default resolution first when I start up the game. Anti-Aliasing makes not much of a different too as I can still clearly see the pixels on the edge of the models.
One thing that I hate most from the game is that you need to complete the entire story before it unlocks the Hardcore mode for ToTD and Directors Cut mode for HoTD and after completing the Directors Cut, then only for the Hardcore Mode to unlock. The Directors Cut allows you to explore addtional places or rooms which was not made available before but 80 to 85% is still the same old chapter.
There is a multiplayer option but I haven't found the opportunity to try them out as there are no community.
So overall, this is a pretty decent game if you can overlook the above set back, even better if its on sale!
