Dark Souls is an action role-playing video game developed by FromSoftware and published by Namco Bandai Games for PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, and Microsoft Windows. A spiritual successor to FromSoftware's Demon's Souls, it is the second installment in the Souls series of games. The game was self-published and released in Japan in September 2011, and worldwide by Namco Bandai Games the following month.
In August 2012, the "Prepare to Die" edition of Dark Souls was released for Windows, featuring additional content previously unavailable to PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 users. In October 2012, the additional content from the Windows version was released as downloadable content for consoles under the subtitle Artorias of the Abyss. Dark Souls takes place in the fictional kingdom of Lordran. Players assume the role of a cursed undead character who begins a pilgrimage to discover the fate of his kind.
Dark Souls received critical acclaim upon its release and is considered to be one of the best video games ever made, with critics praising its combat depth, intricate world design, and deeply rooted lore. However, the game's difficulty received mixed reviews. While some praised the challenge it provides, others criticized it for being unnecessarily unforgiving. The PC version of the game was less well-received, with criticism aimed at numerous technical issues, bugs, and crashes. By April 2013, the game had sold over two million copies worldwide. The PC version was the second most played Games for Windows Live title in 2012 based on unique users. The game spawned two sequels, Dark Souls II and III, released in 2014 and 2016 respectively.

The Cave is less of a full fledged adventure game and more of a compartmentalized adventure game. You choose 3 of 7 characters to enter the cave and each character will have their own puzzle level with 3 constant puzzle levels that the player must always play through.
For the old school adventure aficionados, the Cave won't be a challenge and may not live up to the experiences of games such as Monkey Island. For the rest the Cave sits as an enjoyable puzzle game with simple control schemes and interesting puzzle levels.
There are 7 total characters each with a different special ability, the only issue I have with the abilities is that most of them are really only used in their specific levels, otherwise some of the abilities are pretty useless through out the rest of the game. There are characters that will allow you to get through certain puzzles quicker than normal but no puzzle requires a character outside of the main character for that story. Each character has their own story to tell, mostly told through their own level as well as through the storyboards that you pick up throughout the game.
Due to only being able to play 3 characters at a time, multiple playthroughs of the game are needed to see everyone's ending. This only causes problems when you have to play the default puzzles that always show up in the game. It would have been better if there was say 6 default puzzles and 3 random ones would be dropped in everytime you played to keep the player guessing as to which puzzle was next. I got bored of the default puzzles real quick after playthrough 5 and up.
The main dialogue in the game comes from the Cave itself and is really well written. Sure you'll get bored of it after playing through the game several times but on first play through it's enjoyable to listen to.
The Cave is an adventure game worth playing but don't come in expecting it to replicate the old school adventure games.

I didn't buy The Cave immediately when it was originally released and this is mainly because I'm not a Ron Gilbert, Tim Schafer, or Double Fine fanboy. I like all of those things, but the only Ron Gilbert game I ever played was Maniac Mansion (which was great, but I was like 8 years old), and both Tim Schafer and Double Fine have shown me that they can do as much bad as good sometimes (cough ... Brutal Legend .. cough). I did eventually acquire The Cave though and having finally played it, found I enjoyed it.
Right up front, the presentation of this game is top notch. The art, controls (I used an Xbox controller), and sound were excellent. The core conceit of the game design (choosing 3 out of 7 characters to go through the cave) I felt was a bit lacking though. The game makes concessions for your not having certain characters (and their abilities) with you and with the exception of completely optional cave painting unlocks and very minor shortcuts, your choice of characters is purely narrative. This isn't horrible, but it means you'll have to play through the game 3 times to get all the character stories and content, repeating the non-character specific areas of the game each time.
The actual control of the multiple characters works rather well and for the most part the puzzles designed to rely on them are interesting as opposed to frustrating. My one gripe with the controlling multiple characters is the backtracking that takes place for each one in many instances. While there are checkpoint-like locations where the two other characters will instantly appear at the side of your controlled character in order to alleviate the tedium of treading the same ground again, some puzzles still require going back and forth through the same area with two or more characters in order to solve a puzzle.
In the end, The Cave is a pleasant blend of adventure and puzzle genres with what I would consider to be an entry-level to intermediate difficulty. What it may lack in complexity it makes up for in charm and I'd recommend it if you're looking for a mild puzzler with good personality.

"It's a killer puzzle-box, designed to scare me to death, and I'm trapped inside. Must be Christmas!"
This is a very enjoyable Portal-like puzzle game (70ish levels, maybe 20 hours). The gameplay is just as enjoyable as Portal 2 (which is one of my all-time favorites). The ambient music and voice acting are very good. When I first stated playing, The default settings gave me motion sickness and had to put this title aside for a bit. Checking the discussion pages showed that others had the same issues. I did find a solution (Field of View to maximum, Mouse sensitivity to minimum, Motion blur off, tweaking the quality until I could keep the FPS at 60). It helps that I have a GTX 970M graphics card on my laptop. I stongly recommend doing this before you get started (it would even help if the mouse sensitivity could be further dropped).
The first two chapters are very easy, teaching the player how to get used to the game world (similar to the first 10 levels of the original Portal). Then the difficulty ramps up and the fun begins. There are a total of 70ish levels, and many more interactable items than Portal 2 (i.e. light-bridge). Had to peek at the discussions for a hint on a chapter 4 and 5 puzzle, the others I eventually got on my own.
Some of the puzzles involve time-dependent actions, maybe more-so than in Portal 2.
Bought this on sale, I'd even pay full price for this. HIghly recommended. Definitely got the value for my money.

With only a single jumpscare in the beginning to weed out the weak, and absolute psychological trauma throughout, Cry of Fear is the scariest game I have personally ever played. It will scare you as a viewer, it will scare you as a gamer, it will scare you as a human being, and with the sole exception of the initial beginning jumpscare, Cry of Fear knows it doesn't need loud noises to do this. Sometimes, fear is the silent enemy the size of a two story building, slowly walking its way toward you over a long distance, and the luck of discovering him before he reaches your location. Fear is the choice between Health, Light, and a Weapon when you can only choose two, and the dark of the forest is black as pitch. Fear is what you make of it, and this game will show you the way.
It's difficult to put into words the sheer quality contained within this deceptively simple-looking masterpiece. It may be free, it may have started out as a mod for Half Life, but don't be fooled. Cry of Fear is both my favorite Horror Game of all time, and one of my favorite games period. Since playing it, I've found myself innoculated to the entire horror genre of games a whole. No game has scared me quite like Cry of Fear has, and I flit from horror game to horror game now in an attempt to recreate the feeling. But in a word, what truly sold me, among some of it's other incredible qualities:
Dedication.
Going back through the game again with Developer Commentary enabled, you really begin to understand what a passion project this game was. Team Psykskallar mapped out locations in their own hometown and remade them faithfully in game. There is one particular audio track near the end of the game, during which it is storming, when mentions that the lightning sounds in game were actually recorded from actual lightning storms that the team recorded outside their building.
It might not seem like much, but in the days of over-produced cookie cutter Triple-A garbage that comes out year after year, The passion Team Psykiller showed just to get a simple audio recording for background noise impressed the hell out of me.
I could talk about this game's "Fear Factor" (which is substantial, and has easily stood the test of time). I could talk about the gameplay (the inventory system is particular is genius), I could talk about the story (which even after the first playthrough will still make you feel uncomfortable), but in the end, all you need to know about Cry of Fear is the amount of passion that went into this game. It is a game few can handle, it is a game made with love, and if you are looking for a game that will scare the life out of you without breaking your eardrums, look no further.
Good Luck.

I almost couldn’t believe the premise of this shooter when I first saw it. Really…you kill zombies by typing words correctly? Although I’ve admittedly not played the House of the Dead games outside of arcades, I felt like I couldn’t pass up this opportunity when I saw it. I’ve never played the original House of the Dead: Overkill either, although it is baked-in along with this new keyboard-based game.

As far as game mechanics go, it’s pretty much exactly what it advertises – words will pop up on the screen above zombies, and your success is based upon how quickly and accurately you can key in those words. Your characters move from room to room on rails, sometimes barreling through an entire squadron of undead, other times not moving forward until you’ve essentially committed zombie genocide. This is one of the few games in which I feel the DLC is needed, as it increases the dictionary of words used with interesting themes, such as a Shakespeare pack or a sports lexicon. Some of the words and phrases are absolutely wacky, and I loved the challenge it provided for both my fingers and my mind.

As for the story – that’s where the real charm of this game is found. The entire adventure is presented as a grindhouse-style flick, and there’s a filter over the action that shows film noise and burns, which I felt really set a tone right from the start. Every cutscene is appropriately ludicrous and crass; the main characters swear and curse with incredible conviction, which is actually addressed within the dialogue itself during the few quiet moments between levels. Traveling between setpieces, the characters will occasionally make a comment on their situation, or their relationship in regards to each other. It’s an incredibly honest approach to the standard zombie apocalypse gore fest, and at one point the male protagonists recognize that they are stereotypical macho men going who have to save the strongest female protagonist. I really wasn’t expecting a type-‘em-up zombie game to have an interesting, existential view of the genre as a whole, and yet there it was.

Otherwise, the game is comparatively offensive and comical as an episode of South Park. You’ll hear scat jokes as you attack a giant-headed, wheelchair-bound, Stephen-Hawking-esque zombie, for example. But, the game stays so consistent with how ham-fisted it is with being distasteful that it actually is engaging and fun throughout. Had the game attempted to be serious and grim, it would have failed miserably.

I did attempt to play the original House of the Dead: Overkill which is included, but the options for controller support is very scant. There’s no option to adjust the reticle sensitivity, and as a result I felt like the crosshairs were flying all over the screen, even during slow-motion sections. It feels like the typing aspect of this game is the main attraction, which certainly isn’t a bad thing.

I don’t know the next time that one of these House of the Dead typing games will be released, but I enjoyed my time with this one so much that I’ll probably grab whatever comes next as well. Recommended for anyone looking for something entirely new to the shooting genre.

This is one of the few Free to Play games out there that is truley free, as in, there is no way to spend money on this game. No weapon skins, no map packs, no membership. All the content is readily available from the moment you install the it. This is quite commendable, since with the amount of weapons, maps and gamemodes currently in the game there's easily 100 hours+ worth of content.
The gameplay is unique in that it rewards slowing down to take your shots, but still highly emphasises moving about in order to avoid getting hit. Whiskey bottles that restore your health are scattered throught the maps, but recharge slowly so encourage learning the maps well and having good positioning in order to maxime the time you stay alive. Drinking whiskey also causes your screen to sway, making it harder to hit enemies the drunker you are, which makes for an interesting twist on health gain since it has a tangible downside.
Positioning is key due to a variety of factors, such as most weapons having long reload times, Chests that have higher tier weapons and whiskey that restores health are scattered throughout each map, and the fact that many players will constantly be moving about means that you need to know what might be where and when.

The game is great if you just want to sit down, relax, and have a good ol' game of cowboy shooting, however, there is a ranking system and leader board for each of the official game modes if you want to play in a more competetive way. Also, many of the guns have very high skill ceilings. For example, the Sharps Rifle is a one hit kill sniper rifle which functions just like the AWP in CS:GO, only it's far more punishing if you miss, since it only loads one shot at a time. It can only be obtained from the golden chest, giving death some actual weight and encouraging you to take more caution with the weapon.
The last note I have is the approach to gun balance. Every kill you get awards you notriety, which is essentially just points. Different weapons award different amounts of notriety depending on how powerful they are, e.g. the Colt Navy and the Colt Walker arre both six shot revolvers, however the Navy takes three shots to the body to kill an enemy, whereas the Walker only takes one.
The Navy on the other hand reloads far faster and awards 10 notriety per kill, whilst the Walker takes ages to reload and only awards 4 notriety. In addition, the Walker can only be obtained from the golden chest, whilst you can spawn with the Navy.
This allows powerful weapons to exist in the game without them being straight upgrades to the weaker weapons. Limiting the availbility of the weapons also means that dying to them doesn't make them feel overpowered, since once you kill the person using the weapon you don't have to worry about it again for a while, or can even pick it up and use it yourself.
The system function much like having the Golden Gun in Goldeneye, and the game does a great job of replicating that feeling of splitscreen multiplayer shooters from many years ago.
On the whole, the good things:
I'd say any downsides of the game differ from person to person, I can't personally thing of anything major that makes my experience worse other than my own performance, but other people may find other things that they dislike about it, whether it be the design, or the maps, or the gamemodes.
At the end of the day you're not losing anything by downloading it and giving it a try, so that's what I recommend you do.
I wouldn't say it's a great game in the sense that it'll blow your socks off with its graphics or high tech engine or revolutionary new mechanics or whatever, I would say it's a great game in the sense that everything it does,

I want to like this game, but there's a few fundamental problems with it's current F2P model, and just the game in general, that make it more frustrating than fun.
My biggest issue is that you rarely get to do what you want to do. Now that it's an F2P model, this is BAD. I wouldn't mind playing different classes if I had things unlocked for them, but 6 hours in I've barely been able to unlock a single character. I've only been able to use that character twice in about 12 matches because it always gives me a different class to play, often times when I'm the only person with priority set to that specific class. I can't think of any other F2P game where you can spend hours grinding the currency and still not get to use the thing you unlocked. It's especially bad because free players literally only have 2 permanent unlocked characters, that being Markov the Assault guy and Goliath, the monster. It's either them, or whoever is free at every role that week.
Also, the monster is simply not a satisfying game experience for someone not familiar with the game. I understand some people love it and do well with it, but new players are not those people. Even reading some guides on how to succeed with the limited Monster choice I have access to at the moment, I find I'm dead after the first or second dome nearly every game. The concepts to avoid being tracked well enough that you can at least reach Stage 2 are simply not taught to you in the tutorial and even after a few hours of play are still completely foreign. Every time I've been the Monster, I've been completely rolled and I'm not sure what I could have done different.
It's a game doomed to fail because the gameplay experience isn't consistent. Being the monster or being one of the hunters is a COMPLETELY different experience. Being good at one doesn't translate to being good at the other. Because of these reasons, I cannot recommend this game beyond a couple of hours. By all means, give it a shot yourself because hey free game with really high production values, but it just wasn't for me.

Here is the second part of the
series, with a new protagonist and even a new historical era for us to discover. After Medieval Middle East in the first game, Renaissance Italy sure is a livelier place and a time period to experience. But not without the infamous cloak and dagger politics either. Boy, was all these a great improvement over the first title! In means of story, things are just getting started; and in means of gameplay, Ubisoft learned from experience and managed to set the bar higher.
So, what happens after Desmond's realization that the war between assassins and templars never ended? Well, I warn you that next two paragraphs will contain spoilers concerning the first game, so if you are yet to play the original title and willing to do at some point, skip this part. At the end of our previous game, Desmond and Lucy broke out of the Abstergo lab, with the revelation Lucy was an assassin all along. Now, they are staying low in an assassin hideout, while a team works with a new version of Animus on Desmond, to try and find information concerning other Pieces of Eden, buried deep within Desmond's memories. As various clues we have gathered at the end of the previous chapter implied, we skip a generation to arrive Renaissance Italy in out memory line to track the next Piece of Eden, and as a result, we are introduced with a new ancestor of Desmond: Ezio Auditore de Firenze.
Series of memories here in this chapter, covers Ezio's lifespan from his birth 'till his mid-forties, portraying a story of betrayal, vengeance, acceptance and frustration as the end reveals a grander bite than poor Ezio ever bargained for. Soon after our story starts, the young Florentine nobleman's mischief and debauchery comes to a sudden end with a persecution, that will change his life forever. From there on, he vows to hunt parties responsible for the tragedy that befall on him, and we accompany him as he proceeds with it. After silent, stubborn and arrogant Altair; Ezio is a contrasting protagonist, with a Mediterranean sense of humor and a taste for all kinds of earthly delights, yet also the meticulous, with a libertarian outlook that all assassins share. Whom would I prefer? Well, I think I'm still an Altair gal at this point, but we'll be together with Ezio for two more games, so that can change.
The setting is Renaissance Italy, and we travel through and between Florence and Venice, witnessing the rise and fall of Medici and Borgia families, decades in between. Cities are bustling with all kinds of arts, wonderous examples of Renaissance architecture and various discoveries of engineering. As another trademark of AC series, we are to encounter many historical figures, either as allies or foes; and live a part of history itself under an exciting conspiracy twist. All characters are impressively fleshed out, with their own accurate backgrounds and agendas. The cityscapes are well used in this one too, with genuine landmarks; and every scene is another opportunity for a breath-taking screenshot.
The gameplay itself improved considerably too, with countless side quests to deal, parkour missions to run, assassination contracts to accept, assassin tombs to discover, templar vaults to raid and a good deal of collectibles that actually serve various purposes upon their completion! There are also imprints left by the previous subject of experiment labeled as "the truth" for us to discover the origin of all this conflict. Upon discovery, these clues present us some really complicated, yet well thought puzzles, deciphering bits of information about assassin and templar involvement in history! As another bonus of the gameplay, money is introduced, so you can look for treasure, rob your defeated foes, accumulate an income and rebuild your family villa in Monteriggioni – and even adorn your halls with famous artworks of the era too. Sure, there are a couple of downsides to the game, like most weaponry that we will encounter providing little to no improvement aside a couple chosen ones, or climbing AI still being ridiculously clumsy – but nothing that would break your immersion. At the end of the day, you are in for hours of gameplay which you wouldn't be bored of, not even for a second.
If you are yet to experience
series, this is a good enough place to start, covering the basics of the previous game and improving upon it in means of playability. This is where things get interesting, revealing the centuries long conspiracy a bit more. We'll see more of Ezio to come in
- the second part of Ezio Trilogy - and see what else fate stores for the beloved Renaissance assassin.

I used to be a big fan of Typing of the Dead. I thought it was a cool way to teach people how to type with speed and accuracy. However, this game... It's just not fun. I might not have the credibility of those who have done full run throughs or played this game for over 7 hours, but hear me out.
The most important part of any game is the first impression of it. If the first impression is not very exciting, then this game will not be very appealing towards its audience. This game has that same problem: a very weak first impression. It tries to make a very floppy story with cliche's everywhere in its comedic-satire on the whole film industry. However, that lackluster story makes this game really hard to play.
Along with, the biggest selling point to the first Typing of the Dead was that it had fun phrases that were childish, but could make you laugh. This game does not really have those, if they are later in the game then I have not seen them being that I'm only on level 4. That lack of fun, childish phrases really siphons the whole thought about the game being about learning how to type.
This game lacks the sheer fun quality to it. Am I saying that this is a bad game? No, it's just not fun. I would not recommend buying this game. I would try to find the original (if you still can) and playing that because it is much more fun than this game.

This game is absolutely fantastic. 10/10 in my book (for early access)
Graphics: The graphics are top notch. This is a very pretty game with great optimization. Currently driving 1440p with a GTX 1070, i7 6700k, and 16 gigs at 2100mhz. My frames are a steady 60FPS and dip occasionally into the 50s when Im near hydrogen particles. (I guess that needs worked on a bit). Have yet to find a visual bug of any sort in my experience thus far.
Crafting: The crafting mechanic is solid. You will need to gather nodes to build or craft anything. Its the typical survival/crafting play style. Mine nodes to build this thing, which will allow you to build this thing, and so on...
Survival aspect: Kind of non existent at the moment. Your food and water will go down slowly over time but its nothing that a few berries and a glass of water wont fix. When you get into a fight and your suit is breached nothing a little endless ducktape cant cure. Its much easier at this current time than say games like Rust, Ark, The Forest, ect...
The PVE is awesome but anyone with a couple hours experience in any FPS game will have the wildlife wipped.
Overall game mechanics: This is where the game really shines. Everything has a certain polish not common in early access games. The attention to detail is a breath of fresh air and really puts yourself into the game. All the little things like third person animations and gun play all seam very tight and right. The inventory is well thought out. The droids that follow you around and do your bidding is just well, awesome.
Multiplayer: Ehhh, kinda there, kind of not... I bought this for my friend and I and we really just had a hell of a time. The colony system seems to not be working correctly yet and spawning so far away from each other was a drag. Would like to see some form of a friend option when in game to see each others locations and base sites. Tried to play on several populated servers but could not build anything so whats the point?
Conclusion: This is an awesome early access single player game in its current state. I can not wait! for more content and fixes from the devs. If you have a decent video card you will benefit greatly from the amazing graphics. I recommend this game to everybody. For the price you cant loose. 10/10 all day long.

Fistful of Frags is the best worst game I've ever played. It's ridiculous, and it's annoying, but it's also hilarious. It's got a really solid community, and something about it is unbelievably fun to me. It's difficult for me to explain why I like it so much because it's such a weird, goofy game. But I really believe that this game survives because of its quirks.
It's free, and it's subject to change. If you don't like that, this game definitely isn't for you. If you want a consistent, clean experience, don't even waste your time here. However, I think that this unpredictable nature is what gives the game its charm. One day you'll hop on to find your favorite maps arranged slightly differently or see a change in the loadout options, and you have to be okay with it.
Don't take Fistful of Frags seriously. If you want a serious, fast paced multiplayer FPS, many of those exist, and you won't find it here. If you want a lighthearted, fun, and funny game to play when you aren't in the mood to experience some large, beautiful thing, Fistful of Frags is a great game to have in your library.

Where do I even begin?
Well, there's roughly 70 puzzles (10 per chapter) + intermission areas. The quality of the textures are okay, but they do have a tendency to go out of focus so you might encounter some eye strain. If there was music, I didn't notice nor remember what it sounds like.
T.O.M. has a great voice and personality. Ava, less than so but still good. Lot of mystery and intrigue going around and a lot of things that make you go "wait, what is this?" and stuff. Weird stuff. Good weird. The optional stuff just makes things weirder.
Controversial subject matter. Personally, I'm heavily one-sided on this material in regards to the game's plot, but I see the potential for an argument to ensue. The execution of this subject matter, though: fantastic. Like, I was torn at one point and I didn't know what was right or wrong. Cognitive dissonance at its finest. Messes with your humanity, in a way, and tears your mind in two between what's logical and what's moral and stuff.

Now as far as puzzle games go this is a very good game, it will never match the portal series and trying to compare any other game to it will fail. If a game however, was to even come close? it would be this. It has no humour and the portal humour is one of a kind, the story is short but sweet and the mechanics really do make you think. The story explores the ideas of consciousness, morality, and not surprisingly the Turing Tests. It's intelligent, bonus puzzles reveal bonus transcripts or video logs that add to the story, the game is very well made and I had to think about it and the answers a lot more than I have other games.
To keep it short, if you like puzzle games or even story games, you'll love this. If you're looking for humour and a casual game it's not for you, but i highly reccomend this game and so do many others.

The comparisons between this, Portal, and The Talos Principle are well founded, and I compare them myself as follows.
Portal is essentially the perfect base. It is an excellently polished game, with good story and atmosphere, excellent gameplay and balance, and a good amount of polish. The game is just as long as it needs to be.
Talos takes great gameplay and story, but it scales up the challenge far too much for the common audience. It is the longest of the three, but doesn't last too long, being the most full of the three games.
Then there is this game. It is the most story focused of the three, after after playing the other two I'm actually rather disappointed. It has 70 levels with 7 bonus puzzles, as compared to portal's 19 +epilogue, but I ended up spending more time to finish portal than this. The puzzles are more of a gateway to the story than real challenges, and most can very easily be completed within a minute, with the most difficult taking me no more than 5 to figure out. The game suffers from quantity over quality, as none of the puzzles are memorable. On top of that, there is very little noticable polish, with a most of the stylistic choices being more of an annoyance than adding to the experience. The main character's walk animation in non-puzzle maps gets in the way more than anything, and the visual filters that are applied to certain situations, such as moving between puzzles are either disorienting, or difficult to look at for any period of time, or both. And gameplay-wise, there is a notable lack of polish, as even the most basic action of putting a puzzle piece into a port requires more precision than should be necessary. There is even descrepancies in the story, with timelines being poorly put together. There is a lot of story that can be gathered from the environment, including audio logs and readable texts, but none of this is acknowledged in the game whatsoever and can be completely skipped with no real impact. The story props only tell you what is going to be directly stated in required voice overs later on in the game anyways.
Now, with all of that being said, this is an excellent game by it's own merit. There is clever puzzle design, and very good puzzles later on, though they do feel a bit too short. There is a fantastic plot twist that introduces a very interesting and decently implemented puzzle mechanic. And the ending is incredibly powerful and decently set up.
If I could ask for anything more from this game, it would be more content, and more polish. The story is good, but there is so much more to be built upon thats just either passed over quickly or ignored.

It can be argued that The Turing Test is not as deep and complex than Portal or the Talos Principle, and that the puzzles are way easier, but it also can't be denied that the game was really well done. If the puzzles seam too easy for you, each chapter offers an additional puzzle that requires to think way way out of the box to be solve, and will reward you with more information, not essential, but giving you more insight into the philosophy of the game.
The graphic are not looking to impress you. It's basic Unreal Engine graphic, which is good, since we can focus on solving those puzzles (I'm not joking, in Talos Principle, I spent so much time sight seeing, which is good too, but somehow makes you take a bit too long to finish), and the sound atmosphere and music score are discreet and help you focus.
Well, I liked that game obviously. I liked the story, which is really well explored, I liked the puzzles which were at the right balance between diificulty and casuality (and always very logical) so you don't get frustrated and wait too long on each one, and I liked that there were additional information hidden behind some more unusual puzzle.
I hope to see more games from this team.

This one gets a mixed review from me.
The Cave calls itself a puzzle-platformer, but the puzzles are on the trivial side "Here's a locked door. And look -- there is key. Oh, what should you do?". The platforming is also on the easy side and mainly a way to have something to do while ferrying said key to said door.
The environments are visually interesting. Each character has their own ability, and a unique game section, most of which have some combination of plot/backstory related to that character.  That's the highlight of the game; it is fun to see the special areas, and a few of them have genuinely interesting puzzles.
Except there is one extremely annoying aspect: You can take three characters per game. So to experience all seven stories, you will have to play the game three times -- and the common areas aren't interesting enough to make play number three be other than a drag. Oh, and if you avoid spoilers by not reading how to do the achievements until after your play-through, it is quite likely to need a fourth play-through.
So, it is a mixed bag. You will have to decide whether the annoying ones outweigh the potential fun.

The Cave is a 2D side-scroller, puzzle platformer game. You choose a combination of 3 out of the 7 characters and descend to the Cave. The Cave features great humor and comedy especially the narration itself. The puzzles are not that challenging. Only two character stories gave me a hard a time. (The Monk and The Time Traveler) Each character story has their own key puzzle part. (meaning a "hard" part of the story) The combination of characters you choose affects your path through the cave but not entirely since there will be parts of your journey where you'll be doing the same puzzle over and over again especially when you tend to miss quite a lot of the collectible Cave paintings. For the whole part, the Cave is a bit short since I'm more indulged in heavy puzzle games making The Cave puzzles not much of a challenge but it's a game worth playing. I recommend this game to anyone who wants to experience a humor and comedy like no other with the addition of great stories and a puzzle platformer gameplay. This price is a bit too high for the game itself so I also highly encourage anyone to buy it when it's on sale, more preferably when it's on a 66% discount or higher.
Pros:
+ Good graphics
+ Great narration (has a lot of humor)
+ Has great storylines with their own unique twists (One story per character)
Cons:
+ The puzzles are very repetitive when you want to clear the game with a new set of characters.
+ The Price is too much for the gameplay itself.
Overall, it's a great game and I totally enjoyed the game and story despite the easy puzzles.

While not refined and overall great as other survival-horror games such as Silent Hill 2 or the old Resident Evil games, this game does provide an awesome experience of horror, along with providing an incredible showcase of what modders can really do even with a roughly 20 year old engine.
Singleplayer is great, and like other survival horror games there are unlockables scattered throughout the game which you can unlock and use in future playthroughs. There are mods for the game which include custom maps, which are also great, although obviously not the main reason for playing this game.
The multiplayer is also great, although many miss the multiplayer since there are no visible servers in the server menu. What you have to do is port forward, or use Hamachi or other programs to get multiplayer working, all of which can be set up by the guides in the community, very helpful guides too. The soundtrack is also pretty good, immersing you into the game more. In true survival horror fashion there are multiple endings which play if certain perameters are met, all which equal up to 4 endings with a secret ending too.
Don't be afraid to pick this up, especially since it's free on Steam or on ModDB. Do note that this game has a lot of technical issues, so don't be afraid to seek help if you encounter a problem. If you like this game then you should also check out Afraid of Monsters, made by the same guys as the people who made Cry of Fear.

Cry of Fear is a game made by same dev who made Afraid of Monsters mod for Half-Life 1. Cry of Fear actually started as another mod for Half-Life 1 and is available as a mod too, becoming stand-alone game only in 2013.

Some more. Otherwise, all jolly atmospheres and enemies that twitch around and scream at you, begging for a shotgun.

ACR (so far) has added more about Subject 16 and his place in everything, which is fascinating. AC2, though, seems to have a lot more material. The storyline was long, deep, and ended in a way I couldn't have predicted. It's too late after Portal, Antichamber, etc. to really capitalise on that, and its lack of VR capability means it doesn't capture a market it's perfect for. Yet as a product taken out of context, it's still a very good title that doesn't outstay its welcome.
As a puzzle game, its puzzles are perhaps the most important aspect. There's only one puzzle you can't do at first (it's an optional one), although you could guess your way to the answer if you had the patience, but generally the puzzles are all pretty easy. There's one or two that require a bit more thought or bending of the rules, though I don't think most players will struggle with it at all.
The other main aspect of the game is its story, and I think this is where it excels. The story is really quite captivating and thought-provoking, and I felt like I was constantly trying to work out where it'd go or how it'd resolve itself, and it goes quite deep. It's not ARG level, but some players will definitely want to replay this game a few times to get all the story pieces together.
Overall;
A great story that, despite easy and largely unfrustrating puzzles, is well worth the time.

This game takes a simple concept and turns into an experience that is very clever. There are 600 puzzles total, giving you many puzzles for a low price.
Horizontal words are arranged in rows. Reading these lines will give you the clue about what the word they want you to guess is. You can move the letters in these horizontal rows in order to create the answer to the solution vertically (the white column).
Although the clues are minimilistic, it gives you enough of a clue that you usually able to figure it out. Puzzles range from 3 letter words to 8 letter words. There are different themes, and depending on your knowledge, some puzzles can be very challenging. The movie pack for example is probably one of the more cryptic ones, given that they are only allowed to give you so much information. Even when you are stumped, you can use a clue to reveal one letter at a time to help with the puzzle. The clues recharge quickly, and there are no penalties, allowing you to use them as many times as you'd like. Even when the clues are a bit far fetched and difficult to figure out, it's not too hard. Comparitively, the rest of the game is pretty easy to figure out.
It has a nice relaxing sound track and easy achievements. It does not have cloud saves - so make sure not to do 39/40 puzzles in one pack on one computer and then move to another one, you won't be able to continue where you left off. Would recommend this to people who love crossword puzzles or other similar puzzle type games.

Fun, creative word game.
How it works:  You are given a clue arranged in words stacked on top of each other forming a sentence.  One word per line.  Using that clue you have to move the words left or right until the correct letters for the solution are in the lighted up vertical line.  You can see examples in the screenshots and game's description.
The game is arranged in different categories.  3 letter words, 4 letter words, etc. up to 8 letters, then categories like Food, Science, Animals, Fashion, and Misc. categories.
To be honest the game is fairly easy.  There is a cheat button which will reveal one of the letters.  I have used that a few times when I was stumped and didn't want to sit there thinking forever.
What I really like about the game is the creative clue descriptions.  They had to really be clever sometimes to have only so many words and with the correct letters for the clue.
This would be a nice family game.  Everyone sit around the screen and the first to shout out the answer wins a point.  Keep going until a set number of points is reached or a time limit, whatever you decide.  So far it's been family-friendly, no risque words, but I have not completed the game yet, so don't take my word for it yet.
The pace is pretty quick, until you get stumped.  I play for about 15 minutes a day before I get bored and want to play something else.  So this is not one of those puzzle games where you play for hours at a time.
Overall, I recommend this game.  Price is cheap and seems good for the amount of content you get.  Graphics are minimal, as seen in screenshots.  Sounds are limited; I think there's a sound for getting a word right but I don't remember much else.

phrase shift is almost like a crossword in some ways; testing your knowledge and vocabulary, but it works differently, in which you slide words for individual letters to form the answer vertically.
it's a fun game in general, but there are some quirks to it. firstly, it's very american. *spoiler*
secondly, some of the 'descriptions' feels almost forced on and/or abstract, just to have the letters available. this makes the puzzle almost awkward and confusing sometimes. of course, i do appreciate that it's not easy to find words that could make up the description sometimes, that still has the letters needed to form the answer.
finally, i think the 'reveal' button, should have a more limited usage. perhaps just once or twice per round tops. this is because this feature makes the game 'too easy' to beat i suppose. or perhaps do away with it altogether, and add a 'hint' or 'clue' button, where a brief, but further description is given, without revealing any letters. would add to the challenge a bit more.
all in all, it's a good concept, but could still do with some work. one thing that comes to mind, is perhaps breaking free of some american-centric questions, like name of places and presidents (unless it's something, or someone famous where the rest of the world has a chance of answering, like a lincoln or kennedy), and widen it to a more global thing. questions involving europe, asia, africa, the rest of the world too. just a thought.
i'm leaning towards a thumbs up still, because it's a good concept. would like to see a sequel perhaps, with some rework to it; maybe sometime in the near future.

This little puzzle game has a lot going for it, probably - it's an interesting concept, it's very cheap, and it's vaguely reminiscent of solving crossword puzzle hints. In the end, though, I can't recommend it.
Some clues are insultingly simple, such as the one with "bee" as a solution. Others, especially in the "movies" section, are impossible without either extensive guesswork or specific cultural knowledge. (For that matter, some of the "movies" puzzles contain spoilers!) And some phrases aren't especially difficult, but just kind of stretch things in an awkward way. There are even a couple cases where a puzzle or solution is repeated! So many answers are simple enough that I want to recommend this game for English learners... but they'd be completely stymied by the more obscure or awkward puzzles.
In the end, despite the crossword puzzle comparison, *none* of these puzzles gave me an especially deep feeling of satisfaction to solve. Everything was either trivial, frustrating, or just kind of blah. Perhaps most damning of all is that while I was solving the puzzles, I made a little challenge for myself to see if I could maximize the number of columns I lined up for each solution. That's right, I had to make a game within the game to keep it even mildly interesting.
I'm left with the feeling that we're actually seeing the wrong end of things: the actual *fun* game contained within this idea would be a social game where you've given the solution, have limited time to come up with a phrase like the ones that form these puzzles, and then vote on who came up with the best phrase. In other words, what we're seeing here is just the results of the real game, which the creator(s) already played without us.

This game blew my mind in so many ways. Going to break this down into pros and cons.
Cons
-Some (maybe just one) puzzles might not be solvable on your own depending on your system configuration.
-If you don't enjoy games that lack game over screens, this might not tickle your fancy.
-While the puzzles are interesting, they aren't really the most challenging.
Pros
-Just about everything else.
The writing is amazing. The world really feels alive and, like any good example of world building, you get a sense that there's a ton of information that shapes the world that you never even really see. All of the characters are relatable and it's not hard at all to grow attached to them. Some are even so interesting and amusing you'll start missing one off characters that you only see once. There are things done here that you don't see very often and the entire narrative is presented in a fresh and new way. If you enjoy story driven games, this is a MUST grab.
The gameplay is very simple. Standard walk around and interact with the world. Nothing out of the ordinary for adventure games. The interesting bits come in when the game takes full advantage of your computer and does things outside of boundries of the game itself to present puzzles and even drastically enhance the story. Some of what they did here on a technical level actually shocked me. Especially upon realizing that this was all made in RPG Maker. There's nothing complex here, but it's definitely interesting to experience.
The game's music is beautiful and adds vastly to the atmosphere. It's not something I would personally listen to in the car or on its own, but lovers of soundtracks will get a kick out of this.
The graphics and visuals are amazing if not breath taking. The designs of just about everything in the game stands out and is memorable and the "splash pages" you get for certain scenes only add to that.
As I mentioned in cons, if you aren't interested in games where most of the value lies in the story? This might not be for you. However, for the vast majority of people, I would highly recommend getting this game.

I'll start this review with saying that if you are on the edge, please, just play this game. It's worth every second that you will put into it. And honestly, this is a game best played knowing nothing more than the name.
That said,
OneShot is an RPG Maker adventure puzzle game. When I first started looking at this game, a few other games immediately came to mind. The RPG Maker pixel aesthetics reminded me of Yume Nikki, OFF, and Undertale. After playing this game, I have to say that these four games bear more similarities than just titles. Although not as bleak as Yume Nikki, the "lost in a foreign world" and "am I dreaming" concepts are easily found. In narration and style, I'd say the game is most similar to OFF, but a lot of the mechanics remind me of some of the more surreal parts of Undertale. The game is about 4 hours long, which isn't much, although there is definitely replay value. OFF and Yume Nikki offer similar playtimes, but at no cost. Undertale, on the other hand, arguably has more replay value than OneShot, yet comes at the same price. However, OneShot definitely goes to show that good things do come at a price. By the time you reach the end of this clever, cute, and entertaining game, you will be happy you parted with those ten dollars. Please buy this.

In my opinion, the best AC title to date (sorry Origins, I love you very much but ACII's still on top). The graphics may be outdated for some more nit-picky players, and AC1 actually has better graphics (at least, in my opinion), but ACII still manages to be an incredibly immersive experience. Its main locations (Firenze, Venezia, Forlì, Monteriggioni and San Gimignano) have their own characteristic aura and their own charms and even soundtrack. Firenze is passionate, colorful and vibrant. Venezia is colorful but at the same time it retains a "dreamy" feel to it. Forlì is gloomy and humid. Monteriggioni feels like home, not only because it is the headquarters of the Assassin Order, but because it's warm and welcoming. San Gimignano is a small but busy medieval city, and feels imponent. I have personally been to Firenze and Venezia before playing the game and I'm being serious when I say that the game brought me back to those cities.
Story-wise, it's very compelling. There was no moment in which I felt like the story was dragging out. And unlike other AC titles, ACII is a game that lets you become attached to the secondary characters. They have their own story and character development.
It surely is not as good as Brotherhood graphically or gameplay-wise (in Brotherhood you have many more combat and weapons options), however I do think that ACII is the best game out of the two. Brotherhood has far more side content (also very much varied), but the main story is just not as compelling as ACII's.
ACII is a classic, not only for Assassin's Creed fans, but for any gamer who enjoys a great game. If you haven't played it yet, do give it a try. If you're too scared of spending money on something you're not sure you're going to like (like me), watch a gameplay or two on Youtube, and see if you'd like to take on the experience yourself. I did it that way and found so many things on my own that those gameplays had never shown. It was totally worth it.

There are many things one could say about Dishonored.
You admire the gameplay, which ranges from stealthy non-lethal, hold-your-breath-so-they-don't-hear-you mischief to hearth pounding swordplay and tactical assassinations.
You could go on for hours about the characters, both Corvo and the NPC's.  Such as how every character has a distinct personality, and how the protagonist Corvo's character is portrayed perfectly without him ever speaking.
You could complement the story, which follows a linear path while still allowing for you, the player, to shape Corvo's personality and change the outcome of the world around you in such a way that sometimes, even when you win, you feel like you lost.
You could speak of the DLC's, which unlike many tacky add-ons and half-baked pieces of gameplay that were cut out before release, actually manage to be as high quality as the main game, while acting as a perfect experiment for the devs to test the powers they used in the second game, and bridge the stories between the two in a way that lacks spoilers, while allowing people who pick up the second game to have more context for who the villains and hero's are.
All of these things and more could be discussed, but I'll just leave it with this:
This game made me laugh.  This game brought me to the verge of tears.  This game made me angry.  This game made me smile.  This game made me consider my own morality and what actions actually warrant a lethal response.  Even with a story that typically takes about 8-10 hours, I can honestly say that Dishonored is possibly my most enjoyed game of all time.  I recommend this game to anybody and everybody, you will not regret it.

Good points missing, bad things introduced.
If you've played the previous games in the series like I have, you would probably have high expectations from this game. Equally possible, however, is the disappointment that you may find. The previous ToD I and II were truly awesome games with a thoughtful design of gameplay and at the same time focused on their educational aspect. Unfortunately much of their these are actually missing in this installment.
For starters, in this game you won't find any keyboards and Dreamcasts, which were just signatures for the previous game. Also missing were the items like molotov cocktails available for pick up, which added fun and could be life-savers. In place of these were concept arts, audio tracks, 3D models which are unlockable. Worse still, these are not collected by typing certain letters or words like you would in the previous games, but by pressing TAB key, which is rather meaningless. As these are not as noticeable as they should, this could mean that you may be better off just to press TAB key every now and then. In-game challenges (e.g. defeat 30 zombies) with rewards are also non-existent. Maintaining combos only gets your a better score instead of life bonuses. Gameplay is also straightforward without twists like answering a question as in the previous games.
Compared to the previous installments, this game is rather easy at NORMAL or HARD difficulty. But the hardcore mode, which put emphasis on accuracy, could on the other hand be too hard. In this mode, if you make a mistake in the middle of a word then the phrase would change and you will have to start over again. You would also have to type spaces, which you may find quite annoying if you're used to the previous games or the non-hardcore mode. To make things worse, if you are too slow the zombies would just keep attacking you, unlike in the previous games where they would slow down after you lost a life and give you a chance to pick up momentum again. This, coupled with the fact that you have to restart when miss, could cost you two or three lives when you make a single mistake, which could be rather frustrating. In addition, I've been in times when I noticed my mistake only after a few letters, only to know that I was already locked on the new phrase(s) which contained some same letters, which could be very confusing as I was wondering where I was. Although it could have been a good idea to require spaces as in the real world, the game failed in this aspect by not having any visual cues for spaces. Therefore I am always wondering if I've typed the spaces as I am so used to the previous games, and have lost many lives either because I had to stop and think or because I remembered it wrong, which means retyping the phrase. Another problem is the difficulty to figure out which text box corresponds to the zombie closest to you. At times I have to wait until the box changes to red before I could be sure, which could be too late. If you've noticed, in the previous installments the words got harder if you were doing well and vice versa, which kept you always under pressure to improve. It is not the case in this game.
The game offers unlimited credits at the cost of half your score, which I find not as challenging as the previous games. Also, as long as you finish a level you will unlock the next, no matter what difficulty you attempted. The minigames are somewhat cosmetic and meaningless, instead of focus on a particular area (e.g. accuracy, reflexes, special keys) helping you to improve.
All in all, this game did not inherit much of the merits from the previous games and boils down to a dull and repetitive gameplay with a few nuisances. That said, I suppose the game is not that bad if you forget the previous installments.

I'm just going to be blunt here because this game speaks for itself. To describe it in one sentence would be "One big glorious shared masturbation between Tim Schafer and the other Double Fine guys and every single one of their fans".
The way I see it, this is like Psychonauts but with the focus entirely on dialog and character development. It's also what Psychonauts would have been like if it were not for EA and LucasArts being moral watchdog pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥ It explores pretty dark motivations and is not afraid of showing fairly brutal murder that the cartoony aesthetic makes more grim for some reason. Especially because of how The Cave reacts to it so non-chalantly. He's seen this cycle repeat for thousands of years.
This is where the spoilers start. From what I can tell The Cave is a purgatory of sorts. Characters are stuck in a loop of reincarnation and retreading their paths until they can not be total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and be redeemed. It really makes the playthroughs seamless from both a story and technical standpoint.
Speaking of technical standpoint, from the perspective of a programmer I am absolutely in love with this game for a few reasons. Firstly, it uses Buddha (appropriate name hm?) which as far as I can tell is an engine that Double Fine wrote for their stuff in house and uses Lua as an extension language. They used it for Costume Quest and probably Stacking and others. I deeply admire and respect when people write engines that are reusable and aren't just marketing throw-aways. Damn shame that Double Fine is keeping it proprietary though.
Besides that, the story justifies the reuse of game assets marvelously. It uses mostly the same map but with minor changes for each character that opens pathways and other branches. It gets a little bit repetitive when you're doing the generic transition levels but still. I rarely see such a robust way of extending a game in a non-intrusive manner.

Or let's say you garrison a frontline. Even if you didn't started an attack order troops will try to disobey orders and advance which will break the line. This is especially stupid when playing a minor nation with less manpower - I always play such nations.
Naval movement is a mess. As stated above troops will suicide when trying to defend a land line using boats to reach their destination EVEN if landline is available and infrastructure is fine - so no major delay is expected.
However if you try to attack - game says - you need sea/air superiority first.
This is cheap mechanics, just a lazy way to force you to play by the game rules.
Guess what Devs - this is a 2-way street - for you this is mechanics, for me it's disliking the game.
But bottom line ... If you get it on promotion - buy it. ;)
Negative P.S. to Devs: Car Mechanic Simulator 15 has more frequent updates.
Positive P.S. to Devs: Last update really was step in the right direction for the optimization of the game.
Give credit when credit is due.

I personally spent so much damned time waiting for this game, convinced it would be everything I love from HOI3, but with better graphics, and a much smoother interface. What I got instead was an extremely watered down, and extremely incomplex game compared to its predecessor. While in HOI3 I could spend hours micromanaging an entire front for a couple days, or automate it all but a small 'Special Operations' unit under my direct command, HOI4 seems to take in favour of having the entire game automated.
I enjoy the factory system, but it seems not well fleshed out compared to just following HOI3 BICE's method and adding different industry modifying plants, in addition to the IC system. Combat is boring and the entire game slows to a crawl due to the lack of propper army balancing. As Turkey I should not be able to single handedly conquer the Soviet Union, it should not be physically possible, at least not for a few hundred years.
The game also lacks in the political spectrum, which HOI3 was not well known for either, though somehow Paradox managed to make it worse. Instead of having 6+ different political parties, many with differing ideologies or ministers or rules which would affect how you play, you have 4 ideologies. No Social Democrats vs Market Liberals, now it is Democratic, Fascist, Communist, or non-aligned, which disappears quickly enough with no way to bring it back.
Overall I would like to like this game, but it is a world sandbox which starts in 1936, not a World War Two Grand Strategy Game, which is what was advertised.

Word puzzle game where you are presented with a serious of clues and you have to slide the individual words horizontally to form the answer vertically made up of one letter of each of the clue words.
There are 600 puzzles in the game made up of 3 to 8 letter answers spread across 15 40 puzzle themed sets. While most of the clues are quite elegant, some are obtuse and others unintentionally misleading. There is a clue system where you can reveal one letter at a time of the answer if you get stuck so your progress is never impeded for too long. One note: this is an American game so uses American synonyms and spelling, not British.
There are some bugs almost completely contained to the level selection screen and what happens after you hit next puzzle. As you progress through a puzzle set the game will invariably skip at least two levels for some reason meaning you will have to go back to the puzzle selection screen after each set is "complete" achievement wise to finish off the ones the game skipped. The selection screen can also bug out showing half of one and half of another or nothing at all.
All in all this is a very nice little word puzzle game, well recommended. It should take somewhere about 3-4 hours and you can get 100% achievements just for finishing it. Maybe some sort of steamworks integration to allows others to make puzzle sets could be next on the horizon.

This is no Dishonored 2, Watchdogs 2, or Rollercoaster Tycoon World (I wouldn't touch that game though), but more of a good buy for a new genre of play on 'Words-Within-Words' word game.
Reminds of the clean puzzle game Polarium (DS) and Polarium Advanced (GBA), where you are given a preset of ready made puzzles and if you finish them all, that is pretty much it, with expection to their modes of clearing out random falling blocks (DS) and a time attack mode (GBA).
I would have liked to seen a custom mode, where you can make your own puzzles, but I wonder how curation would be regulated when it comes to correctly spelling the word or not. Nonetheless, it's a great starter for this new way of word games.

Is a detective game where you're playing as Detective Solomon Bixby. The game has 10 different cases to offer. The first 5 which has an estimate of 25 minutes to completion and the rest of the 5 cases have an estimate of 30, 35 and 45 minutes being the maximum estimate. Which also happens to be the FINALE chapter. I do not like the typography. At first, I thought there was something wrong with the game but I got used to it. There are not many characters in game either. It's somewhat an openworld game but it feels like we're playing in a ghost town.
The game has a nice feel to it. All that neon lighting and the retro look this game has, it feels pretty good to be playing it. The music goes fine with it. However, I think there should at least be an objective tab where players could look up what exactly they should be going after. Since there is no subtitles and there isn't going to be any updates including the subtitles, the very least thing that could be done is setting up an Objective tab that tells players what should be done.
Graphics for both Low and High settings are good. But you get that full retro experience only when you're playing in High graphics settings. This is only because when you've set the graphics to low, all the lighting effects and smoke effects are turned off. So there's no way you can experience the cool neon style lighting and most other graphics. I really loved the retro look this game has to offer.

That's about all the errors I have found in my 1.4hrs of gameplay.
An overpriced game which clearly does not deserve to be overpriced. It would've been better if Charizmo were a little bit patient and didn't have to leave me while I was doing a little sightseeing. It would've been better if the elevators were working efficiently and I didn't have to walk all the way from Bixby's office to the Reef Lounge. It would've been better if the game costed a little cheaper.

I think this game's world broke my brain. The game is basically going from one location to another, following clues, and expects you to learn the world layout, but after an hour I still can't remember where any corridor or doors lead. Not a single one. It's the most confusing world I have ever encountered in a game. Navigating Vietcong's VC tunnels was a breeze compared to this. After my whole experience was running around trying to find the navigation guide robot, I admit defeat. Trying to follow the rare signs also always led me somewhere completely else. And that is after dancing in front of the sign, trying to make the white reflection blocking most of it away. (Can be fixed by turning post-processing off, but then the game looks really bad, and its looks are what has drawn me to it, and the best part of it for me).
Stuff that doesn't help is a really high mouse sensitivity that you cannot change, and the entire menu and all the ui text being in a fancy font, in red color, and overlaid over busy backdrops, making it really difficult to read.
I feel bad for not liking this game, because I really like its look and the setting, but the whole thing being about navigation while being impossible to navigate would make me insane. But that's me, maybe others don't have this problem, and I hope that's correct, because I feel this game has something to offer, and effort went into its making - which is something that you don't encounter that much these days on Steam.

I really wanted to like this because after wading through a sea of low effort retro 2D pixel platformers, running into a 3D game using a modern engine is like an oasis!  Or it should be.
Some effort went into making this puzzle/walker game where you "investigate" crimes by walking around and pressing "E" every now and then, but not enough... the gameplay is kind of dead, and it feels incomplete.
The artwork is... unique?  There's shiny metal hats?  It's like the dev saw Bioshock and thought it would be better if there was no shooting or interaction with stuff, and a *lot* more neon, terrible, barely legible fonts, and weird nonsensical map layout.  And no NPCs.   Not kidding about the super high contrast neon everything garish colour scheme, either.  I got eyestrain after 5 minutes.
It plays smoothly enough in 4K so in terms of the game engine, well, that works, but unfortunately, even though it's a first person 3D game, the weak/nonexistent gameplay and wacky offputting art style kill this one pretty quick.

This is one of those games that would score a really high from face value but once you get to the actual game part of it all you get is flaws in execution and story telling.
-First of all and probably the most evident thing about the game is how it looks. This game has really great aesthetic. It's this mix of neon cyber-noir (screenshots for reference) that actually works incredibly well. The game mixes so many colors, shapes and fonts that end up forming captivating and interesting scenarios to look at and explore.
-The atmosphere is really good as well, you can really get involved in the game's world from the little sounds and the audio cue's around you.
-Both of these are what make the exploration so enjoyable. Feels like there's always something that catches your eye and you always feel like there's more to see. Due to it's nature you're never afraid to explore anything that catches your eye, the game gives you complete freedom to go where you want and that's another one of it's strongest points.
Screenshots:
The storytelling is really poor. The game lacks a proper structure which really ends up hurting it. The scenario works so hard to captivate you it's sad that the storytelling kinda throws it all away due to all the flaws it has. Flaws that come in the form of poor voice acting, weak script and frail event structure.
Another thing that kinda ends up working in a negative way for the game is it's gameplay, or it's lack of it. You do very little in this game, to put it in a short way all you end up doing is following the dots to complete the picture. Using this analogy the dots are all in the right spots, it's just that you don't understand what the picture is when you finish and it leaves you feeling quite unsatisfied.
Honestly I won't recommend this game at full price, the content and the gameplay are just to weak. But if you see it at a buck during a major steam sale or in a bundle I would say the great visual design and atmospheric exploration make it a worthy pick up, which is why I'm giving this game a positive recommendation.

Door to Door.  Hmm...  this game is hard to rate.  I really wanted to like it, and I do in some aspects, but what's most disappointing is the fact that this game could have been something really special.  Unfortunately, it falls short of being a great game.
Pros:
The graphics are beautiful
For the most part, you must find and follow clues
A rich and extremely detailed world
Very large and diverse areas to explore
Cons:
The cases are very silly (not funny silly, stupid silly)
The game takes your clues and solves the case for you (too much hand holding)
Most, if not all of the jokes fall flat
There is no notebook that you can reference
Cons that the developer is up front about:
There are no subtitles (some of the voices are hard to understand)
There are no other people (bots) in this city
Because the game was made with an older version of unreal engine, it made it impossible to fix or modify the game to accommodate the ladder, however, since the developer said this in the update section, I wouldn't dock them for it.  The only reason I'm mentioning it here is someone may insist on subtitles or a populous.
For new players, the city is very difficult to navigate, but there is "Charizmo" .  However, not all of the locations are listed so you may want to familiarize yourself with the city before you solve the cases.  There is no time limit so you can take all the time you want.
Despite it's shortcomings, I do like this game... somewhat.  Is it worth $6.99 (at the time of this review)?  Well, no.  I would wait for a sale if you want to give this game a shot.

A reasonable puzzle game. Reminiscent of the talos principle (including a cute little easter egg) but a lot simpler and shorter. The difficulty of puzzles remains pretty low and new mechanics are being added pretty continuously, which means they need to keep the relative difficulty curve low and reset it to convey the new mechanics pretty consistently. I'm no messiah with the puzzle games but this was pretty easy to knock out in 4 hours and some change, including sitting through the epilogue a few times to find out if the ending changed depending on your choice.
Soundtrack is reasonable but nothing special, atmopshere is solid but the ending and the central premise of the game philosophically feels disconnected from the primary ingame conflict. The Turing Test imagery feels tacked onto an unrelated story (or arguably the other way around) and there isn't much impact between the two even at the end.
If you're a huge fan of puzzle games its probably worth picking up on sale, but I wouldn't recommend paying full price for it. Sorry guys! Its a solid offering just not really comparable to some of the obvious competition.

In a nutshell: needs more work but a solid foundation. It's a tentative 'yes' from me but unless you are really keen to try this I'd hold off until it's further down the line. I've played my fair share of early access games and, well, this really puts the *early* in EA.
As it stands the game is barely a proof of concept, it's the kind of thing you'd show someone to say "this is a viable idea" - just a taste of a good game. What is there is good, but not much. Many things exist in only the most rudimentary capacity: there's a level system which does nothing, many of the structures in the game are outright non-functional (when I tried to build a gas tank structure the game even popped up with a flashing "structure not implemented" message), the progression is rather minimal but it is there.
The game looks really good and the controls are nice and fluid - it doesn't have that clunky, amateurish feel that plagues a lot of survival games. The basebuilding is fairly standard, and similar to subnautica - prefab bits which snap together. Interestingly lots of the base parts have individual elements (eg. each 'wall' is it's own section) which hopefully means this will be utilised (say, reinforcing certain walls and stuff).
The enemies which are there are quite simplistic, for the most part just charging straight at you and not posing any real difficulty. I suspect (read: hope) more variety will be introduced down the line, but there is already a sandworm which leaps out of the ground to devour you, so hopefully more stuff like that is in the works.
Vehicles are fun to drive and very satisfying: there's a bike, several varieties of rovers, a spaceship you can fly around and into orbit a la No Man's Sky and even a mechwarrior-esque bipedal mech. Sadly as it stands there's not much to do other than craft these vehicles at the moment

The Cave was a big disappointment for me. I used to consider myself a Double Fine fan, considering practically every DF title to be an instant purchase. However, I consider their more recent releases to be of much lower quality than I would expect from a developer I admired so. The Cave was the first of these.
First off, as a puzzle platformer, most of the puzzles in the game aren't particularly challenging or interesting, often consisting of a simple "find key, open door." Some puzzle mechanics are fun, such as the Time Traveller's ability to alter events in the past to change a level's layout in the future. Mechanics such as these aren't very common, as many of the puzzles are generic so that any character can complete them, likely to avoid conflicts in your party composition.
Every character has their own backstory which covers how or why they arrived at the titular Cave, but after going through the first couple of characters' levels, you'll notice the common theme pretty quickly and the story exploration becomes uninteresting. It almost feels like an attempt to make "another Psychonauts" by the nature of its writing, with The Cave's backstory exploration echoing similarly to the repressed memories in Psychonauts. However, many may find The Cave's characterization extremely lacking in comparison. Its humor is there but it lacks the quality writing underneath which made other DF titles work so well.
The Cave tops off its first (very short, no more than 4-5 hour) playthrough with a picture montage (yet again reminiscent of the repressed memories in Psychonauts) and a text notification informing you that you have beaten The Cave, rather than any sort of proper ending. The Cave encourages the player to go through the game at least three times to unveil every character's backstory, with the game not "actually" being beaten until then. Due to the repetition of solving many of the same puzzles across each playthrough, I was not interested in finishing the game a second time. The writing wasn't even interesting enough to convince me to power through the repetition of doing them again.
All in all, despite its many weak points, The Cave has a few interesting puzzle mechanics that make it worth playing, especially if it can be grabbed for 75% off or more. Unless it's a title you are very interested in, however, I'd avoid it altogether.
